topics.description: Nguyen et al. (2021) investigate deep active learning for detecting airspace opacity and lung lesions on chest X-ray images from an in-house dataset. The study uses 135,309 images, with 131,030/4,279 split and up to 6,550 labeled examples forming the annotation budget. The goal is to perform image-level classification for specific pathological findings while controlling labeling cost.

topics.title: Subtomogram classification in cryo-ET
topics.description: This topic addresses classification of subtomograms from cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), often using simulated data such as the SHREC’19 dataset. The table lists 25,000 images (24,000/1,000 split) with an initial labeled budget of 10% and query batches of 5%, explicitly tying the task to active learning protocols. The objective is to categorize 3D molecular structures, where labeling is highly specialized and benefits from selective querying.

topics.title: Task types in medical deep active learning
topics.description: This topic highlights the diversity of task types—segmentation, classification, and keypoint localization—used as benchmarks for deep active learning in medical image analysis. Segmentation tasks operate on volumetric data (e.g., CT), classification tasks span disease or severity prediction (e.g., pneumonia presence, calcification level), and keypoint localization targets anatomical landmarks (e.g., cephalometric and hand landmarks). The table illustrates how active learning strategies must adapt to different output spaces and annotation costs across these task categories.

topics.title: Brain structure segmentation from MRI and histology
topics.description: This topic focuses on brain structure segmentation using both MRI and histology data under an active learning scheme. The SATA MRI dataset with 35 volumes uses boundary pixels as the primary annotation target, while an in-house histology brain dataset comprises 15 stacks for structure delineation. The methodology emphasizes efficient acquisition of boundary information and cross-modality segmentation, reducing detailed labeling effort.

topics.title: Polyp segmentation in colonoscopy sequences
topics.description: This topic covers deep active learning for polyp segmentation in colonoscopy video data. The CVC-ClinicDB dataset with 29 sequences (split 23/3/3) is used to learn pixel-level polyp masks. The focus is on selecting informative frames and sequences for annotation to efficiently improve polyp segmentation performance, relevant for computer-aided colonoscopy.

topics.title: Active learning for laparoscopic image segmentation
topics.description: This topic focuses on segmenting laparoscopic surgical images of the gallbladder using deep active learning on the CholecSeg8k dataset. The dataset comprises 8,080 images with a specified split (4,640/1,600/1,640), and experiments make use of only a fraction of data (e.g., 10% labeled) to train segmentation models. Active learning strategies are used to iteratively select the most informative unlabeled frames for annotation, thus reducing manual labeling costs in surgical scene understanding. Bernhardt et al. (2022) illustrate this in the context of laparoscopic image segmentation.

topics.title: Polyp segmentation and lesion classification
topics.description: This topic covers two related endoscopic imaging tasks: polyp segmentation and colonoscopic lesion classification. Polyp segmentation focuses on delineating polyp regions at the pixel level, while colonoscopic lesion classification assigns diagnostic labels at the image or lesion level. The table entries (e.g., sample sizes of 1,000 and 2,717) indicate how datasets are organized for these tasks within deep active learning studies, distinguishing between segmentation and classification as technical objectives.

topics.title: Deep active learning for brain tumors
topics.description: This topic concerns the use of deep active learning methods for brain tumor analysis, focusing on both classification and segmentation tasks. The target entities are brain tumors in medical images, and the processes involve automatically categorizing tumor types and delineating tumor regions. The section indicates a configuration associated with a sample size of 100, reflecting how many images are used in the labeled set or related experimental settings.

topics.title: Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma Tumor MRI Segmentation
topics.description: This topic addresses segmentation of nasopharyngeal carcinoma tumors from MRI scans of the nose region, based on an in-house slice-level dataset. The data involve 1,057 patients with a 7:1:2 split, and 20% labeling is indicated, suggesting a limited annotation budget. The focus is on tumor delineation for treatment planning, an application well-suited to deep active learning due to the high cost of voxel-wise annotations.

topics.title: MRI hippocampus segmentation with MSD dataset
topics.description: This topic concerns hippocampus segmentation from MRI using the MSD (Medical Segmentation Decathlon) dataset. It references a task on anterior and posterior hippocampus segmentation with a dataset size of 9,270 samples split into 7,163/350/1,757 subsets, indicating training/validation/test or similar partitions. Such a setup is well-suited for evaluating deep active learning strategies in organ sub-structure segmentation, where detailed region labeling is required.

topics.title: OCT retinal layer segmentation datasets
topics.description: Kadir et al. (2023) are associated with optical coherence tomography (OCT) eye imaging datasets such as the Duke dataset, where superpixel representations are used and 100 scans are split in a 6:2:2 ratio for training/validation/testing, with annotation percentages as low as 2% and 10%. Additional OCT datasets, AROI (1,136 scans, 6:2:2 split) and UMN (725 scans, 6:2:2 split), are also mentioned for segmentation tasks. These collections support OCT layer segmentation studies under limited-annotation regimes, which is central to evaluating deep active learning in ophthalmic imaging.

topics.title: Carotid ultrasound CUBS dataset
topics.description: Tang et al. (2023) are linked to an ultrasound imaging task focused on the carotid region, using the CUBS dataset. The dataset description notes 3,220 images with a split of 2,016/1,204, along with an additional reported number 159, suggesting a substantial data resource for carotid analysis (e.g., vessel or plaque segmentation). This dataset provides a basis for assessing deep active learning methods in vascular ultrasound imaging.

topics.title: Carotid Intima-Media Segmentation Task
topics.description: This topic concerns a segmentation task focused on the carotid intima-media region, using an in-house dataset. The dataset includes 350 test samples, suggesting a specialized, possibly institution-specific collection rather than a public benchmark. The emphasis is on pixel-level delineation of anatomical structures for vascular assessment within a deep active learning framework.

topics.title: Breast Cancer Metastasis Detection in CAMELYON16
topics.description: This topic focuses on detecting cancer metastases in lymph nodes from breast histopathology using the CAMELYON16 dataset. The input is patch-based, extracted from 398 whole-slide images (270/128 split), with multiple patch sizes (4096, 8192, 12288) and varying numbers of patches per WSI (1, 3, 5). It frames metastasis detection as a classification problem, highlighting design choices in patch sampling and resolution relevant to deep active learning strategies.

topics.title: Colon Histopathology Classification with PathMNIST
topics.description: This topic covers colon histopathology image classification using the PathMNIST dataset. The dataset comprises 107,180 images with a specified split of 89,996/10,004/7,180 for training, validation, and testing, and includes 20 classes. It represents a benchmark histopathology classification setting for evaluating deep active learning methods on multi-class diagnostic tasks.

topics.title: Dataset scale and split design in benchmarks
topics.description: This topic concerns how medical imaging benchmarks are quantitatively characterized by total sample counts and explicit train/validation/test splits. The OrganAMNIST and BloodMNIST entries both specify large numbers of images and detailed partitioning, reflecting standard experimental design for evaluating deep active learning methods. Such structured splits are essential for fair comparison of algorithms, particularly when studying label efficiency and performance under limited annotation budgets.

topics.title: PROMISE 2012 prostate MRI segmentation
topics.description: This topic covers prostate segmentation from MRI slices using the PROMISE 2012 dataset. The dataset contains 1,377 slices split into 1,020/109/248 subsets and is used for a prostate segmentation task evaluated in the context of deep active learning. The work by Qu et al. (2023a) is cited, indicating a NeurIPS 2023 study focusing on this MRI-based segmentation problem.

topics.title: Histopathology nuclei segmentation across multiple organs
topics.description: This topic addresses nuclei segmentation in histopathology images drawn from several organs and datasets. TCGA-KUMAR (seven organs, patch-level, 30 images with 12/4/14 split), TNBC (breast, 50 images with 30/7/13 split), and MoNuSeg (seven organs, 44 images with 30/14 split) are used with only 5% or 7% of data labeled. Hu et al. (2023) in TMI employ these datasets to study deep active learning for nuclei segmentation under extremely limited annotation budgets.

topics.title: Lower extremity MRI dataset setup
topics.description: The section describes an in-house MRI dataset of the lower extremities, associated with IJCARS, used for deep active learning experiments. The data is organized at the volume or slice level, with 119 volumes split into 90 for training, 9 for validation, and 20 for testing. Sampling units can be entire 3D volumes or sets of 190 slices, reflecting different annotation/query granularities in active learning workflows.

topics.title: CheXpert chest X-ray dataset characteristics
topics.description: The CheXpert chest X-ray dataset is presented as a large-scale benchmark for deep active learning in 2D medical imaging. It includes 224,114 X-ray images of the chest, with a split of 223,414/200/500 across training, validation, and test sets. The dataset is image-based (rather than volumetric), and involves 10 target classes, enabling class-imbalanced and large-scale active learning studies.

topics.title: Medical image benchmarks for AL
topics.description: The section lists several benchmark datasets used in medical image analysis, specifying modality, anatomical region, dataset name, sample size and splits, and target clinical task. These include ChestXray14 for thoracic disease diagnosis, BreastMNIST for breast cancer diagnosis, DermaMNIST for skin lesion diagnosis, RetinaMNIST for diabetic retinopathy severity grading, and TissueMNIST for kidney cortex disease classification. Such datasets form the basis for evaluating deep active learning strategies in diverse imaging contexts.

topics.title: Entropy-based uncertainty with pseudo-labeling
topics.description: In breast pathology image classification, active learning is implemented by measuring entropy over model predictions on patches to quantify uncertainty. Patches with high entropy are sent to experts for annotation, while low-entropy patches receive pseudo-labels and are used to augment the training set without manual labeling. This combines uncertainty sampling with semi-supervised learning to improve annotation efficiency. The key entities are patch-level predictions, entropy as an uncertainty metric, and pseudo-label assignment.

topics.title: Category-wise curriculum querying and negative pre-training
topics.description: For histological tissue classification at the patch level, category-wise curriculum querying dynamically adjusts how much uncertainty sampling focuses on each class. This addresses class-dependent difficulty and imbalance by weighting querying effort per category during active learning. Additionally, negative pre-training uses intentionally wrong predictions to better separate visually similar classes, improving discriminative representations before or during active learning. Together, these strategies refine query selection and representation learning in complex multi-class pathology settings.

topics.title: Human-augmenting AI labeling with Core-Set AL
topics.description: A human-augmenting labeling system leverages active learning to suggest which WSI patches experts should annotate and to propose labels via a trained classifier. Core-Set is used as the active learner to select a subset of patches that best represent the data distribution while being informative. This human-in-the-loop workflow significantly reduces pathologists’ workload (around 90%) and can slightly improve data quality across cellular labeling tasks. The process couples query selection, model training, and expert verification in an iterative loop.

topics.title: Attention-based MIL with MC Dropout for querying
topics.description: In MIL-based WSI classification, attention-based MIL architectures are combined with Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout to estimate uncertainty at both the attention (instance importance) and classification levels. For each patch within a WSI, MC Dropout yields predictive distributions from which uncertainties are computed, and patches with the highest uncertainties are selected for expert annotation. This dual uncertainty captures ambiguity in which patches matter and how they should be classified, improving the informativeness of queried instances. The method aligns instance-level querying with the MIL attention mechanism.

topics.title: Open-set active learning for relevant patch selection
topics.description: Because WSIs contain both target classes (e.g., tumors, lymph nodes, normal cells) and many irrelevant non-target tissues (e.g., fat, stroma, debris), open-set active learning is adopted. In this setting, the unlabeled pool includes both target and non-target samples, and the system must simultaneously perform relevance filtering and uncertainty-based querying. By combining feature distribution information with prediction uncertainty, the method selects patches that are both informative and likely to belong to target classes for annotation. This reduces annotation spent on clearly irrelevant or out-of-distribution regions while focusing expert effort on diagnostically meaningful instances.

topics.title: Specialized AL Designs for Segmentation
topics.description: The section emphasizes specialized active learning designs tailored to medical image segmentation, including slice-based annotation, one-shot annotation, and explicit modeling of annotation cost. These designs exploit unique traits of medical imaging data (e.g., volumetric structure, annotation granularity) to make the selection and labeling process more efficient and clinically feasible.

topics.title: Autoencoder-based slice feature learning
topics.description: Autoencoders are used to learn semantic feature representations of each slice in a 3D volume, serving as the basis for selecting key slices. After encoding slices from axial, sagittal, and coronal planes, a selection strategy similar to representativeness-based RA is applied to identify which slices to annotate. This couples unsupervised feature learning with active selection across multiple anatomical planes.

topics.title: Application to 3D knee structure segmentation
topics.description: The slice-based annotation and selection strategy is extended to 3D segmentation of knee cartilage and bone. This shows that the framework is transferable beyond its initial application, supporting complex musculoskeletal structures where 3D context is important but full-volume annotation is costly.

topics.title: Self-attention for enhanced slice features
topics.description: A self-attention module is integrated into the autoencoder to improve the quality of slice-level feature learning. By modeling long-range dependencies within a slice, self-attention can produce more discriminative representations, potentially leading to better identification of key slices for annotation in active learning workflows.

topics.title: Clustering and regional uncertainty in CT
topics.description: For muscle segmentation in CT images, key slices and subregions within them are jointly selected using clustering and uncertainty. Hiasa et al. (2020) first apply clustering to identify representative key slices, then focus annotation on regions within those slices that exhibit high model uncertainty. This two-stage process combines global structural diversity (via clustering) with local informativeness (via uncertainty). It improves annotation efficiency by targeting both important slices and their most ambiguous areas.

topics.title: Hybrid uncertainty-representativeness for slice annotation
topics.description: Recent methods for slice-based annotation combine uncertainty with representativeness to select informative samples. In shoulder MRI musculoskeletal segmentation, Ozdemir et al. (2021) measure uncertainty using the variance across multiple Monte Carlo (MC) dropout runs and measure representativeness using posterior probabilities estimated by an infoVAE. This balances querying slices where the model is unsure with slices that are representative of the data distribution. Such hybrid criteria aim to improve both sample informativeness and coverage of the feature space.

topics.title: Bayesian U-net and MI-based redundancy reduction
topics.description: Li et al. (2024) propose a hybrid deep active learning strategy for musculoskeletal segmentation of lower extremities in MRI and CT. Uncertainty is estimated using a Bayesian U-net, while representativeness is computed via cosine similarity, ensuring both informative and diverse slice selection. They additionally apply mutual information-based criteria to minimize sample redundancy, following Nath et al. (2021), further improving the efficiency of queried samples. This integrated approach achieves strong performance across both MRI and CT datasets.

topics.title: Self-supervised features for one-shot sampling
topics.description: Most one-shot annotation methods in medical imaging combine self-supervised feature learning with tailored sampling strategies. Self-supervised representations (e.g., from VAEs, contrastive learning, or auto-encoding transformations) capture semantic structure without extensive labels, enabling more informed selection of samples within a single round. These learned features then drive criteria like representativeness, diversity, or density for sample selection.

topics.title: RA: VAE-based representativeness sampling
topics.description: The RA method is an early one-shot active learning approach for medical image segmentation that leverages features from a variational autoencoder (VAE). It uses a representativeness strategy in the learned feature space to select informative samples for single-round annotation. RA showed strong performance on gland segmentation in pathological images, whole-heart MRI segmentation, and fungal segmentation in electron microscopic images.

topics.title: Representativeness-based key slice selection
topics.description: Wu et al. proposed a representativeness-based framework focused on selecting key slices for annotation in a one-shot setting. They employ self-learning to obtain semantic representations for each slice, then use these features to propagate expert annotations to unannotated slices. This approach reduces the number of slices needing direct expert labeling while maintaining segmentation quality across the volume.

topics.title: Contrastive features and farthest-first sampling
topics.description: Jin et al. (2022b) integrate contrastive learning features with a farthest-first sampling strategy to realize one-shot annotation. Contrastive learning yields discriminative embeddings, while farthest-first sampling selects samples that are maximally separated in this feature space, promoting diversity and broad coverage. Their method was validated on ISIC 2018 skin lesion and lung segmentation datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness for single-round labeling.

topics.title: Density-based selection via reachable distance
topics.description: Jin et al. (2023b) use auto-encoding transformations for self-supervised feature learning, capturing meaningful structure in unlabeled medical images. In the resulting feature space, they define a notion of reachable distance to estimate local sample density and select high-density samples for annotation in one shot. This favors labeling representative points in dense regions, which can improve generalization while respecting strict interaction limits.

topics.title: Data-driven NLP and label dependence
topics.description: Modern NLP systems are primarily built on data-driven machine learning models whose performance critically depends on both the quality and quantity of labeled training data. Achieving high performance generally requires substantial supervised data, which is not always easy or cheap to obtain. This dependence motivates methods that can make more efficient use of scarce labels.

topics.title: Survey Literature Collection Methodology
topics.description: The authors explain their process for constructing the survey corpus of AL papers for NLP, beginning with a keyword search for 'active' in ACL Anthology titles. This initial set is refined through manual filtering, followed by iterative inclusion of relevant works missed by the keyword search and from other venues discovered via reference chasing. This process underpins the bibliometric counts and the coverage of the survey.

topics.title: Typical Active Learning Procedure Loop
topics.description: Algorithm 1 lays out a standard AL loop: initialize a seed labeled set from the unlabeled pool, train a model, repeatedly select informative instances, obtain annotations, update labeled and unlabeled sets, and retrain until a stopping criterion is met. The main components are the seeding strategy, model training routine, query function, annotation step, and stopping rule. This procedural decomposition structures the rest of the survey.

topics.title: Informativeness-Based Query Strategies
topics.description: One core category of AL query strategies is based on informativeness, where instances are selected because the current model is uncertain about them or expects them to yield the largest performance gain. Metrics such as prediction entropy, margin, or expected error reduction typically operationalize informativeness. The survey devotes a subsection to categorizing and comparing such approaches in NLP.

topics.title: AL for Structured Prediction in NLP
topics.description: The authors point out that applying AL to NLP must handle structured outputs such as sequences and trees, as found in tasks like parsing, sequence labeling, and machine translation. AL methods must therefore reason about informativeness at the level of structured instances or substructures, which complicates query design and uncertainty estimation. A dedicated subsection surveys these structured prediction–specific techniques.

topics.title: Active Learning with Advanced Learning Techniques
topics.description: The survey discusses integrating AL with advanced learning paradigms, particularly modern deep learning approaches. This includes using neural architectures, transfer learning, or semi-supervised techniques within the AL loop to better exploit both labeled and unlabeled data. A subsection surveys how these advanced methods interact with query strategies and model training dynamics.

topics.title: Initialization Strategies for Starting AL
topics.description: Starting active learning requires choosing an initial seed set from the unlabeled pool, which can affect convergence speed and stability. The survey identifies this as a distinct design choice, covering methods such as random seeding, diversity-based initialization, or heuristic selection to ensure a reasonable starting model. A subsection systematically reviews these initialization strategies.

topics.title: Output uncertainty and uncertainty sampling
topics.description: Uncertainty sampling selects unlabeled instances for which a single model is most uncertain about its prediction. For probabilistic models, common measures include entropy, least-confidence, and margin sampling; for non-probabilistic models like SVMs, proximity to the decision boundary plays a similar role. These methods have been revisited for modern Transformer-based NLP systems as well.

topics.title: Local region divergence for uncertainty
topics.description: Beyond raw output scores, uncertainty can be measured by how much a model’s predictions vary in an instance’s local neighborhood. If the instance is near a decision boundary, small changes (e.g., nearest-neighbor replacements, adversarial perturbations, or data augmentation) can cause divergent predictions, indicating high uncertainty. Recent work operationalizes this idea using nearest-neighbor search, adversarial attacks, and augmented variants of each instance.

topics.title: Gradient-based expected gradient length querying
topics.description: Gradient-based strategies select instances expected to most strongly affect the model’s parameters, typically measured by the norm of the loss gradient. Since unlabeled instances lack gold labels, the loss and gradients are computed as expectations over possible labels, leading to the Expected Gradient Length (EGL) criterion. EGL has been applied to sequence labeling and speech recognition, with variants that focus specifically on embedding gradients in neural NLP models.

topics.title: Error and ambiguity-based performance predictors
topics.description: A simpler performance-oriented idea is to directly target instances that are currently erroneous or ambiguous for the task model. This can involve training an auxiliary model to predict instance-wise loss, judge correctness of predictions, or determine when expert querying is needed in structured prediction. Inspired by data maps, some methods look for instances with intermediate average correctness over training, and in machine translation, error-prone examples are identified via backward translation (round-trip consistency) or quality estimation models.

topics.title: Density-based representativeness measures
topics.description: Density-based methods prioritize instances that lie in dense regions of the unlabeled data, so that labeled examples are representative rather than outliers. Simple proxies include n-gram or word-count statistics, while more general approaches compute each instance’s average similarity to all others. To reduce computational cost, k-nearest neighbor similarity is often used instead of full pairwise similarity over the pool.

topics.title: Discriminative representativeness versus labeled data
topics.description: Discriminative strategies select unlabeled instances that differ most from the already labeled set, emphasizing coverage of novel features and domains. This can be operationalized with feature-based metrics such as unseen n-grams or out-of-vocabulary words, or via similarity scores that prefer instances dissimilar to labeled examples. More sophisticated methods explicitly train a classifier or adversarial model to distinguish labeled from unlabeled data, and in domain adaptation settings, domain separators serve a similar filtering role.

topics.title: Greedy and clustering-based batch diversity
topics.description: Two main families of methods ensure batch diversity: greedy iterative selection and clustering-based selection. Iterative methods build batches step by step, each time choosing instances that are both useful and dissimilar from those already chosen, and can approximate advanced criteria like coresets or determinantal point processes. Clustering-based approaches partition the unlabeled pool into clusters and select representatives from different clusters, using similarities based on input features, learned representations, model-based similarity, gradients, or masked LM surprisal embeddings.

topics.title: Static hybrid combinations of query criteria
topics.description: Hybrid strategies combine informativeness and representativeness into a single scoring function for each instance. Simple static combinations include weighted sums or multiplicative formulas that merge multiple criteria, such as uncertainty and density. These methods do not adapt during training but provide a straightforward way to balance competing objectives in query selection.

topics.title: Integrated hybrids: clustering, gradients, and DPPs
topics.description: Some methods integrate multiple criteria more organically into a single selection mechanism. Examples include uncertainty-weighted clustering, where cluster selection is biased by instance uncertainty; diverse gradient selection, where gradient vectors encode both uncertainty and diversity; and DPP-based methods that factorize quality (e.g., informativeness) and diversity in a probabilistic selection model. These approaches jointly model what is informative and how to diversify the selected set.

topics.title: Multi-step and dynamic hybrid querying
topics.description: Multi-step querying applies different criteria in sequence, such as first filtering highly uncertain instances and then clustering them, or selecting the most uncertain instance within each cluster. Dynamic hybrids go further by changing the mixture of strategies over time, recognizing that representativeness may matter more in early AL stages while uncertainty becomes more reliable later. Methods like DUAL and GraDUAL formalize this by switching or interpolating between density-based and uncertainty-based selectors, and other work uses predefined monotonic functions to control combination weights throughout the AL process.

topics.title: Active learning for structured prediction
topics.description: Many NLP tasks require predicting structured outputs (e.g., label sequences, parse trees) composed of interdependent variables, which complicates querying and annotation compared to flat classification. A central design decision is whether to query labels for entire structures or only for selected sub-structures. This choice affects how utilities, uncertainties, and annotation workflows are defined and computed.

topics.title: Full-structure active learning utilities
topics.description: When querying full output structures, uncertainty-based strategies such as entropy must evaluate probabilities over an exponentially large output space. This is approximated using dynamic-programming algorithms for tree- and sequence-entropy, or via top-k approximations that treat k-best predicted structures as a proxy for the full space. These techniques adapt standard active learning criteria to settings where explicit enumeration of all structures is infeasible.

topics.title: Disagreement, length bias, and aggregation in full-structure AL
topics.description: For disagreement-based strategies in structured prediction, exact full-structure agreement is often too strict, so partial-disagreement measures and fine-grained scores (e.g., F1 for sequence labeling) are used. Because longer instances tend to appear more uncertain, length normalization is employed to mitigate length bias, though there is debate about whether long sequences should be discouraged. Utilities for a whole structure can also be built by aggregating token- or factor-level scores, using operations such as sums, averages, frequency-weighted sums, or selecting only the least-probable sub-structure.

topics.title: Unequal annotation costs in segmentation
topics.description: The section highlights that common active learning methods assume equal annotation costs per sample, which is unrealistic in medical image segmentation where annotation time can vary significantly. It argues that active learning should explicitly consider annotation costs, such as annotation time, to better support physicians and make querying more practical in clinical settings.

topics.title: Disagreement-time cost model with knapsack AL
topics.description: Kuo et al. (2018) integrate predictive disagreement and estimated annotation time to guide sample selection for intracranial hemorrhage detection in CT scans. Jensen–Shannon divergence between multiple model outputs measures informativeness, while annotation time is approximated using the segmentation boundary length and number of connected components. The selection problem is formulated as a 0–1 knapsack optimization, solved via dynamic programming, to choose the most informative samples under a cost budget.

topics.title: Similarity-based slice annotation cost
topics.description: Shen et al. (2021) estimate the annotation cost of brain tumor slices using a distance measure between queried slices and already-labeled slices. Lower distance is interpreted as lower annotation cost, under the assumption that annotating slices similar to previously labeled ones is faster and easier for experts. This embeds a notion of familiarity into the active learning cost model.

topics.title: Spatially-informed cost and Dice optimization
topics.description: Atzeni et al. (2022) refine annotation cost estimation for brain structure segmentation by accounting for spatial relationships between multiple regions of interest. They also use the average Dice coefficient from previous active learning rounds to predict current Dice performance. Regions are then selected for annotation to maximize the predicted average Dice, linking cost modeling with an explicit segmentation quality metric.

topics.title: Uncertainty-Guided Interactive Fetal Brain Segmentation
topics.description: For MRI fetal brain segmentation, an uncertainty-guided interactive refinement framework is introduced. A specialized network architecture produces multiple segmentation outputs simultaneously; the variance across these predictions is used as an uncertainty metric. Slices with the highest estimated uncertainty are prioritized for human expert interaction, allowing clinicians to focus refinement on the most ambiguous regions, thereby improving segmentation quality with minimal additional annotation.

topics.title: Learnable k-space sampling for MRI
topics.description: Deep learning is used to reconstruct undersampled MRI data where k-space is sampled via either fixed or learnable masks. Traditional approaches use a fixed undersampling mask and a deep model to reconstruct the image, while AL-based approaches learn which k-space locations to sample next. This transforms acquisition into an adaptive sampling problem directly tied to reconstruction quality and imaging speed.

topics.title: Adversarial and RL policies for k-space
topics.description: Adversarial learning and reinforcement learning are used to design active sampling policies in k-space for MRI. Methods include an adversarially trained evaluator that selects the next k-space row, dual deep Q-networks for active sampling decisions, and policy-gradient-based networks that adapt sampling patterns. Rewards are defined via reconstruction metrics such as structural similarity, linking sampling choices to image quality improvements.

topics.title: Joint optimization of acquisition and reconstruction
topics.description: Instead of treating acquisition and reconstruction separately, some MRI approaches jointly optimize the sampling policy and the reconstruction network. This end-to-end training allows the acquisition strategy to adapt to the reconstruction model’s capabilities, potentially yielding better image quality for a given acquisition budget. It exemplifies tightly coupled AL and reconstruction design.

topics.title: Adaptive CT scanning angle selection
topics.description: Active learning is applied to CT by adaptively choosing patient-specific scanning angles. The method tailors the projection directions to each individual, enabling sufficient reconstruction quality with fewer projections. This reduces both radiation exposure and scan duration compared to fixed-angle protocols.

topics.title: Active rescanning in electron microscopy
topics.description: In electron microscopy, an AL pipeline first enhances low-resolution images to high resolution, then predicts regions of interest and reconstruction errors. A weighted determinantal point process (DPP), parameterized by reconstruction error, selects which pixels to rescan to refine the image. This strategy simultaneously maintains low reconstruction error and spatial diversity, focusing acquisition on informative and diverse locations.

topics.title: Limitations of Existing AL Evaluations
topics.description: Active learning (AL) for medical image analysis lacks comprehensive and systematic evaluation on realistic medical datasets. Many studies rely on standard benchmark datasets such as CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, or MedMNIST, which do not fully capture the limited data availability and higher complexity of real-world clinical imaging. This mismatch raises concerns about the clinical applicability of reported performance gains.

topics.title: Inconsistent Gains Over Random Sampling
topics.description: Different AL strategies often exhibit inconsistent performance and do not reliably outperform simple random sampling, especially in classification tasks. Studies, including Munjal et al. (2022) and prior discussion in §4.2, report that no single AL method consistently dominates others and that random sampling can be competitive or even superior when the annotation budget is low. This uncertainty makes it difficult to decide which AL method to adopt for a given medical imaging scenario.

topics.title: Active learning for electron microscopy imaging
topics.description: This topic addresses the use of deep active learning in electron microscopy (EM) for brain imaging, including mouse cortex (SNEMI3D) and human cerebrum data. Methods target accelerated acquisition and analysis of EM volumes by prioritizing which regions or samples to acquire at high resolution and to annotate, thus reducing the immense labeling burden typical of EM datasets. The work referenced (Pineda et al. 2020, MICCAI) explores strategies to efficiently reconstruct or segment neural structures from large-scale EM imagery.

topics.title: CT-based reconstruction datasets
topics.description: Several CT reconstruction benchmarks are referenced, covering lung and spine imaging. Lung CT reconstruction is associated with the AAPM dataset, while spine CT reconstruction uses the VerSe dataset. These datasets support evaluation of reconstruction algorithms in different anatomical regions and CT imaging contexts.

topics.title: Accuracy for Multi-Class Classification
topics.description: Accuracy (ACC) is used as the primary evaluation metric for the multi-class classification task on the NCT-CRC-HE-100K dataset. It measures the proportion of correctly classified samples over the total number of samples, providing a straightforward indicator of overall classification performance. This choice is suitable when class distributions are relatively balanced and all classes are equally important.

topics.title: Test-Set Metrics as Final Results
topics.description: Evaluation metrics are ultimately computed on the testing set and reported as the final results. This practice ensures that performance estimates reflect generalization to unseen data and are not biased by training or validation processes. It provides a fair basis for comparing different models or active learning strategies.

topics.title: Random sampling baseline in AL
topics.description: Random sampling is used as the baseline comparison method in the active learning (AL) evaluation. It selects unlabeled samples uniformly at random without using any model-driven informativeness or diversity criteria. This provides a reference to measure the benefit of more sophisticated query strategies.

topics.title: Classic uncertainty-based AL criteria
topics.description: Confidence, Entropy, and Margin are presented as classic uncertainty-based active learning methods. They compute uncertainty scores from prediction probabilities using three different measures: low maximum confidence, high entropy, and small classification margin indicate greater uncertainty. These scores guide the selection of unlabeled samples expected to most improve the model when labeled.

topics.title: Core-Set as a comparison method
topics.description: The Core-Set method by Sener and Savarese (2018) is listed among the comparison methods for evaluating active learning strategies. Although not described in detail in this section, it is treated as an additional baseline/competitor in the experimental setup alongside uncertainty-based and Bayesian methods.

topics.title: k-Center-Greedy for core-set selection
topics.description: k-Center-Greedy is used as the selection algorithm to balance computational cost and active learning performance. At each step, it greedily selects the point that maximizes the minimum distance to already selected points, approximating the k-center objective in embedding space. This yields a diverse and representative labeled set without the cost of exact optimization.

topics.title: Coarser sub-structures and grouped queries
topics.description: Instead of querying the smallest possible units, many approaches select larger sub-structures (e.g., sub-sequences, head edges, neighborhood pools, phrases) to better align with how annotators read and to reduce context switching. Coarser granularity can alleviate the missed-class effect, where rare or difficult classes are overlooked when sampling too locally. Grouping strategies—such as first selecting uncertain sentences and then uncertain tokens within them, or choosing nearby instances sequentially—further streamline annotation and reduce cognitive load.

topics.title: Computer-assisted and interactive annotation
topics.description: Direct cost reduction can be achieved by tighter model–annotator interaction, such as pre-annotation where models supply best or top-k predictions that annotators correct instead of labeling from scratch. This paradigm underlies post-editing in machine translation and has been shown effective when combined with AL. More interactive systems continuously propagate user corrections back into the model during annotation sessions—e.g., interactive machine translation where the system updates its prediction after each corrected character—thereby reducing human effort further; AL can be integrated into such systems to prioritize which segments to present. Crowdsourcing is highlighted as another complementary cost-reduction mechanism.

topics.title: Reducing wait time in active learning loops
topics.description: Active learning involves iterative cycles of training and querying that impose wait time on annotators, motivating methods to accelerate these stages. Query-time speedups include sub-sampling large unlabeled pools, caching invariant computations, and approximating densities or nearest neighbors with k-NN methods. For training, incremental warm-starting may seem natural but can harm neural performance, so full retraining is often preferred, sometimes paired with using a lightweight model for querying and a stronger model for final training. Additional reductions come from accepting stale model information via batch-mode AL and parallel AL architectures that decouple and continuously run annotation, training, and scoring processes.

topics.title: Distilled and proxy models for querying
topics.description: To improve efficiency without sacrificing too much active learning performance, smaller distilled or proxy models can be used for query selection. Distillation compresses a large pre-trained model into a smaller one that approximates its behavior, enabling faster querying and shorter annotator wait time. Works cited show that these proxy models can be periodically synchronized with the main model via distillation, sometimes combined with pseudo-labeling and sub-sampling to further reduce computational cost.

topics.title: Pretraining and continual transfer in AL
topics.description: Transfer learning is integrated with active learning by initializing models from large pre-trained language models and further adapting them through continual training. Pretrained representations reduce the amount of task-specific annotation needed, while continual training allows incremental adaptation to new domains or tasks during the AL process. Meta-learning is also used to initialize models so they can learn effectively from small actively acquired datasets, and similar transfer ideas are applied to the model-based query policy itself.

topics.title: Transductive, domain, and cross-lingual transfer
topics.description: Transductive learning within active learning transfers information from specific target unlabeled sets, such as other domains or languages, to reduce annotation needs. Methods leverage labeled or unlabeled data from related domains to guide selection and learning in the target domain, and similarly exploit cross-lingual signals when data in one language is scarce. This creates a multi-source scenario where active learning decisions and model updates are informed by heterogeneous but related data distributions.

topics.title: Weak supervision integrated with active learning
topics.description: Weak supervision is combined with active learning by using imperfect or indirect supervision sources such as execution results, structure-based heuristics, gazetteers, and interactively discovered labeling rules. In this setting, actively selected instances may be labeled not only by humans but also by weak labeling functions or auxiliary resources, thereby reducing manual annotation effort. The section illustrates this with examples from semantic parsing, entity representation, sequence labeling, and rule-learning workflows.

topics.title: Data augmentation and query synthesis in AL
topics.description: Data augmentation techniques are applied within active learning to expand training data and improve generalization, using methods such as iterative back-translation, mixup for sequence labeling, and phrase-to-sentence transformations for machine translation. Augmentation can also be tied directly to instance querying, where transformations inform which examples to select. An advanced variant, query synthesis, generates new synthetic instances for annotation instead of sampling from an existing pool, and has shown promise for simpler text classification scenarios despite the challenges of realistic text generation.

topics.title: Random and representativeness-based seeding strategies
topics.description: Random sampling is widely used to initialize AL because it preserves the original data distribution and is simple to apply. More sophisticated representativeness-based strategies select instances near clustering centroids to obtain seed sets that are both representative and diverse. These seeding methods aim to provide a strong starting point before more complex query strategies are applied.

topics.title: Advanced models for AL initialization
topics.description: Advanced learning techniques can assist in selecting informative seed instances before standard AL cycles begin. These include transfer learning and unsupervised methods to capture structure in unlabeled data, as well as language-model-based approaches. Examples include selecting low-probability words for word sense disambiguation or choosing cluster centers using surprisal embeddings from pre-trained contextualized LMs.

topics.title: Uncertainty aggregation in segmentation tasks
topics.description: For segmentation, uncertainty-based methods differ from classification by operating initially at the pixel level. Pixel-wise scores (e.g., probabilities or uncertainty measures per pixel) are first produced, and then aggregated by averaging across pixels to obtain a single uncertainty score per image or sample. This aggregated score is then used for sample selection in active learning.

topics.title: Classification backbone and training setup
topics.description: The classification tasks use ResNet-18 as the backbone network, optimized with stochastic gradient descent with momentum. Training runs for 100 epochs with a batch size of 128, a learning rate of 0.01, momentum of 0.9, and cross-entropy as the loss function. A cosine learning rate decay schedule is applied to achieve smoother convergence during optimization.

topics.title: Dataset-specific augmentations for classification
topics.description: Different data augmentation strategies are applied for two classification datasets to improve generalization. For NCT-CRC-HE-100K, only random horizontal flipping is used, reflecting relatively simple transformations. For ISIC 2020, a richer augmentation pipeline from Zhuang et al. (2018) is followed, including random cropping, flipping, rotation, affine transforms, and color jittering, to model more complex variability in dermoscopic images.

topics.title: U-Net segmentation architecture design
topics.description: Segmentation tasks are handled using a 5-level U-Net architecture, with symmetric encoder and decoder paths. Each level contains two blocks, and each block is composed of a 2D convolution, a dropout layer with probability 0.1, batch normalization, and a leaky ReLU activation. This configuration balances regularization, stable training, and non-linear feature extraction for pixel-wise prediction.

topics.title: Computational environment and software stack
topics.description: Experiments are executed on high-end NVIDIA GPUs (GeForce RTX 3090 and 4090) with CUDA 11.3, indicating requirements for substantial computational resources. The implementation is based on Python 3.8.10 and PyTorch 1.11.0, defining the software environment and deep learning framework used for reproducibility and potential extension.

topics.title: Margin sampling in low-budget regimes
topics.description: This topic describes the behavior of the Margin-based active learning strategy when only a small labeling budget is available. Margin performs well in this regime because it leverages information from wrong predictions between similar classes to select informative samples. This aligns with findings reported in related work (Hu et al. 2023), highlighting the value of uncertainty near decision boundaries for early-stage labeling.

topics.title: Binary skin lesion classification setup
topics.description: The section evaluates deep active learning methods on the ISIC 2020 dataset framed as a binary skin lesion classification task with severe class imbalance. Performance is measured using AUC on a held-out test split, as summarized in Table 7. This setup provides a challenging environment to compare different active learning strategies under realistic clinical class distributions.

topics.title: Equivalence of Confidence and Margin in binaries
topics.description: In the binary classification setting, the Confidence and Margin uncertainty measures become mathematically equivalent, leading the authors to report only Confidence-based results. This reflects that the score ordering induced by these two strategies is identical when only two classes are present. Consequently, Margin is omitted from the comparative analysis.

topics.title: Random vs uncertainty-based query strategies in ASD
topics.description: ASD values are reported for multiple acquisition strategies: Random, Confidence, Entropy, and Margin sampling. Each strategy is associated with mean ± standard deviation ASD values across several budget levels, such as Random (4.71 ± 1.13 down to 2.21 ± 0.73) and Confidence (6.63 ± 2.05 down to 2.22 ± 0.62). These results compare purely random selection with uncertainty-based methods that rely on confidence scores, entropy, or decision margins from the model. The comparison indicates how different query strategies impact boundary accuracy in deep active learning for medical image segmentation.

topics.title: Core-Set Under Low-Budget Early Rounds
topics.description: The Core-Set method performs well on both mean DSC and ASD during early rounds in a lower budget scenario. This suggests that Core-Set is particularly effective when label budgets are small, helping to rapidly improve both overlap and boundary accuracy with limited annotations. Its early-round advantage highlights the role of representative subset selection in data-efficient segmentation.

topics.title: Dataset choices for computing stopping metrics
topics.description: The dataset used to compute stopping metrics can significantly affect the stability and reliability of stopping decisions. Improperly chosen sets may lead to unstable measurements, motivating the use of a separate unlabeled dataset for monitoring. Since many stopping metrics do not require gold labels, this auxiliary dataset can be large to reduce variance, though increased size can also introduce practical concerns such as longer evaluation wait times.

topics.title: Curriculum learning integrated with AL
topics.description: Curriculum learning arranges training instances in a meaningful or progressively harder order, and can be combined with AL to guide which examples to query and when. This integration considers both informativeness (from AL) and pedagogical ordering (from curriculum learning) to improve training efficiency and model performance.

topics.title: Model efficiency and wait time in AL
topics.description: Model efficiency is emphasized as crucial in AL to reduce the annotator’s wait time between query selection and labeling. Because AL involves repeated retraining or updating models as new labels arrive, computational efficiency and system latency directly affect the practicality and user experience of AL systems.

topics.title: Applying AL to complex NLP tasks
topics.description: The survey notes that AL has been used mainly for simple classification, while more complex tasks like text generation, NLI, and QA remain underexplored. These tasks involve richer outputs and more complex inputs, making unlabeled data collection and annotation harder, yet early work suggests AL can still aid data collection and model training for them.

topics.title: AL beyond direct target labeling
topics.description: AL can query not only task labels but also auxiliary supervision such as features, rationales, explanations, evaluations, or symbolic rules. By selecting informative instances for these richer annotation types, AL can support tasks like feature labeling, rationale collection, explanation annotation, and rule discovery to enhance downstream models.

topics.title: Practical deployment challenges of AL
topics.description: Most AL research simulates annotation using existing labeled datasets, overlooking real-world issues like true annotation cost, efficiency and wait time, data reuse, and when to start or stop AL. In practice, AL processes are often non-repeatable, making the choice of query strategies and hyperparameters critical yet difficult, and addressing these challenges is key for wider industrial adoption.

topics.title: Cross-domain transfer of AL methods
topics.description: The limitations section highlights that many AL techniques, particularly querying strategies developed in computer vision, may be transferable to NLP tasks. It advocates looking beyond NLP-specific work and leveraging insights and algorithms from other domains to improve AL for language applications.

topics.title: Need for comparative AL experiments
topics.description: The survey acknowledges the lack of empirical comparisons across AL strategies within the work itself, pointing to a broader need for systematic experimental studies. Comparative benchmarks evaluating multiple AL methods under shared conditions could yield more actionable guidance for practitioners selecting strategies for specific NLP tasks.

topics.title: Supervised models in remote sensing
topics.description: The section highlights the widespread use of statistical learning models—especially Support Vector Machines and neural networks—for supervised classification of land use from modern satellite imagery. It notes their effectiveness on very high spatial and spectral resolution data, framing them as state-of-the-art techniques in remote sensing image classification.

topics.title: Training set representativeness and cost
topics.description: Performance of supervised classifiers is described as heavily dependent on how representative the training data are of the underlying classes. Constructing such appropriate training sets is portrayed as difficult and expensive, since it often requires extensive manual analysis via visual inspection or field surveys followed by sample labeling.

topics.title: Sampling Diversity via BADGE and Core-Set
topics.description: Both BADGE and Core-Set are identified as methods that enhance sampling diversity in the active learning process. By diversifying the selected samples, these methods aim to cover different regions of the data space and avoid redundant annotations, which can accelerate model improvement. This diversity-focused selection is presented as a key factor behind their strong early performance in segmentation metrics.

topics.title: Late-Round Superiority of Uncertainty and Random Sampling
topics.description: In later active learning rounds, uncertainty-based methods and even random sampling catch up and improve in both mean DSC and ASD. This suggests that once the model has been sufficiently initialized with diverse, informative samples, simpler selection strategies can still yield strong incremental gains. The observed trend is consistent with earlier findings referenced in the survey, indicating a shift in the relative benefits of complex selection strategies over the course of AL.

topics.title: L2 and cosine distances on embeddings
topics.description: This topic defines how L2 and cosine distances are computed over feature embeddings of images in deep active learning. Each image sample x is mapped to a d-dimensional feature vector z, and the L2 distance is calculated as the Euclidean norm of the difference between two embeddings, while the cosine distance is derived from one minus the cosine similarity between them. These formulas formalize how image similarity is quantified in the feature space for AL methods.

topics.title: Budget-dependent metric performance on datasets
topics.description: This topic summarizes empirical results comparing L2 and cosine distances across multiple medical imaging datasets and labeling budgets. On NCT-CRC-HE-100K, both metrics perform similarly at all budgets, whereas on ISIC 2020 and ACDC, L2 is better in early rounds (low budget) but cosine becomes competitive or superior as more samples are selected (high budget). The findings lead to a recommendation that L2 is generally preferable for low-budget scenarios, while cosine distance may be more advantageous when the annotation budget is high and the model is more mature.

topics.title: Uncertainty as a driver in AL
topics.description: Uncertainty is emphasized as a central signal in active learning, guiding which samples should be queried for annotation. The section suggests that current uncertainty estimates can be improved so that they more directly correspond to where the model is likely to be wrong, instead of merely being numerically high. This reframing positions uncertainty as a tool to expose model weaknesses rather than a generic confidence score.

topics.title: Querying samples with inaccurate predictions
topics.description: The text proposes that active learning performance can be enhanced by preferentially querying samples on which the model currently makes incorrect predictions. This contrasts with querying solely based on high uncertainty and implies a tighter coupling between error detection and query strategy. The idea is that an ideal uncertainty measure should correlate strongly with prediction inaccuracy, making error-prone samples more likely to be selected.

topics.title: Learnable performance estimation for QC
topics.description: This topic describes learnable performance estimation methods for automated quality control (QC) of deep model outputs in medical image analysis. Examples include the Segment Anything Model (SAM) providing IoU estimates per mask, deep generative models predicting Dice scores for cardiac MRI segmentation, and auxiliary networks predicting Dice for brain tissue segmentation. These approaches estimate segmentation quality directly and are proposed as promising tools to support uncertainty-based active learning and mitigate model over-confidence.

topics.title: Probability calibration for uncertainty-based AL
topics.description: This topic covers probability calibration as a means to address over-confidence in deep models used for uncertainty-based active learning. Calibration measures the alignment between predicted probabilities and true outcomes, with over-confident models being poorly calibrated; examples include polyp classifiers where confidence should match actual polyp prevalence. The text discusses that ensembles can be better calibrated than MC Dropout, and Dirichlet-based methods consider all prediction outcomes, but most approaches only propose improved uncertainty metrics and perform post-hoc calibration. Existing calibration methods often require additional labeled datasets, highlighting the open problem of integrating calibration directly into uncertainty-based active learning pipelines.

topics.title: Diffusion models with superior generative quality
topics.description: Diffusion models are highlighted as a newer class of generative models achieving state-of-the-art image quality. They iteratively denoise random noise into coherent images, and recent work (Kazerouni et al., 2023) demonstrates that they can surpass GANs on standard generative benchmarks. This improved fidelity and diversity make them attractive candidates for data generation within active learning frameworks.

topics.title: Text-to-image diffusion for flexible generation
topics.description: Text-to-image diffusion models, exemplified by Stable Diffusion, are described as revolutionizing image generation by conditioning on natural language prompts. Their high-quality, text-guided outputs enable users to specify semantic content and appearance details directly through text. This controllability can support more targeted synthesis of rare or informative cases for active learning in medical imaging contexts.

topics.title: ControlNet for structure-conditioned diffusion
topics.description: ControlNet is introduced as an extension that allows diffusion models to follow detailed structural conditions, such as sketches or segmentation masks. By injecting additional control signals, it preserves global semantics from text while aligning local structures to given guidance maps. This mechanism can generate anatomically consistent or label-aligned images that are valuable for annotation-efficient learning and structured data augmentation.

topics.title: Integrating diffusion models into deep AL
topics.description: The section emphasizes that systematically exploring diffusion models within deep active learning remains an open research direction. Potential integrations include using diffusion-based generators to propose informative queries, synthesize hard or underrepresented cases, or model uncertainty in the data space. The authors position this as a promising avenue to surpass current GAN-centric AL strategies, especially in medical image analysis.

topics.title: Foundation models in active learning
topics.description: The section highlights how visual foundation models such as CLIP, SAM, and large language models like GPT-4 are shifting paradigms in medical image analysis and computer vision. These models, rich in prior knowledge, open new opportunities to redesign and improve active learning (AL) pipelines by leveraging their generalizable representations. The focus is on how this new class of models changes the context in which AL is developed and applied.

topics.title: Core methods in deep active learning
topics.description: The survey is described as comprehensively reviewing core methodological approaches in deep active learning. This implies coverage of key query strategies, model architectures, and selection criteria that underpin how deep active learning systems are designed and evaluated. These core methods form the technical foundation upon which more specialized and application-specific techniques are built.

topics.title: Active learning tailored to medical imaging
topics.description: The survey specifically focuses on active learning methods that are customized for medical image analysis tasks. Such tailoring can involve adapting query strategies, model designs, or annotation interfaces to the unique properties of medical images (e.g., 3D volumes, multi-modal data) and clinical labels. The conclusion underscores the importance of domain-specific adaptations rather than generic active learning pipelines.

topics.title: Challenges adapting classical AL to deep learning
topics.description: When transferring traditional active learning methods to deep learning, feature representations become dynamically learned and evolve during training, making pre-computation of pairwise distances or similarities for representativeness-based measures infeasible. Additionally, DNNs tend to be over-confident in their predictions, which can undermine uncertainty estimation for unlabeled samples. Although prior work has comprehensively summarized DAL methods, a lack of cross-dataset, cross-task experimental comparisons makes it difficult to know which DAL algorithms suit which tasks.

topics.title: DeepAL+ benchmarking toolkit for DAL
topics.description: DeepAL+ is a DAL benchmark toolkit that re-implements 19 DAL methods, extending a previous toolkit (DeepAL) that contained 11 highly-cited approaches before 2018. It upgrades prior implementations, adds more recent and highly-cited DAL algorithms, and expands the range of tasks and datasets to include standard image benchmarks (MNIST, CIFAR, SVHN), medical image analysis, and object recognition with spurious correlations. Using DeepAL+, the authors conduct comparative experiments across multiple tasks, analyzing factors such as batch size, number of training epochs per AL iteration, and timing costs. The toolkit is designed to be extensible, enabling easy integration of new tasks, datasets, DAL algorithms, and base models, and is publicly released on GitHub.

topics.title: Gradient-based active learning criteria
topics.description: Gradient-utilizing strategies estimate the impact of labeling a sample by examining gradients of the loss with respect to model parameters. They approximate how much the model would change if a candidate point were labeled and used for training, often via gradient norms or influence scores. This aligns selection with expected parameter updates rather than just prediction scores. Such methods are particularly suited to deep networks where gradients carry rich sensitivity information.

topics.title: Representative diversity-based DAL strategies
topics.description: Representative/diversity-based deep active learning (DAL) aims to select samples that are diverse and representative of the unlabeled pool. The section lists three main mechanisms: clustering, discriminative learning, and point processes. Concrete example methods include K-means-based selection, the Corset approach, Cluster-Margin, DAL, VAAL, WAAL, BADGE (DPPS version), and Active DPP, each operationalizing diversity or representativeness differently.

topics.title: Uncertainty-based deep active learning
topics.description: Uncertainty-based DAL selects unlabeled samples exhibiting high uncertainty, explicitly distinguishing aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Aleatoric uncertainty stems from inherent randomness in data generation processes, while epistemic uncertainty arises from limited model knowledge and can be reduced with more data. The text notes that many such DAL measures are adapted from pool-based active learning techniques developed for classical machine learning tasks, and that these methods form a standard family of querying strategies.

topics.title: Requirements for compact, informative training sets
topics.description: The section concludes that desirable training sets should be small yet constructed 'in a smart way,' focusing on discriminative pixels that accurately capture class boundaries. This requirement is especially critical for very high spatial or spectral resolution classification, where feature spaces are large and complex but training information is limited.

topics.title: Pool-based active learning notation
topics.description: The section formally defines the labeled training set X = {x_i, y_i} with class labels y_i in {1, …, N} and feature vectors x_i in a d-dimensional input space ℝ^d. It also defines the unlabeled set U = {x_i}, a large pool of candidate pixels (u ≫ l) from which the algorithm selects samples to be labeled. This establishes the pool-based setting common in active learning for remote sensing.

topics.title: Iterative sampling and model adaptation
topics.description: Active learning algorithms are described as iterative sampling schemes in which the classification model is regularly updated by incorporating newly labeled pixels. The new samples are chosen to be those most beneficial for improving model performance, typically based on some informativeness criterion. This captures the core process of alternating between sample selection, labeling, and model refinement.

topics.title: Heuristic-based candidate evaluation and ranking
topics.description: Each unlabeled candidate in the pool is scored with a user-defined heuristic that quantifies its interest for labeling. The candidates are then ranked according to this heuristic score, guiding which samples are most informative to query. This mechanism allows the algorithm to prioritize samples expected to most improve the model.

topics.title: Uncertainty reduction as selection objective
topics.description: The selection strategy aims to target areas where the model exhibits low confidence. By adding such uncertain samples to the training set, the algorithm forces the classifier to resolve these regions of uncertainty, simultaneously seeking to maximize performance gain. This articulates the underlying objective guiding the heuristic used in candidate selection.

topics.title: Bagging-based committee construction
topics.description: A committee of classifiers is built using bagging, where k training sets are generated by drawing with replacement from the original labeled data. Each bootstrapped set is used to train a separate classifier, and the committee collectively predicts labels for unlabeled candidate pixels. This results in k labelings for each candidate pixel, forming the basis for estimating uncertainty. The approach leverages only a part of the available labeled pixels in each bag to induce diversity among committee members.

topics.title: Multi-view committees via feature partitioning
topics.description: High-dimensional remote sensing data are handled by splitting the original feature space into multiple disjoint subsets or views, and building a committee of classifiers, each operating on a different view. For hyperspectral images, these views can be derived from the block-diagonal structure of the covariance matrix, so that each block defines a feature subset. Each view produces an independent classification of the same pixel, enabling disagreement-based or entropy-based query heuristics similar to nEQB. This multi-view construction underpins the later definition of the AMD selection rule.

topics.title: SVM decision function and confidence
topics.description: This topic details the SVM decision function used in active learning, including the kernel-based representation, dual coefficients, and support vectors. It highlights how the absolute value of f(xi), the distance from a sample to the hyperplane, serves as a confidence indicator, with larger margins implying more certain classifications. The entities involved include kernels K(xj, xi), support vectors xj with non-zero αj, and binary labels yj.

topics.title: Large margin heuristics visualization
topics.description: The section introduces a three-class toy example to illustrate large margin active learning heuristics for SVMs. Distances from decision hyperplanes are visualized by color intensity, with black indicating points on or near the decision boundary and white indicating maximal distance. The MS (Margin Sampling) and MCLU heuristics are compared by showing that areas of maximal uncertainty correspond to regions minimizing their respective objective functions (Eq. (7) and Eq. (9)). Additional subfigures depict absolute per-class distances to each hyperplane.

topics.title: Alternative names for margin sampling
topics.description: The text notes that the margin sampling heuristic appears in the literature under several different names. These include “most ambiguous,” “binary level uncertainty,” and “SVMSIMPLE,” reflecting slight terminological variations across studies. Despite the naming differences, these methods all implement the same core idea of querying samples near the SVM decision boundary.

topics.title: Predictive entropy over posterior probabilities
topics.description: This topic describes the mathematical formulation of predictive entropy HM[y|x] as −∑_k p_M(y = k | x) log p_M(y = k | x). The entropy is computed over the posterior label probabilities p_M(y | x) given by the classifier M for each class k. It quantifies the uncertainty of the model’s prediction for a given input by measuring how spread out the probability mass is across classes.

topics.title: Least Confidence active learning heuristic
topics.description: Least Confidence (LeastConf) is an uncertainty-based query strategy that selects data points x for which the model M has the lowest posterior probability on its most likely predicted label ŷ. The acquisition function is defined as α_LeastConf(x, M) = − p_M(ŷ | x), so higher acquisition scores correspond to lower model confidence. This method focuses solely on the top predicted class probability as a proxy for uncertainty, without considering the full predictive distribution over labels.

topics.title: Variation Ratios as lack-of-confidence measure
topics.description: Variation Ratios (VarRatio) is presented as a method similar to Least Confidence that also targets the model's lack of confidence in its predictions. Its acquisition function is α_VarRatio(x, M) = 1 − p_M(ŷ | x), which measures how far the top predicted class probability is from full certainty. Like LeastConf, it relies on the most likely label’s posterior probability but expresses uncertainty as a complement (1 minus that probability).

topics.title: Mutual information-based acquisition function
topics.description: The BALD score is defined as the mutual information between the model’s predictions y and the posterior distribution over parameters p(ω|D_l). This is expressed as the difference between the predictive entropy H_M[y|x] and the expected conditional entropy E_{p(ω|D_l)}[H_M[y|x, ω]]. The first term measures overall predictive uncertainty, while the second term averages uncertainty conditioned on specific parameter settings, isolating epistemic uncertainty due to parameter uncertainty. This decomposition is central to how BALD quantifies and selects informative data points.

topics.title: Mean Standard Deviation uncertainty measure
topics.description: Mean Standard Deviation (MeanSTD) is an acquisition function that maximizes the average predictive variance over all k classes for a sample. It computes the variance of class probabilities under a Bayesian posterior over model parameters and averages these variances, prioritizing points with high predictive dispersion across stochastic forward passes. This targets samples where the model’s class probability estimates are most unstable, indicating high epistemic uncertainty.

topics.title: Clustering and CoreSet representative selection
topics.description: Representative/diversity-based strategies such as KMeans and CoreSet aim to select batches that approximate the overall data distribution in a feature space. KMeans iteratively chooses centroids proportional to squared distances from existing centroids, while CoreSet operates in the model’s penultimate layer h(x), repeatedly picking the point farthest from its nearest labeled neighbor. These methods view the selected points as a proxy for the full dataset, emphasizing coverage of the feature space.

topics.title: Cluster-Margin for diverse low-confidence sampling
topics.description: Cluster-Margin combines clustering with margin-based uncertainty to choose diverse, low-confidence samples. It first performs hierarchical agglomerative clustering with average linkage to structure the unlabeled pool, then identifies points within clusters that have the lowest margin scores (least confident predictions). Finally, it filters these to a diverse subset of size b, differing from CoreSet by performing clustering only once as a preprocessing step.

topics.title: Weighted-sum combination and DPP balancing
topics.description: Weighted-sum optimization combines uncertainty and representativeness scores into a single acquisition value via α = α_uncertainty + β α_representative, but introduces a hyperparameter β and mismatched score formats (scalar vs matrix). Exploitation-Exploration is an example that subtracts a similarity term from entropy-based uncertainty to reduce redundancy while promoting diversity. DPPs are highlighted as a natural way to jointly account for per-sample uncertainty and pairwise diversity without extra hyperparameters, though exact sampling incurs O(N³) complexity.

topics.title: Two-stage combined selection strategies
topics.description: Two-stage (or multi-stage) optimization refines candidate sets sequentially using different criteria, often first selecting an informative subset and then enforcing diversity. WAAL first trains a discriminative network on labeled vs unlabeled data and then uses it for batch selection. BADGE computes gradient embeddings in the first stage and clusters them with KMeans++ in the second, whereas DBAL prefilters to the top ρb most uncertain points and then clusters them into b groups, choosing samples near cluster centers.

topics.title: Data-aspect enhancements: pseudo-labeling
topics.description: Data-aspect DAL enhancements use pseudo-labeling to exploit large unlabeled pools without explicit annotation. CEAL assigns pseudo-labels to high-confidence (low-entropy) predictions and includes them in subsequent training iterations, effectively enlarging the labeled set. This approach requires confidence thresholds as hyperparameters; poor tuning can introduce erroneous labels and harm performance.

topics.title: Loss function modification via adversarial objectives
topics.description: Altering the target model’s loss function is proposed as another route to enhancing DAL. WAAL introduces a min–max loss that leverages unlabeled data to better discriminate between labeled and unlabeled samples during training. This adversarial-style objective aims to shape the feature space so that selected unlabeled batches are both diverse and distributionally informative for label acquisition.

topics.title: Ensemble-based uncertainty: MC Dropout and ensembles
