topics.title: Uncertainty estimation and class statistics
topics.description: The section highlights that estimating classification confidence (e.g., probabilities or margins) can be unreliable when it depends heavily on estimated class statistics, as in Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). Poorly estimated class means and covariances can propagate into misleading uncertainty measures, negatively affecting active learning sample selection. A similar issue arises for committee-based methods using bagging when each bag contains only a small portion of the original samples, making committee disagreement unstable.

topics.title: Handling complex manifolds via feature-space modeling
topics.description: For data lying on complex manifolds, redundancy among samples can severely degrade the quality of the active learning sampling and the resulting training set. The text advocates modeling relationships among samples in feature space to better capture manifold structure and select representative pixels. Methods such as kernel k-means within MCLU-ECBD and hMCS, as well as distance to support vectors in the cSV heuristic, are cited as concrete strategies to exploit this relational structure.

topics.title: Sequential sampling with moving sensors
topics.description: In scenarios where moving sensors acquire samples sequentially via an automatic device, batch-based querying is unnecessary and potentially inefficient. The priority shifts to models and heuristics with very low computational cost that can be updated rapidly and suggest the next sampling location almost in real time. Within this context, BT (e.g., breaking ties) and KL-max heuristics are identified as particularly suitable due to their favorable computational properties.

topics.title: Legend for algorithm characteristics
topics.description: The table defines a compact legend to encode properties of active learning algorithms: B for binary vs. M for multiclass problems, q as the number of candidate samples, k as the number of learners in a committee, S as batch size, and SVs as support vectors. Checkmarks (✓) and crosses (×) indicate the presence or absence of specific features. This notation supports concise comparison across multiple methods in supervised remote sensing image classification.

topics.title: Ongoing research on active sampling heuristics
topics.description: The text highlights that research on active learning for remote sensing is active and evolving, with new heuristics for active sampling continuously developed. The community in remote sensing and signal processing keeps proposing and testing novel selection strategies, indicating that the current survey is not exhaustive. This underscores a dynamic field with ongoing methodological innovation.

topics.title: Active selection in semi-supervised classification
topics.description: This topic concerns actively selecting unlabeled pixels to improve semi-supervised classification in remote sensing imagery. Active learning strategies query the most informative unlabeled pixels so that limited labeling effort yields maximal gain in classifier performance. It focuses on the interaction between labeled and unlabeled data under a semi-supervised learning regime.

topics.title: Spatially adaptive active learning heuristics
topics.description: Spatially adaptive heuristics adjust active learning query strategies based on spatial properties of the image, such as neighborhood structure or spatial context. Instead of treating each pixel independently, these methods exploit spatial patterns to guide which samples to label. This leads to more efficient learning in spatially correlated remote sensing data.

topics.title: Active learning for cross-domain model adaptation
topics.description: This topic addresses using active learning to adapt models across different domains or scenes, such as transferring a classifier from one geographic area or sensor condition to another. By selectively querying labels in the target domain, the model can be efficiently adapted while minimizing annotation cost. It focuses on domain shift and transfer learning in remote sensing classification.

topics.title: Contextual information in query heuristics
topics.description: Here, the focus is on extending active learning heuristics beyond purely spectral criteria to explicitly incorporate contextual information such as positional data and texture. While current methods largely rely on spectral features or embed context only as additional attributes in the data vector, the text highlights the lack of heuristics that directly reason over spatial position and texture. This involves designing query strategies that model spatial relationships and local image structure.

topics.title: Robustness of uncertainty-based heuristics to noise
topics.description: This topic concerns the vulnerability of uncertainty-driven active learning heuristics to high levels of image noise, particularly in synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data. Since these methods rely on model uncertainty at the pixel level, heavy noise can render uncertainty estimates unreliable and the heuristics ineffective. The text notes that designing noise-robust active learning strategies for such conditions remains an open and largely unexplored research area.

topics.title: AI Systems Approaching Expert Performance
topics.description: AI-powered systems for medical image analysis have achieved performance comparable to human experts in several clinical tasks. The text highlights applications such as skin cancer classification, lung cancer screening with CT, polyp detection during colonoscopy, and prostate cancer detection in whole-slide images. These systems can be integrated into clinical workflows to improve diagnostic accuracy and assist less-experienced clinicians.

topics.title: Deep Learning Foundations for Image Analysis
topics.description: Deep learning models act as the core component of AI-based medical image analysis systems, learning complex patterns directly from raw images and generalizing to unseen cases. Their strength lies in robust feature extraction and generalization capabilities, which have driven major advances in medical image analysis. However, these models typically depend on large-scale human-annotated datasets, exemplified by the ImageNet dataset widely used in computer vision.

topics.title: Workflow challenges in digital pathology
topics.description: In digital pathology, pathologists must examine tissue slices under high-magnification microscopes and continuously adjust magnification due to complex tissue structures. This examination is slow, typically requiring 15 to 30 minutes per slide, and accurate annotation is even more challenging than mere inspection. The need for detailed interpretation across varying magnifications greatly increases cognitive and time demands on pathologists.

topics.title: Limitations of crowdsourcing for medical images
topics.description: While crowdsourcing significantly reduces annotation costs for general computer vision tasks, it is poorly suited for medical image analysis. High-quality medical labels require domain-specific medical knowledge and clinical expertise, and even for simpler tasks, crowd workers tend to produce lower-quality annotations than trained professionals. Privacy concerns further restrict the use of open crowdsourcing platforms for sensitive medical data.

topics.title: Expert annotation burden and variability
topics.description: Replacing crowd workers with clinical experts shifts the bottleneck to the high cost and time demands of expert annotation. For example, a radiologist may need about 60 minutes to manually segment brain tumors per patient, with high hourly compensation, making large-scale labeling very expensive. To reduce bias, multiple annotation rounds or multiple annotators per case are often used, introducing intra- and inter-annotator variability that further increases annotation cost and complexity.

topics.title: Existing surveys on active learning
topics.description: Previous surveys have examined active learning from several angles, including the role of humans in developing and deploying deep learning in medical imaging, AL for segmentation with imperfect annotations, and AL as a label-efficient learning method focusing on model and data uncertainty. Other general AL surveys in machine learning and computer vision have provided foundational introductions and reviewed deep AL developments in CV and NLP, as well as taxonomies of model-driven and data-driven sample selectors and fair re-implementations of high-impact methods. These works form the background against which the current medical imaging-focused survey is positioned.

topics.title: Identified gaps in current AL surveys
topics.description: The section highlights several limitations of existing AL surveys: rapid methodological progress has outpaced current reviews, leaving new ideas and techniques under-covered. There is insufficient synthesis on combining AL with other label-efficient methods, despite this being a recognized future direction. Moreover, few surveys systematically evaluate AL methods on medical imaging datasets, and current reviews insufficiently address AL’s elevated importance under high medical annotation costs.

topics.title: Scope and paper selection of this survey
topics.description: The survey aims to comprehensively cover AL for medical image analysis, including core methods, integration with label-efficient techniques, and domain-specific adaptations. Papers are primarily sourced from medical image analysis using keyword-based searches on Google Scholar and arXiv, then expanded via citation tracing. Seminal AL works from general computer vision are also included to maintain a coherent taxonomy, and the surveyed works are largely drawn from top-tier journals and conferences, totaling 164 AL works with 234 references.

topics.title: Canonical active learning problem settings
topics.description: Active learning is framed around three primary problem settings: membership query synthesis, stream-based selective sampling, and pool-based active learning. Each setting defines different assumptions about how unlabeled samples are obtained and how queries to the oracle are made. This classification underpins the formulation and comparison of active learning strategies across applications, including medical image analysis.

topics.title: Stream-based selective sampling under memory constraints
topics.description: Stream-based selective sampling assumes that unlabeled samples arrive sequentially in a stream, and the learner must immediately decide whether to query their labels. This setting is well-suited for environments with limited memory, such as edge computing devices, because it does not require storing a large pool of data. However, it typically ignores correlations between samples in the stream, which may limit selection efficiency.

topics.title: Batch-mode selection in deep active learning
topics.description: When multiple samples are selected for labeling at once, the process is termed batch-mode active learning. Deep active learning typically assumes batch-mode pool-based settings because retraining deep models after each individual annotation is computationally impractical, and a single labeled example rarely yields a significant performance gain. Consequently, the survey treats batch-mode pool-based active learning as the default setup for deep active learning methods it reviews.

topics.title: Sample selection via informativeness functions
topics.description: In each round, an informativeness function I evaluates every sample in the unlabeled pool Du_t to quantify its utility for model improvement. Based on these scores, a sampling strategy S selects a batch of the most informative samples to form the queried set Dq_t. This mechanism focuses annotation effort on samples expected to maximally benefit the deep model f_{θ_{t−1}}.

topics.title: Queried and unlabeled datasets with budget
topics.description: The queried dataset Dq_t in round t is a subset of the unlabeled pool Du_t, defined by applying the sampling strategy S to informativeness evaluations I(x, f_{θ_{t−1}}). The annotation budget b governs how many samples are selected per round, enforcing b = |Dq_t| ≪ |Du_t| to ensure only a small fraction of data is labeled. This formalization explicitly distinguishes unlabeled, queried, and budget-constrained subsets within each iteration.

topics.title: Oracle-based annotation and dataset update
topics.description: After selection, the queried set Dq_t is sent to an oracle, typically medical experts such as doctors, who provide ground-truth annotations. These newly labeled samples are then incorporated into the labeled dataset Dl_t, updating it for subsequent training and selection rounds. This step operationalizes human-in-the-loop learning by coupling algorithmic selection with expert annotation.

topics.title: Hybrid and Learnable Sampling Approaches
topics.description: This topic addresses query strategies that combine multiple selection criteria or learn the sampling policy directly. Hybrid sampling fuses uncertainty, representativeness, and class-balance cues, while learnable sampling uses neural networks or reinforcement learning to optimize query decisions end-to-end. Such methods aim to adapt sampling behavior to task-specific characteristics rather than relying on fixed heuristics.

topics.title: Annotation-efficient Strategies and Cost Modeling
topics.description: This topic deals with reducing and modeling annotation costs in medical imaging. It includes slice-based annotation (labeling only selected slices in volumetric scans), one-shot annotation (annotating minimal examples), and explicit consideration of 'Annotation Cost'. These strategies aim to align active learning with realistic clinical workflows where expert time is limited and labeling is expensive.

topics.title: Active learning dataset update rules
topics.description: The section formalizes how labeled and unlabeled datasets are updated in each active learning round. Newly queried samples D_q^t, once labeled by the oracle, are added to the labeled set D_l^t and simultaneously removed from the unlabeled pool D_u^t. This iterative refinement of D_l and D_u underpins the active learning loop and ensures no sample is selected twice.

topics.title: Supervised deep model training in AL loop
topics.description: After oracle annotation in each round, the deep learning model f_θ_t is trained in a fully supervised way on the current labeled set D_l^t. The training objective is expressed as minimizing an expected loss L(f_θ(x), y) over (x, y) ∈ D_l^t, written compactly as L(x, y; θ). This step produces updated parameters θ_t that are then used for subsequent sample selection.

topics.title: Iterative versus one-shot active learning
topics.description: The section contrasts the standard multi-round active learning process with one-shot strategies. In the iterative setting, steps of selection, annotation, and training are repeated until an annotation budget is exhausted or a target performance is reached. By contrast, one-shot active learning performs sample selection in a single pass without multiple rounds, changing how the model and querying strategy are designed.

topics.title: Imaging modalities and segmentation tasks overview
topics.description: The figure caption fragments indicate that the survey’s overall framework spans multiple medical imaging modalities and tasks, including MRI, CT, and Electron Microscopy, with a focus on medical image segmentation. Interactive segmentation and density-based methods are highlighted within this framework, signaling key application areas where deep active learning is applied. These elements situate the formal AL loop within concrete medical imaging contexts.

topics.title: Survey contribution on sampling strategies
topics.description: This survey claims a unique contribution by explicitly defining sampling strategies as core methods of active learning, rather than treating them as secondary. It reviews how to design better sampling strategies and summarizes all cited AL works, including their uncertainty/representativeness metrics and sampling approaches. These methods and metrics are systematized and detailed in a comprehensive table (Table 2).

topics.title: Prediction-probability uncertainty metrics
topics.description: This topic covers classical uncertainty measures computed directly from a model’s prediction probabilities p = Softmax(fθ(x)) over C classes. Metrics include Least Confidence (1 − max_i p_i or equivalently using max_i p_i with ↓ direction), Entropy (−∑_i p_i log p_i with ↑ direction), Margin (difference between top-1 and top-2 class probabilities with ↓ direction), and Mean Variance of class probabilities (↑ direction). These metrics quantify how spread or peaky the predicted distribution is, and serve as basic uncertainty scores in active learning query strategies.

topics.title: Uncertainty for medical image active learning
topics.description: Uncertainty estimation is positioned as crucial for deploying deep learning in clinical practice, where medical images exhibit high variability and training data are limited. Predictive uncertainty allows models to flag ambiguities, artifacts, and unseen patterns, making it a natural informativeness metric in active learning. Samples with higher uncertainty are treated as harder and more error-prone, so querying and annotating them helps the model learn novel patterns and improve overall performance.

topics.title: Aleatoric, epistemic, and predictive uncertainty
topics.description: Uncertainty is decomposed into aleatoric uncertainty (AU) and epistemic uncertainty (EU). AU represents data-driven noise such as motion or metal artifacts in MRI/CT and cannot be reduced by collecting more data, while EU reflects model uncertainty due to unlearned knowledge and can be reduced with additional labeled data. In practice, most active learning work does not explicitly separate AU and EU, so 'uncertainty' typically refers to predictive uncertainty, the combined effect of both, because disentangling the two is difficult and often offers limited practical benefit.

topics.title: Taxonomy of uncertainty-based active learning
topics.description: Uncertainty-based active learning methods are organized into five main categories: multiple inference, gradient-based uncertainty, performance estimation, uncertainty-aware models, and adversarial-based uncertainty. Multiple inference methods include MC Dropout, data disagreement, model disagreement, and model ensembles; gradient-based approaches use gradients, Fisher Information, or influence functions; performance estimation employs surrogate metrics or learnable performance predictors; uncertainty-aware models encompass evidential deep learning and mixture density networks; adversarial-based methods leverage adversarial samples and adversarial training. This taxonomy structures the design space of uncertainty exploitation beyond simple probability-based measures.

topics.title: Model ensembles and snapshot ensembles for AL
topics.description: Model ensemble approaches train multiple independent deep models whose predictions are combined to estimate uncertainty, often outperforming MC dropout but at higher computational cost. Snapshot ensembles reduce this overhead by capturing multiple model checkpoints along a single training trajectory using cyclic learning rate schedules, though naïve variants may underperform full ensembles. An improved snapshot ensemble maintains optimization trajectories across active learning rounds with parameter regularization and can surpass standard ensembles. Additionally, stein variational gradient descent is used to train diverse ensembles for organ and tumor segmentation in CT and MRI, improving performance over competing methods.

topics.title: Query-by-Committee model disagreement in segmentation
topics.description: Model disagreement, formalized as Query-by-Committee (QBC), selects samples where multiple models’ outputs diverge most, indicating high epistemic uncertainty. Suggestive Annotation (SA) trains several segmentation networks via bootstrapping and uses prediction variance as a disagreement metric, achieving strong performance in gland and lymph node segmentation. Other works train multiple distinct segmentation models and measure disagreement (e.g., prediction variance or KL divergence between teacher and student models) to prioritize cases for annotation in tasks like abdominal multi-organ and carotid intima-media segmentation.

topics.title: CAM-based disagreement and geometric uncertainty metrics
topics.description: Some approaches leverage class activation maps (CAMs) and geometric similarity measures to refine disagreement-based active learning. In polyp segmentation, multiple decoders are trained on CAMs from a classification network, and both model disagreement (entropy and Dice between decoder outputs) and CAM disagreement (Dice between CAMs and decoder outputs) are used to select informative samples; low model but high CAM disagreement cases are turned into pseudo-labels for semi-supervised learning. Other methods quantify disagreement between CAMs using Hausdorff distance or between MC dropout predictions via vote entropy, capturing spatial or categorical uncertainty for tasks such as rib fracture detection.

topics.title: Data disagreement via input perturbations and viewpoints
topics.description: Data disagreement methods avoid training many models by instead perturbing inputs (e.g., augmentations or viewpoint changes) and measuring predictive inconsistency across these variants. KL divergence is a central metric, used to compare predictions for different augmented CT scans in COVID diagnosis and different viewpoints in 3D scenes, with higher KL indicating more informative samples. Extensions include an input-end committee that randomly augments inputs and quantifies classification and localization disagreement using cross-entropy and variance, respectively, providing a flexible framework for image-level and region-level uncertainty estimation.

topics.title: Feature-space interpolation disagreement with prototypes
topics.description: Feature-space interpolation strategies assess whether unlabeled data introduce novel information by interpolating between unlabeled feature vectors and labeled class prototypes. If the interpolated point’s prediction disagrees with the prototype’s label, this is interpreted as evidence that the unlabeled sample lies in a region not well represented by existing labels and should be annotated. This prototype-based disagreement mechanism has shown improvements across multiple datasets and settings, offering a representation-level perspective on uncertainty beyond raw prediction variance.

topics.title: Expected Gradient Length for exudate classification
topics.description: As an early application, expected gradient length is used to select informative samples in an exudate classification task on eye fundus images. Otálora et al. (2017) adopt the classic expected gradient length criterion to drive annotation decisions, leveraging the connection between gradient magnitude and sample value. This illustrates how traditional gradient-based active learning ideas are applied in medical imaging.

topics.title: Manifold-projected gradients for MRI segmentation
topics.description: Dai et al. propose an active learning method that projects segmentation loss gradients onto a learned data manifold to guide sample selection. A variational autoencoder (VAE) is first trained to capture the manifold of MRI brain images, and then a segmentation model is trained whose Dice-loss gradients are computed on labeled data. Query samples are chosen based on the components of these gradients that lie along the manifold, aiming to focus on realistic and informative variations. Their extended work demonstrates superior performance in both MRI brain tumor and whole-brain segmentation tasks.

topics.title: Layer-wise and last-layer Fisher approximations
topics.description: To make FI-based active learning feasible in deep models, approximations are introduced that reduce computational cost. Sourati et al. compute FI using average gradients per network layer instead of full parameter-wise matrices, and they rely on expected empirical loss (Eq. 5) to obtain gradients without labels; this method improves brain extraction performance across ages and pathologies. Ash et al. further simplify the approach by computing the FI matrix only for the last layer, and their gradient computation matches the BADGE framework, which uses last-layer gradient embeddings. These approximations retain much of FI’s informativeness while avoiding full quadratic complexity.

topics.title: Influence function-based sample selection
topics.description: Liu et al. apply influence functions to choose unlabeled samples expected to most positively affect model performance when labeled. The influence of a sample is computed using gradients of the loss on the labeled set and the inverse Hessian of the empirical risk (Eq. 9), capturing how upweighting that sample would perturb model parameters and downstream loss. Because unlabeled samples lack ground-truth, their gradients in the influence expression are approximated using gradients of the expected empirical loss. This yields an AL criterion grounded in classical robust statistics but adapted to deep models in medical imaging.

topics.title: BADGE-style gradients for medical segmentation
topics.description: The section alludes to extending the BADGE framework, which uses gradient embeddings from the last layer, to medical image segmentation tasks. It is mentioned in the context of semantic segmentation of laparoscopic surgical images and in Ash et al. (2021), where only the last-layer FI matrix is computed with BADGE-like gradients. This indicates a design where gradient-based diversity and uncertainty, encoded at the final layer, guide active sample selection in dense prediction problems. Such adaptations aim to transfer BADGE’s classification-oriented strategy to pixel-wise medical segmentation settings.

topics.title: Surrogate metrics via prediction agreement
topics.description: Surrogate metrics approximate performance by exploiting prediction agreement or intermediate representations, serving as upper or lower bounds of loss or evaluation scores. Examples include computing the intersection over union (IoU) across multiple MC dropout predictions and correlating it with the true Dice coefficient, and averaging Dice scores between intermediate and final layers under deep supervision. These surrogates show strong linear correlations with real task metrics, making them effective proxies for performance in medical image segmentation.

topics.title: Cyclic Output Discrepancy (COD) as loss surrogate
topics.description: Cyclic Output Discrepancy (COD) measures the norm of the change in network outputs between two consecutive annotation rounds. Within limited training iterations, sample loss is shown to be bounded by this output difference, making COD a surrogate for both loss and downstream evaluation metrics. Samples with high COD are preferentially selected, as empirical results demonstrate that higher COD is associated with higher loss and poorer performance.

topics.title: Combining loss prediction with diversity and disagreement
topics.description: Some methods enhance learnable loss estimation by integrating it with other active learning criteria such as model disagreement and sample diversity. In COVID diagnosis and colonoscopy polyp analysis under federated active learning, predicted loss is combined with prediction disagreements and diversity measures to select informative and diverse samples across distributed clients. This composite strategy aims to improve both uncertainty targeting and coverage of the data space.

topics.title: Loss ranking prediction instead of regression
topics.description: Recognizing that active learning primarily needs an uncertainty ordering rather than exact loss values, loss regression is relaxed to predicting relative loss ranks. Kim et al. (2021) replace the loss regressor in LLAL with a ranking module derived from RankCGAN, directly optimizing for correct ordering of sample uncertainties. This rank-based estimation empirically surpasses exact loss regression for sample selection.

topics.title: Uncertainty-aware deep models in AL
topics.description: This topic covers deep models that inherently model predictive distributions rather than point estimates, such as VAEs and probabilistic U-Nets. These models output full distributions over predictions, reducing over-confidence compared to deterministic networks and providing built-in uncertainty estimates. They require only a single forward pass at inference, lowering computational and time costs for active learning pipelines.

topics.title: Multi-label EDL using Beta distributions
topics.description: In multi-label chest X-ray classification, EDL is adapted by decomposing the Dirichlet distribution into multiple Beta distributions, one per class label. Each Beta distribution models the evidential uncertainty for a specific label, and its entropy is used as the aleatoric uncertainty metric for annotation. This enables uncertainty-aware active learning in a multi-label medical imaging setting.

topics.title: EDL-based active domain adaptation
topics.description: Here, EDL is employed within an active domain adaptation framework to select samples under both data and distributional uncertainty. Samples exhibiting high distribution uncertainty (domain shift) and high data uncertainty are prioritized for annotation. This evidential approach tailors active learning to settings where source and target data distributions differ.

topics.title: KL-divergence-driven adversarial attacks for uncertainty
topics.description: Here, adversarial attacks are constructed by maximizing the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the model’s predictions on original and perturbed inputs under a bounded perturbation norm. The KL divergence quantifies how much the prediction distribution changes under small adversarial noise, capturing local sensitivity of the classifier. Samples for which this divergence is maximized, given the perturbation constraint, are deemed more uncertain and are selected for annotation. This leverages distributional disagreement under adversarial perturbations as an uncertainty metric.

topics.title: Adversarial training with classifier disagreement
topics.description: This topic describes an adversarial training scheme that alternates optimization of a shared feature extractor and multiple classifiers to surface uncertain samples. Two classifiers are trained on labeled and unlabeled data: first, classifiers are updated while the feature extractor is fixed to increase disagreement and expose ambiguous regions; next, the feature extractor is updated against fixed classifiers to reduce the discrepancy between labeled and unlabeled representations. After several alternations, samples that induce the largest classifier disagreements are identified as most informative and are annotated. The method combines adversarial objectives in representation learning with disagreement-based active learning.

topics.title: Distribution Misalignment and Dataset Bias
topics.description: In feature space, uncertain samples tend to lie near the decision boundary, so uncertainty-based selection skews the queried set toward this region. As a result, the distribution of queried samples diverges from the overall data distribution, introducing dataset bias. This misalignment can cause a performance drop and motivates considering relationships among samples during querying.

topics.title: Limitations of Uncertainty as Informativeness Metric
topics.description: Uncertainty-based AL under-exploits the visual content of each sample and the inter-sample relationships, focusing instead on model confidence alone. This limitation leads to outlier selection and distribution misalignment. Consequently, the authors argue for designing new informativeness metrics that explicitly encode sample characteristics and their relationships.

topics.title: Feature Representations in Medical Image AL
topics.description: Medical images are high-dimensional and contain complex, often non-obvious information about lesions, tissues, and anatomical or functional structures. Good feature representations lower dimensionality while encoding anatomical, histological, pathological, and functional cues relevant to clinical tasks. Because of this, representativeness-based querying is typically executed in the learned feature space rather than raw image space.

topics.title: Clustering-based active learning framework
topics.description: Clustering-based active learning exploits the fact that similar medical images cluster together in feature space, enabling selection of representative samples via clustering on embeddings. Data are partitioned into clusters and cluster centroids are chosen for annotation, leveraging the data’s inherent structure while remaining easy to implement. This provides a straightforward query strategy that focuses labeling effort on diverse, representative points.

topics.title: Coarse-to-fine clustering for nuclei segmentation
topics.description: Lou et al. propose a two-level clustering strategy using K-Means for nuclei segmentation in pathological images. They first perform coarse-level clustering to broadly group patches and then fine-level clustering within these groups to refine selection. The goal is to identify particularly informative image patches for labeling, improving segmentation quality while keeping annotation costs low.

topics.title: Active learning via ROI correctness judgment
topics.description: In connectomics, Lin et al. first predict a semantic mask for each unlabeled sample and then reformulate active learning as judging whether each predicted region of interest (ROI) is correct. This shifts the labeling task from full annotation to verification of model-generated segmentations. The approach narrows annotation to critical ROIs where model predictions may be unreliable, increasing efficiency.

topics.title: Two-stream VAE-based clustering in connectomics
topics.description: Lin et al. train two separate feature extractors based on variational autoencoders (VAEs): one on segmentation masks and another on unlabeled images. These two streams provide complementary feature spaces for clustering in active learning. In particular, they apply mask-level clustering using mask features to group ROIs with similar appearances, guiding selection of diverse and uncertain regions for annotation in connectomics.

topics.title: Hierarchical mask and image-level clustering
topics.description: The approach first forms clusters based on segmentation masks and then performs additional clustering at the image level within each mask cluster. This hierarchical strategy separates structural (mask-based) similarity from broader visual (image-based) similarity. Such a design aims to better capture fine-grained object-level patterns before aggregating image-level characteristics. It is particularly suitable for medical images where object shape and appearance both carry diagnostic information.

topics.title: Two-stream clustering vs feature concatenation
topics.description: Two-stream clustering processes mask features and image features in separate streams, instead of concatenating them into a single feature vector. The results indicate that this separation prevents image features from overwhelming the contribution of mask features during clustering. As a consequence, structural information encoded in masks is preserved, leading to more balanced and meaningful clusters. This highlights the importance of feature-stream decoupling in multi-modal or multi-feature clustering setups.

topics.title: Application to synapse and mitochondria analysis
topics.description: The described clustering method is applied to tasks such as synapse detection and mitochondria segmentation in medical images. These are fine-scale, structure-focused problems where accurate delineation and recognition of small biological entities are critical. The method achieves excellent performance on these tasks, suggesting that its design is well-suited to capturing the complex shapes and appearances of subcellular structures. This demonstrates the utility of advanced clustering strategies in biomedical image analysis.

topics.title: Cover-based representativeness in active learning
topics.description: Cover-based active learning casts representativeness as a covering problem in feature space, analogous to placing spheres whose centers are selected samples to cover all data points. Two main formulations are discussed: set cover, which enforces complete coverage of the dataset, and maximum cover, which aims to cover as much as possible without strict completeness. Both are NP-hard but admit near-optimal greedy solutions that iteratively pick samples covering the largest number of remaining points. The trade-offs include large radii and outlier selection risk under set cover, versus more flexible coverage and reduced outlier bias under maximum cover.

topics.title: Maximum-cover-based Segmentation Active Learning (SA)
topics.description: Segmentation Active learning (SA) is an early representativeness-based method that first queries highly uncertain samples and then selects representative ones under a maximum cover formulation. Representativeness of an unlabeled sample is defined via cosine similarity to its most similar queried sample, and a global representativeness score sums these over all unlabeled samples. SA uses a greedy strategy to add points that maximally increase this representativeness measure, effectively generalizing the discrete maximum cover problem to continuous similarities in [0,1]. This framework became a foundation for many later cover-based active learning approaches in medical image analysis.

topics.title: Medical imaging extensions of SA-style maximum cover
topics.description: Several works extend the SA maximum-cover framework to diverse medical image tasks by modifying feature extraction, similarity measures, or the selection protocol. Examples include quantizing segmentation networks to improve accuracy and reduce memory, using VAEs with hierarchical clustering to define clusters and select representative points per cluster (RA), and inverting the similarity measure to 1−sim(·,·) to emphasize diversity in breast cancer segmentation. Other variants use self-supervised feature extractors and SIFT-based keypoints to select template images with maximal average cosine similarity for few-shot keypoint detection, or shift from set cover to maximum cover with graph-based greedy algorithms (ProbCover) to avoid outlier selection. Collectively, these methods illustrate how representativeness via maximum cover is adapted to segmentation, detection, and few-shot scenarios in medical imaging.

topics.title: Submodular formulations for cover-based active learning
topics.description: Set cover and maximum cover objectives can be expressed with submodular set functions, which exhibit diminishing returns: the marginal gain of adding an element decreases as the selected set grows. When an informativeness function I is monotone and submodular, greedy selection of samples that maximize the marginal gain in I yields near-optimal solutions in linear time, naturally modeling the idea that earlier queries should be most informative. Although methods like SA and RA were not explicitly framed this way, their objectives align with submodular formulations that encourage both representativeness and diversity. Typical pipelines involve computing pairwise similarities, defining a submodular objective over candidate subsets, and solving it greedily.

topics.title: Similarity-based distribution discrepancy metrics
topics.description: Similarity-based discrepancy approximates distribution distance via pairwise sample similarity, such as average cosine similarity between feature vectors from labeled and unlabeled sets. In medical segmentation tasks, samples far from the labeled set and close to the unlabeled set are selected, while graph-based methods like UncertainGCN use GCNs to model sample relationships and pick unlabeled nodes with lowest similarity to labeled ones. Prototype-based object detection methods build class or feature prototypes (sometimes incorporating prediction entropy) and query samples far from these labeled prototypes.

topics.title: Extensions of adversarial discrepancy-based AL
topics.description: Several methods extend VAAL by modifying the representation, supervision signal, or discriminator architecture to enhance active learning. Multimodal variants adapt the VAE to reconstruct multiple medical image modalities from a single-modality latent code, enabling cross-modal consistency in tasks such as brain tumor segmentation and chest X-ray classification. Other works remove adversarial training, replace binary discriminator labels with sample uncertainty, combine VAE and supervised-model features, or add extra discriminators distinguishing real from VAE-reconstructed features so that selection modules favor both uncertain and representative samples. Additional hybrids feed learning-loss predictions together with VAE features into the discriminator to enrich the selection signal.

topics.title: Optimal transport and continuous candidate selection
topics.description: Some methods formalize active learning as an optimal transport problem that minimizes the Wasserstein distance between labeled and unlabeled sets using self-supervised feature representations. Mixed-integer programming is employed to guarantee globally convergent and diverse sample selection, ensuring a well-spread labeled set in feature space. Other approaches treat candidate points as continuous variables in feature space, optimizing them to be close to unlabeled neighbors and far from labeled samples, then querying the nearest real samples; this optimization objective is shown to be equivalent to minimizing the Wasserstein distance.

topics.title: MMD and taxonomy of discrepancy measures
topics.description: Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) quantifies the distance between two distributions as the difference between their kernel-mean embeddings, effectively comparing mean feature representations in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. In active domain adaptation, MMD is used to measure the distance between source and target domains and to select target samples that are simultaneously representative and diverse. The section also clarifies that Wasserstein distance belongs to the family of integral probability metrics (IPM), while MMD belongs both to IPM and to the broader category related to H-divergence, and references external work for a more detailed taxonomy of such discrepancy measures.

topics.title: InfoVAE-based density estimation for MRI AL
topics.description: In shoulder MRI musculoskeletal segmentation, infoVAE is used to estimate sample density for both labeled and unlabeled sets. Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) replaces KL divergence as the regularization term during training, and the encoder’s posterior probability serves as the density metric. Samples with high density relative to the unlabeled pool but low density relative to the labeled dataset are prioritized for annotation, balancing representativeness and novelty.

topics.title: Fixed-representation and end-to-end density AL variants
topics.description: Wang et al. propose two variants of density-based active learning: one with fixed feature representations and another trained end-to-end. The fixed-representation variant resembles TypiClust but explicitly maximizes distances among selected samples to enhance diversity. The end-to-end variant jointly learns feature representations and sample selection using a learnable k-means clustering module, simultaneously optimizing cluster assignments and embeddings under a local smoothness constraint. This integrates representation learning and density-based selection into a unified training pipeline.

topics.title: Computational trade-offs in AL methodologies
topics.description: Methodologically, cover-based AL involves solving an NP-hard problem and relies on greedy linear-time approximations whose distance from the optimal solution is unknown in practice. This makes it difficult to assess how much AL performance could improve with truly optimal coverage. Density-based AL replaces this NP-hard optimization with density estimation, which is generally more computationally efficient. Thus, density-based strategies offer a more tractable alternative while still guiding sample selection via inferred data distribution structure.

topics.title: Diversity sampling in deep active learning
topics.description: Diversity sampling aims to reduce redundancy among queried samples in active learning so that the annotation budget is not wasted on highly similar instances. By encouraging selection of less redundant data, it mitigates overfitting to a small, homogeneous training set and improves model performance. The section outlines four main diversity strategies: clustering, farthest-first traversal, determinantal point processes (DPPs), and methods tailored to specific informativeness metrics.

topics.title: Random partitioning into stochastic batches
topics.description: Random selection is repurposed for diversity by partitioning the entire dataset into stochastic batches, which are then scored and selected based on batch-level uncertainty. In prostate and hippocampus segmentation tasks, the highest-uncertainty random batches were annotated, leading to consistent improvements of multiple uncertainty-based active learning methods under extremely low annotation budgets. This shows that simple random batch partitioning can act as an effective diversity mechanism when combined with uncertainty scoring.

topics.title: Fisher information-based SDP diversity selection
topics.description: Fisher information (FI)-based active learning methods formulate batch selection as a semidefinite programming (SDP) problem that maximizes information gain while controlling redundancy. Different solvers and algorithms address the computational challenges of SDP: some work relies on off-the-shelf commercial solvers, while others introduce greedy algorithms tailored to high-dimensional feature spaces. These FI-SDP formulations provide a principled way to promote diversity grounded in information theory.

topics.title: Image hashing and locality-sensitive diversity
topics.description: Image hashing for diversity sampling compresses each image into a compact feature representation, such as its first principal component, and then uses locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) to bucket similar images together. Samples are drawn uniformly across buckets so that the labeled set spans many distinct regions of the feature space, reducing redundancy. Applied to skin lesion analysis, this method shows how simple hash-based partitioning can operationalize diversity in large-scale image pools.

topics.title: Long-Tail Class Distributions in Medical Tasks
topics.description: Many medical image classification problems exhibit a long-tail distribution, where a small number of classes are frequent and numerous rare classes have few examples. The section cites tasks such as skin lesion classification and whole-slide image classification as typical examples. These long-tail distributions complicate model learning because standard training objectives are dominated by common classes.

topics.title: Overfitting Majority and Underfitting Minority Classes
topics.description: Training deep learning models on imbalanced datasets tends to cause overfitting to majority classes and underfitting to minority classes. Majority classes are modeled very accurately but may not generalize well, while minority classes are poorly represented and lead to low sensitivity or recall. This imbalance in learning performance undermines the clinical reliability of medical image classifiers.

topics.title: Diversity sampling for imbalanced COVID-19
topics.description: In a class-imbalanced COVID-19 image classification dataset, multiple informativeness scores and sampling strategies were compared within an active learning framework. The findings indicated that diversity-based sampling, which prioritizes querying heterogeneous samples, is better suited than other strategies for mitigating class imbalance. This highlights diversity as a key selection criterion when majority and minority classes are unevenly represented.

topics.title: Tail-aware VAE–copula active sampling
topics.description: Jin et al. assumed that samples closer to the tail of the feature distribution are more likely to be from minority classes, equating tail probability with minority-class likelihood. They trained a variational autoencoder (VAE) for feature extraction and used copula models to estimate tail probabilities over these features, then combined clustering with unequal probability sampling to select informative samples. This tail-aware active learning approach was validated on the long-tailed ISIC 2020 skin lesion dataset.

topics.title: Threshold-based minority class querying
topics.description: In blood cell detection under microscopy, Sadafi et al. designed an active learning rule that requests expert annotations when the predicted probability for the minority class exceeds a fixed threshold (0.2). This simple decision rule targets labeling efforts at cases likely to belong to the underrepresented class, improving class coverage without complex modeling. The strategy directly couples classifier confidence with annotation triggering.

topics.title: Bayesian error decomposition for AL imbalance
topics.description: Choi et al. proposed estimating the probability that a classifier will make a mistake on a given sample and decomposing this error probability into three components via Bayes’ rule. They trained a VAE to model the likelihood of the data given a predicted class, and an auxiliary classifier on VAE features to estimate class priors and class-specific mislabeling probabilities. By jointly considering these three probabilities for query selection, they reduced class imbalance effects in active learning and showed good performance on stepwise class-imbalanced CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.

topics.title: Uncertainty-based optimization for class balance
topics.description: Bengar et al. introduced an optimization-based active learning framework that explicitly maintains class balance while using uncertainty as a primary selection signal. When querying uncertain samples, the method compensates for underrepresented classes by adding the most confident samples from those minority classes to the query batch. This produces a more balanced labeled set over time, improving learning stability under class imbalance.

topics.title: Class-balanced region sampling for segmentation
topics.description: In segmentation-focused active learning, some methods select regions or patches rather than full images, which risks missing rare or small structures such as the optic chiasma or optic nerve in head-and-neck multi-organ segmentation. To address this, Cai et al. and Wu et al. developed class-balanced region sampling strategies that bias region selection toward areas containing rare object classes. These strategies ensure that annotation effort covers critical but small anatomical structures within a region-querying AL setup.

topics.title: Hybrid sampling with multiple metrics
topics.description: Hybrid sampling in active learning addresses the challenge of effectively integrating multiple informativeness metrics when selecting unlabeled samples. Instead of relying on a single criterion, hybrid methods combine different notions such as uncertainty and representativeness to guide annotation. This aims to exploit complementary strengths of various metrics to improve label efficiency, especially in medical image analysis scenarios.

topics.title: Multi-round sampling strategy
topics.description: Multi-round sampling sequentially applies different informativeness metrics, first filtering a subset of candidates by one metric and then refining selection within this subset using another. This staged strategy is popular in medical image analysis for its simplicity and flexibility, as demonstrated in several cited works. It enables a coarse-to-fine selection process where an initial metric narrows the pool and a secondary metric optimizes the final batch for annotation.

topics.title: Combining representativeness and uncertainty
topics.description: Hybrid strategies often pair representativeness with uncertainty to balance coverage of the data distribution and model improvement. One example performs representativeness sampling conditioned on uncertainty scores to reduce redundancy in the selected set, ensuring diverse but informative samples. Another approach uses dynamic weights to allocate labeling budget between representativeness and uncertainty, prioritizing typical data early and uncertainty-focused refinement later as the model matures.

topics.title: Metric fusion for hybrid sampling
topics.description: Metric fusion directly combines multiple informativeness scores into a single composite measure for sample selection. A simple instantiation is summing different metrics and querying samples with the highest aggregated values, enabling straightforward joint optimization of several criteria. This approach is widely adopted in medical-domain active learning, offering a more integrated alternative to sequential, multi-round strategies.

topics.title: Ranked batch-mode adaptive metric fusion
topics.description: Ranked batch-mode active learning adaptively fuses multiple metrics when selecting batches of samples, rather than using fixed, predetermined combinations. It typically ranks unlabeled instances using several criteria and then integrates these rankings or scores to construct an optimal query batch. This adaptive fusion aims to better capture evolving informativeness patterns during the active learning process.

topics.title: Reinforcement learning formulation of sample selection
topics.description: Sample selection is framed as a reinforcement learning problem where the learner and dataset form the environment, and the neural selector acts as the agent. The agent repeatedly chooses a limited number of samples for annotation and receives rewards that reflect the impact of these choices on downstream model performance. These rewards are used to train the neural selector’s policy, enabling adaptive, performance-driven sampling strategies.

topics.title: Actor-critic neural selector for medical images
topics.description: An actor-critic framework is used where the actor implements the neural selector and the critic network evaluates the quality of selected samples. This setup learns to choose samples that most effectively improve medical image classification performance. The method is reported to perform excellently in lung CT disease classification and diabetic retinopathy classification from fundus images.

topics.title: Probabilistic policy networks with REINFORCE
topics.description: A probabilistic policy network is employed as the neural selector, outputting distributions over samples to query. Rewards are designed to encourage selection of diverse and representative data points, aligning the sampling process with coverage of the data manifold. The policy is trained using the REINFORCE algorithm, a classic policy-gradient method for updating stochastic policies from reward signals.

topics.title: Few-shot and meta-learning neural selectors
topics.description: Beyond standard RL formulations, learnable sampling can also be cast as few-shot learning or approached via meta-learning to train neural selectors. These perspectives aim to learn sampling strategies that generalize across tasks or datasets, enabling rapid adaptation with limited labeled data. Such methods leverage prior experience to guide which samples are most beneficial to label in new scenarios.

topics.title: Leveraging idle unlabeled samples in AL cycles
topics.description: In standard active learning cycles, many unlabeled samples remain unused for training, effectively sitting idle while only queried samples are labeled and learned from. The text highlights this inefficiency and proposes combining active learning with semi-supervised learning so that both labeled and unlabeled images contribute to model training. This joint utilization can enhance data efficiency and model performance without increasing annotation demands. It reframes unlabeled pool data as a training asset rather than mere query candidates.

topics.title: Uncertainty estimation with MC dropout
topics.description: Within the CEAL framework for melanoma segmentation, Monte Carlo (MC) dropout is used to estimate prediction uncertainty. By performing multiple stochastic forward passes with dropout enabled at test time, the method computes variability in predictions as an uncertainty measure. These uncertainty estimates guide which medical image samples are selected for expert annotation versus pseudo-labeling.

topics.title: Refining pseudo-labels with dense CRFs
topics.description: In medical image segmentation, dense conditional random fields (CRFs) are applied to refine pseudo-labels generated by deep models. This post-processing step enforces spatial and appearance consistency across pixels, correcting local misclassifications in the initial pseudo-labels. Such refinement improves the quality of supervision when training segmentation networks with pseudo-labeled data.

topics.title: Curriculum-based hard and easy sample selection
topics.description: For Gleason grading in prostate cancer histopathology, samples are categorized into hard and easy via curriculum learning. Hard samples, which are likely more informative or challenging, are always sent for oracle (expert) annotation. Easy samples are then further analyzed based on training behavior to decide whether they should be pseudo-labeled or discarded.

topics.title: Training loss for label-noise detection
topics.description: Training loss on easy samples is used as a proxy for label reliability in the pseudo-labeling process. Easy samples with low training loss are assumed to have reliable pseudo-labels and are included to assist training, whereas easy samples with high loss are treated as noisy and excluded. This mechanism adaptively filters pseudo-labeled data to reduce the impact of label noise in deep active learning for medical images.

topics.title: Integrating consistency-based SSL into AL
topics.description: Several works integrate semi-supervised learning methods that rely on consistency regularization into active learning pipelines for medical image analysis. Examples include combining MeanTeacher, VAT, and NoTeacher with AL for chest X-ray classification, and coupling a proposed COD method with MeanTeacher. Another line combines density-based active learning with multiple semi-supervised strategies, showing that such hybrids can outperform standard active learning and semi-supervised baselines.

topics.title: Consistency-based sample informativeness in AL
topics.description: Consistency is also used as a criterion to measure sample informativeness for active learning selection. In a semi-supervised AL framework, each unlabeled sample is passed through the model multiple times with random augmentations, and a consistency loss is defined by the variance between the multiple outputs. Samples exhibiting lower consistency (higher variance) are deemed more informative and are selected for annotation. This joint use of consistency for both semi-supervised training and query strategy leads to significant performance gains.

topics.title: Single vs multiple inference strategies
topics.description: The methodologies are categorized into single-model inference and multiple-inference schemes for estimating uncertainty. Single-model methods rely on one deterministic pass to compute measures like distance to the decision boundary, while multiple-inference strategies (e.g., MC Dropout or data disagreement across inferences) approximate distributions over predictions. This distinction reflects different ways to capture epistemic uncertainty in deep active learning.

topics.title: Single-model uncertainty sampling strategies
topics.description: This topic covers deep active learning that relies on a single predictive model and classical uncertainty-based query strategies. Acquisition functions such as Least Confidence, Margin, and Entropy are used to score unlabeled samples, often selecting the Top-k highest-uncertainty instances for annotation. Pseudo-labeling may be applied to leverage model predictions on unlabeled data, integrating semi-supervised learning with active selection.

topics.title: Ensemble-based multi-criterion acquisition functions
topics.description: This topic describes ensemble-based deep active learning that evaluates unlabeled data using multiple acquisition criteria simultaneously. Metrics such as Entropy, BALD (Bayesian Active Learning by Disagreement), Least Confidence, and Variance are computed from ensemble predictions to capture different facets of epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty. Samples are then ranked and the Top-k most informative instances are selected at each iteration.

topics.title: Entropy, Least Confidence, and Variance Measures
topics.description: Uncertainty sampling in deep active learning commonly employs prediction entropy, least confidence, or variance to rank unlabeled samples. Entropy and least confidence operate on the output probability distribution, while variance is often derived from multiple inferences to capture prediction instability. These simple metrics underpin several single-model and committee-based strategies in the survey.

topics.title: Contextual and Coverage-Based Diversity Criteria
topics.description: Beyond simple distance-based diversity, some methods explicitly model contextual diversity and coverage of the data manifold. Cover-based and contextual diversity criteria focus on selecting samples that collectively span different regions and semantic contexts in the feature space, which is crucial for complex medical images. These approaches emphasize set-level properties rather than only individual sample informativeness.

topics.title: Hybrid Fusion of Uncertainty and Diversity
topics.description: Hybrid fusion methods combine multiple selection signals—such as uncertainty, diversity, and discrepancy—into a unified acquisition strategy. For example, they may jointly optimize for high entropy and large feature-space distance, or blend MC Dropout uncertainty with data disagreement and clustering. These composite strategies seek to balance informativeness with representativeness in medical image annotation.

topics.title: Uncertainty estimation strategies in DAL
topics.description: The table catalogs multiple uncertainty estimation approaches used in deep active learning, including multiple inferences via MC Dropout, model ensembles, and model disagreement, as well as single-model entropy, margin, BvSB, probability of misclassification, and MDN-based uncertainty. It also lists gradient-based uncertainty (e.g., Fisher Information, influence functions) and performance-estimation-based uncertainty that relies on predicted loss or segmentation quality. These strategies define how each method quantifies epistemic or aleatoric uncertainty over unlabeled medical images. They form the primary criterion for ranking candidate samples for annotation across the surveyed works.

topics.title: Adversarial training and adversarial querying
topics.description: Some surveyed works leverage adversarial mechanisms to drive active learning, either by training with adversarial examples or by explicitly generating adversarial samples for querying. The table shows approaches that use adversarial training combined with classifier disagreement or margins, and methods that use adversarial samples scored by KL divergence and Bhattacharya coefficient. These techniques aim to identify boundary or hard-to-classify cases that are especially informative for improving model robustness. They connect adversarial robustness objectives with active sample selection in medical imaging.

topics.title: Task-specific and radiomic selection metrics
topics.description: The table records the use of task-specific performance and shape metrics such as IoU, Dice score, Hausdorff distance, and temporal output discrepancy as basic selection criteria, particularly for segmentation tasks. It also lists medical imaging–specific descriptors like multivariate radiomics features, deep saliency features, saliency maps, and kurtosis to characterize lesion or organ appearance. These domain-specific metrics allow active learners to target anatomically or clinically meaningful errors rather than purely statistical uncertainty. They underscore the adaptation of deep active learning to medical image analysis requirements.

topics.title: Hybrid and multi-round sampling strategies
topics.description: Several methods combine multiple criteria—such as uncertainty and representativeness—or alternate them across rounds, forming hybrid sampling strategies. These are denoted as 'Hybrid - Multi-round' or 'Hybrid - Equal Split', indicating iterative schemes where, for example, some samples are chosen by energy/entropy while others are selected by density or consistency constraints. Such hybridization aims to mitigate the weaknesses of any single criterion and adapt acquisition to model state over successive active learning rounds. Consistency-based or pseudo-label components are often integrated into these hybrid pipelines.

topics.title: Semi-supervised and self-supervised integration
topics.description: The table highlights methods that integrate semi-supervised learning (e.g., pseudo-labeling) and self-supervised learning (SSL) into deep active learning workflows. SSL signals—such as the loss of a pretext task—are used as additional metrics to guide selection, while pseudo-labeling extends supervision to unlabeled data during training between acquisition steps. These techniques aim to exploit the large unlabeled pool more fully, reducing annotation requirements while maintaining performance. Their presence is indicated in the 'SemiSL' and 'SelfSL' columns with entries like 'Pseudo-label' and 'Self-supervised Learning / Loss of Pretext Task'.

topics.title: Dice-based performance estimation for querying
topics.description: Some active learning methods in medical image segmentation estimate sample-wise segmentation quality using Dice-based metrics to drive selection. Performance can be predicted via learnable models or surrogate estimators that approximate the Dice score without ground truth labels. Samples with lower estimated Dice (i.e., poorer expected performance) are prioritized for annotation, directly linking the acquisition function to the target evaluation metric. This approach reframes uncertainty as expected task performance rather than purely probabilistic uncertainty.

topics.title: Cosine similarity-driven query selection
topics.description: Cosine similarity is used to measure angular similarity between feature embeddings of medical images or slices, guiding selection of samples that are dissimilar from already labeled ones. In active learning, minimizing cosine similarity to labeled examples promotes diversity and exploration of underrepresented regions of feature space. This is often combined with other criteria, such as coverage or clustering, to form a more robust selection strategy.

topics.title: Saliency-guided graph-based Top-k querying
topics.description: This topic combines saliency maps with graph-based methods and Top-k selection criteria. Saliency maps highlight important regions in medical images, which are then integrated into a graph representation to prioritize structurally and diagnostically relevant samples. A Top-k strategy selects the k most informative nodes, balancing local saliency and global graph structure.

topics.title: Curriculum learning with noisy sample detection
topics.description: This topic involves using curriculum learning strategies alongside noisy sample detection in deep active learning. The system orders samples from easy to hard, while simultaneously detecting and handling potentially noisy or mislabeled images. This helps stabilize training and prevents the model from being misled by unreliable annotations, particularly common in large medical datasets.

topics.title: Top-k pseudo-label based selection
topics.description: This topic focuses on using pseudo-labels and Top-k criteria to drive sample selection. A model assigns provisional labels to unlabeled images; those with high confidence or meeting specific Top-k scoring rules are selected either for automatic inclusion or for prioritized human annotation. This leverages the model’s current knowledge to expand training data more efficiently.

topics.title: Multi-inference data disagreement metrics
topics.description: This topic describes active learning strategies based on multiple inferences and data disagreement. The same image is evaluated multiple times (e.g., via augmentations or stochastic forward passes), and disagreement is quantified using metrics like cross-entropy and variance across predictions. Images with the largest disagreement are selected, as they indicate regions of model uncertainty and potential informational gain.

topics.title: Single-model uncertainty scoring heuristics
topics.description: Some surveyed approaches rely on single-model predictions and compute heuristic uncertainty scores directly from output probabilities. Examples include Best-versus-Second-Best (BvSB) margins and the distance of predicted probabilities to 0.5 as measures of classifier ambiguity. These lightweight metrics avoid ensemble overhead while still providing guidance for query selection.

topics.title: Self-supervised and pseudo-label signals for querying
topics.description: Some methods integrate self-supervised or pseudo-label signals to guide active sample selection. One approach uses the loss from self-supervised pretext tasks as an acquisition metric, assuming higher pretext loss indicates underrepresented or hard samples. Others exploit consistency and pseudo-label quality, where samples with unstable or unreliable pseudo-labels under augmentations or clustering are prioritized for annotation.

topics.title: Discrepancy-based semantic and distinctive scoring
topics.description: The method leverages discrepancy-based measures using semantic and distinctive scores to guide active learning. These scores quantify how much samples differ in feature/semantic space, helping identify informative unlabeled instances. This is combined with a hybrid fusion strategy and disagreement among classifiers to prioritize samples. A Top-k selection mechanism is applied to choose the most informative examples.

topics.title: Confidence-based routing to active learning
topics.description: Samples for which the model’s prediction confidence falls below a threshold are diverted from semi-supervised training to active learning. These uncertain instances are then considered for expert annotation, ensuring labeling resources focus on the most ambiguous cases. This mechanism tightly couples confidence estimation with the active learning loop.

topics.title: Balanced uncertainty and adversarial instability selection
topics.description: Two specialized selectors are used to choose unlabeled samples for oracle annotation: a balanced uncertainty selector and an adversarial instability selector. The balanced uncertainty selector aims to pick samples that are both uncertain and class-balanced, while the adversarial instability selector targets instances whose predictions are unstable under adversarial perturbations. This integrates model uncertainty and adversarial robustness into the active learning criterion.

topics.title: Dataset size limits semi-supervised AL
topics.description: Semi-supervised learning combined with active learning can be successful, but its effectiveness is restricted by the overall dataset size, which is often small in medical imaging. This limitation reduces the potential gains from leveraging unlabeled data and constrains model performance improvements. The text highlights that medical image datasets are typically relatively small compared to other domains, exacerbating this issue.

topics.title: Self-supervised learning on raw medical images
topics.description: Self-supervised learning is proposed as a way to exploit the large quantities of raw, unlabeled medical images stored in hospital information systems. The core idea is to use the data itself to define pretext tasks and supervision signals, enabling pre-training on large unlabeled datasets. This approach aims to mine hidden information from these images without requiring human annotation.

topics.title: Combining active learning with self-supervision
topics.description: The section proposes integrating active learning strategies with self-supervised learning to achieve higher annotation efficiency than random sampling. Active learning would guide which samples to label on top of a self-supervised pre-trained backbone, aiming to maximize performance gains per labeled example. This combination targets more efficient use of expert annotations in medical imaging tasks.

topics.title: Supervised pre-trained models for cold-start AL
topics.description: Early cold-start solutions leverage fully supervised models pre-trained on large datasets such as ImageNet to guide initial sample selection in medical imaging tasks. Zhou et al. combine entropy and disagreement as informativeness metrics, where disagreement is quantified as the KL divergence between prediction probabilities of different patches from the same sample. Randomness is added to balance exploration and exploitation in the selection strategy. Experiments on colonoscopy and CT pulmonary embolism datasets show superior performance over competing methods under cold-start conditions.

topics.title: CALR and BIRCH-based clustering selection
topics.description: CALR uses features from a contrastive learning-based extractor and applies BIRCH clustering to group unlabeled samples for initial labeling in cold-start AL. Within each cluster, it selects samples with maximum information density, aiming to capture representative and informative points. BIRCH is chosen over k-Means because it is less sensitive to outliers and can better identify noisy samples, improving robustness of the initial labeled set. This method exemplifies clustering-driven selection on self-supervised features under cold-start constraints.

topics.title: Graph-based greedy initial sample selection
topics.description: A graph-based greedy algorithm is proposed by Yehuda et al. to choose optimal initial samples using self-supervised feature representations. Samples are modeled as nodes in a graph, with edges reflecting similarity, and a greedy procedure selects a subset that optimizes criteria such as coverage or diversity. This approach seeks to systematically balance representativeness and redundancy in the initial labeled pool. It exemplifies combinatorial optimization applied to cold-start AL using unsupervised embeddings.

topics.title: Contrastive-loss based cold-start AL
topics.description: Chen et al. (2023b) use the loss from momentum contrastive learning to address the cold-start problem in active learning for medical image analysis. They assume that higher contrastive losses indicate samples more representative of the underlying data distribution. Unlabeled data are clustered with k-Means, and within each cluster the samples with the highest contrastive loss are selected for annotation, which helps mitigate class imbalance and improve anomaly detection when few labeled samples are available. The approach is validated on PathMNIST, OrganMNIST, and BloodMNIST datasets.

topics.title: One-bit annotation with contrastive AL
topics.description: Zhang et al. (2022b) propose an active learning setting where oracles provide only a one-bit feedback indicating whether a prediction is correct, instead of a full class label. Contrastive learning is then used to pull representations of correctly predicted samples closer and push those of incorrectly predicted samples away from their predicted class representations. This design reduces annotation complexity while still improving model performance, outperforming other active learning baselines in terms of bit information efficiency.

topics.title: Contrastive AL for class mismatch filtering
topics.description: Du et al. (2021, 2022) integrate contrastive learning into active learning to handle class distribution mismatch, where unlabeled data may contain samples outside the labeled dataset’s class distribution. By carefully defining negative samples in the contrastive loss, their method filters out mismatched-class samples and emphasizes informative in-distribution samples for querying. The extended work adds theoretical analysis, more experiments, and incorporates existing label information into the framework to strengthen its practical effectiveness.

topics.title: Redundancy in Full-Image Annotation
topics.description: In fine-grained medical imaging tasks like segmentation and detection, labeling entire images can be redundant and waste annotation budget. Large, easily segmented organs (e.g., liver, spleen) do not require dense labeling to improve model performance. In contrast, small, hard-to-segment organs such as the esophagus and adrenal glands would benefit more from focused annotation. This highlights the mismatch between uniform full-image labeling and the heterogeneous difficulty across anatomical structures.

topics.title: Combining Uncertainty and Annotation Cost
topics.description: Some patch-selection strategies jointly optimize for both information gain and labeling effort by combining uncertainty with estimated annotation cost. The learner prioritizes patches that are not only uncertain but also cheaper or faster to annotate, balancing performance improvements against human workload. This leads to more cost-effective active learning compared to uncertainty-only selection.

topics.title: Uncertainty Sampling with Latent-Space Mixup
topics.description: In retinal vessel segmentation, patches with the highest predictive uncertainty are queried for annotation, focusing expert effort on the hardest regions. Latent-space mixup is then applied between labeled and unlabeled samples to encourage linear relationships in the feature space, effectively regularizing the model. This exploits unlabeled patches to enhance generalization and improve performance under limited annotations.

topics.title: Spatial Confidence Aggregation over Patches
topics.description: For whole-slide pathology images, local patch confidences can be spatially aggregated to derive region-level uncertainty. Each slide is split into patches, per-patch confidence (e.g., maximum predictive probability) is computed, and a 5×5 mean filter aggregates neighboring confidences into a regional metric. Regions corresponding to low aggregated confidence (high uncertainty) are then prioritized for annotation, capturing spatial context rather than treating patches independently.

topics.title: Adaptive Non-Square Patch Selection
