However, its performance is highly sensitive to hyper-parameters of the LossNet component, particularly the feature size determined by the fully connected layer, and it fails on more complex datasets like EMNIST and TinyImageNet despite extensive tuning. The difficulty is linked to predicting target loss in settings with many categories, but this can be mitigated by using a pre-trained backbone (e.g., pre-trained ResNet18), which provides better feature representations and substantially improves LPL’s effectiveness.

topics.title: WAAL limitations on many-class datasets
topics.description: Weighted Adversarial Active Learning (WAAL) exhibits similar failure patterns to LPL on datasets with many categories, such as EMNIST and TinyImageNet. The method struggles to extract sufficiently diversified features in these high-class-count settings, leading to degraded performance. The comparison on CIFAR100 further supports the explanation that dataset category complexity can hinder WAAL’s ability to construct effective representations.

topics.title: Marginal benefit and high cost of AdvBIM
topics.description: AdvBIM augments DAL training with adversarial samples, computed via an adversarial distance r for each unlabeled sample at every iteration, but does not achieve performance gains comparable to LPL. Because the adversarial examples are crafted using the current backbone model, the additional robustness they provide is limited, resulting in only marginal improvements. The method is extremely time-consuming and computationally prohibitive, to the point that experiments on large datasets like EMNIST and TinyImageNet could not be completed.

topics.title: WAAL robustness to epochs and diversity modeling
topics.description: In the ablation study, WAAL consistently outperforms Entropy and BADGE and is notably less sensitive to the number of training epochs, achieving stable AUBC (around 0.825) even with as few as 5 epochs and showing little change up to 30 epochs. The robustness is attributed to WAAL’s explicit modeling of diversity among samples and its use of unlabeled data to build better representations, which reduces data bias. This property is particularly attractive for DAL, as effective performance can be maintained with fewer training epochs, saving computation time.

topics.title: Group-wise accuracy metrics on Waterbird
topics.description: The Waterbird dataset is partitioned into four groups based on bird type and background: {(waterbird, water), (waterbird, land), (landbird, land), (landbird, water)}. Besides overall accuracy, the study reports mismatch accuracy (for the spurious/background-mismatched groups {(waterbird, land), (landbird, water)}) and worst-group accuracy (the minimum accuracy among all four groups). These metrics quantify performance under distribution shift and group imbalance, revealing robustness and fairness properties of DAL methods.

topics.title: Enhancing techniques in LPL and WAAL
topics.description: LPL and WAAL use additional enhancing mechanisms—loss prediction and leveraging unlabeled-data information—to guide query selection in deep active learning. On Waterbird without pretraining, these techniques can outperform standard uncertainty or clustering-based methods in overall accuracy by extracting more informative signals from the data. However, both methods struggle on the worst group under both pretraining regimes, likely because group imbalance biases loss prediction and unlabeled-data statistics, harming performance on minority or hardest subgroups.

topics.title: Enhancement Methods Beyond Acquisition Functions
topics.description: The text discusses the limited gains from solely designing new acquisition functions and highlights alternative enhancement strategies such as learning loss prediction (LPL) and enlarging batch size per acquisition round. It notes that these methods do not generalize well across all tasks and stresses the need for more universal enhancement approaches. Cluster-Margin is cited as a method that scales active learning to very large batch sizes (100K–1M), illustrating both progress and the difficulty of surpassing such scalability.

topics.title: Integrating DAL with Semi- and Self-Supervision
topics.description: There is a research trend toward combining deep active learning (DAL) with semi-supervised and self-supervised learning (S4L) to better exploit unlabeled data. Work by Chan et al. suggests that a significant portion of DAL's benefits can be absorbed by strong S4L techniques, based on extensive empirical comparisons. A key future direction is to design DAL pipelines that more effectively leverage unlabeled data in very low-label regimes.

topics.title: Domain-Specific DAL in Autonomous Driving and Medicine
topics.description: DAL is proposed as a promising tool for data-insufficient, safety-critical domains such as autonomous driving and medical image analysis. In autonomous driving, active learning for nighttime detection of pedestrians and bicycles significantly improved mean average precision compared to manually selected training data. In medical imaging, the prevalence of rare but critical diseases and the high cost of expert annotation make class imbalance and rare-class emphasis central design concerns for DAL strategies. The text underscores that each domain has distinct requirements, motivating task- and domain-specific DAL research.

topics.title: Labeling requirements for deep learning
topics.description: Due to their complex architectures and high capacity, deep learning models require large quantities of labeled samples for effective training. The availability of large-scale annotated datasets has therefore become a key enabler for DL performance. This creates a dependency between DL success and the cost and effort of obtaining high-quality labeled data.

topics.title: Historical evolution of deep learning
topics.description: This topic covers the chronological development of deep learning models from early neural network formulations to modern deep architectures. It mentions the McCulloch-Pitts model, the introduction of backpropagation, the first RNNs, LeNet as an early DNN, Deep Belief Networks, and AlexNet’s breakthrough performance on ImageNet. It highlights how improvements in computing power and architectures led to superior results across visual, language, and speech tasks.

topics.title: Data greed and labeling bottlenecks in DL
topics.description: The text emphasizes that DL’s recent breakthroughs depend heavily on massive labeled datasets, making it highly data-greedy. It explains that while unlabeled data are easy to obtain, manual annotation is costly, especially in expert domains such as COVID-19 lung lesion labeling, medical imaging, speech recognition, remote sensing, robotics, and specialized NLP tasks. This creates a practical bottleneck and motivates methods that maximize performance gains from a small number of labeled samples.

topics.title: Active learning query scenario paradigms
topics.description: The section categorizes AL approaches by application scenario into membership query synthesis, stream-based selective sampling, and pool-based active learning. Membership query synthesis allows the learner to query labels for any point in input space, including synthetically generated samples. Stream-based selective sampling decides online for each incoming sample whether to query its label, whereas pool-based methods evaluate the entire unlabeled pool and select the best samples based on ranking. These paradigms define how and when label queries are made in practice.

topics.title: Convolutional Neural Network as baseline DL
topics.description: The section references a convolutional neural network (CNN) as a common deep learning model used as the baseline architecture when comparing DL, AL, and DeepAL. CNNs serve as the feature extractor and prediction model whose parameters are later adapted within the active learning process.

topics.title: Device resource constraints and AL strategy
topics.description: The text contrasts mobile devices, which require timeliness and have limited storage and computation, with larger devices that have ample resources. It notes that the commonly used pool-based sampling strategy in AL research is more suitable for large, resource-rich devices, implying that alternative strategies may be needed for constrained mobile platforms.

topics.title: Label budget and stopping conditions
topics.description: Both the pool-based AL cycle and the DeepAL workflow are described as iterative processes that terminate when a label budget is exhausted or when predefined stopping conditions are satisfied. This highlights the importance of explicitly modeling annotation cost (budget) and designing stopping strategies to decide when further querying is no longer beneficial.

topics.title: Importance of AL query rule design
topics.description: Active learning (AL) begins from unlabeled datasets and relies on carefully designed query rules to select the most informative samples for labeling. These rules aim to minimize labeling cost while maximizing model performance. Consequently, the quality and design of query rules are central to the overall effectiveness of AL methods, and there is extensive research focused on this aspect.

topics.title: Scalability to high-dimensional data
topics.description: Active learning methods face significant challenges when applied to high-dimensional data such as images, text, and video. Many existing approaches were developed and evaluated primarily on low-dimensional problems, limiting their direct applicability to complex, real-world domains. This scalability issue constrains the broader deployment of traditional AL techniques in modern deep learning settings.

topics.title: Feature extraction limitations in AL
topics.description: Traditional active learning typically operates on pre-extracted features and lacks the capability to learn feature representations jointly with querying. In contrast, deep learning models are designed, either manually or automatically, to perform high-performance feature extraction as part of end-to-end training. This gap means that classical AL frameworks often cannot fully exploit the representational power of deep models without additional integration mechanisms.

topics.title: Model uncertainty and overconfident softmax
topics.description: Uncertainty-based query strategies are central in Active Learning, but directly applying them to Deep Learning is problematic because DL models tend to be overconfident. The softmax output (Softmax Response, SR) is an unreliable confidence measure and can perform worse than random sampling when used for sample selection. This highlights a core challenge in using standard DL outputs for AL uncertainty estimation.

topics.title: Batch Query Strategies for Deep AL
topics.description: Empirical work shows that traditional heuristic query strategies designed for one-by-one selection may fail when applied to deep learning in batch settings. Consequently, many researchers develop batch query methods that simultaneously optimize the information content and diversity of selected samples, better matching the training dynamics of deep models.

topics.title: Decomposition of DeepAL research components
topics.description: The DeepAL framework is decomposed into two core parts: active learning (AL) query strategies applied to the unlabeled dataset, and deep learning (DL) model training methods. Additional research axes include methods for improving model generalization and strategies for deciding when to stop querying. This decomposition structures the subsequent survey sections that analyze each component systematically.

topics.title: Pool-based DeepAL optimization formulation
topics.description: In the pool-based setting, DeepAL defines an unlabeled dataset Uₙ with sample space X, label space Y, and joint distribution P(x, y), and a current labeled set Lₘ. Using a deep model f: X → Y, the goal is to design a query strategy Q that selects Lₘ ⊆ Uₙ to minimize the expected loss E(x,y)[ℓ(f(x), y)] while keeping m ≪ n. This formalizes DeepAL as choosing a minimal labeled subset that achieves a desired accuracy, highlighting that the query strategy Q is central to reducing labeling cost.

topics.title: Acquisition function for batch selection
topics.description: Within BMDAL, the acquisition function a_batch(B, f_θ(L)) evaluates a candidate batch B of unlabeled samples given the current labeled training set L (also denoted D_train) and model f_θ. The optimal batch B* is defined as the subset of U that maximizes this acquisition score, formalizing batch selection as an arg max optimization over all possible subsets. This provides a general mathematical template under which specific batch criteria, such as uncertainty or diversity, can be instantiated.

topics.title: Redundancy issue in independent batch selection
topics.description: Constructing batches by independently selecting top-scoring samples can yield sets of highly similar, information-rich points that provide redundant information to the model. Such redundancy wastes labeling resources and does not significantly improve the model’s understanding of the data distribution. This motivates more sophisticated batch acquisition strategies that explicitly account for relationships and diversity among samples, beyond independent uncertainty scores.

topics.title: Exploration-P: balancing uncertainty and redundancy
topics.description: Exploration-P addresses limitations of early BMAL methods that over-rely on similarity and exploitation of boundary samples, leading to batches that poorly represent the feature-space distribution. It uses a deep neural network to learn feature representations, computes sample uncertainty via entropy, and aggregates uncertainty over a selected set S as E(S) = Σ E(xᵢ). Redundancy within S is quantified by R(S), a sum of pairwise similarities Sim(xᵢ, xⱼ) based on learned features and a similarity matrix M. The final objective I(S) = E(S) − α/|S|·R(S) promotes batches with high total uncertainty and low redundancy, explicitly trading off exploration and exploitation.

topics.title: Hybrid AL queries: uncertainty and diversity
topics.description: The section discusses hybrid active learning query strategies that explicitly weight uncertainty and redundancy/diversity within a mini-batch. A scalar α is introduced to balance these components, so that selected samples are both informative (high uncertainty) and non-redundant (diverse). This hybridization aims to improve the effectiveness of batch selection compared to using either criterion alone.

topics.title: Diverse Mini-Batch Active Learning (DMBAL)
topics.description: DMBAL augments K-means-based selection by weighting cluster optimization with sample informativeness, jointly considering information volume and diversity under a mini-batch query setting. It is designed to scale from generalized linear models to deep learning, enhancing both scalability and batch diversity. The method focuses on constructing diverse yet informative mini-batches for labeling.

topics.title: Dataset-dependent suitability of AL strategies
topics.description: The text highlights that diversity-based and uncertainty-based query strategies do not suit all datasets equally, and their effectiveness depends on dataset statistics. Diversity-based methods perform better with richer category content and larger batch sizes, whereas uncertainty-based methods are preferable for smaller batches and less rich content. In BMAL settings with unfamiliar, potentially unstructured data, it is hard to pre-select the appropriate strategy.

topics.title: Practical dominance of uncertainty-based querying
topics.description: Despite the superior performance of hybrid strategies, the text notes that uncertainty-based active learning remains widely used in deep learning. This is primarily because uncertainty measures integrate conveniently with softmax output layers, simplifying implementation. Thus, practical considerations still favor pure uncertainty sampling in many deep AL systems.

topics.title: Bayesian neural network formulation for AL
topics.description: The section formalizes deep Bayesian active learning by defining a probabilistic neural network with parameters θ having a prior p(θ), usually Gaussian, and a softmax likelihood p(y=c|x,θ). It introduces the posterior p(θ|X,Y) via Bayes’ rule and the predictive distribution for a new point as an expectation over this posterior. This Bayesian formulation underpins uncertainty-aware acquisition functions in deep models.

topics.title: DBAL with BCNNs and MC-dropout
topics.description: DBAL [72] combines Bayesian Convolutional Neural Networks with active learning, adapting the BALD acquisition function to high-dimensional deep learning settings. It models CNN weights with Gaussian priors and employs variational inference to approximate the posterior, while in practice MC-dropout is often used as a low-cost stochastic regularization technique to draw posterior samples. MC-dropout has been shown to be equivalent to variational inference in this context and yields good empirical performance on real datasets.

topics.title: Limitations and critiques of DBAL methods
topics.description: The text reports several critiques of DBAL-style approaches. A core-set method argues DBAL is unsuitable for large datasets due to its need for batch sampling, and another analysis claims that using dropout at test time yields performance similar to standard neural network softmax responses as uncertainty measures. Furthermore, DEBAL attributes DBAL’s overconfident predictions to pattern collapse in variational inference, motivating ensemble-based Bayesian active learning variants.

topics.title: ACS-FW Bayesian core-set optimization
topics.description: ACS-FW (Active Bayesian CoreSets with Frank-Wolfe optimization) reconstructs the batch structure in active learning to optimize a sparse subset that approximates the log-posterior of the full dataset. It uses the Frank–Wolfe algorithm, together with random projections, to select a Bayesian core set that scales to large data while retaining posterior fidelity. Compared with entropy- and BALD-based strategies, ACS-FW achieves better coverage of the overall data manifold.

topics.title: Deep probabilistic ensembles for DBAL
topics.description: Deep Probabilistic Ensembles (DPEs) use a regularized ensemble of deep networks to approximate a deep Bayesian neural network. The method maintains multiple models whose diversity is controlled by regularization, and uses their predictive variability as a proxy for Bayesian uncertainty. DPEs are evaluated on large-scale visual active learning experiments to assess their classification performance and usefulness as uncertainty estimators.

topics.title: ActiveLink for KG link prediction
topics.description: ActiveLink is a deep active learning framework for link prediction in knowledge graphs that adopts a Bayesian perspective on neural link predictors. It extends uncertainty sampling by exploiting the structural information of the knowledge graph, yielding a task-specific acquisition function. This method targets efficient querying in relational domains where links (triples) rather than independent instances are labeled.

topics.title: Meta-learning-based unbiased incremental training
topics.description: ActiveLink addresses the bias introduced by naive incremental training in iterative active learning, where retraining from scratch is costly and simple fine-tuning overweights either new or early-selected data. In each AL iteration, it updates model parameters with newly selected samples and then approximates a meta-objective that anticipates future prediction performance based on previously selected samples. This meta-learning-based procedure balances the influence of new and past data, providing an approximately unbiased estimate of model parameters over the evolving labeled set.

topics.title: Core-set based density methods and FF-Active
topics.description: Density-based methods in deep active learning focus on selecting a core set of points that represents the overall data distribution, thereby reducing labeling cost while preserving coverage of the feature space. FF-Active implements this idea by performing farthest-first traversal in the neural activation space to pick diverse points, and is related to Exploration-P which uses early-stage random queries to improve exploration and avoid low-diversity traps. These approaches emphasize representativeness and diversity of the selected subset rather than pure uncertainty.

topics.title: Discriminative Active Learning with density awareness
topics.description: Discriminative Active Learning (DAL) also frames active learning as a binary classification problem between labeled and unlabeled data, but explicitly aims to make the two sets indistinguishable. By sampling from the unlabeled pool in proportion to data density, DAL avoids overfocusing on sparse regions and instead reflects the true distribution more faithfully. The approach is conceptually general and can be transferred beyond standard classification tasks to other problem types.

topics.title: Dataset characteristics, gradient analysis, and ensembles
topics.description: Gradient Analysis (GA) evaluates the relative importance of images in common datasets and serves as a general tool for understanding diversity and utility of training examples. Its findings show that some datasets exhibit nearly uniform sample importance, making small subsampling ineffective and cautioning against blindly using tiny sub-datasets in active learning. Additionally, comparative studies indicate that ensemble-based active learning can better handle class imbalance and produce more calibrated uncertainty estimates than Monte Carlo dropout–based Bayesian methods or density-based approaches.

topics.title: Standard Active Learning Pipeline Structure
topics.description: The standard AL pipeline is decomposed into three components: an oracle providing labeled data, a predictor (e.g., a Bayesian Neural Network) that learns from labeled data and outputs predictive uncertainty, and a guide that uses a fixed, hard-coded acquisition function. The acquisition function selects the next unlabeled sample to query, and this process repeats in cycles. This structure highlights the rigidity of traditional acquisition functions compared to adaptive approaches.

topics.title: Reinforced Active Learning (RAL) with Policy BNN
topics.description: RAL replaces the fixed acquisition function in standard AL with a Bayesian policy network that learns a sampling policy via reinforcement learning. A BNN predictor produces probabilistic outputs, which are aggregated into a comprehensive probability distribution and passed to a BNN probabilistic policy network. This policy network receives oracle feedback each labeling round and updates the acquisition function to better select optimal query points for the current dataset.

topics.title: Deep Reinforcement Active Learning for Person Re-ID
topics.description: DRAL extends the reinforcement learning-based query strategy to the person re-identification task using a deep reinforcement active learning framework. For each query anchor (probe), an agent sequentially selects candidate instances from a gallery pool to be labeled by the oracle with binary feedback (positive/negative). The state encodes similarity relationships among instances, and rewards derived from oracle feedback guide the agent to adjust its querying policy to obtain high-quality samples.

topics.title: Active-iNAS: Joint Active Learning and NAS
topics.description: Active-iNAS challenges the assumption that a suitable deep learning model architecture is fixed prior to active learning and focuses on jointly optimizing both the model and the query strategy. It uses neural architecture search (NAS) to dynamically explore effective model architectures while actively selecting informative samples. This integration aims to find architectures that are particularly well-suited to the evolving labeled set in DeepAL, instead of relying on a predesigned model.

topics.title: SSAL multi-phase training across AL cycles
topics.description: SSAL proposes a semi-supervised active learning regime that orchestrates unsupervised, supervised, and semi-supervised training phases across AL iterations to maximize use of available data without increasing labeling cost. Before AL begins, labeled and unlabeled data are used for unsupervised pretraining; in each AL cycle, the model is first trained in a supervised manner on labeled data and then refined via semi-supervised learning on all data. This constitutes a new training methodology where different learning paradigms are systematically combined within the AL loop.

topics.title: Training methods and data utilization
topics.description: This topic highlights that exploring model training procedures and data utilization techniques in Deep Active Learning (DeepAL) can yield performance gains larger than merely changing query strategies. By better exploiting existing labeled and unlabeled data without increasing labeling cost, these methods mitigate the issue of having too few actively queried samples to effectively update deep models. It emphasizes optimizing how data is used in training rather than only focusing on which data to query.

topics.title: Two-stage uncertainty in deep models
topics.description: This topic explains why traditional uncertainty-based query strategies from shallow models are not directly applicable to deep learning models. A deep model is conceptualized as comprising a feature extraction stage and a task learning stage, each contributing its own uncertainty. Relying solely on the last-layer output underestimates the true predictive uncertainty, because it ignores uncertainty arising in earlier feature representations. The section introduces this two-stage uncertainty perspective, illustrated conceptually in Fig. 8.

topics.title: AL-MV multiview layer-based uncertainty
topics.description: AL-MV (Active Learning with Multiple Views) treats outputs from different hidden layers of a CNN as distinct views of the data. It explicitly models uncertainty at both the feature extraction and task learning stages by considering uncertainties from multiple intermediate layers. The algorithm adaptively weights the uncertainty from each layer to obtain a more accurate overall uncertainty estimate for sampling decisions. This multiview aggregation aims to improve query quality compared with using only the final layer.

topics.title: Multilevel U-Net DeepAL for segmentation
topics.description: This topic describes a Deep Active Learning framework for finger bone segmentation built on Deeply Supervised U-Net. It uses outputs from multiple segmentation hidden layers together with the final layer output as inputs to the active learning component. These multilevel predictions are integrated to evaluate the 'information size' or informativeness of each sample for querying. By leveraging deep supervision and multi-scale features, the method refines uncertainty estimation for medical image segmentation tasks.

topics.title: Stabilizing Predictions (SP) stopping strategy
topics.description: The SP method proposes an AL stopping strategy based on prediction stability over an unlabeled 'stop set' drawn from the pool. At each iteration, the model’s predictions on this stop set are monitored, and querying stops once these predictions stabilize, under the assumption that a well-trained model exhibits stable outputs. This approach avoids extra annotation costs because the stop set remains unlabeled, aligning with the budget-conscious goals of active learning. Although introduced for AL in general, it is also applicable to DeepAL.

topics.title: Query strategies for model uncertainty
topics.description: To address uncertainty in deep models within DeepAL, the survey highlights several query strategy families: uncertainty-based and hybrid methods, Deep Bayesian Active Learning (DBAL), and density-based techniques. These approaches aim to select informative samples by leveraging confidence scores, Bayesian uncertainty estimates, and data distribution structure. The table cites multiple works under each category, reflecting active research on optimizing query policies.

topics.title: AL criteria integrated into deep belief networks
topics.description: One line of work integrates active learning criteria directly into deep belief networks (DBNs) for classification. The combined system is then evaluated on various real uni-modal and multi-modal datasets, exploring how AL-driven sample selection interacts with DBN feature learning. This represents an early example of fusing deep generative models with AL strategies.

topics.title: Active transfer learning for hyperspectral images
topics.description: Subsequent work on HSI classification combines active learning with transfer learning to mitigate cross-domain disparities. One approach uses AL to initialize the HSI labeling process and then performs transfer learning, recommending the construction and linking of higher-level features between source and target HSI data. Another proposes a unified deep network with active transfer learning to achieve strong classification performance with fewer labeled samples.

topics.title: Committee-based DeepAL for object detection
topics.description: A DeepAL framework for object detection employs a layered architecture as a 'query by committee' to select images for annotation. The method also adopts an exploration–exploitation trade-off strategy, balancing querying highly uncertain examples with exploring diverse regions of the data space. This reduces labeling costs while training robust object detectors for domains such as autonomous driving and other real-world applications.

topics.title: Transfer learning and AL for wildlife monitoring
topics.description: Deep neural networks are combined with transfer learning and active learning to identify and count species in camera trap imagery. For UAV-based wildlife detection, transfer sampling (TS) is introduced to locate corresponding regions between source and target datasets, enabling more effective domain transfer. Active sampling focuses labeling on informative or transferable regions, improving detector reusability across different environments while conserving annotation effort.

topics.title: Self-paced DeepAL for pulmonary and bone segmentation
topics.description: DASL introduces Nodules R-CNN for pulmonary nodule segmentation, generating segmentation masks as examples and combining active learning with self-paced learning (SPL) to progressively select informative yet learnable samples, thus reducing labeling effort. A related Nodule-plus Region-based CNN extends this idea to 3D CT nodule detection and segmentation using a deep self-paced active learning (DSAL) strategy that leverages both labeled and unlabeled data. Deep-supervised active learning for finger bone segmentation iteratively fine-tunes the model and uses intermediate hidden-layer outputs as selection criteria, achieving comparable segmentation quality to full annotation with fewer labeled samples.

topics.title: Active learning for visual imitation navigation
topics.description: In navigation tasks, imitation learning uses first-person visual observations and teacher actions to train a student agent to predict appropriate actions in its own environment. The system employs deep convolutional networks for feature extraction and imitation policy learning, and then integrates active learning to query additional samples where the model’s confidence is low. By selectively adding these uncertain examples to the training set, the navigation strategy is substantially improved using relatively few labeled demonstrations.

topics.title: Curriculum-based active learning for translation
topics.description: A curriculum learning framework related to active learning controls which training samples are presented to a machine translation model over time. It dynamically chooses examples based on the estimated difficulty of each sample and the current competence of the model, effectively shaping the learning schedule. This adaptive curriculum improves training efficiency and yields notable accuracy gains, and its underlying idea informs richer sample selection strategies in DeepAL.

topics.title: Addressing Sampling Bias in Active Text Classification
topics.description: [166] focuses on the sampling bias problem that arises in deep active text classification, where iterative selection can skew the labeled set. Using large-scale text corpora from [250], the work studies how AL strategies affect data distribution and classification performance. The methods generally outperform traditional AL baselines, indicating better handling of sampling bias in deep settings.

topics.title: Active Deep Networks with RBMs for Sentiment
topics.description: [257] builds an Active Deep Network (ADN) using Restricted Boltzmann Machines to integrate unsupervised pretraining on both labeled and unlabeled data. Within a semi-supervised framework, active learning is used to jointly select labeled data and refine the classifier, exploiting large pools of unlabeled text. This yields competitive performance on sentiment classification by improving generalization with minimal labels.

topics.title: DeepAL for News Accuracy Detection
topics.description: [22] proposes a human-computer collaborative system for detecting misleading or false news content using deep active learning. The model operates with 1–2 orders of magnitude fewer labeled samples than fully supervised baselines, yet improves detection performance. Reduced annotation needs accelerate convergence and yield about 25% average performance gains in news accuracy detection.

topics.title: ALPNN for EEG Report Concept Extraction
topics.description: [141] introduces an Active Learning Policy Neural Network (ALPNN) to identify concepts and relationships in large collections of EEG (electroencephalogram) reports. The model actively selects which samples to annotate, improving extraction of clinical knowledge from semi-structured text. This supports scalable construction of clinical knowledge bases from EEG narratives.

topics.title: Online Active Learning for Open-Domain Dialogue
topics.description: [13] applies an online AL strategy to deep models for open-domain dialogue systems that interact with real users. The system incrementally learns from user feedback in each dialogue round, querying for information when most beneficial. This setup enables continual improvement of conversational quality with limited annotation overhead.

topics.title: Hidden-Space Uncertainty for VQA Active Learning
topics.description: [104] observes that conventional AL strategies, which estimate uncertainty in the output space, can fail on tasks like Visual Question Answering (VQA) where multiple phrasings are correct. Output-based uncertainty can be overestimated, sometimes performing worse than random sampling. To address this, [104] proposes measuring uncertainty in the model’s hidden representation space, better handling paraphrasing and improving AL effectiveness for VQA generation.

topics.title: MLFS: DeepAL for Gene and miRNA Selection
topics.description: MLFS (Multi-Level Feature Selection) [101] integrates deep learning and active learning to select genes and miRNAs based on expression profiles. The method performs multi-level feature selection while incorporating known biological relationships between miRNAs and genes. It is applied to miRNA expansion tasks, aiming to identify informative molecular features with fewer labeled experiments.

topics.title: Risk-Aware DeepAL for Robot Trajectories
topics.description: [8] introduces a risk-aware resampling technique that leverages active learning with deep models and existing solvers to optimize robot trajectories, particularly for collision avoidance in environments with moving obstacles. This approach reduces the cost of failure by focusing data collection on risky regions of the state space and is validated on a real nano-quadcopter. [258] further proposes an active trajectory generation framework for training a DNN-based inverse dynamics model, systematically designing informative trajectories for control learning.

topics.title: DALAUP for Anchor User Prediction
topics.description: DALAUP (Deep Active Learning for Anchor User Prediction) [37] presents a DeepAL framework for identifying anchor users in social networks. By actively selecting which users to label, the method reduces annotation cost while improving prediction accuracy for anchor users, who often link different platforms or communities. This supports more efficient social network analysis under label scarcity.

topics.title: Early Research Stage of DeepAL
topics.description: Compared with traditional deep learning and active learning, DeepAL is characterized as being in a preliminary research stage. As a result, there are relatively few classic or foundational works, yet the paradigm is argued to have similarly broad application scenarios and practical value as standard deep learning methods.

topics.title: Taxonomy of DeepAL Applications and Datasets
topics.description: To support access to concrete use cases, the survey classifies and summarizes DeepAL application scenarios and the datasets used across related work. These classifications are detailed in another section of the paper and compiled in a summary table, enabling readers to see how DeepAL has been instantiated across different domains and data resources.

topics.title: Variability in random sampling baselines
topics.description: The performance of the random sampling baseline (RSB) in DeepAL experiments varies substantially across studies, even under seemingly identical settings. For instance, using 20% labeled CIFAR-10 data, RSB performance reported in one study is 13% higher than in another; similarly, under 40% labeled CIFAR-100 with VGG16 as feature extractor, reported results differ by 8%. These discrepancies complicate fair comparison of DeepAL methods and highlight sensitivity to experimental choices.

topics.title: Conflicting findings on AL strategies
topics.description: Studies report conflicting conclusions regarding the relative effectiveness of diversity-based, uncertainty-based, and random sampling strategies in DeepAL. Some work claims diversity-based querying consistently outperforms uncertainty-based methods and that uncertainty-based approaches can even underperform RSB, while more recent research disputes this hierarchy. This inconsistency raises questions about how robust these strategy comparisons are to datasets, architectures, and experimental setups.

topics.title: Role of ablation and transfer experiments
topics.description: Ablation studies and transfer experiments are proposed as necessary tools for understanding and validating DeepAL improvements. Ablation experiments help isolate which components or modifications are responsible for observed performance gains, while transfer experiments test whether an active learning strategy can reliably select high-value samples across different datasets. Together, these methods support more principled development and assessment of DeepAL algorithms.

topics.title: Hyperspectral image classification with DeepAL
topics.description: Deep active learning is used for classifying hyperspectral images, where each pixel contains a high-dimensional spectral signature. Datasets such as PaviaC, PaviaU, Botswana, Salinas Valley, Indian Pines, Washington DC Mall, and Urban serve as benchmarks. Query strategies aim to select the most informative pixels or regions to label, addressing the high annotation cost and spectral complexity in remote sensing imagery. Performance is typically measured by classification accuracy across land-cover or material classes versus labeling effort.

topics.title: Biomedical image classification via DeepAL
topics.description: Deep active learning is applied to biomedical image analysis tasks such as pathology slide classification, EEG-related image patterns, and other medical image recognition problems. Example datasets include Erie County, EEG recordings, BreaKHis, SVEB, and SVDB, which contain specialized medical signals or images. Because medical labels require expert annotators, DeepAL prioritizes the most informative samples to reduce the number of labeled exams or image patches needed. Evaluation often considers diagnostic accuracy and label-efficiency on clinically relevant datasets.

topics.title: DeepAL for video-based autonomous navigation
topics.description: In video processing, deep active learning is used for tasks related to autonomous navigation, where agents must interpret sequential visual or simulated sensory data. The Mash-simulator dataset is used to study how agents acquire informative experiences for navigation decisions. Query policies can prioritize trajectories or frames that improve a navigation model the most, given limited labeling or interaction budgets. This connects DeepAL with reinforcement or imitation learning in dynamic environments.

topics.title: Gene expression-based cancer analysis
topics.description: In the biomedical 'Other' category, deep active learning is used for gene expression analysis related to cancers such as breast cancer (BC), hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and lung cancer. High-dimensional gene expression profiles require expert-curated labels (e.g., cancer subtype, prognosis), making label-efficient learning crucial. DeepAL selects the most informative patient samples for genomic annotation or validation, helping build accurate predictive models with fewer labeled profiles. This supports precision medicine by focusing costly biological validation where it matters most.

topics.title: Robotics control and navigation with DeepAL
topics.description: Deep active learning is used in robotics to select informative interactions or trajectories for learning control policies. Datasets like EATG and Crazyflie 2.0 capture robotic behavior or flight data. By querying the most informative states or actions for expert feedback or labeling, robots can learn navigation and control tasks with fewer demonstrations. This ties DeepAL to sample-efficient robot learning in real-world environments.

topics.title: Social network and location intelligence
topics.description: Deep active learning is used in social network analysis leveraging data from platforms like Foursquare and Twitter. Tasks may involve location prediction, user profiling, or content categorization based on check-ins and social posts. Given the massive volume of social data, DeepAL focuses human labeling on the most informative users, posts, or locations. This supports efficient construction of models for recommendation, mobility analysis, or social behavior understanding.

topics.title: TUH EEG clinical signal dataset
topics.description: The TUH EEG corpus offers large-scale electroencephalogram recordings, often with clinical labels such as seizure events or other neurological conditions. In deep active learning, this dataset underpins studies where models query the most informative EEG segments for expert annotation to reduce labeling costs in medical time-series analysis.

topics.title: Bitcraze robotics and drone platform
topics.description: Bitcraze provides small aerial robots and related hardware/software platforms that can be used to collect embodied sensory data (e.g., vision, IMU) in robotics experiments. Within deep active learning scenarios, such platforms enable interactive data acquisition, where the robot’s actions can be driven by an active learning policy to gather the most informative observations.

topics.title: Non-specific application scenarios category
topics.description: The mention of 'Non-specific application scenarios' suggests a category of datasets or use cases that do not fit neatly into a single, clearly defined application domain. These scenarios are relevant in deep active learning when methods are evaluated across heterogeneous tasks, emphasizing generality of query strategies rather than domain-specific optimization.

topics.title: Hybrid supervised and unsupervised training schemes
topics.description: Training optimization in deep active learning increasingly focuses on integrating labeled datasets, unlabeled datasets, and generated data (e.g., via GANs) within a unified training scheme. This includes hybrid training methods that combine unsupervised, semi-supervised, and supervised learning throughout the active learning cycle. Such approaches are expected to produce larger performance gains than changing the selection strategy alone, by better exploiting all available data types.

topics.title: Leveraging unlabeled and generated data
topics.description: Unlabeled and synthetically generated datasets are used to compensate for the scarcity of labeled examples in deep learning and the limited number of labeled samples selected by active learning. By exploiting these additional data sources, models can make fuller use of available information without incurring extra annotation costs. This helps mitigate the dependency of deep models on large labeled training sets.

topics.title: Limits of over-reducing labeled subsets
topics.description: The text warns against blindly striving to train models on ever smaller labeled subsets. In datasets with high content variety and many samples, the relative difference in importance between individual samples may be negligible, reducing the benefit of aggressive subset minimization. This implies that extreme reduction of labeled data can undermine performance gains expected from active learning.

topics.title: Mixed improvement strategies for DeepAL
topics.description: There is no inherent conflict between advances in query strategies, training schemes, task independence, and computational efficiency, so combining these directions into mixed improvement strategies is advocated. Such integrated approaches can jointly reduce labeling costs and broaden application scenarios for DeepAL. Nonetheless, the field is characterized as still being in its infancy, indicating substantial room for future development.

topics.title: Query Strategy Optimization in DeepAL
topics.description: This topic focuses on designing and comparing query strategies tailored to deep neural networks within active learning. It includes uncertainty-based, diversity-based, and representativeness-aware sampling methods that select the most informative unlabeled instances for annotation. The optimization problem typically trades off informativeness, redundancy, and computational cost in the context of large-scale deep models.

topics.title: Pool-based versus stream-based active learning
topics.description: Traditional pool-based active learning assumes a fixed pool of unlabeled observations from which instances are selected for labeling, a setting that may not match dynamic real-world environments. In contrast, stream-based (online) active learning continuously receives data in a stream and must decide, on arrival, whether to query each observation. This online setting allows real-time adaptation to changing data distributions but also imposes sequential decision and resource constraints.

topics.title: Survey gap in online active learning
topics.description: Existing surveys either focus on pool-based active learning or on online learning from data streams under the assumption that all labels are available. Apart from a prior review centered on fuzzy-model-based online active learning, recent developments in broader online active learning methods have not been synthesized. This creates a gap for scenarios where labels are scarce or expensive in streaming contexts, motivating the need for this survey.

topics.title: Terminology: stream-based AL vs selective sampling
topics.description: The text clarifies that some authors use a narrow definition of stream-based active learning focused purely on selecting informative stream observations for model fitting. Under this view, deciding which observations to query during prediction time is termed online selective sampling. The survey adopts a broader perspective, encompassing all methods that select informative data points to label from a data stream in an online manner.

topics.title: Keyword-based literature search strategy
topics.description: The authors describe a systematic literature search on SCOPUS and Google Scholar using a specific set of query terms related to online and stream-based active learning. The keywords include various phrasings such as “on-line active learning”, “online active learning”, “stream-based active learning”, “single pass active learning”, “online selective sampling”, “sequential selective sampling”, and combinations of “active learning” with “data stream”. This strategy is designed to capture diverse terminology used in the domain of active learning for data streams.

topics.title: Relevance screening and paper selection
topics.description: Each retrieved paper is reviewed individually to assess its relevance to online active learning. Irrelevant works are eliminated based on this screening, and some papers that lack the specified keywords but still employ online active learning methodologies or are pertinent to the discussion are manually added. This reflects a mix of automated retrieval and expert judgment in the selection process.

topics.title: Snowballing through reference analysis
topics.description: Beyond the initial keyword search, the authors extend their corpus by including related papers found in the reference lists of already reviewed strategies. This reference-based expansion aims to capture additional relevant work and provide a more complete view of the field, especially studies that might not be easily discoverable through keyword queries alone. It contributes to understanding the broader context and ‘bigger picture’ of active learning for data streams.

topics.title: Active learning scenarios in data streams
topics.description: This topic covers the different deployment scenarios in which stream-based active learning operates, such as fully supervised streams, partially labeled streams, and evolving environments with concept drift. Each scenario imposes constraints on how often labels can be queried, how quickly models must adapt, and what assumptions can be made about data distribution. These scenario distinctions guide the design of suitable active querying strategies.

topics.title: Classification of online active learning approaches
topics.description: This topic focuses on taxonomies and classification schemes for organizing online active learning methods for data streams. Approaches may be grouped by query strategy (e.g., uncertainty-based, density-based), model type (single vs. ensemble), handling of concept drift, or label budget management. Such a classification helps compare methods, identify gaps, and structure the state-of-the-art landscape.

topics.title: Evaluation strategies and performance metrics
topics.description: This topic concerns how to evaluate stream-based active learning algorithms, including metrics and protocols tailored to evolving data and limited labels. It involves assessing predictive performance over time (e.g., prequential accuracy), label efficiency, adaptation to concept drift, and computational cost, often under streaming evaluation setups. Appropriate evaluation strategies are critical to fairly compare algorithms and understand trade-offs between accuracy and labeling cost.

topics.title: Synthesis of methods and future research
topics.description: This topic addresses summarizing existing online active learning methods and outlining future research directions. It involves comparing methodological families, identifying common design patterns, and highlighting open problems such as more robust drift-aware querying, better integration with semi-supervised learning, or improved evaluation standards. Such synthesis guides subsequent work in the field.

topics.title: Supervised learning problem formulation
topics.description: Supervised learning is framed as learning a function that maps input variables (covariates) to an output variable (response). This function is estimated from a labeled dataset consisting of many input–output pairs. The focus is on using these labeled examples to train predictive models for tasks such as classification or regression.

topics.title: Motivation for active learning usage
topics.description: Active learning is motivated by scenarios where obtaining labels is difficult, costly, or impractical for all available data. Under a labeling budget constraint, only a subset of unlabeled observations can be queried. Properly selected labeled subsets can enable classification or regression models to reach performance comparable to using all labels, while using only a small fraction of the available observations.

topics.title: Margin-based query strategies
topics.description: Margin-based active learning focuses on selecting instances that lie close to the current decision boundary of the classifier, where prediction uncertainty is highest. By querying labels for these borderline points, the learner aims to refine the boundary most efficiently, improving classification performance with fewer labeled examples. This strategy is often used with margin-based models such as SVMs or linear classifiers.

topics.title: Diversity and density-based selection
topics.description: Diversity- and density-based methods exploit structural information in the data to select instances that are both representative of the underlying distribution and diverse from already labeled points. Techniques include using Mahalanobis distance to find observations far from labeled samples, clustering to pick cluster representatives, and graph-based methods to model relationships among labeled and unlabeled instances. Semi-supervised strategies such as label propagation on graphs can guide the selection of influential or poorly propagated nodes to label.

topics.title: Hybrid active learning strategies
topics.description: Hybrid strategies combine multiple selection criteria to exploit complementary strengths, such as uncertainty, diversity, and representativeness. For example, one can first partition the input space via clustering and then apply margin-based sampling within each region to pick the most uncertain representative instances. These methods aim to balance local informativeness with global coverage of the data distribution.

topics.title: Macro scenarios of active learning
topics.description: Active learning methods are organized into three macro scenarios based on how unlabeled instances are provided to the learner and how queries are formed. This categorization abstracts over specific query strategies to emphasize the flow of information, the interaction with the oracle, and the constraints on which instances can be queried. Understanding these scenarios helps practitioners choose suitable active learning setups and compare algorithms fairly across different application contexts.

topics.title: Batch size selection in active learning
topics.description: In pool-based active learning, the batch size k (number of instances labeled per iteration) governs how frequently the model is retrained and how many new instances are added. Smaller k allows more frequent updates of the selection criteria, but risks higher computational cost due to repeated training. Larger k, as in adding fixed percentages of the dataset, is more practical for large models where retraining is expensive, but increases the risk of redundant labeling. Thus, k embodies a problem- and model-specific trade-off between computational efficiency and avoiding redundant labels.

topics.title: Uncertainty-based acquisition in pool-based AL
topics.description: Pool-based active learning methods often rely on uncertainty-based instance selection, where candidate data points are scored by how uncertain the model is about their labels. These criteria are operationalized through acquisition functions, which map model predictions to informativeness scores. Combining uncertainty measures with acquisition functions like entropy, mutual information, or variation ratio enables more principled selection of instances whose annotations are expected to be most beneficial. This framework links model predictive distributions with label-query decisions.

topics.title: Mutual information and variation ratio criteria
topics.description: Beyond entropy, mutual information and variation ratio are alternative acquisition metrics derived from model predictions. Mutual information captures the expected reduction in uncertainty about model parameters or predictions after observing a label, emphasizing instances that can most change the model. Variation ratio measures how frequently the most probable class appears across predictions (e.g., in ensembles or Bayesian samples), with lower ratios indicating higher uncertainty. These measures help select a diverse set of highly uncertain points, complementing pure entropy-based selection.

topics.title: Real-time sampling in manufacturing
topics.description: In chemical and manufacturing processes, a learner predicts product quality under strict time constraints for sampling decisions, often to preserve traceability in high-volume production. Online active learning selects which process observations to label in real time so that models for quality prediction, predictive maintenance, and visual inspection can be continuously updated. The key entities are production batches or items, quality measurements, time windows for decision-making, and evolving predictive models.

topics.title: Sequential decisions in streaming media and trials
topics.description: For video streaming platforms and clinical trials, users or patients arrive sequentially and cannot be accumulated into a large candidate pool. Online active learning must decide on the fly whether to label or enroll each arriving subject or interaction to optimize learning or trial outcomes. This involves trade-offs between information gain, user or patient burden, and strict timing or recruitment constraints.

topics.title: NLP text classification with online AL
topics.description: In text classification tasks such as sentiment analysis and spam detection, data points like messages or documents arrive continuously. Online active learning frameworks decide in real time which texts to label so that the model can be updated incrementally and maintain or improve accuracy. Entities include incoming text streams, labeling actions, and continuously refined classifiers.

topics.title: Unsupervised preprocessing in semi-supervised learning
topics.description: One category of semi-supervised methods is unsupervised preprocessing, which applies techniques such as dimensionality reduction, clustering, or feature extraction to the combined labeled and unlabeled dataset before supervised training. This transformation aims to produce a representation where informative samples are easier to identify and model parameters are better estimated when few labels are available. In online active learning, this includes using pre-trained networks to extract salient features from unlabeled instances prior to initiating the sampling routine, thereby guiding more informative query choices.

topics.title: Autoencoders for online active learning
topics.description: An autoencoder is trained on all available unlabeled data to learn a compressed representation that improves downstream online active learning. In this setting, the learned features are then used with linear regression models to enhance prediction and query selection under streaming conditions. This exploits the structure of unlabeled data without requiring additional labels.

topics.title: Wrapper methods with pseudo-labels
topics.description: Wrapper methods rely on one or more supervised learners trained jointly on labeled data and pseudo-labeled unlabeled data. Two core variants are self-training, using a single model that assigns pseudo-labels to confidently predicted examples, and co-training, where multiple models exchange their most confident predictions to generate pseudo-labels for each other. These methods integrate semi-supervised learning into the active learning loop.

topics.title: Pseudo-labels and confirmation bias risk
topics.description: Pseudo-labels help exploit unlabeled data in label-scarce environments but can induce confirmation bias. When models trust their own or peers’ pseudo-labels too strongly, they may reinforce early mistakes, degrading performance. Managing this risk is crucial when incorporating pseudo-labeled data into active learning pipelines.

topics.title: Confirmation bias in active query strategies
topics.description: In a broader active learning context, confirmation bias refers to query strategies that preferentially select examples supporting the current model hypothesis. Such selection neglects challenging or contradictory instances that could drive model improvement, leading to overconfident yet brittle models. Designing acquisition functions that avoid this bias is critical for robust learning.

topics.title: Graph-based regularization and sampling
topics.description: Graph-based methods construct a graph over all data points and train a supervised model with a loss combining standard supervised terms and a regularization that enforces similar predictions for connected nodes. In online active learning, the graph encodes similarity relationships that guide query selection, such as choosing points in low-density regions or far from existing labeled examples. This couples semi-supervised smoothness assumptions with structure-aware active sampling.

topics.title: Industrial quality control as stationary stream
topics.description: Industrial quality control is presented as an example where data streams can be treated as stationary due to controlled operating conditions. Control actions at regular intervals and continuous maintenance of system components stabilize the process, leading to relatively consistent data distributions. Stationary stream classification methods can leverage this stability to monitor product quality and detect anomalies with fewer assumptions about distribution shifts.

topics.title: Human activity recognition from wearable data
topics.description: Human activity recognition using wearable devices is described as another application of stationary data stream classification. Data from sensors on fitness trackers or similar devices generates a continuous stream representing activities like walking, running, or sleeping, assumed to be relatively stable in distribution over time. Models can be updated in real time as new labeled examples arrive, enabling continuous personalization and improvement of activity classification.

topics.title: Real-time intrusion detection under cyberattack drift
topics.description: This topic focuses on real-time intrusion detection systems that monitor computer networks and must detect emerging forms of cyberattacks. Because attack patterns evolve, the underlying data distribution shifts, requiring classification models that adapt over time to maintain detection performance in streaming network data.

topics.title: Random sampling versus specialized strategies
topics.description: This topic contrasts naive random sampling with more advanced online active learning strategies. Random sampling selects instances from the data stream uniformly for annotation, ignoring informativeness. In contrast, specialized strategies target scenarios where labeling resources are limited or costly and where the data distribution may be non-stationary, requiring informed, adaptive selection to maintain model performance over time.

topics.title: General framework and drift adaptation
topics.description: This topic refers to a general framework that captures the main components shared across online active learning algorithms, with configurable options highlighted via callouts. The framework encompasses processes such as instance selection, querying, and model update in a streaming context. It also interfaces with drift detection and adaptation mechanisms that monitor changes in data distribution and trigger model adaptation, as detailed in referenced flowcharts.

topics.title: Mistake-driven perceptron updates with selective labels
topics.description: When a label is queried and the prediction is incorrect, the model is updated via the standard perceptron rule w_t = w_{t−1} + M_t y_t x_t, where M_t is an indicator of a prediction mistake. If the label is not requested, the weight vector remains unchanged, so learning occurs only on queried examples where errors are observed. This couples label querying with mistake-driven updates, reducing annotation cost while maintaining an online learning process.

topics.title: Smoothing-based sampling probability function
topics.description: The section introduces a sampling probability Pt defined as Pt = δ / (δ + |pt|), where δ ≥ 1 is a smoothing parameter. This formulation yields a sampling distribution equivalent to a previously defined one (Eq. 3), but restricts the smoothing parameter to values not smaller than 1. The sampling probability modulates how likely an example is queried based on a score pt, affecting the shape of the sampling distributions illustrated for b-sampling and logistic sampling.

topics.title: Minimax gradient-based conservative selection
topics.description: To mitigate the risks of aggressively focusing on misclassified examples under label noise, Bordes et al. propose a more conservative selection strategy based on a minimax gradient criterion. Instead of directly choosing the most misclassified points, examples are selected for updating wt according to how they influence a worst-case (minimax) gradient objective. This aims to provide more robust updates that are less sensitive to noisy labels and erroneous boundary estimates.

topics.title: Role of model confidence in sampling
topics.description: Beyond label reliability, the section stresses that confidence in the model itself must be considered when sampling is based solely on model predictions. Hao et al. (2018b) argue that margin-based sampling may be suboptimal when the model is not sufficiently confident, implying that query strategies should account for model uncertainty in addition to prediction margins. This connects active sampling quality directly to the model’s calibration and stability over time.

topics.title: Variance-aware soft margin querying strategy
topics.description: The sampling decision uses a variance-adjusted soft margin that combines the absolute margin with a correction term ct depending on the margin variance νt. The correction term ct = −(η/2)(1/(νt + 1/γ)) is designed so that high variance (low confidence) increases the incentive to query labels, while low variance reduces it. A composite quantity ρt = |pt| + ct is computed: if ρt ≤ 0 the label is always queried; if ρt > 0, the label is queried with probability Pt = δ / (δ + ρt), introducing a Bernoulli sampling mechanism that smoothly trades off uncertainty and labeling cost.

topics.title: Cost-sensitive loss for imbalanced data streams
topics.description: To handle class-imbalanced streaming applications, a cost-sensitive variant of the loss function is introduced. This modification assigns different costs to errors from different classes, biasing the learner to pay more attention to minority or more critical classes. The approach is positioned within the broader context of imbalanced data stream analysis.

topics.title: Cold-start with imbalanced multiclass ELMs
topics.description: Qin et al. (2021) highlight the cold-start issue specifically in imbalanced multiclass settings using extreme learning machines (ELMs). In such datasets, some classes have very few instances, severely degrading the model’s predictive ability for those classes, especially early on. They extend an existing active learning framework to multiclass classification and propose a sampling strategy that jointly considers instance uncertainty and diversity, using pairwise diversity measures to avoid redundant queries and to better represent under-represented classes.

topics.title: Differentially private online SVM active learning
topics.description: A differentially private online active learning method based on SVMs randomizes the classical margin-based querying strategy of Tong and Koller. The informativeness of a point x_t is modeled as c(t) = exp(−d(x_t, w_t)), where d(x_t, w_t) = |⟨w_t, x_t⟩| / ||w_t|| is its distance to the current SVM hyperplane. In the non-private setting, labels are queried for points within a margin band around the hyperplane (c(t) > τ, equivalently d(x_t, w_t) ≤ log 1/τ), but to ensure privacy the method replaces this deterministic rule with randomized decisions.

topics.title: Mini-batch strategies for private SGD training
topics.description: For training under differential privacy, the method introduces two mini-batch strategies to mitigate the slow convergence that can result from adding noise in private stochastic gradient descent. By grouping streaming instances into mini-batches before applying noisy updates, the approach aims to balance privacy guarantees with optimization efficiency. This is contextualized with references to prior work on private SGD algorithms.

topics.title: Online active learning with reject option
topics.description: Reject option classifiers allow the learner to abstain from making a prediction when instances are highly ambiguous, mitigating the high cost of misclassification errors, as in medical diagnosis tasks. Shah and Manwani study online active learning for such classifiers, where deciding to reject versus predict is integral to the model’s operation. The framework is tailored to streaming data where each new instance may be predicted, rejected, or queried for a label.

topics.title: Double ramp loss for label querying
topics.description: The reject option classifier uses a non-convex double ramp loss ℓ_dr, where parameter updates occur only in a specific linear region of the loss. The label of the current example xt is queried only if |f_t(xt)| lies within [ρ_t − 1, ρ_t + 1], the interval where the loss is linear and informative for updating. The parameter ρ defines the bandwidth of the rejection region, controlling which instances fall into the 'reject' versus 'predict' zones.

topics.title: Bayesian online active learning framework
topics.description: Fujii and Kashima propose a Bayesian online active learning framework based on policy-adaptive submodularity to handle data streams. It distinguishes between a stream setting, where labeling decisions can be delayed within a time window, and a secretary setting, where decisions must be taken immediately upon arrival. The framework is general enough to cover tasks such as active classification, active clustering, and active feature selection under streaming conditions.

topics.title: Adaptive submodular maximization in streams
topics.description: The Bayesian framework is grounded in adaptive submodular maximization, extending classical submodular maximization characterized by diminishing returns of adding elements to a set. By updating the set function as new observations arrive, the method adapts to the evolving data distribution and current state of knowledge. This adaptivity aims to exploit streaming data more efficiently, improving model performance under limited labeling budgets.

topics.title: Disagreement-based online active learning theory
topics.description: Huang et al. introduce a disagreement-based active learning framework for online settings, formalized over a hypothesis space H with VC dimension d and a Tsybakov noise model. Each classifier h ∈ H maps observations xt to binary labels yt ∈ {0,1}, and pairwise disagreement is quantified by d(h1, h2) = P[h1(x) ≠ h2(x)]. The induced disagreement region, where committee members predict differently, underpins sampling strategies that query labels only on informative, contentious instances.

topics.title: Label complexity and regret objectives
topics.description: Online active learning is formalized as a policy π = ({v_t}, {λ_t}), where v_t encodes whether a label is queried and λ_t is the prediction rule at time t. The performance over a time horizon T is evaluated via label complexity, defined as the expected number of queried labels E[Q(T)], and regret, defined as the expected excess number of classification errors with respect to an optimal hypothesis h*. The algorithm’s goal is to minimize label complexity subject to a constraint on regret, balancing labeling cost and predictive performance.

topics.title: Disagreement-based query region in online learning
topics.description: The learner maintains a version space H_t of candidate hypotheses and defines a region of disagreement D(H_t) as points where at least two hypotheses in H_t predict different labels. Initially, the version space is the full hypothesis class H and the disagreement region is the whole input space X. At each time t, if the current instance x_t falls inside D(H_t), the learner queries its label; otherwise, it predicts with an arbitrary classifier from H_t. This mechanism drives selective querying based on current model uncertainty.

topics.title: Version space pruning via empirical error thresholds
topics.description: After each iteration t, the learner uses the collected labeled set Z_t of size M to estimate the empirical error ε_{Z_t}(h) for all classifiers in H and identify the current best classifier h*_t. The version space is then updated by removing hypotheses whose empirical error exceeds that of h*_t by more than a threshold ε_{Z_t}(h, h*_t). This threshold controls how aggressively the version space is pruned, mediating a trade-off between reducing label complexity (by shrinking the disagreement region) and limiting regret (by avoiding elimination of good classifiers.

topics.title: Surrogate-loss active learning with pseudo-labels
topics.description: Desalvo et al. (2021) extend disagreement-based online active learning to a framework using surrogate losses and weak labels. At each time step, the learner may either query the true label y_t or assign a pseudo-label ŷ_t, and both true and pseudo-labeled instances form a set S_t that combines Z_t and Ŷ_t. The empirical risk ε_{S_t}(h) is computed over this mixed set, effectively integrating active learning with semi-supervised learning to optimize the sampling and learning strategy.

topics.title: Bayesian active learning for activity recognition
topics.description: For online human activity recognition with sensor data, a semi-supervised active learning strategy leverages a pre-trained conditional restricted Boltzmann machine to extract generic features robust to different sensor layouts. Instance selection follows a Bayesian approach aimed at minimizing uncertainty over model parameters by comparing current model uncertainty (from data up to time t) with the expected risk conditioned on the potential label y_t. The discrepancy between these quantities indicates the impact of acquiring the current label on model uncertainty. A dynamically adaptive threshold is used to decide whether the expected risk justifies querying the label.

topics.title: Decay-weighted expert loss and potential
topics.description: The section discusses how expert advice algorithms maintain a cumulative loss Ri,t−1 for each expert, updated with an exponential decay factor η so that recent mistakes are weighted more heavily than older ones. It explains that the Generalized Forecaster (GF) operates by minimizing, at each time step, the worst-case increase in a potential function over all possible label outcomes. This potential function assigns a value to each expert that reflects the quality of its advice based on its decay-weighted past performance. These mechanisms underpin how expert weights and influence are adapted over time in online prediction.

topics.title: Active multiple kernel learning with random features
topics.description: A related framework applies online active learning to multiple kernel learning (MKL) using random feature approximation. The Active MKL (AMKL) algorithm employs an ensemble of N kernel functions within a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), where each kernel-based function 1fi,t(xt) is optimized independently in a local step. In a subsequent global step, the learner combines these N kernel functions to construct a best-approximation function ft(xt) for prediction on sequentially arriving data. This setup leverages MKL’s ability to capture diverse data characteristics while maintaining online, incremental updates suitable for streaming and active settings.

topics.title: Regret-minimizing kernel ensemble weighting
topics.description: The method constructs a learned kernel-based predictor f̃t(xt) as a weighted combination of N kernel functions fi,t, with weights vi,t chosen to minimize regret over the time horizon T. Weights are computed via exponential weighting of past losses on labeled instances: ωi,t = exp(−ηg ∑_{τ∈A_{t−1}} ℓ(f̂i,τ(xτ), yτ)), where A_{t−1} indexes queried points and ηg is a tunable parameter. Normalizing ωi,t yields vi,t, which balance the contribution of each kernel according to historical performance relative to the best kernel function f*i,t. This framework ties instance labeling decisions to an adaptive ensemble of kernel predictors optimized on previous labeled data.

topics.title: Confidence-based instance selection via kernel agreement
topics.description: Instance selection relies on a confidence condition that measures the similarity of predictions among the weighted kernel ensemble, controlled by a tolerance threshold δ > 0. The criterion max_{1≤j≤N} ∑_{i=1}^N vi,t ℓ(f̃i,t(xt), f̃j,t(xt)) ≤ δ enforces that, for an unlabeled instance, all kernels’ predictions are sufficiently close under the loss ℓ, indicating high agreement. When this condition holds, the system can refrain from querying the label, interpreting high consensus as high confidence. This selection rule is analogous to the condition used in AEWAF by Hao et al. (2018a), adapting expert agreement to a kernel-based ensemble.

topics.title: Distribution shifts in drifting data streams
topics.description: Active learning strategies in this category address online classification in time-varying data streams where the underlying data distribution changes over time. The text distinguishes distribution shifts based on whether they affect the feature distribution p(x) or the conditional distribution p(y|x). A covariate shift is defined as a change that only impacts p(x) while leaving p(y|x) unchanged. This categorization sets the stage for analyzing and designing active learning methods tailored to different types of drift.

topics.title: Limitations of unsupervised drift detection
topics.description: The text explains that purely unsupervised drift detection struggles to capture true concept drifts when the input distribution p(x) remains unchanged but the conditional relationship between x and y changes. In such cases, labels are necessary to recognize that the mapping from features to labels has shifted. This highlights a fundamental limitation of relying only on unlabeled data for detecting concept drift in active learning scenarios. It motivates combining limited supervised signals with unsupervised detectors.
