topics.title: Pseudo-label propagation using k-nearest neighbors
topics.description: The section describes augmenting active learning decisions with pseudo-labels inferred from already labeled neighbors. For an unlabeled queried point, its label is estimated through a weighted majority vote among its k-nearest neighbors, propagating known labels through the feature space. Both true labels and these pseudo-labels are then used to assess the utility of incoming data points. This semi-supervised mechanism enriches label information under latency and sparsity, improving utility estimation in streaming active learning.

topics.title: Drift-aware dual-classifier management
topics.description: The algorithm maintains a primary classifier and conditionally spawns a new classifier when the drift detector raises a warning. During a warning phase, the new classifier is trained in the background with labeled examples while the original classifier remains in use. Upon confirmed drift detection, the new classifier replaces the old one, and its training continues, enabling smoother adaptation to concept drift while avoiding abrupt model changes.

topics.title: Simulated labeling via bagging and fuzziness
topics.description: To avoid redundant queries when labels are delayed, the method identifies a region Dn+ = Dn\Wn where queried labels are not yet available. Instead of re-querying similar instances, it simulates incoming labels by using a bagging approach that averages utility estimates over multiple simulated labelings, thus approximating the effect of future supervision. An alternative simulation based on fuzzy labeling is also considered to represent label uncertainty more explicitly.

topics.title: Class-imbalance-aware uncertainty thresholds
topics.description: Instance selection is based on predictive uncertainty measured by the best-versus-second-best margin for multi-class classification. After a passive initialization pool, a per-class threshold θi is computed (Eq. 31) as a function of class-specific sample counts and a constant m controlling threshold size, so that querying behavior can differ across classes. Class imbalance is further addressed through class-specific training weights and dynamic adjustment of these thresholds to bias selection toward minority-class instances.

topics.title: Chunk-based drift detection and selection
topics.description: A data stream S is partitioned into fixed-length chunks whose adjacent distributions are compared to detect concept drift. After a drift is identified, a multi-objective optimization problem is formulated to select query candidates from the current batch that are both relevant and diverse. Relevance is defined as a point’s contribution to the emerging concept, while diversity is quantified via the Pearson correlation coefficient among instances in the same region, encouraging informative yet non-redundant labeling.

topics.title: Meta-learned uncertainty thresholds per window
topics.description: Another approach samples the most uncertain instances from each chunk but uses a meta-learning framework to fine-tune the uncertainty threshold for each window. By adapting this threshold based on meta-level information, the method aims to reduce the number of labels requested while preserving effective adaptation to new concepts. This window-wise tuning balances exploration of changing regions of the feature space with labeling cost constraints.

topics.title: Damped sliding window weight decay
topics.description: Dynamic classifiers are assigned gradually decaying weights based on a damped sliding window mechanism. Each dynamic classifier weight is initialized at 1/D and then updated according to its creation time using the recurrence in Eq. (34). More recent dynamic classifiers receive higher weights to emphasize detection of sudden concept drifts, while older ones have smaller weights and contribute to identifying gradual drifts. This temporal weighting scheme encodes recency into the ensemble’s decision process.

topics.title: Hybrid random–uncertainty instance selection
topics.description: The instance selection strategy combines uncertainty sampling with random sampling to choose which data points in the stream should be labeled. Uncertainty is based on the margin of ensemble predictions, while random sampling ensures coverage of regions far from the current decision boundary. This hybrid design addresses the limitation of pure uncertainty sampling, which may miss concept changes that occur away from the boundary. Similar ideas are reused in chunk-based ensemble active learning, where Zyblewski’s budget labeling strategy selects both random and informative examples measured via a support function threshold (interpreted as distance to the decision boundary in binary problems).

topics.title: Clustering-based active learning with stable classifiers
topics.description: Halder et al. (2023) extend a framework with stable and dynamic classifiers by inserting a clustering step on each data block. The goal is to train a new stable classifier on instances that are simultaneously informative and representative, selected from clusters formed in each incoming block. This integrates cluster structure into the design of online active learning for time-varying data streams.

topics.title: Density-peak clustering for representative sample selection
topics.description: Zhang et al. (2023) employ density-peak clustering to identify the most representative data points in each batch of a data stream. They detect incomplete clusters in the dynamic feature space via the 'altitude' of data points and then query labels from those regions in subsequent iterations. This targets areas that are underrepresented or poorly formed in the current clustering structure.

topics.title: Bi-criteria GGMM-based active learning with drift handling
topics.description: Mohamad et al. (2018) introduce a bi-criteria active learning algorithm that combines input-space density and label uncertainty. Density is modeled with a growing Gaussian mixture model (GGMM) that forms clusters and estimates data density, creating a new cluster when a point’s Mahalanobis distance to its nearest cluster exceeds a closeness threshold. Label uncertainty and concept drift are handled via a Bayesian logistic regression model whose parameters evolve over time, linking evolving class boundaries with the streaming data’s cluster structure.

topics.title: Discrepancy-based incremental model updating
topics.description: The model is updated incrementally using a discrepancy measure defined as the difference between the model’s uncertainty on an instance xt before and after its true label yt is added to the training set. The query strategy uses a b-sampling approach to preferentially select instances that are expected to contribute most to the current error. This couples an uncertainty-change metric with error-focused sampling for online active learning in data streams.

topics.title: Cognitive dual density-uncertainty query strategy
topics.description: Liu et al. (2021) propose an online active learning strategy that combines local density and classifier uncertainty to select informative and representative instances under concept drift and noise. Local density is defined as the number of times an observation is the nearest neighbor of other instances, computed within a sliding 'cognition window' over the stream. Inspired by Ebbinghaus’s law of human memory, the method uses a memory-strength-based policy to decide when the cognition window is refreshed, addressing both gradual and abrupt drifts. Labeling decisions are controlled by two thresholds, one on local density and one on classifier uncertainty.

topics.title: Time-decay Bayesian probit framework for streams
topics.description: Chu et al. (2011) propose an online framework based on a Bayesian probit model with time-decay to handle evolving data streams. Online Bayesian learning maintains a posterior distribution over the linear classifier’s weight vector wt, while time-decay strategies downweight older examples to cope with concept drift and emphasize recent data. An online approximation technique supports weighted examples, following Minka (2001), and various sampling strategies are explored using entropy-based, function-value-based, and random selection criteria. This integrates probabilistic modeling, temporal weighting, and multiple query heuristics for streaming active learning.

topics.title: Conflict and ignorance for stream active learning
topics.description: In single-pass active learning for evolving classification models, query decisions are based on conflict and ignorance. Conflict captures when an incoming instance lies near the decision boundary between classes, indicating label ambiguity, while ignorance measures the distance of the instance from the labeled training data in feature space, indicating unexplored regions. These two criteria guide which streaming instances should be labeled to most effectively improve the classifier.

topics.title: Uncertainty-driven active learning for evolving regression
topics.description: For evolving regression models, online active learning combines ignorance in the input space with uncertainty in model outputs and parameters. Predictive uncertainty is quantified using confidence intervals via locally adaptive error bars, and overlapping fuzzy rules are merged with a dedicated approach to refine the rule base. Parameter uncertainty is assessed using the A-optimality criterion, an alphabetic optimality measure that aims to minimize the average variance of parameter estimates.

topics.title: Variable uncertainty thresholds and low-support rules
topics.description: An alternative active learning strategy for recurrent fuzzy classifiers uses a dynamic threshold based on the variable uncertainty strategy. Instead of directly exploiting output uncertainty, the method adaptively adjusts the threshold that determines when to query labels, focusing updates on rules with low support formed from few observations. This emphasizes improving underrepresented regions of the rule base and addresses the what-to-learn question in recurrent fuzzy model training.

topics.title: D-optimality for fuzzy model parameter selection
topics.description: A recent online active learning strategy for fuzzy models introduces criteria based on D-optimality in the consequent space. D-optimality is used to reduce parameter uncertainty by selecting instances that maximize the determinant of the information matrix, thereby improving the precision of parameter estimates in the consequents of fuzzy rules. This embeds classical optimal experimental design principles into active learning for evolving fuzzy systems.

topics.title: Spherical potential-based novelty thresholds
topics.description: Subramanian et al. propose a meta-cognitive component that evaluates the novelty of incoming data points using a knowledge measure called spherical potential, a concept studied in kernel-based methods. This spherical potential is used to set a threshold deciding whether a new fuzzy rule should be added to capture the knowledge in the current sample. The work contrasts this label-efficient novelty criterion with a prediction-error-based threshold relying on hinge loss, which is less suitable under label scarcity.

topics.title: Certainty-based querying in visual inspection streams
topics.description: For visual inspection quality control, images are evaluated in a single pass and those selected for querying are stored in a buffer to be labeled later by an oracle. The buffer size defines a trade-off between promptly updating the classifier and limiting frequent human interventions. An active learning strategy is used that queries samples when model certainty, computed differently for a random forest (best-versus-second-best margin) and an evolving fuzzy classifier (conflict and ignorance measures), falls below a threshold.

topics.title: Hotelling T² and SPE for AL sampling
topics.description: Cernuda et al. employ a latent-structure-based query strategy using Hotelling T² and squared prediction error (SPE) statistics, classical tools from multivariate statistical process control and anomaly detection. These statistics measure the distance between the current labeled training set and a new unlabeled data point; high values indicate that the observation violates the current model and is thus informative to query. Implementations combine these criteria with principal component regression or partial least squares, and newly labeled samples trigger retraining of a Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy model using a sliding window over the data stream.

topics.title: Optimal experimental design and active learning
topics.description: Optimal experimental design is presented as a closely related field to active learning, focusing on designing experiments that enable efficient parameter estimation or improved prediction while minimizing the number of labeled runs N. It develops optimality criteria that balance resource efficiency with model performance. The traditional framework considered here is based on linear regression models, connecting classical design of experiments with active learning objectives.

topics.title: Linear regression and OLS estimation
topics.description: The section defines a linear regression model y = Xβ + ε with N observations and d input variables, where ε is Gaussian noise with covariance σ²I. It explains that if XᵀX is full rank, the ordinary least squares (OLS) estimator for the regression coefficients β is given by (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy. This sets the foundation for later discussion of design properties and parameter uncertainty.

topics.title: Moment matrix and design geometry
topics.description: The moment matrix M = XᵀX / N is introduced as a key object in design optimality criteria, encapsulating information about the design geometry. Since XᵀX governs the estimation of β, its structure (eigenvalues, determinant) reflects how informative the design is for parameter estimation. Optimal design methods exploit these properties to evaluate and compare experimental designs.

topics.title: Confidence ellipsoid for regression parameters
topics.description: Assuming Gaussian noise, the estimator β̂ has a Normal distribution with covariance σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹, which induces a confidence ellipsoid for the true parameter vector β. The ellipsoid is defined via quadratic forms in (b − β̂) involving XᵀX, and its volume is inversely proportional to √det(XᵀX), while the axis lengths scale with 1/λᵢ, the eigenvalues of XᵀX. This geometric interpretation underlies how optimality criteria assess designs via ellipsoid size and shape.

topics.title: From offline to streaming optimal design
topics.description: Traditional optimal design methods are used in offline experimental settings, where all design points can be pre-determined before data collection. In streaming scenarios, data points arrive sequentially and the design must be adapted online, requiring modifications of classical optimality-based approaches. This motivates strategies that incrementally select which incoming observations to label to approximate an optimal design.

topics.title: Online A-optimal design under heteroskedasticity
topics.description: Fontaine et al. extend online optimal design to settings with heteroskedastic noise, where the variance of the response depends on the covariates. Their objective is to optimally allocate a fixed labeling budget across covariates so that the variances of the estimated regression coefficients are balanced, in line with A-optimality principles. This results in adaptive selection policies that consider both design geometry and non-constant error variance.

topics.title: Conditional D-optimality for streaming selection
topics.description: Cacciarelli et al. propose a Conditional D-optimality (CDO) algorithm that extends norm-thresholding ideas to D-optimal design in streaming settings. The design is made marginally D-optimal given an initial labeled set, and incoming observations are selected by applying a D-optimality-based thresholding rule to augment this set. The method exploits the link between D-optimality and prediction variance, yielding a sequential selection strategy that improves the determinant of the information matrix as new data arrive.

topics.title: Warm-up set and KDE threshold estimation
topics.description: Before starting active querying, the learner passively collects a warm-up set of j unlabeled observations from the stream to estimate the covariance structure of the data. Using eigendecomposition and whitening of both the initial design X and warm-up set W, the algorithm computes representations Z and V in a normalized space. Kernel density estimation (KDE) over V is then used to select a threshold τ such that the norm-thresholding rule achieves the desired sampling rate α. This procedure initializes τ and is periodically updated as the labeled design grows.

topics.title: Outlier-robust double-threshold sampling region
topics.description: To mitigate the tendency of design-optimality sampling to focus on outliers, the authors describe bounding the selection region with two thresholds τ1 and τ2. Only points whose leverage x_t^T (X^T X)^{-1} x_t falls between these bounds are eligible for labeling, defining an annular region in the transformed feature space. The upper threshold τ2 controls a trade-off between avoiding high-leverage outliers and still exploring uncertain regions of the input space. This modification aims to preserve predictive performance in the presence of outliers.

topics.title: MAB as sequential experimental design
topics.description: Multi-armed bandit (MAB) problems are framed as a special case of sequential experimental design, where each arm pull is an experiment chosen to maximize an outcome over time. The learner must identify the arm with the highest expected reward among several arms with different reward distributions. This setting parallels active learning, as both involve sequential decisions (arm pulls or label queries) with feedback guiding future choices to optimize reward or model accuracy.

topics.title: Regret minimization in bandits
topics.description: Regret minimization in MAB focuses on maximizing cumulative reward across many trials, equivalently minimizing the loss relative to always playing the best arm. Algorithms must carefully balance exploration of lesser-known arms to improve reward estimates with exploitation of the currently best-estimated arm. This paradigm is suited to applications such as treatment design, online advertising, and recommender systems, where ongoing rewards are critical.

topics.title: Pure exploration bandit strategies
topics.description: Pure exploration methods aim to identify the best arm with high confidence or under a fixed budget of arm pulls, rather than maximizing cumulative reward. The main objective is to learn an accurate model of the reward structure while minimizing the number of measurements or labels, often motivated by safety or cost constraints on interventions. This setting is relevant to domains such as drug discovery and soft sensor development, where safe and efficient experimentation is crucial.

topics.title: G-optimality and XY-allocation for bandits
topics.description: In the offline pure exploration setting for linear bandits, Soare et al. analyze the problem using the G-optimality criterion from experimental design, which seeks to minimize the maximum prediction variance over a design space. They introduce the XY-allocation algorithm, a specific strategy for allocating pulls across arms to achieve near G-optimal experimental designs. This connects classical optimal design theory with sample-efficient bandit exploration.

topics.title: LSTM-based policy for label vs. predict
topics.description: Woodward and Finn (2017) propose a reinforcement learning approach in which, at each time step, the learner must choose between predicting a label for xt or paying to query its true label yt. The policy π*(st) is optimized over states st to balance the cost of label requests versus the cost of incorrect predictions, with rewards assigned for requesting a label (Rreq), making a correct prediction (Rcorr), or an incorrect prediction (Rinc), where Rcorr and Rinc are modeled as negative due to associated costs. The action-value function is approximated using an LSTM neural network with a linear output layer, enabling the policy to exploit temporal dependencies in the sequence of decisions.

topics.title: Learning-curve evaluation of active learning
topics.description: Active learning strategies are evaluated by comparing them to passive random sampling through learning curves that track model performance versus the number of labeled examples. Metrics such as accuracy, F1 score, or root mean square error on a holdout test set are plotted. The curve’s asymptote and slope capture overall performance and sample efficiency, with steeper slopes indicating faster performance gains per labeled example.

topics.title: Non-parametric tests for strategy comparison
topics.description: To rigorously compare multiple active learning sampling strategies, non-parametric statistical tests are recommended. For pairwise comparisons, the sign test and the Wilcoxon signed-ranks test are proposed, while for more than two strategies, Friedman tests (including aligned-ranks and Iman–Davenport correction) and the Quade test are suggested. These tests assess whether observed performance differences between active and passive strategies are statistically significant across tasks or datasets.

topics.title: MOA framework for stream evaluation
topics.description: MOA (Massive Online Analysis) is an open-source software suite for data stream mining that implements both holdout and prequential evaluation strategies. It provides infrastructure to run and compare online learning and active learning algorithms on streaming data. Many studies in the survey use MOA as their experimental platform for evaluating online active learning strategies. Its inclusion of multiple evaluation protocols makes it a de facto standard tool in this research area.

topics.title: Train-on-queried, test-on-full-dataset protocol
topics.description: Some works adopt a non-standard protocol where models are trained only on queried (labeled) data but evaluated on the entire dataset, including instances seen during training. This differs from strict prequential test-then-train, where each instance is tested before becoming part of the training set. Such a protocol can lead to partial overlap between training and test data, which may bias performance estimates. It reflects a batch-style evaluation layered on top of an active querying process.

topics.title: Window-based batch evaluation in streams
topics.description: Window-based evaluation assesses prediction accuracy over all observations within the current batch or window of a data stream. Models are evaluated on each window as a unit, reflecting performance over recent data rather than on a per-instance basis. This approach can smooth short-term fluctuations and is useful when data naturally arrive in batches. It diverges from strictly online, instance-level prequential evaluation while still respecting temporal structure.

topics.title: Network protocol identification with AL
topics.description: Online active learning is used for network protocol identification, where traffic data streams must be classified into protocol types under changing conditions. Zhang et al. (2020a) propose a method to select the most representative instances on the fly, focusing labeling effort where it most benefits the model. This approach enables continual adaptation of the protocol classifier to dynamic data distributions.

topics.title: Limits of deep AL in stream settings
topics.description: Many effective deep active learning strategies for computer vision rely on clustering or computing pairwise similarities between image embeddings to select diverse or informative samples. Such operations typically require multiple passes over the dataset or substantial storage, making them ill-suited to single-pass, stream-based scenarios. Consequently, these deep AL methods are not easily adaptable to online learning from data streams.

topics.title: Uncertainty-based AL for 3D objects
topics.description: For stream-based classification of 3D objects, online active learning can rely on traditional models combined with uncertainty sampling. Narr et al. (2016) employ a Mondrian forest classifier, an efficient online alternative to random forests, and query labels for images with high classification uncertainty. This design balances computational efficiency with focused labeling of the most ambiguous 3D object instances.

topics.title: Vision-based process monitoring with AL
topics.description: Online active learning is applied to vision-based process monitoring to reduce the effort required for manual image labeling while tracking industrial or operational processes. Rožanec et al. (2022) first extract visual features using a pre-trained ResNet-18 model, then employ online active learning to decide which images should be annotated. This combination leverages deep feature representations with selective labeling to make process monitoring more scalable.

topics.title: Feature-filtered streaming active learning
topics.description: A mutual-information-based feature selection step retains only √n of the original features to train an online classifier, where n is the number of observations in the training set. This reduced feature set is then used with a simple uncertainty-based active learning strategy. The approach is combined with several streaming classification algorithms, including Hoeffding trees, Hoeffding adaptive trees, stochastic gradient trees, streaming logistic regression, and streaming k-nearest neighbors.

topics.title: Gradient-based diversity sampling for DNNs
topics.description: For deep streaming active learning, each incoming example is represented by the gradient of the cross-entropy loss with respect to the last-layer parameters, using the model’s argmax prediction as a pseudo-label. The selection probability of a point is made proportional to the determinant of the updated covariance matrix of gradient representations, favoring examples that contribute novel information. This determinant-based criterion encourages diversity and coverage in the gradient space of the selected batch.

topics.title: Slice-aware budgeting in streaming object detection
topics.description: In autonomous driving scenarios, streaming camera data includes heterogeneous and imbalanced conditions such as clear, foggy, and rainy weather. A streamline approach is proposed to actively allocate labeling budget across these slices, prioritizing those where the model underperforms rather than sampling proportionally to their frequency. This counters the tendency of passive sampling to under-represent rare but critical conditions in the training data.

topics.title: Diversity-based online AL for vehicle faults
topics.description: For autonomous cars, a diversity-based online active learning strategy is used to improve fault detection. The method focuses on selecting diverse informative examples to reduce the false alarm rate while enabling the system to learn about previously unseen faults. This tailors active sampling to safety-critical anomaly and fault detection in automotive systems.

topics.title: Active learning in compressor optimization loops
topics.description: An industrial framework is introduced that couples a thermodynamics-based simulator of a centrifugal compressor with a Gaussian Process surrogate model and an online active learning module. The goal is to minimize the power absorbed during the boil-off process by adaptively selecting new experimental operating points. Simulator, surrogate, and optimizer interact in real time, with active learning guiding which experiments to run to efficiently explore and optimize compressor behavior.

topics.title: SBAD framework single-pass sampling
topics.description: The SBAD framework (Manjah et al., 2023) structures online active learning for data streams into sampling, fine-tuning, and evaluation phases. Sampling is performed in a single pass over the stream using a thresholding mechanism to decide which instances to query. This design aims to respect streaming constraints while still selecting informative examples.

topics.title: Scalability of online active learning
topics.description: Online active learning algorithms must remain computationally efficient and scalable to cope with large datasets and high-velocity data streams. The time to make sampling decisions must be lower than the process feed rate; otherwise, buffers are required, which undermines the benefits of true online operation. As data volume and speed increase, computational demands can become prohibitive, limiting real-world deployment.

topics.title: Model interpretability in active querying
topics.description: Beyond selecting the most informative instances, it can be important to explain why particular samples are queried, especially in high-stakes domains. Providing interpretable rationales for query choices helps practitioners in areas like healthcare and manufacturing better understand both the model behavior and the underlying problem. This links active learning with explainability and user trust requirements.

topics.title: Real-time label availability in streams
topics.description: The section assumes that queried data points from a stream receive labels immediately. This real-time label availability is treated as a foundational condition for many active learning methods in streaming settings. It directly influences how quickly the model can adapt to incoming data and support subsequent querying decisions.

topics.title: Implementation challenges and annotation tools
topics.description: Despite its advantages, real-time annotation introduces practical implementation challenges, such as coordinating timely human or system responses and integrating them seamlessly into the learning pipeline. The section notes that these issues need to be addressed through advanced data annotation tools, which can support efficient labeling workflows in streaming environments.

topics.title: Batch-mode active learning with streamed sampling
topics.description: This topic addresses training deep neural networks from data streams under memory constraints, where instances are sampled in real time but labels and model updates are deferred until a batch is formed. The approach combines streaming data acquisition with batch-mode active learning, in which queried instances are accumulated and then labeled and used for model updates in batches. This design balances computational and memory limitations with the need for timely sampling decisions in streaming environments.

topics.title: Active learning on data streams
topics.description: The section emphasizes the specific challenge of performing active learning when data arrive as a continuous stream and decisions must be made in real-time. Methods must select the most informative data points on-the-fly, under constraints such as limited labeling budgets and evolving data distributions. This contrasts with pool-based active learning where the full dataset is available in advance.

topics.title: Nonlinear regression and Bayesian optimization
topics.description: A key future direction is to develop online active learning strategies tailored to regression models, especially beyond linear models and linear bandits. The section notes growing interest in using Bayesian optimization techniques for active learning in nonlinear regression problems, where the goal is to select query points that improve function estimates efficiently. These methods can exploit probabilistic surrogate models to balance exploration and exploitation in streaming contexts.

topics.title: Object detection in data stream AL
topics.description: Object detection appears as a specialized task within online active learning for data streams, treated with single-model strategies. Both stationary and batch-processed settings are represented, suggesting interest in selectively labeling complex structured outputs (e.g., bounding boxes) under streaming constraints. This indicates an extension of AL for streams beyond standard classification and regression to more complex computer vision tasks.

topics.title: Limits of ensemble and batch online methods
topics.description: This topic highlights that ensemble models and batch-based approaches, although dominant in online classification, rely on assumptions that may break in real-world streaming applications. When data arrive continuously and resources are constrained, forming batches or maintaining multiple models may be infeasible. This motivates investigation into alternative online learning and sampling paradigms better suited to strict temporal or memory budgets.

topics.title: Query strategies for online active learning
topics.description: The survey reviews strategies for selecting the most informative data points in an online setting, where instances arrive sequentially. Key query mechanisms include uncertainty sampling, diversity sampling, query by committee, and reinforcement learning-based approaches. These methods aim to optimize which instances are labeled under limited annotation budgets while the data stream evolves. The topic concerns query selection criteria, model informativeness measures, and sequential decision-making policies.

topics.description: This topic describes the open access licensing terms under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. It specifies permitted uses such as sharing, adaptation, distribution, and reproduction, provided appropriate credit is given, a license link is included, and changes are indicated. It also distinguishes between materials covered by the article’s license and third-party content that may require separate permission. A reference link is provided for readers to access the full license terms.

topics.title: Data-driven NLP and label dependence
topics.description: Modern NLP systems are primarily built on data-driven machine learning models whose performance critically depends on both the quality and quantity of labeled training data. Achieving high performance generally requires substantial supervised data, which is not always easy or cheap to obtain. This dependence motivates methods that can make more efficient use of scarce labels.

topics.title: Survey Literature Collection Methodology
topics.description: The authors explain their process for constructing the survey corpus of AL papers for NLP, beginning with a keyword search for 'active' in ACL Anthology titles. This initial set is refined through manual filtering, followed by iterative inclusion of relevant works missed by the keyword search and from other venues discovered via reference chasing. This process underpins the bibliometric counts and the coverage of the survey.

topics.title: Typical Active Learning Procedure Loop
topics.description: Algorithm 1 lays out a standard AL loop: initialize a seed labeled set from the unlabeled pool, train a model, repeatedly select informative instances, obtain annotations, update labeled and unlabeled sets, and retrain until a stopping criterion is met. The main components are the seeding strategy, model training routine, query function, annotation step, and stopping rule. This procedural decomposition structures the rest of the survey.

topics.title: Informativeness-Based Query Strategies
topics.description: One core category of AL query strategies is based on informativeness, where instances are selected because the current model is uncertain about them or expects them to yield the largest performance gain. Metrics such as prediction entropy, margin, or expected error reduction typically operationalize informativeness. The survey devotes a subsection to categorizing and comparing such approaches in NLP.

topics.title: AL for Structured Prediction in NLP
topics.description: The authors point out that applying AL to NLP must handle structured outputs such as sequences and trees, as found in tasks like parsing, sequence labeling, and machine translation. AL methods must therefore reason about informativeness at the level of structured instances or substructures, which complicates query design and uncertainty estimation. A dedicated subsection surveys these structured prediction–specific techniques.

topics.title: Active Learning with Advanced Learning Techniques
topics.description: The survey discusses integrating AL with advanced learning paradigms, particularly modern deep learning approaches. This includes using neural architectures, transfer learning, or semi-supervised techniques within the AL loop to better exploit both labeled and unlabeled data. A subsection surveys how these advanced methods interact with query strategies and model training dynamics.

topics.title: Initialization Strategies for Starting AL
topics.description: Starting active learning requires choosing an initial seed set from the unlabeled pool, which can affect convergence speed and stability. The survey identifies this as a distinct design choice, covering methods such as random seeding, diversity-based initialization, or heuristic selection to ensure a reasonable starting model. A subsection systematically reviews these initialization strategies.

topics.title: Output uncertainty and uncertainty sampling
topics.description: Uncertainty sampling selects unlabeled instances for which a single model is most uncertain about its prediction. For probabilistic models, common measures include entropy, least-confidence, and margin sampling; for non-probabilistic models like SVMs, proximity to the decision boundary plays a similar role. These methods have been revisited for modern Transformer-based NLP systems as well.

topics.title: Local region divergence for uncertainty
topics.description: Beyond raw output scores, uncertainty can be measured by how much a model’s predictions vary in an instance’s local neighborhood. If the instance is near a decision boundary, small changes (e.g., nearest-neighbor replacements, adversarial perturbations, or data augmentation) can cause divergent predictions, indicating high uncertainty. Recent work operationalizes this idea using nearest-neighbor search, adversarial attacks, and augmented variants of each instance.

topics.title: Gradient-based expected gradient length querying
topics.description: Gradient-based strategies select instances expected to most strongly affect the model’s parameters, typically measured by the norm of the loss gradient. Since unlabeled instances lack gold labels, the loss and gradients are computed as expectations over possible labels, leading to the Expected Gradient Length (EGL) criterion. EGL has been applied to sequence labeling and speech recognition, with variants that focus specifically on embedding gradients in neural NLP models.

canonical_topics.name: Uncertainty and Gradient-Based Query Strategies
canonical_topics.description: Uncertainty- and informativeness-based querying remains a central pillar of deep active learning. Classical output-based criteria such as entropy, least-confidence, margin sampling, and distance to the decision boundary select instances where the model’s predictions are most uncertain. Gradient-based approaches, such as Expected Gradient Length (EGL), instead target points expected to induce the largest parameter updates, often computed as an expectation over possible labels. In deep neural models, these methods are adapted to probabilistic softmax outputs, margin-like scores, and gradient norms on embeddings or specific layers. Recent work revisits these strategies for Transformer-based NLP systems, analyzing when they improve data efficiency and how they interact with model calibration.

canonical_topics.name: Neighborhood Divergence for Deep Uncertainty Estimation
canonical_topics.description: Neighborhood-divergence methods estimate uncertainty by examining how a model’s predictions change under small perturbations in the input space. For a given instance, nearest-neighbor replacements, adversarial perturbations, or data augmentation can produce variants whose prediction diversity reveals proximity to decision boundaries. In deep active learning, these techniques exploit the geometry of neural representation spaces to better capture epistemic uncertainty than raw output scores alone. Implementations often rely on efficient nearest-neighbor search or adversarial attack algorithms over deep embeddings. Such criteria are then used as query functions to prioritize instances whose local regions exhibit high predictive instability.

canonical_topics.name: Deep Active Learning with Modern Learning Paradigms
canonical_topics.description: Deep active learning frequently combines query strategies with advanced training paradigms such as modern neural architectures, transfer learning, and semi-supervised learning. Neural encoders and large pretrained language models provide rich representations that can change how informativeness and diversity are measured. Transfer learning allows active selection to focus on domain adaptation, deciding which target-domain examples to label when starting from a pretrained model. Semi-supervised and consistency-based techniques further exploit unlabeled data, interacting with the query strategy to avoid redundancy and overfitting. The survey examines how these components jointly influence label efficiency, stability, and overall performance in NLP tasks.

canonical_topics.name: Deep Active Learning for Structured NLP Prediction
canonical_topics.description: Applying deep active learning to NLP often involves structured outputs such as sequences, trees, or alignments. Query strategies must reason about informativeness at the level of entire structures, spans, or tokens, rather than single-class labels. For neural sequence labeling, parsing, and machine translation models, this leads to criteria defined over sequence-level uncertainties, marginal token distributions, or surrogate losses. Some approaches decompose structured uncertainty to identify the most informative substructures, while others operate on full-sequence predictions or n-best lists. The survey reviews these specialized methods and their empirical behavior across structured NLP tasks.

canonical_topics.name: Initialization Strategies for Deep Active Learning Loops
canonical_topics.description: The choice of initial labeled seed set can strongly affect the stability and convergence of deep active learning. Random seeding is simple but may yield poor coverage for high-dimensional neural representations. Alternative strategies use diversity criteria, clustering in embedding space, or heuristic rules to ensure that the first training iterations produce a reasonably calibrated model. For deep networks, robust initialization can mitigate early-stage overfitting and reduce the risk of query bias in subsequent rounds. The survey systematically reviews these initialization strategies and their impact on label efficiency and final performance.

topics.title: Error and ambiguity-based performance predictors
topics.description: A simpler performance-oriented idea is to directly target instances that are currently erroneous or ambiguous for the task model. This can involve training an auxiliary model to predict instance-wise loss, judge correctness of predictions, or determine when expert querying is needed in structured prediction. Inspired by data maps, some methods look for instances with intermediate average correctness over training, and in machine translation, error-prone examples are identified via backward translation (round-trip consistency) or quality estimation models.

topics.title: Density-based representativeness measures
topics.description: Density-based methods prioritize instances that lie in dense regions of the unlabeled data, so that labeled examples are representative rather than outliers. Simple proxies include n-gram or word-count statistics, while more general approaches compute each instance’s average similarity to all others. To reduce computational cost, k-nearest neighbor similarity is often used instead of full pairwise similarity over the pool.

topics.title: Discriminative representativeness versus labeled data
topics.description: Discriminative strategies select unlabeled instances that differ most from the already labeled set, emphasizing coverage of novel features and domains. This can be operationalized with feature-based metrics such as unseen n-grams or out-of-vocabulary words, or via similarity scores that prefer instances dissimilar to labeled examples. More sophisticated methods explicitly train a classifier or adversarial model to distinguish labeled from unlabeled data, and in domain adaptation settings, domain separators serve a similar filtering role.

topics.title: Greedy and clustering-based batch diversity
topics.description: Two main families of methods ensure batch diversity: greedy iterative selection and clustering-based selection. Iterative methods build batches step by step, each time choosing instances that are both useful and dissimilar from those already chosen, and can approximate advanced criteria like coresets or determinantal point processes. Clustering-based approaches partition the unlabeled pool into clusters and select representatives from different clusters, using similarities based on input features, learned representations, model-based similarity, gradients, or masked LM surprisal embeddings.

topics.title: Static hybrid combinations of query criteria
topics.description: Hybrid strategies combine informativeness and representativeness into a single scoring function for each instance. Simple static combinations include weighted sums or multiplicative formulas that merge multiple criteria, such as uncertainty and density. These methods do not adapt during training but provide a straightforward way to balance competing objectives in query selection.

topics.title: Integrated hybrids: clustering, gradients, and DPPs
topics.description: Some methods integrate multiple criteria more organically into a single selection mechanism. Examples include uncertainty-weighted clustering, where cluster selection is biased by instance uncertainty; diverse gradient selection, where gradient vectors encode both uncertainty and diversity; and DPP-based methods that factorize quality (e.g., informativeness) and diversity in a probabilistic selection model. These approaches jointly model what is informative and how to diversify the selected set.

topics.title: Multi-step and dynamic hybrid querying
topics.description: Multi-step querying applies different criteria in sequence, such as first filtering highly uncertain instances and then clustering them, or selecting the most uncertain instance within each cluster. Dynamic hybrids go further by changing the mixture of strategies over time, recognizing that representativeness may matter more in early AL stages while uncertainty becomes more reliable later. Methods like DUAL and GraDUAL formalize this by switching or interpolating between density-based and uncertainty-based selectors, and other work uses predefined monotonic functions to control combination weights throughout the AL process.

topics.title: Active learning for structured prediction
topics.description: Many NLP tasks require predicting structured outputs (e.g., label sequences, parse trees) composed of interdependent variables, which complicates querying and annotation compared to flat classification. A central design decision is whether to query labels for entire structures or only for selected sub-structures. This choice affects how utilities, uncertainties, and annotation workflows are defined and computed.

topics.title: Full-structure active learning utilities
topics.description: When querying full output structures, uncertainty-based strategies such as entropy must evaluate probabilities over an exponentially large output space. This is approximated using dynamic-programming algorithms for tree- and sequence-entropy, or via top-k approximations that treat k-best predicted structures as a proxy for the full space. These techniques adapt standard active learning criteria to settings where explicit enumeration of all structures is infeasible.

topics.title: Disagreement, length bias, and aggregation in full-structure AL
topics.description: For disagreement-based strategies in structured prediction, exact full-structure agreement is often too strict, so partial-disagreement measures and fine-grained scores (e.g., F1 for sequence labeling) are used. Because longer instances tend to appear more uncertain, length normalization is employed to mitigate length bias, though there is debate about whether long sequences should be discouraged. Utilities for a whole structure can also be built by aggregating token- or factor-level scores, using operations such as sums, averages, frequency-weighted sums, or selecting only the least-probable sub-structure.

canonical_topics.name: Error- and Loss-Based Query Predictors
canonical_topics.description: Error- and ambiguity-based approaches select instances by explicitly predicting where the task model is likely to fail. Auxiliary models can be trained to approximate instance-wise loss, estimate correctness of current predictions, or flag cases where expert intervention is needed, especially in structured prediction tasks. Inspired by data maps, some methods target examples with intermediate or unstable correctness over training, which tend to be most informative. In machine translation and related sequence tasks, error-prone candidates can also be identified via round-trip consistency checks (back-translation) or quality estimation models that predict translation adequacy and fluency without reference labels.

canonical_topics.name: Representativeness and Batch Diversity Criteria
canonical_topics.description: Representativeness-based methods favor unlabeled instances from dense regions of the data space so that newly labeled examples reflect common patterns instead of outliers. Density can be approximated with simple statistics like n-grams or word counts, or via similarity-based measures such as average similarity to all (or k-nearest) pool instances in an embedding space. Complementary discriminative criteria prioritize instances that differ most from the labeled set, using feature coverage metrics (e.g., unseen n-grams, out-of-vocabulary tokens) or classifiers trained to distinguish labeled from unlabeled data, including domain separators in adaptation settings. For batch-mode active learning, greedy selection and clustering-based methods further ensure diversity by iteratively picking examples that are dissimilar from already chosen points or by selecting representatives from different clusters. These strategies often rely on input features, learned representations, model-based similarities, gradients, or surprisal-based embeddings to jointly capture coverage and diversity.

canonical_topics.name: Hybrid Informativeness–Diversity Query Strategies
canonical_topics.description: Hybrid active learning strategies combine informativeness (e.g., uncertainty, expected error reduction) with representativeness or diversity into unified selection mechanisms. Static hybrids use fixed formulas—such as weighted sums or multiplicative combinations—to score each instance, trading off uncertainty with density or dissimilarity in a simple, non-adaptive way. Integrated hybrids more tightly couple criteria, for example by performing uncertainty-weighted clustering, encoding both uncertainty and diversity in gradient vectors, or using determinantal point processes that factorize quality and diversity terms. Multi-step hybrids apply criteria sequentially, such as filtering on high uncertainty then clustering, or selecting the most uncertain element within each cluster. Dynamic hybrids further adapt the mixture of strategies over time, often emphasizing representativeness early when the model is weak and shifting toward uncertainty later, using schemes like DUAL, GraDUAL, or predefined scheduling functions to control this evolution.

canonical_topics.name: Active Learning for Structured Prediction
canonical_topics.description: Active learning for structured prediction deals with outputs such as sequences, trees, or graphs whose components are interdependent, making query design and annotation more complex than for flat classification. A key choice is whether to query full structures or only specific sub-structures, which directly impacts utility definitions, computational cost, and annotator workload. For full-structure querying, uncertainty measures like entropy must operate over an exponentially large output space, and are typically approximated with dynamic-programming algorithms for sequence- and tree-entropy or with top-k surrogate distributions over the best-scoring structures. Disagreement-based methods often relax exact structure agreement, instead using partial-overlap measures (e.g., token-level F1) and addressing length bias through normalization, while debating whether longer sequences should be penalized or favored. Utilities for entire structures can also be built by aggregating token- or factor-level scores via sums, averages, frequency-weighted schemes, or by focusing on the least confident sub-structures to concentrate annotation on the most contentious regions.

Density-based methods prefer instances lying in dense regions, using proxies such as n-gram statistics, word-count features, or similarity-based density in an embedding space, often approximated with k-nearest neighbor similarity for scalability. canonical_topics.description: Structured prediction tasks in NLP, such as sequence labeling and parsing, produce interdependent outputs that complicate query design and annotation workflows. A key decision is whether to query full output structures or only selected sub-structures, which directly affects how utilities, uncertainties, and labeling costs are defined. For full-structure querying, uncertainty-based utilities like entropy must operate over exponentially large output spaces, and are approximated using dynamic-programming formulations for sequence or tree entropy, or via top-k approximations that treat a k-best list as a proxy for the full distribution. Disagreement-based strategies similarly face challenges: exact whole-structure agreement is often too strict, so partial-disagreement metrics and task-specific scores (e.g., F1 over sequence labels) are employed, along with length normalization to mitigate biases toward longer instances. More generally, utilities can be constructed by aggregating token- or factor-level scores—through sums, averages, frequency-weighted sums, or focusing on the least probable sub-structures—enabling practical deep active learning in complex structured output spaces.

topics.title: Coarser sub-structures and grouped queries
topics.description: Instead of querying the smallest possible units, many approaches select larger sub-structures (e.g., sub-sequences, head edges, neighborhood pools, phrases) to better align with how annotators read and to reduce context switching. Coarser granularity can alleviate the missed-class effect, where rare or difficult classes are overlooked when sampling too locally. Grouping strategies—such as first selecting uncertain sentences and then uncertain tokens within them, or choosing nearby instances sequentially—further streamline annotation and reduce cognitive load.

topics.title: Computer-assisted and interactive annotation
topics.description: Direct cost reduction can be achieved by tighter model–annotator interaction, such as pre-annotation where models supply best or top-k predictions that annotators correct instead of labeling from scratch. This paradigm underlies post-editing in machine translation and has been shown effective when combined with AL. More interactive systems continuously propagate user corrections back into the model during annotation sessions—e.g., interactive machine translation where the system updates its prediction after each corrected character—thereby reducing human effort further; AL can be integrated into such systems to prioritize which segments to present. Crowdsourcing is highlighted as another complementary cost-reduction mechanism.

topics.title: Reducing wait time in active learning loops
topics.description: Active learning involves iterative cycles of training and querying that impose wait time on annotators, motivating methods to accelerate these stages. Query-time speedups include sub-sampling large unlabeled pools, caching invariant computations, and approximating densities or nearest neighbors with k-NN methods. For training, incremental warm-starting may seem natural but can harm neural performance, so full retraining is often preferred, sometimes paired with using a lightweight model for querying and a stronger model for final training. Additional reductions come from accepting stale model information via batch-mode AL and parallel AL architectures that decouple and continuously run annotation, training, and scoring processes.

topics.title: Distilled and proxy models for querying
topics.description: To improve efficiency without sacrificing too much active learning performance, smaller distilled or proxy models can be used for query selection. Distillation compresses a large pre-trained model into a smaller one that approximates its behavior, enabling faster querying and shorter annotator wait time. Works cited show that these proxy models can be periodically synchronized with the main model via distillation, sometimes combined with pseudo-labeling and sub-sampling to further reduce computational cost.

topics.title: Pretraining and continual transfer in AL
topics.description: Transfer learning is integrated with active learning by initializing models from large pre-trained language models and further adapting them through continual training. Pretrained representations reduce the amount of task-specific annotation needed, while continual training allows incremental adaptation to new domains or tasks during the AL process. Meta-learning is also used to initialize models so they can learn effectively from small actively acquired datasets, and similar transfer ideas are applied to the model-based query policy itself.

topics.title: Transductive, domain, and cross-lingual transfer
topics.description: Transductive learning within active learning transfers information from specific target unlabeled sets, such as other domains or languages, to reduce annotation needs. Methods leverage labeled or unlabeled data from related domains to guide selection and learning in the target domain, and similarly exploit cross-lingual signals when data in one language is scarce. This creates a multi-source scenario where active learning decisions and model updates are informed by heterogeneous but related data distributions.

topics.title: Weak supervision integrated with active learning
topics.description: Weak supervision is combined with active learning by using imperfect or indirect supervision sources such as execution results, structure-based heuristics, gazetteers, and interactively discovered labeling rules. In this setting, actively selected instances may be labeled not only by humans but also by weak labeling functions or auxiliary resources, thereby reducing manual annotation effort. The section illustrates this with examples from semantic parsing, entity representation, sequence labeling, and rule-learning workflows.

topics.title: Data augmentation and query synthesis in AL
topics.description: Data augmentation techniques are applied within active learning to expand training data and improve generalization, using methods such as iterative back-translation, mixup for sequence labeling, and phrase-to-sentence transformations for machine translation. Augmentation can also be tied directly to instance querying, where transformations inform which examples to select. An advanced variant, query synthesis, generates new synthetic instances for annotation instead of sampling from an existing pool, and has shown promise for simpler text classification scenarios despite the challenges of realistic text generation.

topics.title: Random and representativeness-based seeding strategies
topics.description: Random sampling is widely used to initialize AL because it preserves the original data distribution and is simple to apply. More sophisticated representativeness-based strategies select instances near clustering centroids to obtain seed sets that are both representative and diverse. These seeding methods aim to provide a strong starting point before more complex query strategies are applied.

topics.title: Advanced models for AL initialization
topics.description: Advanced learning techniques can assist in selecting informative seed instances before standard AL cycles begin. These include transfer learning and unsupervised methods to capture structure in unlabeled data, as well as language-model-based approaches. Examples include selecting low-probability words for word sense disambiguation or choosing cluster centers using surprisal embeddings from pre-trained contextualized LMs.

canonical_topics.name: Structured query granularity and grouped annotation
canonical_topics.description: This topic studies querying at coarser structural units rather than at the smallest token level in deep active learning pipelines. Methods select sub-sequences, dependency edges, neighborhood pools, or whole phrases and sentences to better match how annotators read and reason about text. Coarser granularity reduces context switching and cognitive load, since annotators label meaningful chunks instead of scattered isolated items. It also mitigates the missed-class effect, where rare or difficult classes may be overlooked when sampling too locally. Grouped querying strategies, such as first selecting uncertain sentences and then uncertain tokens within them or querying spatially or semantically neighboring instances, further streamline the annotation workflow.

canonical_topics.name: Interactive annotation and computer-assisted labeling
canonical_topics.description: This topic focuses on tighter interaction between models and annotators to reduce labeling cost in deep active learning. Computer-assisted annotation provides pre-annotations or top-k predictions that humans correct, turning labeling into a post-editing task rather than annotation from scratch. Interactive systems continuously update their predictions in response to user corrections, as in interactive machine translation where each keystroke or corrected segment triggers model adaptation. Active learning is integrated to select the most informative segments for display, maximizing the impact of human effort. Crowdsourcing can complement these techniques by distributing pre-annotated or interactively chosen instances across many non-expert annotators.

canonical_topics.name: Efficient active learning with proxy models
canonical_topics.description: This topic addresses reducing wait time and computational cost in deep active learning loops while preserving query quality. Query-time speedups include sub-sampling large unlabeled pools, caching invariant computations, and approximating densities or nearest neighbors with fast k-NN-style methods. On the training side, practitioners often favor full retraining over naive incremental warm-starting for neural models, but may use lightweight surrogate models during querying and reserve heavier models for final training. Distilled or proxy networks approximate larger models and can perform uncertainty estimation and selection much faster, periodically synchronized via knowledge distillation and sometimes augmented with pseudo-labeling or sub-sampling. Additional efficiencies come from batch-mode active learning and parallel architectures that decouple and continuously run annotation, training, and scoring processes.

canonical_topics.name: Transfer and pretraining strategies for active learning
canonical_topics.description: This topic investigates how transfer learning and pretraining can reduce annotation requirements in deep active learning. Large pre-trained language models provide strong initial representations, so active learning starts from a high-capacity encoder that needs fewer task-specific labels to reach good performance. Continual and transductive training adapt models to new domains or specific unlabeled target sets during the active learning process, allowing query strategies and models to exploit information from related domains. Cross-domain and cross-lingual setups leverage labeled or unlabeled data from other distributions or languages to guide selection in low-resource targets. Meta-learning and related techniques can also initialize models or query policies themselves so they adapt quickly from the small, actively acquired datasets.

canonical_topics.name: Weak supervision and data augmentation in AL
canonical_topics.description: This topic explores combining weak supervision and data augmentation with deep active learning to reduce reliance on expensive human labels. Weak supervision sources such as heuristics, programmatic labeling rules, gazetteers, execution results, or structural signals provide noisy but cheap labels that complement human annotations. Active learning policies can choose which instances should be sent to humans versus weak labelers, or which examples are most useful for refining labeling rules in semantic parsing, entity recognition, and other structured prediction tasks. Data augmentation further expands training sets via techniques like back-translation, mixup for sequence labeling, and phrase-to-sentence transformations for machine translation. Query synthesis extends this idea by generating new synthetic instances for annotation rather than sampling from an existing pool, which has shown particular promise for simpler text classification scenarios.

topics.title: Dataset choices for computing stopping metrics
topics.description: The dataset used to compute stopping metrics can significantly affect the stability and reliability of stopping decisions. Improperly chosen sets may lead to unstable measurements, motivating the use of a separate unlabeled dataset for monitoring. Since many stopping metrics do not require gold labels, this auxiliary dataset can be large to reduce variance, though increased size can also introduce practical concerns such as longer evaluation wait times.

topics.title: Curriculum learning integrated with AL
topics.description: Curriculum learning arranges training instances in a meaningful or progressively harder order, and can be combined with AL to guide which examples to query and when. This integration considers both informativeness (from AL) and pedagogical ordering (from curriculum learning) to improve training efficiency and model performance.

topics.title: Model efficiency and wait time in AL
topics.description: Model efficiency is emphasized as crucial in AL to reduce the annotator’s wait time between query selection and labeling. Because AL involves repeated retraining or updating models as new labels arrive, computational efficiency and system latency directly affect the practicality and user experience of AL systems.

topics.title: Applying AL to complex NLP tasks
topics.description: The survey notes that AL has been used mainly for simple classification, while more complex tasks like text generation, NLI, and QA remain underexplored. These tasks involve richer outputs and more complex inputs, making unlabeled data collection and annotation harder, yet early work suggests AL can still aid data collection and model training for them.

topics.title: AL beyond direct target labeling
topics.description: AL can query not only task labels but also auxiliary supervision such as features, rationales, explanations, evaluations, or symbolic rules. By selecting informative instances for these richer annotation types, AL can support tasks like feature labeling, rationale collection, explanation annotation, and rule discovery to enhance downstream models.

topics.title: Practical deployment challenges of AL
topics.description: Most AL research simulates annotation using existing labeled datasets, overlooking real-world issues like true annotation cost, efficiency and wait time, data reuse, and when to start or stop AL. In practice, AL processes are often non-repeatable, making the choice of query strategies and hyperparameters critical yet difficult, and addressing these challenges is key for wider industrial adoption.

topics.title: Cross-domain transfer of AL methods
topics.description: The limitations section highlights that many AL techniques, particularly querying strategies developed in computer vision, may be transferable to NLP tasks. It advocates looking beyond NLP-specific work and leveraging insights and algorithms from other domains to improve AL for language applications.

topics.title: Need for comparative AL experiments
topics.description: The survey acknowledges the lack of empirical comparisons across AL strategies within the work itself, pointing to a broader need for systematic experimental studies. Comparative benchmarks evaluating multiple AL methods under shared conditions could yield more actionable guidance for practitioners selecting strategies for specific NLP tasks.

topics.title: Supervised models in remote sensing
topics.description: The section highlights the widespread use of statistical learning models—especially Support Vector Machines and neural networks—for supervised classification of land use from modern satellite imagery. It notes their effectiveness on very high spatial and spectral resolution data, framing them as state-of-the-art techniques in remote sensing image classification.

topics.title: Training set representativeness and cost
topics.description: Performance of supervised classifiers is described as heavily dependent on how representative the training data are of the underlying classes. Constructing such appropriate training sets is portrayed as difficult and expensive, since it often requires extensive manual analysis via visual inspection or field surveys followed by sample labeling.

canonical_topics.name: Datasets for Active Learning Stopping Criteria
canonical_topics.description: The choice of dataset used to compute stopping metrics in active learning strongly influences the stability and reliability of stopping decisions. Using the same training pool can bias or destabilize estimates, motivating the use of a separate monitoring set. Because many stopping criteria rely on model outputs rather than gold labels, this auxiliary dataset can be unlabeled and relatively large to reduce variance. However, larger monitoring sets increase evaluation time and system latency, which is especially critical for deep models retrained frequently during active learning. Designing stopping datasets therefore requires balancing statistical stability, computational cost, and responsiveness to model changes.

canonical_topics.name: Integrating Curriculum Learning with Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: Curriculum learning can be combined with active learning to control not only which examples are queried, but also the order in which they are presented to the model. Instead of selecting purely by uncertainty or informativeness, the system can enforce a pedagogical progression from simpler to more complex instances. This integration aims to stabilize training dynamics, improve sample efficiency, and mitigate catastrophic forgetting in deep models. Designing such curricula requires criteria that jointly capture example difficulty, informativeness, and diversity over the active learning loop. The resulting frameworks can adapt the curriculum as the model improves, continually reshaping both query selection and presentation order.

canonical_topics.name: System Efficiency and Deployment Constraints in Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: Practical deployment of active learning hinges on computational efficiency and low annotator wait time. Deep models must often be retrained or at least incrementally updated after each batch of queried labels, turning training cost and inference speed into critical bottlenecks. Long delays between query selection and availability of updated predictions can degrade annotator experience and make interactive labeling workflows infeasible. Real-world deployments are typically non-repeatable, so choices of model architecture, query strategy, and hyperparameters must be robust under tight resource constraints. Addressing these efficiency and latency challenges is essential for moving active learning from simulated studies into reliable industrial systems.

canonical_topics.name: Active Learning for Complex NLP Tasks and Cross-Domain Transfer
canonical_topics.description: Most active learning research focuses on relatively simple classification tasks, leaving complex NLP problems such as text generation, natural language inference, and question answering underexplored. These tasks involve structured, high-dimensional outputs and nuanced inputs, which complicate both uncertainty estimation and annotation workflows. At the same time, many query strategies and heuristics developed in domains like computer vision may be transferable to these NLP settings with appropriate adaptation. Leveraging cross-domain insights can help design query criteria, acquisition functions, and model architectures better suited for complex language tasks. Systematic studies are needed to understand how methods from other modalities perform and must be modified when applied to sequence-to-sequence and reasoning-heavy NLP problems.

canonical_topics.name: Active Learning with Rich and Auxiliary Supervision
canonical_topics.description: Active learning can target more than just primary task labels, extending to auxiliary supervision such as feature annotations, rationales, explanations, evaluations, or symbolic rules. By selectively querying informative instances for these richer annotation types, systems can build interpretable models, improve sample efficiency, or learn better intermediate representations. For deep models, annotated rationales and explanations can guide attention mechanisms or constrain latent spaces, while rule-like supervision can regularize decision boundaries. Designing acquisition functions that account for the cost and utility of different supervision types is a central challenge. This broader view positions active learning as a general framework for interactive supervision, not just label acquisition.

topics.title: Requirements for compact, informative training sets
topics.description: The section concludes that desirable training sets should be small yet constructed 'in a smart way,' focusing on discriminative pixels that accurately capture class boundaries. This requirement is especially critical for very high spatial or spectral resolution classification, where feature spaces are large and complex but training information is limited.

topics.title: Pool-based active learning notation
topics.description: The section formally defines the labeled training set X = {x_i, y_i} with class labels y_i in {1, …, N} and feature vectors x_i in a d-dimensional input space ℝ^d. It also defines the unlabeled set U = {x_i}, a large pool of candidate pixels (u ≫ l) from which the algorithm selects samples to be labeled. This establishes the pool-based setting common in active learning for remote sensing.

topics.title: Iterative sampling and model adaptation
topics.description: Active learning algorithms are described as iterative sampling schemes in which the classification model is regularly updated by incorporating newly labeled pixels. The new samples are chosen to be those most beneficial for improving model performance, typically based on some informativeness criterion. This captures the core process of alternating between sample selection, labeling, and model refinement.

topics.title: Heuristic-based candidate evaluation and ranking
topics.description: Each unlabeled candidate in the pool is scored with a user-defined heuristic that quantifies its interest for labeling. The candidates are then ranked according to this heuristic score, guiding which samples are most informative to query. This mechanism allows the algorithm to prioritize samples expected to most improve the model.

topics.title: Uncertainty reduction as selection objective
topics.description: The selection strategy aims to target areas where the model exhibits low confidence. By adding such uncertain samples to the training set, the algorithm forces the classifier to resolve these regions of uncertainty, simultaneously seeking to maximize performance gain. This articulates the underlying objective guiding the heuristic used in candidate selection.

topics.title: Bagging-based committee construction
topics.description: A committee of classifiers is built using bagging, where k training sets are generated by drawing with replacement from the original labeled data. Each bootstrapped set is used to train a separate classifier, and the committee collectively predicts labels for unlabeled candidate pixels. This results in k labelings for each candidate pixel, forming the basis for estimating uncertainty. The approach leverages only a part of the available labeled pixels in each bag to induce diversity among committee members.

topics.title: Multi-view committees via feature partitioning
topics.description: High-dimensional remote sensing data are handled by splitting the original feature space into multiple disjoint subsets or views, and building a committee of classifiers, each operating on a different view. For hyperspectral images, these views can be derived from the block-diagonal structure of the covariance matrix, so that each block defines a feature subset. Each view produces an independent classification of the same pixel, enabling disagreement-based or entropy-based query heuristics similar to nEQB. This multi-view construction underpins the later definition of the AMD selection rule.

topics.title: SVM decision function and confidence
topics.description: This topic details the SVM decision function used in active learning, including the kernel-based representation, dual coefficients, and support vectors. It highlights how the absolute value of f(xi), the distance from a sample to the hyperplane, serves as a confidence indicator, with larger margins implying more certain classifications. The entities involved include kernels K(xj, xi), support vectors xj with non-zero αj, and binary labels yj.

topics.title: Large margin heuristics visualization
topics.description: The section introduces a three-class toy example to illustrate large margin active learning heuristics for SVMs. Distances from decision hyperplanes are visualized by color intensity, with black indicating points on or near the decision boundary and white indicating maximal distance. The MS (Margin Sampling) and MCLU heuristics are compared by showing that areas of maximal uncertainty correspond to regions minimizing their respective objective functions (Eq. (7) and Eq. (9)). Additional subfigures depict absolute per-class distances to each hyperplane.

topics.title: Alternative names for margin sampling
