topics.description: The text notes that the margin sampling heuristic appears in the literature under several different names. These include “most ambiguous,” “binary level uncertainty,” and “SVMSIMPLE,” reflecting slight terminological variations across studies. Despite the naming differences, these methods all implement the same core idea of querying samples near the SVM decision boundary.

canonical_topics.name: Compact Informative Training Sets in Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: In deep active learning, training sets should be kept as small as possible while still being highly informative. Rather than sampling pixels uniformly, the labeled set is constructed to concentrate on discriminative regions, especially around class boundaries. This requirement is crucial in very high spatial or spectral resolution settings, where the feature space is large and complex but labeled data are scarce. Designing compact, boundary-focused training sets motivates many active learning criteria that seek samples with maximal expected impact on the decision function.

canonical_topics.name: Pool-Based Active Learning Setup and Iterative Loop
canonical_topics.description: Pool-based active learning assumes an initial labeled set L = {(x_i, y_i)} with class labels y_i ∈ {1,…,N} and feature vectors x_i in a d-dimensional space ℝ^d, together with a large unlabeled pool U = {x_j}. Since |U| ≫ |L|, the learner repeatedly selects a small subset of candidates from U to be labeled by an oracle. After each annotation step, the classifier is retrained or updated using the expanded labeled set. This defines an iterative cycle of sample selection, labeling, and model refinement that is standard in deep active learning and remote sensing applications. The notation and loop structure provide the foundation on which specific query strategies and models are built.

canonical_topics.name: Uncertainty-Based Query Scoring with SVM Margins
canonical_topics.description: In uncertainty-driven deep active learning, each unlabeled candidate in the pool is scored by a heuristic that estimates its potential usefulness for improving the model. For SVM-based learners, the decision function f(x) expressed in terms of kernels, dual coefficients, and support vectors provides a natural confidence measure: the absolute value |f(x)| reflects the distance to the separating hyperplane, with smaller margins indicating higher uncertainty. Candidates are ranked by such scores so that the algorithm queries labels for the most uncertain or informative samples, explicitly targeting regions where the model currently has low confidence. This process can be interpreted as directly aiming to reduce classification uncertainty and sharpen decision boundaries. Margin-based strategies, often referred to as margin sampling, most ambiguous, binary-level uncertainty, or SVMSIMPLE, all implement this same core idea. Visualizations with toy multi-class examples further illustrate how objectives such as Margin Sampling (MS) and MCLU identify areas of maximal ambiguity near SVM decision hyperplanes.

canonical_topics.name: Committee-Based Active Learning via Bagging and Multi-View Features
canonical_topics.description: Committee-based active learning constructs a set of diverse classifiers whose disagreements guide sample selection. One way to build such a committee is bagging, where multiple training sets are produced by sampling with replacement from the labeled data and each bootstrap set trains a separate model, ensuring diversity because each classifier only sees part of the labeled pool. For high-dimensional remote sensing data, an additional source of diversity comes from multi-view learning, where the original feature space is partitioned into disjoint subsets and an independent classifier is trained on each view. In hyperspectral imagery, these views can be derived from block-diagonal structures in the covariance matrix, with each block defining a feature subset. The committee’s multiple predictions for each unlabeled pixel enable disagreement- or entropy-based query heuristics, which underpin selection rules such as those used in advanced multi-view disagreement (AMD) strategies.

topics.title: Significance space construction using SV coefficients
topics.description: Significance space construction (SSC) replaces distance to the SVM hyperplane as the uncertainty measure with a detection problem based on support vector coefficients. Training samples with α_j > 0 (support vectors) are treated as one class and samples with α_j = 0 as the other, defining a second classifier f(x)^SSC for support vector detection. Applied to the unlabeled pool, this classifier predicts which pixels are likely to become future support vectors, and the selection rule x̂_SSC = arg_{x_i∈U} f(x_i)^SSC > 0 focuses on these significant candidates. After identifying this subset, a random selection among the predicted support-vector-like samples is performed for labeling.

topics.title: MCLU-ABD uncertainty-diversity trade-off
topics.description: The MCLU-ABD (multi-class level uncertainty – angle-based diversity) heuristic combines multiclass uncertainty with a kernel-based diversity term. Candidate samples are first restricted to those maximizing the MCLU uncertainty measure, then a query function balances uncertainty f(xi)_MC and normalized kernel similarity to already selected samples using a trade-off parameter λ. This generalizes MAO to arbitrary kernels by normalizing in feature space and explicitly integrating uncertainty and diversity in a single objective.

topics.title: Support-vector-based margin diversification
topics.description: Diversity is enforced by constraining margin sampling to points associated with different closest support vectors, leading to the cSV-based selection rule. This divides the margin in feature space according to the geometric distribution of support vectors, ensuring that queried samples are diverse with respect to the current SVM decision structure. However, it may still select mutually close samples if they are linked to different support vectors, so inter-sample diversity is not guaranteed.

topics.title: Boosting and computational limits of KL method
topics.description: An extension of the KL-divergence approach uses boosting to down-weight previously selected pixels that have become less relevant to the current classifier. This heuristic is practical only with classifiers of low computational cost, because each active learning iteration requires training u+1 models (one per candidate plus the base model). Consequently, it is considered unsuitable for computationally demanding methods such as SVMs and does not naturally support selecting batches of pixels. The topic highlights a trade-off between informativeness of the criterion and computational feasibility in large-scale remote sensing settings.

topics.title: Platt scaling for SVM probability estimates
topics.description: To apply BT with SVMs, decision function outputs are converted into approximate posterior probabilities using Platt’s method. This involves fitting a sigmoid of the form p(y*i = ω|xi) = 1 / (1 + e^(A f(xi, ω) + B)), where A and B are estimated parameters. Although these quantities are not Bayesian posteriors in a strict sense, they serve as practical per-class probability estimates usable by active learning heuristics. This calibration step enables SVMs to participate in probability-based selection criteria like BT.

topics.title: Link between BT and MCLU for SVMs
topics.description: A close relationship is highlighted between the Breaking Ties heuristic and the Margin-based Confidence-based Learning Utility (MCLU) heuristic when using SVM classifiers. By comparing the BT formulation in equation (20) with equation (8), the text notes that both methods effectively target samples with minimal margin between top class hypotheses. This establishes BT as conceptually aligned with margin-based active learning strategies in SVM-based remote sensing classification.

topics.title: Nonlinear manifolds and classifier choice
topics.description: Spectral mean profiles and manifold visualizations reveal high nonlinearity and strong class overlap in the hyperspectral dataset. These characteristics imply that linear decision boundaries are inadequate, leading to poor performance by linear classifiers. Consequently, linear models are explicitly excluded from the subsequent experiments on this dataset.

topics.title: Morphological contextual feature extraction
topics.description: To address spectral similarity between certain land-use classes, 16 contextual bands are derived using morphological opening and closing operators applied to the image. These features are concatenated with the original 4 spectral bands, producing a 20-dimensional representation that captures spatial structure in addition to spectral information. The opening features enhance discrimination of vegetation-related classes, while closing features improve separability of asphalt-related classes such as roads and parking lots.

topics.title: Experimental protocol for active learning
topics.description: The section describes how labeled pixels are iteratively added to the training set (N+5 and N+20 pixels per iteration) and how many iterations are run for three different images until convergence. It specifies different iteration counts for SVM and LDA experiments and configures nEQB with varying committee sizes and proportions of available training data. This protocol defines the process by which the active learning algorithms are evaluated over time.

topics.title: Heuristic families and comparison goals
topics.description: The numerical results compare several active learning heuristics—nEQB, MS, MCLU, MCLU-ABD, and BT—on three datasets, alongside Random Sampling and the base learner (Standard SVM/LDA). Rather than identifying a universally best heuristic, the study aims to characterize the strengths and weaknesses of different method families relative to data characteristics. This framework is intended to guide users in selecting suitable active learning strategies for specific remote sensing problems.

canonical_topics.name: Uncertainty–diversity heuristic families in active learning
canonical_topics.description: This topic covers families of pool-based active learning heuristics that combine uncertainty and diversity, with a focus on margin-based methods such as Breaking Ties (BT), MCLU, and its MCLU-ABD extension. Multiclass uncertainty is quantified from the classifier’s output scores or margins, while diversity is enforced through similarity measures (e.g., kernel or angle-based) so that selected samples both challenge the current decision boundary and are not redundant. A trade-off parameter balances these two components in a single objective, generalizing classic margin and Maximal Angled Orthant (MAO) ideas to arbitrary feature spaces. The comparison of heuristic families emphasizes that no single strategy is universally best; performance depends on data geometry, class overlap, and model capacity. Information-theoretic criteria such as KL-divergence can be more informative but often require training many models per iteration, highlighting a practical trade-off between selection quality and computational cost that also matters for deep active learning.

canonical_topics.name: Probability calibration for active learning
canonical_topics.description: This topic addresses how margin-based classifiers are converted into probabilistic predictors so they can be used with probability-driven active learning criteria. Methods such as Platt scaling fit a sigmoid to raw decision scores, yielding approximate per-class posterior probabilities even for models like SVMs that are not inherently probabilistic. Although these calibrated quantities are not exact Bayesian posteriors, they provide a practical basis for heuristics like entropy sampling, Breaking Ties, or expected error reduction. The same calibration principles extend to deep networks, where calibrated probabilities or logits are crucial for reliable uncertainty estimates in deep active learning. Proper calibration therefore acts as a bridge between deterministic decision functions and probabilistic acquisition functions.

canonical_topics.name: Experimental protocols for active learning evaluation
canonical_topics.description: This topic describes how to design and report experimental protocols for evaluating active learning algorithms over time. Labeled examples are added to the training set in fixed-size batches across multiple iterations, with separate configurations for different models or datasets to ensure fair comparison. Protocols specify the total number of iterations, batch sizes, stopping criteria, and any committee settings for query-by-committee methods, as well as how much of the available labeled data is used for initialization. Performance is typically tracked as a learning curve of accuracy (or another metric) versus labeling effort, allowing different heuristics to be compared on data efficiency. Clear, reproducible protocols are essential for assessing and benchmarking deep active learning strategies in realistic scenarios.

topics.title: Margin-based heuristics with SVM classifiers
topics.description: When using SVM classifiers, the results (Figure 4) show that Margin Sampling (MS) outperforms nEQB and BT, as MS directly ranks candidates using the SVM decision function without extra probability estimation. nEQB suffers from too-small bags of training pixels, and BT has difficulty estimating posterior probabilities via Platt scaling when the initial training set is small, leading to early performance similar to Random Sampling. The analysis concludes that, under SVMs, large-margin heuristics are generally the most reasonable choice among the active learning families considered.

topics.title: MS and MCLU uncertainty criteria
topics.description: The MS and MCLU heuristics are compared as uncertainty-based criteria for selecting informative samples. Both are found to characterize the uncertainty of candidate instances in a similar way, leading to comparable effectiveness in active learning. This suggests that either measure can be reliably used for uncertainty-driven sample selection with SVMs.

topics.title: Spectral diversity via MCLU-ABD
topics.description: Adding a diversity criterion, particularly a spectral diversity measure such as MCLU-ABD, slightly improves classification performance in most cases. The improvement comes with little additional computational cost, and no degradation is observed compared to using uncertainty alone. An exception is noted for the AVIRIS image, where strong spectral mixing reduces the benefit of the diversity criterion.

topics.title: Active sampling for LDA subspace estimation
topics.description: This topic describes how active sampling improves the estimation of the discriminant subspace in LDA by focusing on informative samples. Random sampling can incorporate noise and outliers, biasing the Fisher’s ratio and leading to a suboptimal linear combination of features in the decision function. By strategically querying pixels, the active learner refines the subspace that better separates classes in the feature space.

topics.title: Refining class statistics via heuristic sampling
topics.description: This topic focuses on how heuristic-guided sampling and correct labeling improve estimates of per-class statistics in LDA, specifically class means (positions) and covariances (extents). Better estimates of these parameters lead to more accurate discriminant functions and improved classification performance. The text notes that beyond approximately 330 labeled pixels, the active learning–based training sets outperform standard LDA, yielding more harmonious classification maps.

topics.title: Overall accuracy as performance metric
topics.description: Overall accuracy is used as the primary metric to assess the quality of supervised classification produced by the different algorithms. Accuracy values ranging approximately from 70 to 95 provide a quantitative basis for comparing the effectiveness of RS, MCLU, MCLU-ABD, and the standard SVM as more labeled data are included.

topics.title: Advantages over random pixel selection
topics.description: Active learning heuristics consistently outperform random selection of pixels once convergence is reached. By selectively querying informative pixels, these heuristics achieve higher classification accuracy than random sampling for the same labeling effort. This establishes a clear benefit of informed query strategies over baseline random sampling in supervised remote sensing image classification. The comparison uses random pixel selection as a reference to quantify the added value of active learning.

topics.title: Multi-view strategies for hyperspectral images
topics.description: For high-dimensional hyperspectral images, strategies that leverage the intrinsic data structure are recommended, particularly multi-view heuristics such as AMD and ECBD-ABD. AMD exploits cross-information directly in the spectral band space, while ECBD-ABD selects candidates using spectral angles between pixels to capture spectral similarity. These methods are presented as especially well-suited to the characteristics of hyperspectral data.

topics.title: Uncertainty estimation and class statistics
topics.description: The section highlights that estimating classification confidence (e.g., probabilities or margins) can be unreliable when it depends heavily on estimated class statistics, as in Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). Poorly estimated class means and covariances can propagate into misleading uncertainty measures, negatively affecting active learning sample selection. A similar issue arises for committee-based methods using bagging when each bag contains only a small portion of the original samples, making committee disagreement unstable.

topics.title: Handling complex manifolds via feature-space modeling
topics.description: For data lying on complex manifolds, redundancy among samples can severely degrade the quality of the active learning sampling and the resulting training set. The text advocates modeling relationships among samples in feature space to better capture manifold structure and select representative pixels. Methods such as kernel k-means within MCLU-ECBD and hMCS, as well as distance to support vectors in the cSV heuristic, are cited as concrete strategies to exploit this relational structure.

canonical_topics.name: Margin-Based Uncertainty Sampling with SVMs
canonical_topics.description: Margin-based heuristics such as Margin Sampling (MS) and related criteria like MCLU select points according to their distance to the SVM decision boundary, avoiding the need for fragile probability calibration. Empirical results show that these methods outperform probability-driven strategies like nEQB and BT when training data are scarce, because posterior estimates (e.g., via Platt scaling) are unreliable in the low-sample regime. By relying directly on the decision function values, margin-based active learning achieves more stable and informative query rankings. This insight transfers naturally to deep active learning, where margin-like scores derived from logits or softmax outputs are often more robust than fully calibrated probabilities early in training.

canonical_topics.name: Active Learning with LDA and Class Statistics
canonical_topics.description: In Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), active sampling can substantially improve the estimation of class means and covariances, leading to a better discriminant subspace. Random sampling tends to include more outliers and mislabeled or uninformative points, which can distort Fisher’s ratio and yield a suboptimal linear combination of features. By selectively querying informative pixels, heuristic-driven active learning refines both per-class statistics and the resulting decision boundaries, improving classification accuracy. However, when uncertainty estimates depend heavily on poorly estimated statistics—either in LDA or in bagging-based committees built from small bags—confidence scores and disagreements can be misleading. Designing active learning strategies that acknowledge the unreliability of early-stage class statistics is therefore crucial, including in deep generative or feature-space models that mimic LDA-like assumptions.

canonical_topics.name: Diversity and Structure-Aware Sampling for Hyperspectral Data
canonical_topics.description: For hyperspectral image classification, augmenting uncertainty sampling with diversity criteria such as spectral diversity (e.g., MCLU-ABD) helps reduce redundancy among queried pixels. These methods typically provide small but consistent gains in accuracy with limited additional computational cost, and rarely degrade performance relative to uncertainty-only selection. Structure-aware strategies, including kernel k-means within MCLU-ECBD or distance-to-support-vector heuristics like cSV, explicitly model relationships in feature space to better capture complex data manifolds. Multi-view approaches such as AMD and ECBD-ABD further exploit complementary structure in different spectral representations, making them particularly well suited to high-dimensional hyperspectral data. Together, these ideas inform deep active learning designs that combine uncertainty, diversity, and manifold structure to construct more representative labeled sets.

canonical_topics.name: Advantages of Active Sampling over Random Labeling
canonical_topics.description: In supervised remote sensing image classification, active learning heuristics consistently outperform random pixel selection once sufficient iterations of querying and retraining have occurred. For a fixed labeling budget, strategies that target informative or representative pixels achieve higher overall accuracy than random sampling, demonstrating the value of informed query policies. Using metrics such as overall accuracy across a range of labeled-set sizes provides a clear quantitative basis for comparing active selection methods like MCLU, MCLU-ABD, and standard SVM training against random baselines. This evaluation paradigm is directly applicable to deep active learning, where gains are likewise measured in terms of accuracy or related metrics per unit of annotation effort.

topics.title: Sequential sampling with moving sensors
topics.description: In scenarios where moving sensors acquire samples sequentially via an automatic device, batch-based querying is unnecessary and potentially inefficient. The priority shifts to models and heuristics with very low computational cost that can be updated rapidly and suggest the next sampling location almost in real time. Within this context, BT (e.g., breaking ties) and KL-max heuristics are identified as particularly suitable due to their favorable computational properties.

topics.title: Legend for algorithm characteristics
topics.description: The table defines a compact legend to encode properties of active learning algorithms: B for binary vs. M for multiclass problems, q as the number of candidate samples, k as the number of learners in a committee, S as batch size, and SVs as support vectors. Checkmarks (✓) and crosses (×) indicate the presence or absence of specific features. This notation supports concise comparison across multiple methods in supervised remote sensing image classification.

topics.title: Ongoing research on active sampling heuristics
topics.description: The text highlights that research on active learning for remote sensing is active and evolving, with new heuristics for active sampling continuously developed. The community in remote sensing and signal processing keeps proposing and testing novel selection strategies, indicating that the current survey is not exhaustive. This underscores a dynamic field with ongoing methodological innovation.

topics.title: Active selection in semi-supervised classification
topics.description: This topic concerns actively selecting unlabeled pixels to improve semi-supervised classification in remote sensing imagery. Active learning strategies query the most informative unlabeled pixels so that limited labeling effort yields maximal gain in classifier performance. It focuses on the interaction between labeled and unlabeled data under a semi-supervised learning regime.

topics.title: Spatially adaptive active learning heuristics
topics.description: Spatially adaptive heuristics adjust active learning query strategies based on spatial properties of the image, such as neighborhood structure or spatial context. Instead of treating each pixel independently, these methods exploit spatial patterns to guide which samples to label. This leads to more efficient learning in spatially correlated remote sensing data.

topics.title: Active learning for cross-domain model adaptation
topics.description: This topic addresses using active learning to adapt models across different domains or scenes, such as transferring a classifier from one geographic area or sensor condition to another. By selectively querying labels in the target domain, the model can be efficiently adapted while minimizing annotation cost. It focuses on domain shift and transfer learning in remote sensing classification.

topics.title: Contextual information in query heuristics
topics.description: Here, the focus is on extending active learning heuristics beyond purely spectral criteria to explicitly incorporate contextual information such as positional data and texture. While current methods largely rely on spectral features or embed context only as additional attributes in the data vector, the text highlights the lack of heuristics that directly reason over spatial position and texture. This involves designing query strategies that model spatial relationships and local image structure.

topics.title: Robustness of uncertainty-based heuristics to noise
topics.description: This topic concerns the vulnerability of uncertainty-driven active learning heuristics to high levels of image noise, particularly in synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data. Since these methods rely on model uncertainty at the pixel level, heavy noise can render uncertainty estimates unreliable and the heuristics ineffective. The text notes that designing noise-robust active learning strategies for such conditions remains an open and largely unexplored research area.

topics.title: AI Systems Approaching Expert Performance
topics.description: AI-powered systems for medical image analysis have achieved performance comparable to human experts in several clinical tasks. The text highlights applications such as skin cancer classification, lung cancer screening with CT, polyp detection during colonoscopy, and prostate cancer detection in whole-slide images. These systems can be integrated into clinical workflows to improve diagnostic accuracy and assist less-experienced clinicians.

topics.title: Deep Learning Foundations for Image Analysis
topics.description: Deep learning models act as the core component of AI-based medical image analysis systems, learning complex patterns directly from raw images and generalizing to unseen cases. Their strength lies in robust feature extraction and generalization capabilities, which have driven major advances in medical image analysis. However, these models typically depend on large-scale human-annotated datasets, exemplified by the ImageNet dataset widely used in computer vision.

canonical_topics.name: Active Learning in Semi-Supervised Remote Sensing
canonical_topics.description: This topic studies how to actively select unlabeled pixels to improve semi-supervised classification of remote sensing imagery. The goal is to query the most informative samples so that limited labeling effort yields maximal improvement in classifier performance. It focuses on the interaction between labeled and unlabeled data, where active learning policies guide which pixels receive ground-truth annotations. The setting is particularly relevant when using deep or other complex models that benefit from carefully curated labels rather than large, randomly sampled training sets.

canonical_topics.name: Spatial and Context-Aware Active Learning Heuristics
canonical_topics.description: This topic addresses active learning strategies that explicitly exploit spatial structure and contextual information in images. Instead of treating each pixel or sample independently, query heuristics are adapted based on neighborhood relations, textures, and positional context. The aim is to design selection criteria that reason directly over spatial patterns and local image structure, not just over spectral or feature vectors. Such spatially adaptive heuristics can yield more informative queries and faster learning in spatially correlated data, such as remote sensing imagery. These ideas are particularly powerful when combined with deep models that already encode context but still rely on informative labeled points.

canonical_topics.name: Active Learning for Cross-Domain Model Adaptation
canonical_topics.description: This topic explores how active learning can support adaptation of classifiers across different domains, scenes, or sensor conditions. A model trained in a source domain is transferred to a target domain, and the learner selectively queries labels on target samples to correct for domain shift. The objective is to reduce annotation cost in the target domain while still achieving high performance, making model deployment more scalable. This is especially relevant for deep models in remote sensing, where data distributions can vary drastically across geographic regions or acquisition setups.

canonical_topics.name: Online Active Learning with Moving Sensors
canonical_topics.description: This topic focuses on active learning in scenarios where moving sensors acquire data sequentially, such as along satellite or aerial trajectories. In this setting, batch-based querying is unnecessary or inefficient, and the learner must decide in near real time whether and where to request labels. Emphasis is placed on very low-computation heuristics, such as breaking ties or simple KL-based criteria, that can be updated rapidly as new data arrive. The challenge is to balance computational constraints with informativeness of queries, particularly when deep models are used in resource-limited or onboard environments.

canonical_topics.name: Noise-Robust Uncertainty-Based Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: This topic examines the behavior and limitations of uncertainty-driven active learning heuristics under high noise conditions, such as in SAR imagery. Since these methods rely on model uncertainty at the sample level, strong noise can corrupt probability estimates and lead to misleading query choices. The core challenge is to design selection strategies whose uncertainty measures remain reliable in the presence of noise or to augment them with robustness mechanisms. Developing noise-aware or denoising-integrated active learning schemes is an open research area, particularly for deep models trained on low-SNR remote sensing data.

topics.title: Workflow challenges in digital pathology
topics.description: In digital pathology, pathologists must examine tissue slices under high-magnification microscopes and continuously adjust magnification due to complex tissue structures. This examination is slow, typically requiring 15 to 30 minutes per slide, and accurate annotation is even more challenging than mere inspection. The need for detailed interpretation across varying magnifications greatly increases cognitive and time demands on pathologists.

topics.title: Limitations of crowdsourcing for medical images
topics.description: While crowdsourcing significantly reduces annotation costs for general computer vision tasks, it is poorly suited for medical image analysis. High-quality medical labels require domain-specific medical knowledge and clinical expertise, and even for simpler tasks, crowd workers tend to produce lower-quality annotations than trained professionals. Privacy concerns further restrict the use of open crowdsourcing platforms for sensitive medical data.

topics.title: Expert annotation burden and variability
topics.description: Replacing crowd workers with clinical experts shifts the bottleneck to the high cost and time demands of expert annotation. For example, a radiologist may need about 60 minutes to manually segment brain tumors per patient, with high hourly compensation, making large-scale labeling very expensive. To reduce bias, multiple annotation rounds or multiple annotators per case are often used, introducing intra- and inter-annotator variability that further increases annotation cost and complexity.

topics.title: Existing surveys on active learning
topics.description: Previous surveys have examined active learning from several angles, including the role of humans in developing and deploying deep learning in medical imaging, AL for segmentation with imperfect annotations, and AL as a label-efficient learning method focusing on model and data uncertainty. Other general AL surveys in machine learning and computer vision have provided foundational introductions and reviewed deep AL developments in CV and NLP, as well as taxonomies of model-driven and data-driven sample selectors and fair re-implementations of high-impact methods. These works form the background against which the current medical imaging-focused survey is positioned.

topics.title: Identified gaps in current AL surveys
topics.description: The section highlights several limitations of existing AL surveys: rapid methodological progress has outpaced current reviews, leaving new ideas and techniques under-covered. There is insufficient synthesis on combining AL with other label-efficient methods, despite this being a recognized future direction. Moreover, few surveys systematically evaluate AL methods on medical imaging datasets, and current reviews insufficiently address AL’s elevated importance under high medical annotation costs.

topics.title: Scope and paper selection of this survey
topics.description: The survey aims to comprehensively cover AL for medical image analysis, including core methods, integration with label-efficient techniques, and domain-specific adaptations. Papers are primarily sourced from medical image analysis using keyword-based searches on Google Scholar and arXiv, then expanded via citation tracing. Seminal AL works from general computer vision are also included to maintain a coherent taxonomy, and the surveyed works are largely drawn from top-tier journals and conferences, totaling 164 AL works with 234 references.

topics.title: Canonical active learning problem settings
topics.description: Active learning is framed around three primary problem settings: membership query synthesis, stream-based selective sampling, and pool-based active learning. Each setting defines different assumptions about how unlabeled samples are obtained and how queries to the oracle are made. This classification underpins the formulation and comparison of active learning strategies across applications, including medical image analysis.

topics.title: Stream-based selective sampling under memory constraints
topics.description: Stream-based selective sampling assumes that unlabeled samples arrive sequentially in a stream, and the learner must immediately decide whether to query their labels. This setting is well-suited for environments with limited memory, such as edge computing devices, because it does not require storing a large pool of data. However, it typically ignores correlations between samples in the stream, which may limit selection efficiency.

topics.title: Batch-mode selection in deep active learning
topics.description: When multiple samples are selected for labeling at once, the process is termed batch-mode active learning. Deep active learning typically assumes batch-mode pool-based settings because retraining deep models after each individual annotation is computationally impractical, and a single labeled example rarely yields a significant performance gain. Consequently, the survey treats batch-mode pool-based active learning as the default setup for deep active learning methods it reviews.

topics.title: Sample selection via informativeness functions
topics.description: In each round, an informativeness function I evaluates every sample in the unlabeled pool Du_t to quantify its utility for model improvement. Based on these scores, a sampling strategy S selects a batch of the most informative samples to form the queried set Dq_t. This mechanism focuses annotation effort on samples expected to maximally benefit the deep model f_{θ_{t−1}}.

canonical_topics.name: Expert Annotation Challenges in Medical Imaging
canonical_topics.description: Medical image annotation often requires pathologists and radiologists to inspect large, high-resolution images across multiple magnifications, making the process slow and cognitively demanding. Crowdsourcing is generally unsuitable for such data because accurate labels depend on specialized clinical expertise and are constrained by strict privacy requirements. As a result, annotation must rely on well-compensated experts who may spend tens of minutes per case for tasks like slide assessment or tumor segmentation. To reduce bias, multiple annotators or repeated labeling rounds are frequently used, introducing intra- and inter-observer variability that further increases cost and complexity. These factors create a strong motivation for deep active learning methods that minimize the number of expert-labeled samples needed.

canonical_topics.name: Active Learning Problem Settings and Data Access
canonical_topics.description: Canonical active learning is typically categorized into membership query synthesis, stream-based selective sampling, and pool-based active learning, each defined by different assumptions on how unlabeled data are accessed. In membership query synthesis, the learner can generate synthetic instances to be labeled by an oracle. In stream-based settings, samples arrive sequentially and must be accepted or discarded for labeling on the fly, often under memory or compute constraints such as on edge devices. In pool-based settings, a large static pool of unlabeled data is available, and the learner iteratively selects the most informative subset for labeling. These settings provide the foundational framework for formulating and comparing deep active learning strategies in medical image analysis.

canonical_topics.name: Informativeness-Based Sample Selection in Deep AL
canonical_topics.description: Deep active learning typically relies on an informativeness function that scores each unlabeled sample according to its expected utility for improving the current model. Given a model state and an unlabeled pool, this function produces a value for each candidate, capturing notions such as uncertainty, diversity, or expected loss reduction. A sampling strategy then uses these scores to choose a batch of highly informative samples to query from the oracle. By iteratively retraining on newly labeled batches, this process concentrates expert effort on cases that most effectively enhance model performance under limited annotation budgets.

canonical_topics.name: Batch-Mode Pool-Based Deep Active Learning and Gaps
canonical_topics.description: In deep active learning, batch-mode selection is commonly adopted because retraining large neural networks after each individual annotation is computationally impractical and a single labeled example rarely yields a noticeable performance gain. Most medical imaging applications therefore assume a pool-based setting, where the learner repeatedly selects batches of informative samples from a large unlabeled dataset. Existing surveys have documented this batch-mode, pool-based paradigm but have struggled to keep pace with the rapid methodological progress in deep active learning. Important open issues include limited synthesis of how active learning interacts with other label-efficient techniques, such as semi-supervised or self-supervised learning, and a lack of systematic evaluations on diverse medical imaging benchmarks. These gaps highlight the need for more comprehensive and experimentally grounded surveys of batch-mode deep active learning in clinical domains.

canonical_topics.name: Existing Surveys on Active and Deep Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: Prior surveys have examined active learning from multiple perspectives, including its role as a label-efficient paradigm in medical image analysis and its application to tasks such as segmentation under imperfect annotations. General active learning surveys in machine learning and computer vision have provided foundational introductions and taxonomies of model-driven and data-driven query strategies. More recent overviews address deep active learning in computer vision and natural language processing, offering systematic comparisons and re-implementations of influential methods. Together, these works establish the broader context and methodological baselines against which specialized surveys on deep active learning for medical imaging are positioned.

topics.title: Queried and unlabeled datasets with budget
topics.description: The queried dataset Dq_t in round t is a subset of the unlabeled pool Du_t, defined by applying the sampling strategy S to informativeness evaluations I(x, f_{θ_{t−1}}). The annotation budget b governs how many samples are selected per round, enforcing b = |Dq_t| ≪ |Du_t| to ensure only a small fraction of data is labeled. This formalization explicitly distinguishes unlabeled, queried, and budget-constrained subsets within each iteration.

topics.title: Oracle-based annotation and dataset update
topics.description: After selection, the queried set Dq_t is sent to an oracle, typically medical experts such as doctors, who provide ground-truth annotations. These newly labeled samples are then incorporated into the labeled dataset Dl_t, updating it for subsequent training and selection rounds. This step operationalizes human-in-the-loop learning by coupling algorithmic selection with expert annotation.

topics.title: Hybrid and Learnable Sampling Approaches
topics.description: This topic addresses query strategies that combine multiple selection criteria or learn the sampling policy directly. Hybrid sampling fuses uncertainty, representativeness, and class-balance cues, while learnable sampling uses neural networks or reinforcement learning to optimize query decisions end-to-end. Such methods aim to adapt sampling behavior to task-specific characteristics rather than relying on fixed heuristics.

topics.title: Annotation-efficient Strategies and Cost Modeling
topics.description: This topic deals with reducing and modeling annotation costs in medical imaging. It includes slice-based annotation (labeling only selected slices in volumetric scans), one-shot annotation (annotating minimal examples), and explicit consideration of 'Annotation Cost'. These strategies aim to align active learning with realistic clinical workflows where expert time is limited and labeling is expensive.

topics.title: Active learning dataset update rules
topics.description: The section formalizes how labeled and unlabeled datasets are updated in each active learning round. Newly queried samples D_q^t, once labeled by the oracle, are added to the labeled set D_l^t and simultaneously removed from the unlabeled pool D_u^t. This iterative refinement of D_l and D_u underpins the active learning loop and ensures no sample is selected twice.

topics.title: Supervised deep model training in AL loop
topics.description: After oracle annotation in each round, the deep learning model f_θ_t is trained in a fully supervised way on the current labeled set D_l^t. The training objective is expressed as minimizing an expected loss L(f_θ(x), y) over (x, y) ∈ D_l^t, written compactly as L(x, y; θ). This step produces updated parameters θ_t that are then used for subsequent sample selection.

topics.title: Iterative versus one-shot active learning
topics.description: The section contrasts the standard multi-round active learning process with one-shot strategies. In the iterative setting, steps of selection, annotation, and training are repeated until an annotation budget is exhausted or a target performance is reached. By contrast, one-shot active learning performs sample selection in a single pass without multiple rounds, changing how the model and querying strategy are designed.

topics.title: Imaging modalities and segmentation tasks overview
topics.description: The figure caption fragments indicate that the survey’s overall framework spans multiple medical imaging modalities and tasks, including MRI, CT, and Electron Microscopy, with a focus on medical image segmentation. Interactive segmentation and density-based methods are highlighted within this framework, signaling key application areas where deep active learning is applied. These elements situate the formal AL loop within concrete medical imaging contexts.

topics.title: Survey contribution on sampling strategies
topics.description: This survey claims a unique contribution by explicitly defining sampling strategies as core methods of active learning, rather than treating them as secondary. It reviews how to design better sampling strategies and summarizes all cited AL works, including their uncertainty/representativeness metrics and sampling approaches. These methods and metrics are systematized and detailed in a comprehensive table (Table 2).

topics.title: Prediction-probability uncertainty metrics
topics.description: This topic covers classical uncertainty measures computed directly from a model’s prediction probabilities p = Softmax(fθ(x)) over C classes. Metrics include Least Confidence (1 − max_i p_i or equivalently using max_i p_i with ↓ direction), Entropy (−∑_i p_i log p_i with ↑ direction), Margin (difference between top-1 and top-2 class probabilities with ↓ direction), and Mean Variance of class probabilities (↑ direction). These metrics quantify how spread or peaky the predicted distribution is, and serve as basic uncertainty scores in active learning query strategies.

canonical_topics.name: Dataset Partitions, Budgets, and Oracle Updates
canonical_topics.description: Deep active learning typically maintains three dataset partitions at each iteration: an unlabeled pool, a queried subset, and a labeled training set. A sampling strategy ranks unlabeled examples by an informativeness score computed from the current model, and an annotation budget constrains how many of these can be selected per round. The queried subset is sent to a human oracle (e.g., medical experts) to obtain ground-truth labels. Newly labeled samples are added to the labeled set and removed from the unlabeled pool, ensuring that no example is queried twice. This formalization supports both multi-round (iterative) and one-shot active learning schemes by making the budget, query set, and update rules explicit.

canonical_topics.name: Supervised Deep Model Training in AL Loops
canonical_topics.description: In deep active learning, the model is typically retrained or fine-tuned in a fully supervised manner after each annotation round. The current labeled set defines an empirical risk minimization objective, such as minimizing a task-specific loss over all labeled input–label pairs. Updated parameters are then used to recompute uncertainty or other acquisition scores on the remaining unlabeled pool. The quality and stability of this supervised training step critically affect subsequent query decisions and overall sample efficiency.

canonical_topics.name: Prediction-Probability Uncertainty Metrics for Querying
canonical_topics.description: Classical uncertainty-based query strategies rely on the model’s predictive probability distribution over classes. Common metrics include Least Confidence, which uses one minus the maximum predicted class probability, and Entropy, which aggregates uncertainty across all classes. Margin sampling measures the difference between the top-1 and top-2 predicted probabilities, while mean variance of class probabilities captures dispersion in the prediction vector. These scores quantify how peaked or diffuse the prediction distribution is and serve as basic acquisition functions for selecting informative unlabeled examples in deep active learning.

canonical_topics.name: Hybrid and Learnable Deep AL Sampling
canonical_topics.description: Hybrid sampling strategies combine multiple acquisition signals, such as uncertainty, representativeness, and class balance, into a single query rule. This fusion aims to avoid the weaknesses of any single heuristic and better cover the data distribution while still focusing on ambiguous samples. Learnable sampling approaches go further by parameterizing the query policy itself, often with neural networks or reinforcement learning. These policies are optimized end-to-end to maximize downstream performance or label efficiency, adapting the acquisition behavior to task- and dataset-specific characteristics.

canonical_topics.name: Annotation-Efficient and Cost-Aware Medical DAL
canonical_topics.description: Annotation-efficient strategies in medical deep active learning explicitly model the high cost of expert labeling. Techniques such as slice-based annotation for volumetric scans and one-shot or minimal-example labeling seek to reduce the amount of clinician time per training signal. Cost models may weight samples by expected annotation effort, integrating label cost directly into the acquisition function. By aligning query strategies with realistic clinical workflows and constraints, cost-aware DAL methods strive to maximize performance gains per unit of expert effort.

topics.title: Uncertainty for medical image active learning
topics.description: Uncertainty estimation is positioned as crucial for deploying deep learning in clinical practice, where medical images exhibit high variability and training data are limited. Predictive uncertainty allows models to flag ambiguities, artifacts, and unseen patterns, making it a natural informativeness metric in active learning. Samples with higher uncertainty are treated as harder and more error-prone, so querying and annotating them helps the model learn novel patterns and improve overall performance.

topics.title: Aleatoric, epistemic, and predictive uncertainty
topics.description: Uncertainty is decomposed into aleatoric uncertainty (AU) and epistemic uncertainty (EU). AU represents data-driven noise such as motion or metal artifacts in MRI/CT and cannot be reduced by collecting more data, while EU reflects model uncertainty due to unlearned knowledge and can be reduced with additional labeled data. In practice, most active learning work does not explicitly separate AU and EU, so 'uncertainty' typically refers to predictive uncertainty, the combined effect of both, because disentangling the two is difficult and often offers limited practical benefit.

topics.title: Taxonomy of uncertainty-based active learning
topics.description: Uncertainty-based active learning methods are organized into five main categories: multiple inference, gradient-based uncertainty, performance estimation, uncertainty-aware models, and adversarial-based uncertainty. Multiple inference methods include MC Dropout, data disagreement, model disagreement, and model ensembles; gradient-based approaches use gradients, Fisher Information, or influence functions; performance estimation employs surrogate metrics or learnable performance predictors; uncertainty-aware models encompass evidential deep learning and mixture density networks; adversarial-based methods leverage adversarial samples and adversarial training. This taxonomy structures the design space of uncertainty exploitation beyond simple probability-based measures.

topics.title: Model ensembles and snapshot ensembles for AL
topics.description: Model ensemble approaches train multiple independent deep models whose predictions are combined to estimate uncertainty, often outperforming MC dropout but at higher computational cost. Snapshot ensembles reduce this overhead by capturing multiple model checkpoints along a single training trajectory using cyclic learning rate schedules, though naïve variants may underperform full ensembles. An improved snapshot ensemble maintains optimization trajectories across active learning rounds with parameter regularization and can surpass standard ensembles. Additionally, stein variational gradient descent is used to train diverse ensembles for organ and tumor segmentation in CT and MRI, improving performance over competing methods.

topics.title: Query-by-Committee model disagreement in segmentation
topics.description: Model disagreement, formalized as Query-by-Committee (QBC), selects samples where multiple models’ outputs diverge most, indicating high epistemic uncertainty. Suggestive Annotation (SA) trains several segmentation networks via bootstrapping and uses prediction variance as a disagreement metric, achieving strong performance in gland and lymph node segmentation. Other works train multiple distinct segmentation models and measure disagreement (e.g., prediction variance or KL divergence between teacher and student models) to prioritize cases for annotation in tasks like abdominal multi-organ and carotid intima-media segmentation.

topics.title: CAM-based disagreement and geometric uncertainty metrics
topics.description: Some approaches leverage class activation maps (CAMs) and geometric similarity measures to refine disagreement-based active learning. In polyp segmentation, multiple decoders are trained on CAMs from a classification network, and both model disagreement (entropy and Dice between decoder outputs) and CAM disagreement (Dice between CAMs and decoder outputs) are used to select informative samples; low model but high CAM disagreement cases are turned into pseudo-labels for semi-supervised learning. Other methods quantify disagreement between CAMs using Hausdorff distance or between MC dropout predictions via vote entropy, capturing spatial or categorical uncertainty for tasks such as rib fracture detection.

topics.title: Data disagreement via input perturbations and viewpoints
topics.description: Data disagreement methods avoid training many models by instead perturbing inputs (e.g., augmentations or viewpoint changes) and measuring predictive inconsistency across these variants. KL divergence is a central metric, used to compare predictions for different augmented CT scans in COVID diagnosis and different viewpoints in 3D scenes, with higher KL indicating more informative samples. Extensions include an input-end committee that randomly augments inputs and quantifies classification and localization disagreement using cross-entropy and variance, respectively, providing a flexible framework for image-level and region-level uncertainty estimation.

topics.title: Feature-space interpolation disagreement with prototypes
topics.description: Feature-space interpolation strategies assess whether unlabeled data introduce novel information by interpolating between unlabeled feature vectors and labeled class prototypes. If the interpolated point’s prediction disagrees with the prototype’s label, this is interpreted as evidence that the unlabeled sample lies in a region not well represented by existing labels and should be annotated. This prototype-based disagreement mechanism has shown improvements across multiple datasets and settings, offering a representation-level perspective on uncertainty beyond raw prediction variance.

topics.title: Expected Gradient Length for exudate classification
topics.description: As an early application, expected gradient length is used to select informative samples in an exudate classification task on eye fundus images. Otálora et al. (2017) adopt the classic expected gradient length criterion to drive annotation decisions, leveraging the connection between gradient magnitude and sample value. This illustrates how traditional gradient-based active learning ideas are applied in medical imaging.

topics.title: Manifold-projected gradients for MRI segmentation
topics.description: Dai et al. propose an active learning method that projects segmentation loss gradients onto a learned data manifold to guide sample selection. A variational autoencoder (VAE) is first trained to capture the manifold of MRI brain images, and then a segmentation model is trained whose Dice-loss gradients are computed on labeled data. Query samples are chosen based on the components of these gradients that lie along the manifold, aiming to focus on realistic and informative variations. Their extended work demonstrates superior performance in both MRI brain tumor and whole-brain segmentation tasks.

canonical_topics.name: Uncertainty in Deep Active Learning for Medical Imaging
canonical_topics.description: Uncertainty estimation is central to deep active learning in medical imaging, where data are highly variable and expert annotations are costly. By quantifying predictive uncertainty, models can identify ambiguous cases, artifacts, or out-of-distribution patterns that are most informative to label. Conceptually, uncertainty is often decomposed into aleatoric (data-intrinsic noise) and epistemic (model ignorance) components, but in practice most methods operate on overall predictive uncertainty. Aleatoric uncertainty captures irreducible factors such as motion or metal artifacts, while epistemic uncertainty can be reduced by acquiring more labeled data. Active learning strategies typically target samples with high predictive (often mainly epistemic) uncertainty to improve generalization and safety in clinical deployment.

canonical_topics.name: Taxonomy of Uncertainty-Based Deep Active Learning Methods
canonical_topics.description: Uncertainty-based deep active learning methods can be organized into a taxonomy that clarifies the diverse ways uncertainty is quantified and exploited. Multiple inference approaches estimate uncertainty from repeated stochastic predictions, such as Monte Carlo dropout, model ensembles, and data or model disagreement. Gradient-based methods use gradient norms, Fisher Information, or influence functions to link parameter sensitivity to sample informativeness. Performance-estimation approaches build surrogate or learned predictors of downstream performance to guide querying. Uncertainty-aware models such as evidential networks or mixture density networks output richer uncertainty estimates, while adversarial-based methods probe the model with adversarial examples or adversarial training to expose fragile or uncertain regions of the input space.

canonical_topics.name: Committee and Disagreement-Based Uncertainty in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: Committee and disagreement-based strategies estimate uncertainty by comparing predictions from multiple models, input views, or feature-space prototypes. Classical Query-by-Committee schemes train several segmentation networks or heterogeneous models and select samples with maximal disagreement, quantified via prediction variance, KL divergence, or vote entropy. Model-ensemble approaches, including independent ensembles, snapshot ensembles, and Stein variational ensembles, trade computational cost for stronger uncertainty estimates and often improve performance in medical image segmentation. Data-disagreement methods avoid many models by perturbing inputs or viewpoints and measuring predictive inconsistency across augmentations, enabling fine-grained image- and region-level selection. Extensions leverage class activation maps and geometric distances (e.g., Dice, Hausdorff) or prototype-based feature interpolations to capture spatial and representation-level disagreement, further refining which unlabeled cases introduce genuinely novel information.

canonical_topics.name: Gradient-Based Deep Active Learning for Medical Imaging
canonical_topics.description: Gradient-based deep active learning methods quantify sample informativeness through the sensitivity of model parameters to each training example. Early work applies expected gradient length in medical image classification, selecting fundus images whose gradients have large expected norms, thereby prioritizing samples likely to induce substantial model updates. More advanced approaches project segmentation loss gradients onto a learned data manifold, typically obtained from a variational autoencoder trained on MRI scans, to focus on realistic, clinically plausible directions of change. By ranking unlabeled images according to manifold-aligned gradient components, these methods emphasize cases that most effectively reshape the decision boundary within the true data distribution. Such techniques have demonstrated improved efficiency in annotating complex tasks like brain tumor and whole-brain MRI segmentation.

topics.title: Layer-wise and last-layer Fisher approximations
topics.description: To make FI-based active learning feasible in deep models, approximations are introduced that reduce computational cost. Sourati et al. compute FI using average gradients per network layer instead of full parameter-wise matrices, and they rely on expected empirical loss (Eq. 5) to obtain gradients without labels; this method improves brain extraction performance across ages and pathologies. Ash et al. further simplify the approach by computing the FI matrix only for the last layer, and their gradient computation matches the BADGE framework, which uses last-layer gradient embeddings. These approximations retain much of FI’s informativeness while avoiding full quadratic complexity.

topics.title: Influence function-based sample selection
topics.description: Liu et al. apply influence functions to choose unlabeled samples expected to most positively affect model performance when labeled. The influence of a sample is computed using gradients of the loss on the labeled set and the inverse Hessian of the empirical risk (Eq. 9), capturing how upweighting that sample would perturb model parameters and downstream loss. Because unlabeled samples lack ground-truth, their gradients in the influence expression are approximated using gradients of the expected empirical loss. This yields an AL criterion grounded in classical robust statistics but adapted to deep models in medical imaging.

topics.title: BADGE-style gradients for medical segmentation
topics.description: The section alludes to extending the BADGE framework, which uses gradient embeddings from the last layer, to medical image segmentation tasks. It is mentioned in the context of semantic segmentation of laparoscopic surgical images and in Ash et al. (2021), where only the last-layer FI matrix is computed with BADGE-like gradients. This indicates a design where gradient-based diversity and uncertainty, encoded at the final layer, guide active sample selection in dense prediction problems. Such adaptations aim to transfer BADGE’s classification-oriented strategy to pixel-wise medical segmentation settings.

topics.title: Surrogate metrics via prediction agreement
topics.description: Surrogate metrics approximate performance by exploiting prediction agreement or intermediate representations, serving as upper or lower bounds of loss or evaluation scores. Examples include computing the intersection over union (IoU) across multiple MC dropout predictions and correlating it with the true Dice coefficient, and averaging Dice scores between intermediate and final layers under deep supervision. These surrogates show strong linear correlations with real task metrics, making them effective proxies for performance in medical image segmentation.

topics.title: Cyclic Output Discrepancy (COD) as loss surrogate
topics.description: Cyclic Output Discrepancy (COD) measures the norm of the change in network outputs between two consecutive annotation rounds. Within limited training iterations, sample loss is shown to be bounded by this output difference, making COD a surrogate for both loss and downstream evaluation metrics. Samples with high COD are preferentially selected, as empirical results demonstrate that higher COD is associated with higher loss and poorer performance.

topics.title: Combining loss prediction with diversity and disagreement
topics.description: Some methods enhance learnable loss estimation by integrating it with other active learning criteria such as model disagreement and sample diversity. In COVID diagnosis and colonoscopy polyp analysis under federated active learning, predicted loss is combined with prediction disagreements and diversity measures to select informative and diverse samples across distributed clients. This composite strategy aims to improve both uncertainty targeting and coverage of the data space.

topics.title: Loss ranking prediction instead of regression
topics.description: Recognizing that active learning primarily needs an uncertainty ordering rather than exact loss values, loss regression is relaxed to predicting relative loss ranks. Kim et al. (2021) replace the loss regressor in LLAL with a ranking module derived from RankCGAN, directly optimizing for correct ordering of sample uncertainties. This rank-based estimation empirically surpasses exact loss regression for sample selection.

topics.title: Uncertainty-aware deep models in AL
topics.description: This topic covers deep models that inherently model predictive distributions rather than point estimates, such as VAEs and probabilistic U-Nets. These models output full distributions over predictions, reducing over-confidence compared to deterministic networks and providing built-in uncertainty estimates. They require only a single forward pass at inference, lowering computational and time costs for active learning pipelines.

topics.title: Multi-label EDL using Beta distributions
topics.description: In multi-label chest X-ray classification, EDL is adapted by decomposing the Dirichlet distribution into multiple Beta distributions, one per class label. Each Beta distribution models the evidential uncertainty for a specific label, and its entropy is used as the aleatoric uncertainty metric for annotation. This enables uncertainty-aware active learning in a multi-label medical imaging setting.

topics.title: EDL-based active domain adaptation
topics.description: Here, EDL is employed within an active domain adaptation framework to select samples under both data and distributional uncertainty. Samples exhibiting high distribution uncertainty (domain shift) and high data uncertainty are prioritized for annotation. This evidential approach tailors active learning to settings where source and target data distributions differ.

canonical_topics.name: Fisher Information and Gradient Embedding Approximations
canonical_topics.description: This topic covers approximations that make Fisher information (FI)-based active learning feasible in deep neural networks. Instead of computing the full parameter-wise FI matrix, layer-wise and last-layer approximations use averaged or final-layer gradients to drastically reduce computational and memory costs. These approximations connect naturally to gradient-embedding methods such as BADGE, where last-layer gradients encode both uncertainty and diversity. Such FI-inspired gradient embeddings have been successfully applied to dense prediction tasks like medical image segmentation, preserving much of FI’s informativeness while avoiding full quadratic complexity. The result is a practical class of FI-based acquisition functions scalable to modern deep architectures.

canonical_topics.name: Surrogate Performance Metrics from Prediction Consistency
canonical_topics.description: This topic focuses on surrogate metrics that approximate true task performance by exploiting prediction agreement and output discrepancies. Examples include computing intersection over union (IoU) across multiple Monte Carlo dropout predictions and correlating it with true Dice scores, as well as averaging Dice between intermediate and final outputs under deep supervision. Cyclic Output Discrepancy (COD) extends this idea temporally by measuring the norm of changes in network outputs between successive annotation or training rounds. Under limited training, sample loss can be bounded by COD, making it a useful proxy for both loss and evaluation metrics. These label-free surrogates enable active learning systems to prioritize samples likely to have high true error without requiring ground-truth annotations for scoring.

canonical_topics.name: Learnable Loss Ranking with Diversity and Disagreement
canonical_topics.description: This topic addresses active learning strategies that learn to predict or rank sample losses and combine them with diversity and disagreement signals. Instead of regressing exact loss values, ranking-based approaches train models to order samples by relative uncertainty, which better aligns with the needs of acquisition functions. For example, RankCGAN-inspired modules replace loss regressors in LLAL-style frameworks, directly optimizing for correct uncertainty ordering and improving selection quality. In practical applications such as COVID-19 diagnosis and polyp detection under federated active learning, predicted loss is fused with model disagreement and diversity measures to select informative yet diverse samples across distributed clients. This composite design improves coverage of the data space while still targeting highly uncertain examples.

canonical_topics.name: Probabilistic and Evidential Deep Models for Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: This topic covers deep models that inherently represent predictive uncertainty through probabilistic or evidential outputs. Examples include variational autoencoders and probabilistic U-Nets, which produce full predictive distributions instead of point estimates, reducing overconfidence and providing calibrated uncertainty with a single forward pass. Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) further models uncertainty by treating network outputs as evidence parameters of distributions such as Dirichlet or decomposed Beta distributions in multi-label settings, enabling class-wise aleatoric uncertainty estimation. These evidential representations can be exploited in multi-label medical image classification and in active domain adaptation, where samples with high data and distributional uncertainty are prioritized. Overall, probabilistic and evidential models form a principled backbone for uncertainty-driven deep active learning, especially under distribution shift.

canonical_topics.name: Influence Function-Based Sample Selection in Deep AL
canonical_topics.description: This topic discusses the use of influence functions to guide sample selection in deep active learning. Influence functions estimate how upweighting a candidate sample would perturb model parameters and, consequently, the loss on a validation or labeled set, using gradients and the inverse Hessian of the empirical risk. For unlabeled data, the missing ground-truth is handled by approximating the required gradients with respect to an expected empirical loss. This yields an acquisition criterion grounded in classical robust statistics but adapted to deep models, particularly in medical imaging. By directly targeting samples expected to most improve performance when labeled, influence-function-based selection provides a theoretically motivated alternative to purely heuristic uncertainty measures.

topics.title: KL-divergence-driven adversarial attacks for uncertainty
topics.description: Here, adversarial attacks are constructed by maximizing the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the model’s predictions on original and perturbed inputs under a bounded perturbation norm. The KL divergence quantifies how much the prediction distribution changes under small adversarial noise, capturing local sensitivity of the classifier. Samples for which this divergence is maximized, given the perturbation constraint, are deemed more uncertain and are selected for annotation. This leverages distributional disagreement under adversarial perturbations as an uncertainty metric.

topics.title: Adversarial training with classifier disagreement
topics.description: This topic describes an adversarial training scheme that alternates optimization of a shared feature extractor and multiple classifiers to surface uncertain samples. Two classifiers are trained on labeled and unlabeled data: first, classifiers are updated while the feature extractor is fixed to increase disagreement and expose ambiguous regions; next, the feature extractor is updated against fixed classifiers to reduce the discrepancy between labeled and unlabeled representations. After several alternations, samples that induce the largest classifier disagreements are identified as most informative and are annotated. The method combines adversarial objectives in representation learning with disagreement-based active learning.

topics.title: Distribution Misalignment and Dataset Bias
topics.description: In feature space, uncertain samples tend to lie near the decision boundary, so uncertainty-based selection skews the queried set toward this region. As a result, the distribution of queried samples diverges from the overall data distribution, introducing dataset bias. This misalignment can cause a performance drop and motivates considering relationships among samples during querying.

topics.title: Limitations of Uncertainty as Informativeness Metric
topics.description: Uncertainty-based AL under-exploits the visual content of each sample and the inter-sample relationships, focusing instead on model confidence alone. This limitation leads to outlier selection and distribution misalignment. Consequently, the authors argue for designing new informativeness metrics that explicitly encode sample characteristics and their relationships.

topics.title: Feature Representations in Medical Image AL
topics.description: Medical images are high-dimensional and contain complex, often non-obvious information about lesions, tissues, and anatomical or functional structures. Good feature representations lower dimensionality while encoding anatomical, histological, pathological, and functional cues relevant to clinical tasks. Because of this, representativeness-based querying is typically executed in the learned feature space rather than raw image space.

topics.title: Clustering-based active learning framework
topics.description: Clustering-based active learning exploits the fact that similar medical images cluster together in feature space, enabling selection of representative samples via clustering on embeddings. Data are partitioned into clusters and cluster centroids are chosen for annotation, leveraging the data’s inherent structure while remaining easy to implement. This provides a straightforward query strategy that focuses labeling effort on diverse, representative points.

topics.title: Coarse-to-fine clustering for nuclei segmentation
topics.description: Lou et al. propose a two-level clustering strategy using K-Means for nuclei segmentation in pathological images. They first perform coarse-level clustering to broadly group patches and then fine-level clustering within these groups to refine selection. The goal is to identify particularly informative image patches for labeling, improving segmentation quality while keeping annotation costs low.

topics.title: Active learning via ROI correctness judgment
topics.description: In connectomics, Lin et al. first predict a semantic mask for each unlabeled sample and then reformulate active learning as judging whether each predicted region of interest (ROI) is correct. This shifts the labeling task from full annotation to verification of model-generated segmentations. The approach narrows annotation to critical ROIs where model predictions may be unreliable, increasing efficiency.

topics.title: Two-stream VAE-based clustering in connectomics
topics.description: Lin et al. train two separate feature extractors based on variational autoencoders (VAEs): one on segmentation masks and another on unlabeled images. These two streams provide complementary feature spaces for clustering in active learning. In particular, they apply mask-level clustering using mask features to group ROIs with similar appearances, guiding selection of diverse and uncertain regions for annotation in connectomics.

topics.title: Hierarchical mask and image-level clustering
topics.description: The approach first forms clusters based on segmentation masks and then performs additional clustering at the image level within each mask cluster. This hierarchical strategy separates structural (mask-based) similarity from broader visual (image-based) similarity. Such a design aims to better capture fine-grained object-level patterns before aggregating image-level characteristics. It is particularly suitable for medical images where object shape and appearance both carry diagnostic information.

canonical_topics.name: Adversarial and Disagreement-Based Uncertainty Sampling
canonical_topics.description: This topic covers deep active learning methods that quantify uncertainty via adversarial perturbations and classifier disagreement. Adversarial examples are crafted by maximizing the Kullback–Leibler divergence between predictions on original and perturbed inputs under a bounded norm, so samples with large induced distributional shifts are deemed most informative. In parallel, multi-classifier schemes alternate between updating classifier heads to increase prediction disagreement and updating a shared feature extractor to reduce this discrepancy, thereby exposing ambiguous regions of the input space. Samples that maximize adversarial sensitivity or inter-classifier disagreement are prioritized for annotation, encouraging exploration near complex decision boundaries. These strategies exploit adversarial objectives both to probe model robustness and to define richer uncertainty metrics than raw confidence alone.

canonical_topics.name: Bias from Pure Uncertainty-Based Querying
canonical_topics.description: This topic analyzes how uncertainty-only query strategies can introduce dataset bias in deep active learning. Because such methods preferentially select samples near the current decision boundary, the labeled set can become heavily skewed toward this narrow region in feature space. This distribution misalignment between queried and overall data may harm generalization and lead to overfitting boundary noise or outliers. Moreover, focusing solely on model confidence neglects visual content and inter-sample relationships, which can exacerbate outlier selection. These limitations motivate informativeness measures that integrate uncertainty with diversity, representativeness, and structural relationships among samples.

canonical_topics.name: Feature-Space Representativeness and ROI Verification
canonical_topics.description: This topic addresses how feature representations and task design shape deep active learning for medical images. High-dimensional medical images encode complex anatomical and pathological cues, so representativeness-based querying is typically performed in a learned feature space that compresses yet preserves clinically relevant structure.
