Low-data generative schemes like conditional SinGAN can be trained from a single image–mask pair to produce task-specific segmentation examples when labeled data are extremely scarce. Other methods score synthetic samples for label preservation and redundancy to select only label-consistent, non-overlapping queries from the generative model’s latent space. Early work revealed that low-fidelity or class-ambiguous GAN samples severely limit expert annotation, motivating strategies such as physics-based simulation to automatically label synthetic data at scale.

canonical_topics.name: Implicit Semantic Data Augmentation for Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: Implicit semantic data augmentation (ISDA) can be integrated into deep active learning by perturbing unlabeled samples in feature space rather than in pixel space. For each unlabeled point, multiple semantic augmentations are generated and the diversity among their predictions is used as a signal of informativeness. Samples whose augmentations yield highly diverse outputs are prioritized for annotation, since they likely lie near complex or uncertain decision boundaries. The model is trained jointly on original data and their ISDA-based augmentations, improving robustness and label efficiency. This framework leverages semantic perturbations to better explore informative regions of the feature space during the active learning cycle.

canonical_topics.name: Uncertainty, Representativeness, and Domainness in Active Domain Adaptation
canonical_topics.description: In active domain adaptation, query strategies must simultaneously consider predictive uncertainty and how representative each sample is of the target-domain distribution. Representativeness is often captured via domainness or targetness scores that quantify how strongly a sample belongs to the target domain rather than the source. Effective strategies therefore select target samples that are both highly uncertain and highly target-like, ensuring that labeled data correct model mistakes where they matter most for cross-domain performance. Balancing these criteria helps allocate limited annotation budget to target-domain examples that maximally reduce the adaptation gap. This makes active querying a principled complement to standard domain adaptation techniques.

topics.title: Adversarial learning with importance sampling
topics.description: Su et al. (2020) introduce ADA by combining domain adversarial learning with active learning through importance sampling. A domain discriminator and a task model jointly estimate which target samples are both uncertain for the task and highly different from the source domain. These samples are then prioritized for annotation to simultaneously improve task performance and reduce domain discrepancy.

topics.title: Domainness-aware committee and filtering strategy
topics.description: Fu et al. (2021) integrate query-by-committee, uncertainty, and domainness into an ADA framework. A domain discriminator scores target samples by domainness, while Gaussian kernels filter out anomalous and source-similar target samples to avoid outliers and redundant data. Random sampling is additionally used to enhance diversity among selected images, balancing informativeness and coverage.

topics.title: Uncertainty-weighted clustering of target images
topics.description: Prabhu et al. (2021) apply k-means clustering on target-domain samples and select cluster centers as candidates for annotation. These centers are weighted by predictive uncertainty, so that clusters with more uncertain samples contribute more to the selection. This ensures that chosen images are both diverse in feature space and highly informative for the model.

topics.title: Anchor-based selection for segmentation ADA
topics.description: For segmentation tasks, Ning et al. (2021) introduce anchors built from source-domain class-wise feature concatenations whose cluster centers act as reference anchors. Distances are computed between each target sample and its nearest anchor in this feature space. Target images with the largest distances—indicating poor alignment with source anchors—are queried for annotation to better cover underrepresented or shifted regions.

topics.title: Energy-based image selection in ADA
topics.description: Xie et al. (2022b) adapt the concept of energy, defined as inversely proportional to data likelihood, for ADA. A model trained on the source domain computes energy scores for target-domain samples, with high-energy samples corresponding to low-likelihood, out-of-distribution or shifted data. By selecting high-energy images for annotation, the method targets samples that are representative of the target domain yet substantially different from the source.

topics.title: Prototype inconsistency and uncertainty-based querying
topics.description: Huang et al. (2023) propose selecting target samples that exhibit both high prediction uncertainty and inconsistency with their nearest prototypes. Prototypes summarize class-wise or feature-wise typical patterns, and inconsistency indicates a sample that deviates from these learned norms. This dual criterion aims to capture samples that are both hard for the model and atypical relative to established representations.

topics.title: Dual-reference strategy for tumor segmentation ADA
topics.description: In nasopharyngeal carcinoma tumor segmentation, Wang et al. (2023) propose a dual-reference strategy using both source- and target-domain cues. Source-domain feature representations are clustered to form reference samples, and target images with the highest and lowest similarity to these references are selected. These extremes are interpreted as domain-invariant (high similarity) and domain-specific (low similarity) samples, respectively, jointly improving generalization and adaptation.

topics.title: LabOR: disagreement-based region selection
topics.description: LabOR uses an unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) pre-trained model to generate pseudo-labels for target-domain samples and trains two segmentation heads on these labels. It then maximizes prediction disagreement between the two heads and queries annotations for regions exhibiting the highest disagreement, treating disagreement as an informativeness measure. This strategy enables LabOR to achieve performance close to full supervision while annotating only 2.2% of target-domain regions.

topics.title: Uncertainty and regional impurity for patch querying
topics.description: This approach selects the most informative patches based on a combination of prediction uncertainty and regional impurity. Regional impurity is defined as the number of unique predicted classes within a pixel’s neighborhood, capturing edge or boundary complexity, which often indicates challenging regions. By querying extremely small patches (e.g., 3×3) with high uncertainty and impurity, the method attains near fully supervised performance with only about 5% of the annotation cost.

topics.title: Density-based superpixel selection with GMMs
topics.description: This method models the distribution of superpixels in both source and target domains using Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) as density estimators. It then selects superpixels in the target domain that have high density under the target GMM but low density under the source GMM, identifying representative yet domain-specific regions for annotation. The density-based criterion aims to focus labeling effort on characteristic target structures that are underrepresented or mismatched in the source domain.

canonical_topics.name: Adversarial and Disagreement-Based Sampling for ADA
canonical_topics.description: This topic covers active domain adaptation strategies that exploit adversarial objectives and predictive disagreement to choose informative target samples. One line of work combines a domain discriminator with a task model to estimate both label uncertainty and domain dissimilarity, using importance sampling so that uncertain and highly target-specific images are preferentially annotated. Another line focuses on segmentation, where a UDA-pretrained model with pseudo-labels is equipped with two prediction heads whose disagreement highlights poorly learned regions. By querying images or regions that maximize adversarial mismatch or head-level disagreement, these methods simultaneously improve task accuracy and reduce source–target domain gaps with limited annotation.

canonical_topics.name: Hybrid Uncertainty, Domainness, and Energy Criteria in ADA
canonical_topics.description: This topic integrates uncertainty-based sampling with explicit measures of domainness, data likelihood, and regional complexity for active domain adaptation. Committee-based approaches combine query-by-committee with domainness scores from a domain discriminator, while Gaussian-kernel filters discard anomalous or source-like target samples and random sampling preserves diversity. Energy-based methods treat high-energy (low-likelihood) target images as indicative of out-of-distribution or shifted content, prioritizing them for annotation to better characterize the target domain. At finer granularity, patch-level strategies mix prediction uncertainty with regional impurity, defined by the diversity of predicted labels in a local neighborhood, to focus annotation on complex boundaries and challenging structures. Together, these hybrid criteria aim to balance informativeness, domain shift coverage, and robustness to outliers in the queried set.

canonical_topics.name: Representation- and Cluster-Based Querying for ADA
canonical_topics.description: This topic encompasses active domain adaptation methods that operate in feature space using clustering, anchors, prototypes, and density models to guide querying. Some approaches apply k-means clustering on target features and select cluster centers weighted by predictive uncertainty, ensuring chosen samples are both diverse and informative. Anchor- and prototype-based methods build class-wise reference features from the source or target domain, then query samples that are either far from these anchors, inconsistent with their nearest prototype, or at extreme similarity levels, thereby capturing both domain-specific and domain-invariant patterns. In medical and segmentation settings, dual-reference strategies jointly exploit high- and low-similarity examples, while Gaussian mixture models over superpixels identify regions that are dense under the target distribution but sparse under the source. Collectively, these techniques leverage the geometry and density of learned representations to concentrate labeling effort on structurally representative yet poorly aligned areas of the target domain.

topics.title: Task-specific AL: classification, segmentation, reconstruction
topics.description: The survey outlines that AL methods in medical imaging are organized around specific tasks, namely classification, segmentation, and reconstruction. Each task involves different prediction targets—global image or patient labels, pixel/voxel-wise region delineations, or image restoration and completion—requiring distinct query strategies and model architectures. The section indicates that subsequent discussion will introduce AL works tailored to these varied task types.

topics.title: Clinical Tasks as Image Classification
topics.description: Disease diagnosis, cancer staging, and prognostic prediction in clinical practice are framed as medical image classification problems. This conceptualization allows active learning methods to be applied to a wide range of imaging-based clinical decision tasks by treating them uniformly as label prediction problems over images.

topics.title: General Active Learning with Class Balancing
topics.description: Many active learning approaches for medical image classification reuse general AL strategies rather than domain-specific designs. A common technique is class-balancing sampling, which selects instances from underrepresented classes to compensate for the long-tail distribution typical of medical imaging datasets, thereby improving classifier performance under imbalance.

topics.title: AL Targeted at X-ray and WSI Classification
topics.description: The section focuses on active learning algorithms specifically tailored to chest X-ray and pathological WSI classification tasks. These works adapt AL strategies to handle multi-label chest radiographs and MIL-based WSI formulations, showcasing modality-aware designs beyond generic AL frameworks.

topics.title: Saliency-map aggregation for sample selection
topics.description: Mahapatra et al. (2021) proposed using saliency maps to identify informative chest X-ray samples for annotation in an active learning loop. Per-pixel saliency maps are aggregated into a single scalar score per image, using three strategies: kurtosis of the saliency distribution, multivariate radiomic features, and deep features derived from autoencoders combined with clustering. Comparative results showed that aggregation based on deep autoencoder features yields the most effective selection of informative samples.

topics.title: Boundary-based AL with entropy and pseudo-labels
topics.description: Nguyen et al. (2021) introduced a gist-set mechanism to target samples near the classifier’s decision boundary for annotation, focusing labeling effort where the model is most uncertain. Their strategy sends high-entropy (high-uncertainty) samples to experts for labeling, while assigning pseudo-labels to confident samples to expand training data without manual effort. Momentum updates are incorporated to stabilize predictions over time, reducing fluctuations in sample selection and improving the robustness of the active learning process.

topics.title: Fungal structure analysis in electron microscopy
topics.description: This topic relates to applying deep active learning to electron microscopy images of fungal specimens. The text indicates the use of an in-house dataset, suggesting a specialized application where labeled data are scarce and costly to obtain. Active learning strategies are likely used to select the most informative electron microscopy images or regions for annotation. The goal is to perform accurate segmentation or structural analysis of fungal elements under extreme imaging magnification.

topics.title: Breast Histopathology with BreaKHis Dataset
topics.description: This topic addresses analysis of breast histopathology images using the BreaKHis dataset. The images capture microscopic views of breast tissue, enabling training and evaluation of deep models for differentiating benign from malignant cases. The dataset is a standard benchmark in medical image analysis and is referenced here in the context of a 2019 study by Qi et al. in JBHI.

topics.title: Breast Cancer Diagnosis Classification Methods
topics.description: Breast cancer diagnosis is formulated as an image classification problem, where models predict diagnostic labels from breast-related medical images. The reference to Sadafi et al. (2019) indicates a specific method or study focusing on classification-based diagnosis, likely leveraging deep learning on histopathology or related imaging modalities. Performance would typically be assessed using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, or AUC on labeled datasets.

topics.title: Breast endomicroscopy mosaic classification
topics.description: This topic addresses classification of breast endomicroscopy mosaics, which are composite images acquired with endomicroscopic devices. The dataset contains 1,366 images (1,042/324 split), and the problem is formulated as an image classification task. The referenced work by Gu et al. (2017) explores how deep models can distinguish among different tissue or pathology patterns within these mosaics. Such applications deal with high-resolution, domain-specific imagery where expert labeling is costly.

canonical_topics.name: Task-Specific Deep Active Learning in Medical Imaging
canonical_topics.description: Deep active learning in medical imaging is naturally organized around core prediction tasks such as classification, segmentation, and reconstruction. Classification covers problems like disease diagnosis, staging, and prognosis, where images or patients receive global labels and query strategies focus on image-level uncertainty and diversity. Segmentation tasks require pixel- or voxel-level delineations of anatomical or pathological structures, motivating region-aware query mechanisms and architectures that exploit spatial context. Reconstruction and restoration tasks, such as image completion or enhancement, demand query strategies that prioritize samples with challenging artifacts or missing information. Framing diverse clinical workflows within these task categories clarifies how different model outputs and annotation costs shape the design of effective active learning pipelines.

canonical_topics.name: Query Strategies for Deep Active Learning in Medical Image Classification
canonical_topics.description: Many deep active learning methods for medical image classification adopt and extend general pool-based query strategies rather than designing entirely domain-specific frameworks. A common technique is class-balancing sampling, which preferentially selects instances from underrepresented classes to mitigate the strong label imbalance and long-tail distributions typical of medical datasets. More sophisticated approaches use saliency maps to score unlabeled images, aggregating pixel-wise importance into scalar informativeness measures via statistics such as kurtosis, radiomic descriptors, or deep autoencoder features, with learned deep representations often yielding the most effective sample selection. Boundary-focused methods further target images near the classifier’s decision surface, querying high-entropy, high-uncertainty samples while assigning pseudo-labels to confident examples to expand the training set without extra annotation. Some of these approaches incorporate temporal smoothing or momentum updates to stabilize predictions over iterations, reducing oscillations in the queried set and leading to more robust active learning behavior.

canonical_topics.name: Modality-Aware Active Learning for X-ray and Whole-Slide Pathology
canonical_topics.description: Modality-aware deep active learning methods tailor query strategies to the specific characteristics of chest X-ray and whole-slide pathology images. For chest radiographs, algorithms must often handle multi-label prediction of co-occurring diseases and leverage spatially diffuse abnormalities, encouraging designs that integrate image-level uncertainty with localized attention or saliency. Whole-slide images introduce additional challenges of extreme resolution and multiple-instance learning, where slides are decomposed into tiles or patches and labels are available only at the slide level. Active learning strategies in this setting typically operate at the bag or patch level, selecting informative regions or subsets of tiles that are most likely to refine slide-level diagnoses. These modality-specific adaptations demonstrate that incorporating acquisition physics, label structure, and annotation workflows into the query policy can substantially outperform generic active learning schemes.

topics.title: Infant brain MRI segmentation with iSeg
topics.description: This topic refers to infant brain segmentation from MRI data using the iSeg dataset in the same survey table. The approach is described as operating on 3D patches, indicating volumetric patch-based segmentation for neonatal brain structures. A dataset size of 16,380 patches and a 50% figure (likely related to labeled or selected data proportion) are reported, highlighting data usage characteristics. It represents a neuroimaging segmentation benchmark within medical image analysis for deep (active) learning methods.

topics.title: 2D vs 3D patch-based medical segmentation
topics.description: This topic captures the contrast between 2D and 3D patch-based strategies for medical image segmentation across different modalities and organs. Li and Yin’s colon histopathology gland segmentation uses 2D patches on GlaS, while the infant brain MRI segmentation uses 3D patches on iSeg. The differing patch dimensionalities, dataset sizes, and usage percentages illustrate how patch design and data partitioning vary by task and imaging modality. These choices are central to how deep (active) learning pipelines are structured in medical image analysis.

topics.title: CT hip and thigh muscle segmentation
topics.description: This topic involves muscle segmentation on CT images of the hip and thigh region using data sourced from both TCIA and in-house collections. The data is organized at the slice level, comprising 20 CT volumes, with only 5% of the data indicated as labeled/used at certain stages. The task is explicitly framed as a segmentation problem, reported in Huang et al. (2020) in TMI (2020).

topics.title: Rib fracture recognition in chest X-rays
topics.description: This topic concerns rib fracture recognition in chest X-ray images using an object detection framework. The dataset is in-house, annotated at the region level, and consists of 10,966 images with a 7:1:2 split (likely for different data subsets). Different annotation proportions (0%, 5%, and 10%) are reported, reflecting varying levels of labeled data used in experiments, as described by Shen et al. (2021) in TMI (2021).

topics.title: Musculoskeletal volumetric segmentation tasks
topics.description: The section heading and initial entries indicate a focus on musculoskeletal segmentation, specifically described as "Segmentation" of "volume" data. This suggests tasks where 3D medical image volumes are segmented to delineate musculoskeletal structures, forming a distinct application area within the surveyed deep active learning methods. The emphasis on "volume" differentiates these tasks from 2D image analyses and highlights the need to handle 3D anatomical information.

topics.title: Polyp detection in colonoscopy images
topics.description: Another colonoscopy-related task is polyp detection, also formulated as a classification problem on in-house colonoscopy image data. A larger dataset of 28,250 images (16,300/11,950) is reported, indicating substantial data for detecting polyps within colon imagery. This highlights deep active learning use cases in detecting clinically relevant lesions during colonoscopic examinations.

topics.title: Synthetic bacterial cell microscopy dataset
topics.description: This topic refers to a synthetic microscopy dataset of bacterial cells, described as VGG Cell images. It comprises 150 images with an apparent split of 50/100 (likely train/test or labeled/unlabeled), with 10% of the data used as labeled samples. The dataset supports tasks such as cell counting and keypoint localization, making it suitable for evaluating deep active learning strategies in microscopy imaging.

topics.title: Bone marrow histopathology dataset MBM
topics.description: This topic covers a histopathology dataset of human bone marrow, labeled as MBM. The dataset size is 29 samples with a 15/14 split, which likely corresponds to different subsets such as training and testing or labeled and unlabeled data. It is used as a benchmark for deep active learning methods in histopathological image analysis.

topics.title: MICCAI benchmarks in Xu et al. 2021
topics.description: This topic captures the role of these microscopy and histopathology datasets as benchmarks in the work by Xu et al. (2021). The cited study likely uses the listed MICCAI-related datasets (synthetic microscopy, MBM, ADI, DCC) to evaluate deep active learning techniques for medical image analysis. The mention of the year and citation anchors these datasets to a specific experimental framework in the literature.

topics.title: Retinal vessel segmentation task
topics.description: The section highlights retinal vessel segmentation as the main clinical task, focusing on delineating blood vessels in retinal images. This task is framed as a segmentation problem, where pixel-wise classification of vessels versus background is required. It is listed explicitly as the 'Clinical Task' and 'Technical Task' for the referenced active learning study.

canonical_topics.name: 2D and 3D Patch-Based Medical Image Segmentation
canonical_topics.description: This topic concerns deep (active) learning pipelines that operate on 2D or 3D patches for medical image segmentation. It includes 3D patch-based neonatal brain MRI segmentation on the iSeg dataset and 2D patch-based gland segmentation in colon histopathology (e.g., GlaS). Differences in patch dimensionality, dataset size, and labeled-data proportion shape model capacity, computational cost, and querying strategies in active learning. The design of patch size and dimensionality is central for uncertainty estimation, sample selection, and efficient use of labeled volumes or slides in medical segmentation tasks.

canonical_topics.name: Musculoskeletal CT Volumetric Segmentation with Limited Labels
canonical_topics.description: This topic addresses deep active learning for musculoskeletal segmentation on CT volumes of the hip and thigh. Data are organized at the slice or volume level from both TCIA and in-house collections, with only a small fraction (around 5%) annotated at certain stages. The task is a volumetric segmentation problem targeting muscle structures, as in Huang et al. (TMI 2020). Active learning is used to prioritize the most informative slices or volumes for annotation, improving segmentation performance while keeping labeling effort low in 3D musculoskeletal imaging.

canonical_topics.name: Active Learning for Lesion Detection in Radiology and Endoscopy
canonical_topics.description: This topic covers deep active learning for lesion detection tasks in medical imaging, including rib fracture recognition in chest X-rays and polyp detection in colonoscopy images. In these settings, models are trained in object-detection or image-level classification frameworks on large in-house datasets with region-level or image-level annotations. Studies vary the proportion of labeled data (e.g., 0%, 5%, 10%) and data splits to evaluate how active sample selection accelerates performance gains. The focus is on reducing costly expert annotations for clinically important lesions in radiology and endoscopy while maintaining high sensitivity and specificity.

canonical_topics.name: Microscopy and Histopathology Benchmarks for Deep Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: This topic encompasses microscopy and histopathology datasets used as benchmarks for evaluating deep active learning methods. Examples include a synthetic VGG-based bacterial cell microscopy dataset supporting cell counting and keypoint localization with small labeled subsets, and the MBM bone marrow histopathology dataset with only a few dozen samples split into training and test subsets. Xu et al. (2021) and related work employ these datasets, along with others such as ADI and DCC, to study active learning under extreme data scarcity. These benchmarks highlight challenges like limited sample size, complex morphology, and high annotation cost that motivate active querying strategies.

canonical_topics.name: Retinal Vessel Segmentation with Deep Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: This topic focuses on retinal vessel segmentation framed as a pixel-wise classification task in fundus images. The clinical goal is to delineate retinal blood vessels from background tissue to support diagnosis and monitoring of ocular and systemic diseases. Deep active learning is applied to select the most informative images or regions for manual annotation, reducing the labeling burden in dense segmentation tasks. Studies in this area typically evaluate how different query strategies and label budgets affect vessel delineation accuracy and robustness.

topics.title: Eye imaging modalities: Fundus and OCTA
topics.description: Two eye imaging modalities are referenced: Fundus photography and Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography (OCTA). Both are used for imaging the eye, particularly retinal structures, in the surveyed active learning work. The table associates these modalities with eye-related clinical tasks such as vessel segmentation.

topics.title: DRIVE and ROSE-1 retinal datasets
topics.description: The section lists two datasets used for retinal vessel analysis: DRIVE and ROSE-1. DRIVE is described with 40 images split as 20/20 (commonly train/test), while ROSE-1 is described with 117 images, likely for a similar segmentation task. These datasets serve as benchmarks for evaluating deep active learning methods in retinal vessel segmentation.

topics.title: Airspace opacity and lung lesion diagnosis
topics.description: Nguyen et al. (2021) investigate deep active learning for detecting airspace opacity and lung lesions on chest X-ray images from an in-house dataset. The study uses 135,309 images, with 131,030/4,279 split and up to 6,550 labeled examples forming the annotation budget. The goal is to perform image-level classification for specific pathological findings while controlling labeling cost.

topics.title: Subtomogram classification in cryo-ET
topics.description: This topic addresses classification of subtomograms from cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), often using simulated data such as the SHREC’19 dataset. The table lists 25,000 images (24,000/1,000 split) with an initial labeled budget of 10% and query batches of 5%, explicitly tying the task to active learning protocols. The objective is to categorize 3D molecular structures, where labeling is highly specialized and benefits from selective querying.

topics.title: Task types in medical deep active learning
topics.description: This topic highlights the diversity of task types—segmentation, classification, and keypoint localization—used as benchmarks for deep active learning in medical image analysis. Segmentation tasks operate on volumetric data (e.g., CT), classification tasks span disease or severity prediction (e.g., pneumonia presence, calcification level), and keypoint localization targets anatomical landmarks (e.g., cephalometric and hand landmarks). The table illustrates how active learning strategies must adapt to different output spaces and annotation costs across these task categories.

topics.title: Brain structure segmentation from MRI and histology
topics.description: This topic focuses on brain structure segmentation using both MRI and histology data under an active learning scheme. The SATA MRI dataset with 35 volumes uses boundary pixels as the primary annotation target, while an in-house histology brain dataset comprises 15 stacks for structure delineation. The methodology emphasizes efficient acquisition of boundary information and cross-modality segmentation, reducing detailed labeling effort.

topics.title: Polyp segmentation in colonoscopy sequences
topics.description: This topic covers deep active learning for polyp segmentation in colonoscopy video data. The CVC-ClinicDB dataset with 29 sequences (split 23/3/3) is used to learn pixel-level polyp masks. The focus is on selecting informative frames and sequences for annotation to efficiently improve polyp segmentation performance, relevant for computer-aided colonoscopy.

topics.title: Active learning for laparoscopic image segmentation
topics.description: This topic focuses on segmenting laparoscopic surgical images of the gallbladder using deep active learning on the CholecSeg8k dataset. The dataset comprises 8,080 images with a specified split (4,640/1,600/1,640), and experiments make use of only a fraction of data (e.g., 10% labeled) to train segmentation models. Active learning strategies are used to iteratively select the most informative unlabeled frames for annotation, thus reducing manual labeling costs in surgical scene understanding. Bernhardt et al. (2022) illustrate this in the context of laparoscopic image segmentation.

topics.title: Polyp segmentation and lesion classification
topics.description: This topic covers two related endoscopic imaging tasks: polyp segmentation and colonoscopic lesion classification. Polyp segmentation focuses on delineating polyp regions at the pixel level, while colonoscopic lesion classification assigns diagnostic labels at the image or lesion level. The table entries (e.g., sample sizes of 1,000 and 2,717) indicate how datasets are organized for these tasks within deep active learning studies, distinguishing between segmentation and classification as technical objectives.

topics.title: Deep active learning for brain tumors
topics.description: This topic concerns the use of deep active learning methods for brain tumor analysis, focusing on both classification and segmentation tasks. The target entities are brain tumors in medical images, and the processes involve automatically categorizing tumor types and delineating tumor regions. The section indicates a configuration associated with a sample size of 100, reflecting how many images are used in the labeled set or related experimental settings.

canonical_topics.name: Task Taxonomy in Medical Deep Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: Medical deep active learning benchmarks span several core prediction types, most prominently segmentation, classification, and keypoint or landmark localization. Segmentation tasks often operate on volumetric data such as CT or MRI, requiring dense pixel- or voxel-wise annotations that are expensive to obtain. Classification tasks typically focus on disease presence, severity staging, or subtype prediction from 2D or 3D medical images, where labels are image- or patient-level and may be cheaper but still require expert review. Keypoint localization targets anatomical landmarks, for example in cephalometric X-rays or hand radiographs, where each annotation involves placing multiple precise points. These differing output spaces and annotation burdens strongly influence how active learning query strategies are designed and evaluated across medical applications.

canonical_topics.name: Deep Active Learning for Retinal Vessel Segmentation
canonical_topics.description: Deep active learning is applied to retinal vessel segmentation using imaging modalities such as color fundus photography and Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography (OCTA). Benchmark datasets like DRIVE, with 40 images typically split 20/20, and ROSE-1, with 117 images, provide standard testbeds for evaluating query strategies. The learning objective is to obtain accurate pixel-level vessel masks while minimizing manual delineation effort from ophthalmic experts. Studies in this setting compare different acquisition functions and labeling budgets to see how quickly performance saturates relative to fully supervised baselines. This line of work highlights how modality characteristics and small, carefully curated datasets impact active learning behavior in retinal analysis.

canonical_topics.name: Active Learning for Chest X-ray Opacity and Lesion Detection
canonical_topics.description: Deep active learning has been explored for detecting airspace opacities and lung lesions in large-scale chest X-ray collections. In one representative setup, an in-house dataset of over 135,000 images is partitioned into a large pool and a smaller test set, with only up to around 6,500 images allowed to be labeled under a fixed annotation budget. The task is framed as image-level classification of specific pathological findings, such as consolidation or focal lesions. Active learning strategies iteratively select the most informative unlabeled X-rays to annotate, aiming to approach the performance of fully supervised training while using only a fraction of the labels. This scenario showcases the value of active querying when labels are costly radiological interpretations rather than simple categorical tags.

canonical_topics.name: Active Learning for Brain Structure Segmentation and Tumor Analysis
canonical_topics.description: Deep active learning is used for detailed brain structure analysis across both MRI and histology modalities. In structural segmentation, datasets such as SATA with 35 MRI volumes focus on annotating boundary pixels, while in-house histology stacks (e.g., 15 volumes) require fine-grained delineation of anatomical regions. Complementary work targets brain tumor analysis, combining tumor classification and segmentation on comparatively small labeled image sets on the order of hundreds of cases. Because voxel-level and pixel-level annotations in neuroimaging are extremely time-consuming, active learning methods prioritize regions or samples whose labels are expected to most improve model performance. This enables more efficient use of expert neuroradiology and neuropathology effort across multiple brain imaging tasks.

canonical_topics.name: Active Learning for Colonoscopy Polyp Segmentation and Lesion Classification
canonical_topics.description: In gastrointestinal endoscopy, deep active learning is applied to both polyp segmentation and colonoscopic lesion classification. Datasets such as CVC-ClinicDB, with 29 colonoscopy video sequences split into training, validation, and test subsets, are used to study pixel-level polyp mask prediction. Related classification tasks assign diagnostic labels to images or specific lesions, differentiating between polyp types or other pathological findings. Because annotating full video sequences and dense masks is labor-intensive, active learning strategies aim to select the most informative frames and cases for expert review. This setting illustrates how query design must consider temporal redundancy in videos as well as the different costs of segmentation versus image-level labeling in endoscopic workflows.

topics.title: Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma Tumor MRI Segmentation
topics.description: This topic addresses segmentation of nasopharyngeal carcinoma tumors from MRI scans of the nose region, based on an in-house slice-level dataset. The data involve 1,057 patients with a 7:1:2 split, and 20% labeling is indicated, suggesting a limited annotation budget. The focus is on tumor delineation for treatment planning, an application well-suited to deep active learning due to the high cost of voxel-wise annotations.

topics.title: MRI hippocampus segmentation with MSD dataset
topics.description: This topic concerns hippocampus segmentation from MRI using the MSD (Medical Segmentation Decathlon) dataset. It references a task on anterior and posterior hippocampus segmentation with a dataset size of 9,270 samples split into 7,163/350/1,757 subsets, indicating training/validation/test or similar partitions. Such a setup is well-suited for evaluating deep active learning strategies in organ sub-structure segmentation, where detailed region labeling is required.

topics.title: OCT retinal layer segmentation datasets
topics.description: Kadir et al. (2023) are associated with optical coherence tomography (OCT) eye imaging datasets such as the Duke dataset, where superpixel representations are used and 100 scans are split in a 6:2:2 ratio for training/validation/testing, with annotation percentages as low as 2% and 10%. Additional OCT datasets, AROI (1,136 scans, 6:2:2 split) and UMN (725 scans, 6:2:2 split), are also mentioned for segmentation tasks. These collections support OCT layer segmentation studies under limited-annotation regimes, which is central to evaluating deep active learning in ophthalmic imaging.

topics.title: Carotid ultrasound CUBS dataset
topics.description: Tang et al. (2023) are linked to an ultrasound imaging task focused on the carotid region, using the CUBS dataset. The dataset description notes 3,220 images with a split of 2,016/1,204, along with an additional reported number 159, suggesting a substantial data resource for carotid analysis (e.g., vessel or plaque segmentation). This dataset provides a basis for assessing deep active learning methods in vascular ultrasound imaging.

topics.title: Carotid Intima-Media Segmentation Task
topics.description: This topic concerns a segmentation task focused on the carotid intima-media region, using an in-house dataset. The dataset includes 350 test samples, suggesting a specialized, possibly institution-specific collection rather than a public benchmark. The emphasis is on pixel-level delineation of anatomical structures for vascular assessment within a deep active learning framework.

topics.title: Breast Cancer Metastasis Detection in CAMELYON16
topics.description: This topic focuses on detecting cancer metastases in lymph nodes from breast histopathology using the CAMELYON16 dataset. The input is patch-based, extracted from 398 whole-slide images (270/128 split), with multiple patch sizes (4096, 8192, 12288) and varying numbers of patches per WSI (1, 3, 5). It frames metastasis detection as a classification problem, highlighting design choices in patch sampling and resolution relevant to deep active learning strategies.

topics.title: Colon Histopathology Classification with PathMNIST
topics.description: This topic covers colon histopathology image classification using the PathMNIST dataset. The dataset comprises 107,180 images with a specified split of 89,996/10,004/7,180 for training, validation, and testing, and includes 20 classes. It represents a benchmark histopathology classification setting for evaluating deep active learning methods on multi-class diagnostic tasks.

topics.title: Dataset scale and split design in benchmarks
topics.description: This topic concerns how medical imaging benchmarks are quantitatively characterized by total sample counts and explicit train/validation/test splits. The OrganAMNIST and BloodMNIST entries both specify large numbers of images and detailed partitioning, reflecting standard experimental design for evaluating deep active learning methods. Such structured splits are essential for fair comparison of algorithms, particularly when studying label efficiency and performance under limited annotation budgets.

topics.title: PROMISE 2012 prostate MRI segmentation
topics.description: This topic covers prostate segmentation from MRI slices using the PROMISE 2012 dataset. The dataset contains 1,377 slices split into 1,020/109/248 subsets and is used for a prostate segmentation task evaluated in the context of deep active learning. The work by Qu et al. (2023a) is cited, indicating a NeurIPS 2023 study focusing on this MRI-based segmentation problem.

topics.title: Histopathology nuclei segmentation across multiple organs
topics.description: This topic addresses nuclei segmentation in histopathology images drawn from several organs and datasets. TCGA-KUMAR (seven organs, patch-level, 30 images with 12/4/14 split), TNBC (breast, 50 images with 30/7/13 split), and MoNuSeg (seven organs, 44 images with 30/14 split) are used with only 5% or 7% of data labeled. Hu et al. (2023) in TMI employ these datasets to study deep active learning for nuclei segmentation under extremely limited annotation budgets.

canonical_topics.name: MRI Organ and Tumor Segmentation Benchmarks
canonical_topics.description: This topic covers deep active learning for MRI-based organ and tumor segmentation, including nasopharyngeal carcinoma, hippocampus, and prostate tasks. Representative datasets include an in-house nasopharyngeal carcinoma MRI collection with 1,057 patients (7:1:2 split, around 20% labels), the MSD hippocampus task with 9,270 samples (7,163/350/1,757 split), and PROMISE 2012 prostate MRI with 1,377 slices (1,020/109/248 split). All of these tasks require voxel- or pixel-level delineation of anatomically complex structures, making annotation expensive and time-consuming. They serve as canonical benchmarks for evaluating how deep active learning can reduce labeling effort while maintaining segmentation quality across different organs and institutions.

canonical_topics.name: Ophthalmic and Carotid Ultrasound Segmentation
canonical_topics.description: This topic focuses on deep active learning for segmentation in ophthalmic OCT and carotid ultrasound imaging. It includes OCT retinal layer segmentation on datasets such as Duke (100 scans, 6:2:2 split), AROI (1,136 scans, 6:2:2 split), and UMN (725 scans, 6:2:2 split), where only 2–10% of scans may be labeled. It also covers carotid ultrasound segmentation using the CUBS dataset (3,220 images with reported 2,016/1,204 plus an additional 159 images) and an in-house carotid intima–media dataset with 350 test samples. These applications require precise boundary delineation in noisy, modality-specific images, so they are well suited to studying how active query strategies can target the most informative images or regions under tight annotation budgets.

canonical_topics.name: Multi-Organ Histopathology Nuclei Segmentation
canonical_topics.description: This topic addresses deep active learning for nuclei segmentation in histopathology images drawn from multiple organs and datasets. Key resources include TCGA-KUMAR (seven organs, 30 images with a 12/4/14 split), TNBC (breast, 50 images with a 30/7/13 split), and MoNuSeg (seven organs, 44 images with a 30/14 split). In these benchmarks, only about 5–7% of the data are labeled, reflecting the extreme cost of pixel-wise nuclei annotations. They provide a challenging setting for evaluating active learning strategies that must select the most informative images or regions to annotate while handling cross-organ variability and limited labels.

canonical_topics.name: Histopathology Image Classification Benchmarks
canonical_topics.description: This topic covers deep active learning for histopathology image classification, exemplified by CAMELYON16 and PathMNIST. CAMELYON16 focuses on detecting breast cancer metastases in lymph node whole-slide images, using patch-based inputs extracted from 398 WSIs (270/128 split) at multiple patch sizes and with varying numbers of patches per slide. PathMNIST provides a large-scale colon histopathology benchmark with 107,180 images and a 89,996/10,004/7,180 train/validation/test split over 20 classes. These datasets support systematic evaluation of active learning for multi-class and highly imbalanced diagnostic classification, including how patch sampling, resolution, and acquisition strategies interact under constrained labeling budgets.

canonical_topics.name: Dataset Scaling and Splits for DAL Benchmarks
canonical_topics.description: This topic examines how medical imaging benchmarks for deep active learning are defined in terms of dataset scale and train/validation/test split design. Public datasets such as OrganAMNIST and BloodMNIST, along with others like PathMNIST, explicitly report large sample counts and standardized partitions. Such structured splits are essential for fair comparison of active learning methods, particularly when varying labeled-set sizes or annotation budgets over fixed test sets. The topic emphasizes that clear reporting of data scale, splits, and labeling fractions is crucial for reproducible and interpretable evaluations of label efficiency in deep active learning.

topics.title: Lower extremity MRI dataset setup
topics.description: The section describes an in-house MRI dataset of the lower extremities, associated with IJCARS, used for deep active learning experiments. The data is organized at the volume or slice level, with 119 volumes split into 90 for training, 9 for validation, and 20 for testing. Sampling units can be entire 3D volumes or sets of 190 slices, reflecting different annotation/query granularities in active learning workflows.

topics.title: CheXpert chest X-ray dataset characteristics
topics.description: The CheXpert chest X-ray dataset is presented as a large-scale benchmark for deep active learning in 2D medical imaging. It includes 224,114 X-ray images of the chest, with a split of 223,414/200/500 across training, validation, and test sets. The dataset is image-based (rather than volumetric), and involves 10 target classes, enabling class-imbalanced and large-scale active learning studies.

topics.title: Medical image benchmarks for AL
topics.description: The section lists several benchmark datasets used in medical image analysis, specifying modality, anatomical region, dataset name, sample size and splits, and target clinical task. These include ChestXray14 for thoracic disease diagnosis, BreastMNIST for breast cancer diagnosis, DermaMNIST for skin lesion diagnosis, RetinaMNIST for diabetic retinopathy severity grading, and TissueMNIST for kidney cortex disease classification. Such datasets form the basis for evaluating deep active learning strategies in diverse imaging contexts.

topics.title: Entropy-based uncertainty with pseudo-labeling
topics.description: In breast pathology image classification, active learning is implemented by measuring entropy over model predictions on patches to quantify uncertainty. Patches with high entropy are sent to experts for annotation, while low-entropy patches receive pseudo-labels and are used to augment the training set without manual labeling. This combines uncertainty sampling with semi-supervised learning to improve annotation efficiency. The key entities are patch-level predictions, entropy as an uncertainty metric, and pseudo-label assignment.

topics.title: Category-wise curriculum querying and negative pre-training
topics.description: For histological tissue classification at the patch level, category-wise curriculum querying dynamically adjusts how much uncertainty sampling focuses on each class. This addresses class-dependent difficulty and imbalance by weighting querying effort per category during active learning. Additionally, negative pre-training uses intentionally wrong predictions to better separate visually similar classes, improving discriminative representations before or during active learning. Together, these strategies refine query selection and representation learning in complex multi-class pathology settings.

topics.title: Human-augmenting AI labeling with Core-Set AL
topics.description: A human-augmenting labeling system leverages active learning to suggest which WSI patches experts should annotate and to propose labels via a trained classifier. Core-Set is used as the active learner to select a subset of patches that best represent the data distribution while being informative. This human-in-the-loop workflow significantly reduces pathologists’ workload (around 90%) and can slightly improve data quality across cellular labeling tasks. The process couples query selection, model training, and expert verification in an iterative loop.

topics.title: Attention-based MIL with MC Dropout for querying
topics.description: In MIL-based WSI classification, attention-based MIL architectures are combined with Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout to estimate uncertainty at both the attention (instance importance) and classification levels. For each patch within a WSI, MC Dropout yields predictive distributions from which uncertainties are computed, and patches with the highest uncertainties are selected for expert annotation. This dual uncertainty captures ambiguity in which patches matter and how they should be classified, improving the informativeness of queried instances. The method aligns instance-level querying with the MIL attention mechanism.

topics.title: Open-set active learning for relevant patch selection
topics.description: Because WSIs contain both target classes (e.g., tumors, lymph nodes, normal cells) and many irrelevant non-target tissues (e.g., fat, stroma, debris), open-set active learning is adopted. In this setting, the unlabeled pool includes both target and non-target samples, and the system must simultaneously perform relevance filtering and uncertainty-based querying. By combining feature distribution information with prediction uncertainty, the method selects patches that are both informative and likely to belong to target classes for annotation. This reduces annotation spent on clearly irrelevant or out-of-distribution regions while focusing expert effort on diagnostically meaningful instances.

topics.title: Specialized AL Designs for Segmentation
topics.description: The section emphasizes specialized active learning designs tailored to medical image segmentation, including slice-based annotation, one-shot annotation, and explicit modeling of annotation cost. These designs exploit unique traits of medical imaging data (e.g., volumetric structure, annotation granularity) to make the selection and labeling process more efficient and clinically feasible.

topics.title: Autoencoder-based slice feature learning
topics.description: Autoencoders are used to learn semantic feature representations of each slice in a 3D volume, serving as the basis for selecting key slices. After encoding slices from axial, sagittal, and coronal planes, a selection strategy similar to representativeness-based RA is applied to identify which slices to annotate. This couples unsupervised feature learning with active selection across multiple anatomical planes.

canonical_topics.name: Medical Imaging Benchmarks for Deep Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: A diverse set of medical imaging benchmarks underpins empirical evaluation of deep active learning methods. These include volumetric lower-extremity MRI data with volume- or slice-level sampling units, enabling experiments on different annotation granularities in 3D. Large 2D datasets such as CheXpert and ChestXray14 provide hundreds of thousands of chest X-rays with predefined train/validation/test splits and multiple disease labels, supporting large-scale and class-imbalanced active learning studies. Additional benchmarks like BreastMNIST, DermaMNIST, RetinaMNIST, and TissueMNIST cover breast cancer, skin lesion, retinal, and kidney tissue classification, respectively, broadening coverage across modalities and anatomical regions. Together, these datasets allow systematic comparison of query strategies across scale, modality, label imbalance, and annotation cost settings.

canonical_topics.name: Deep Active Learning for Histopathology and Whole-Slide Images
canonical_topics.description: Deep active learning in histopathology often operates at the patch level, combining uncertainty sampling with semi-supervised learning via pseudo-labeling: high-entropy patches are sent to experts, while low-entropy patches receive pseudo-labels to expand the training set without additional annotation. Category-wise curriculum querying adjusts sampling pressure per class, addressing class-dependent difficulty and imbalance, while negative pre-training with intentionally wrong predictions helps to better separate visually similar categories before or during active learning. Human-augmenting labeling systems use Core-Set selection to propose representative and informative patches and tentative labels, allowing experts to verify rather than annotate from scratch and thereby reducing workload. In multiple-instance learning for whole-slide image classification, attention-based MIL models coupled with Monte Carlo Dropout provide uncertainty estimates both over instance importance and slide-level predictions, guiding which patches within a slide should be reviewed. Open-set active learning further filters out clearly irrelevant or out-of-distribution tissue by combining feature distribution information with prediction uncertainty, ensuring annotation effort focuses on diagnostically meaningful regions.

canonical_topics.name: Active Learning Designs for Segmentation and Slice Selection
canonical_topics.description: Specialized active learning designs for medical image segmentation take into account the volumetric structure of data and the high cost of pixel-level annotation. Strategies such as slice-based annotation and one-shot annotation aim to maximize spatial coverage and model improvement per unit of labeling effort, while explicitly modeling annotation cost to prioritize cheaper but still informative queries. Unsupervised feature learning with autoencoders is used to obtain semantic representations of slices from different anatomical planes, enabling the selection of key slices that best summarize a 3D volume. Representativeness-based selection on these learned features identifies a compact subset of slices for annotation, reducing expert workload while preserving segmentation performance. Together, these methods adapt query granularity and selection criteria to the unique demands of volumetric medical image segmentation.

topics.title: Application to 3D knee structure segmentation
topics.description: The slice-based annotation and selection strategy is extended to 3D segmentation of knee cartilage and bone. This shows that the framework is transferable beyond its initial application, supporting complex musculoskeletal structures where 3D context is important but full-volume annotation is costly.

topics.title: Self-attention for enhanced slice features
topics.description: A self-attention module is integrated into the autoencoder to improve the quality of slice-level feature learning. By modeling long-range dependencies within a slice, self-attention can produce more discriminative representations, potentially leading to better identification of key slices for annotation in active learning workflows.

topics.title: Clustering and regional uncertainty in CT
topics.description: For muscle segmentation in CT images, key slices and subregions within them are jointly selected using clustering and uncertainty. Hiasa et al. (2020) first apply clustering to identify representative key slices, then focus annotation on regions within those slices that exhibit high model uncertainty. This two-stage process combines global structural diversity (via clustering) with local informativeness (via uncertainty). It improves annotation efficiency by targeting both important slices and their most ambiguous areas.

topics.title: Hybrid uncertainty-representativeness for slice annotation
topics.description: Recent methods for slice-based annotation combine uncertainty with representativeness to select informative samples. In shoulder MRI musculoskeletal segmentation, Ozdemir et al. (2021) measure uncertainty using the variance across multiple Monte Carlo (MC) dropout runs and measure representativeness using posterior probabilities estimated by an infoVAE. This balances querying slices where the model is unsure with slices that are representative of the data distribution. Such hybrid criteria aim to improve both sample informativeness and coverage of the feature space.

topics.title: Bayesian U-net and MI-based redundancy reduction
topics.description: Li et al. (2024) propose a hybrid deep active learning strategy for musculoskeletal segmentation of lower extremities in MRI and CT. Uncertainty is estimated using a Bayesian U-net, while representativeness is computed via cosine similarity, ensuring both informative and diverse slice selection. They additionally apply mutual information-based criteria to minimize sample redundancy, following Nath et al. (2021), further improving the efficiency of queried samples. This integrated approach achieves strong performance across both MRI and CT datasets.

topics.title: Self-supervised features for one-shot sampling
topics.description: Most one-shot annotation methods in medical imaging combine self-supervised feature learning with tailored sampling strategies. Self-supervised representations (e.g., from VAEs, contrastive learning, or auto-encoding transformations) capture semantic structure without extensive labels, enabling more informed selection of samples within a single round. These learned features then drive criteria like representativeness, diversity, or density for sample selection.

topics.title: RA: VAE-based representativeness sampling
topics.description: The RA method is an early one-shot active learning approach for medical image segmentation that leverages features from a variational autoencoder (VAE). It uses a representativeness strategy in the learned feature space to select informative samples for single-round annotation. RA showed strong performance on gland segmentation in pathological images, whole-heart MRI segmentation, and fungal segmentation in electron microscopic images.

topics.title: Representativeness-based key slice selection
topics.description: Wu et al. proposed a representativeness-based framework focused on selecting key slices for annotation in a one-shot setting. They employ self-learning to obtain semantic representations for each slice, then use these features to propagate expert annotations to unannotated slices. This approach reduces the number of slices needing direct expert labeling while maintaining segmentation quality across the volume.

topics.title: Contrastive features and farthest-first sampling
topics.description: Jin et al. (2022b) integrate contrastive learning features with a farthest-first sampling strategy to realize one-shot annotation. Contrastive learning yields discriminative embeddings, while farthest-first sampling selects samples that are maximally separated in this feature space, promoting diversity and broad coverage. Their method was validated on ISIC 2018 skin lesion and lung segmentation datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness for single-round labeling.

topics.title: Density-based selection via reachable distance
topics.description: Jin et al. (2023b) use auto-encoding transformations for self-supervised feature learning, capturing meaningful structure in unlabeled medical images. In the resulting feature space, they define a notion of reachable distance to estimate local sample density and select high-density samples for annotation in one shot. This favors labeling representative points in dense regions, which can improve generalization while respecting strict interaction limits.

canonical_topics.name: Hybrid Uncertainty–Representativeness Slice Selection
canonical_topics.description: Hybrid slice-based active learning methods for medical image segmentation jointly exploit uncertainty and representativeness at both slice and subregion levels. Representative key slices are first identified, for example via clustering in feature space, to ensure broad coverage of global anatomical variability. Within these slices, uncertainty measures such as Bayesian or Monte Carlo dropout estimates are used to focus annotation on ambiguous subregions. Representativeness can be quantified with latent-space distances or cosine similarity, while mutual information-based redundancy reduction prevents repeatedly querying highly similar samples. This family of approaches has been successfully applied to CT and MRI musculoskeletal segmentation, including extensions to complex 3D structures where full-volume annotation would be prohibitively expensive.

canonical_topics.name: Self-Attention for Slice-Level Feature Learning
canonical_topics.description: In slice-based deep active learning pipelines, self-attention modules are integrated into autoencoders or encoders to enhance slice-level feature representations. By modeling long-range spatial dependencies within a slice, self-attention produces more contextual and discriminative embeddings than purely local convolutional features. These richer representations improve downstream query criteria such as uncertainty, representativeness, and diversity when selecting key slices for annotation. As a result, the active learner can more reliably identify informative slices and regions, improving segmentation performance under limited annotation budgets.

canonical_topics.name: Self-Supervised Features for One-Shot Annotation
canonical_topics.description: One-shot active learning methods for medical image segmentation increasingly rely on self-supervised or generative feature learning to guide a single, highly effective annotation round. Variational autoencoders and related models (e.g., RA-style approaches) learn latent spaces in which representativeness-based sampling selects a small set of images or slices that best cover the data distribution. Other methods use contrastive learning to obtain discriminative embeddings and apply farthest-first sampling to maximize diversity among queried samples. Auto-encoding transformations and self-learning strategies can also yield features in which density-based criteria, such as reachable distance, identify high-density and thus highly representative samples, while label propagation reduces the need for direct expert annotation of every slice. Across modalities and tasks, these self-supervised feature spaces enable principled representativeness, diversity, and density-based selection tailored to stringent one-shot annotation constraints.

topics.title: Unequal annotation costs in segmentation
topics.description: The section highlights that common active learning methods assume equal annotation costs per sample, which is unrealistic in medical image segmentation where annotation time can vary significantly. It argues that active learning should explicitly consider annotation costs, such as annotation time, to better support physicians and make querying more practical in clinical settings.

topics.title: Disagreement-time cost model with knapsack AL
topics.description: Kuo et al. (2018) integrate predictive disagreement and estimated annotation time to guide sample selection for intracranial hemorrhage detection in CT scans. Jensen–Shannon divergence between multiple model outputs measures informativeness, while annotation time is approximated using the segmentation boundary length and number of connected components. The selection problem is formulated as a 0–1 knapsack optimization, solved via dynamic programming, to choose the most informative samples under a cost budget.

topics.title: Similarity-based slice annotation cost
topics.description: Shen et al. (2021) estimate the annotation cost of brain tumor slices using a distance measure between queried slices and already-labeled slices. Lower distance is interpreted as lower annotation cost, under the assumption that annotating slices similar to previously labeled ones is faster and easier for experts. This embeds a notion of familiarity into the active learning cost model.

topics.title: Spatially-informed cost and Dice optimization
topics.description: Atzeni et al. (2022) refine annotation cost estimation for brain structure segmentation by accounting for spatial relationships between multiple regions of interest. They also use the average Dice coefficient from previous active learning rounds to predict current Dice performance. Regions are then selected for annotation to maximize the predicted average Dice, linking cost modeling with an explicit segmentation quality metric.

topics.title: Uncertainty-Guided Interactive Fetal Brain Segmentation
topics.description: For MRI fetal brain segmentation, an uncertainty-guided interactive refinement framework is introduced. A specialized network architecture produces multiple segmentation outputs simultaneously; the variance across these predictions is used as an uncertainty metric. Slices with the highest estimated uncertainty are prioritized for human expert interaction, allowing clinicians to focus refinement on the most ambiguous regions, thereby improving segmentation quality with minimal additional annotation.

topics.title: Learnable k-space sampling for MRI
topics.description: Deep learning is used to reconstruct undersampled MRI data where k-space is sampled via either fixed or learnable masks. Traditional approaches use a fixed undersampling mask and a deep model to reconstruct the image, while AL-based approaches learn which k-space locations to sample next. This transforms acquisition into an adaptive sampling problem directly tied to reconstruction quality and imaging speed.

topics.title: Adversarial and RL policies for k-space
topics.description: Adversarial learning and reinforcement learning are used to design active sampling policies in k-space for MRI. Methods include an adversarially trained evaluator that selects the next k-space row, dual deep Q-networks for active sampling decisions, and policy-gradient-based networks that adapt sampling patterns. Rewards are defined via reconstruction metrics such as structural similarity, linking sampling choices to image quality improvements.

topics.title: Joint optimization of acquisition and reconstruction
topics.description: Instead of treating acquisition and reconstruction separately, some MRI approaches jointly optimize the sampling policy and the reconstruction network. This end-to-end training allows the acquisition strategy to adapt to the reconstruction model’s capabilities, potentially yielding better image quality for a given acquisition budget. It exemplifies tightly coupled AL and reconstruction design.

topics.title: Adaptive CT scanning angle selection
topics.description: Active learning is applied to CT by adaptively choosing patient-specific scanning angles. The method tailors the projection directions to each individual, enabling sufficient reconstruction quality with fewer projections. This reduces both radiation exposure and scan duration compared to fixed-angle protocols.

topics.title: Active rescanning in electron microscopy
topics.description: In electron microscopy, an AL pipeline first enhances low-resolution images to high resolution, then predicts regions of interest and reconstruction errors. A weighted determinantal point process (DPP), parameterized by reconstruction error, selects which pixels to rescan to refine the image. This strategy simultaneously maintains low reconstruction error and spatial diversity, focusing acquisition on informative and diverse locations.

canonical_topics.name: Cost-Aware Active Learning for Medical Segmentation
canonical_topics.description: Cost-aware active learning for medical image segmentation explicitly models that not all samples require the same annotation effort. Annotation cost can be estimated from properties such as boundary length, number of connected components, similarity to previously labeled slices, or spatial relationships between regions of interest. Informativeness measures (e.g., model disagreement) are combined with these cost estimates, and selection is often cast as a constrained optimization problem such as a 0–1 knapsack under a time or effort budget. Some approaches further link cost models directly to segmentation quality metrics, such as maximizing predicted average Dice score across regions, to prioritize annotations that most efficiently improve performance.

canonical_topics.name: Uncertainty-Guided Interactive Fetal Brain Segmentation
canonical_topics.description: Uncertainty-guided interactive fetal brain segmentation uses model uncertainty to focus expert effort on the most ambiguous image regions. A specialized network architecture generates multiple segmentation hypotheses, and the variance across these predictions serves as an uncertainty indicator. Slices or regions with the highest uncertainty are prioritized for expert interaction and refinement, while confident areas are left untouched. This deep active learning strategy reduces overall annotation time and improves segmentation quality by tightly coupling model-driven uncertainty estimates with targeted human corrections.

canonical_topics.name: Deep Active Acquisition Policies for MRI k-Space
canonical_topics.description: Deep active acquisition for MRI treats k-space sampling as a sequential decision problem guided by reconstruction objectives. Instead of using fixed undersampling masks, learnable sampling policies decide which k-space locations to acquire next, often in tandem with a deep reconstruction network. Policies can be trained via adversarial learning, reinforcement learning (e.g., deep Q-networks or policy-gradient methods), or differentiable mask optimization. Reconstruction metrics such as structural similarity or pixel-wise error define the reward or loss, directly tying sampling decisions to image quality. This leads to adaptive, data-driven acquisition strategies that improve reconstruction fidelity under strict sampling budgets.

canonical_topics.name: Adaptive CT Projection Angle Selection via Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: Adaptive CT projection angle selection frames scan design as an active learning problem over candidate viewing angles. For each patient, the system iteratively chooses the most informative projection directions rather than following a fixed-angle protocol. Selection policies aim to maintain or improve reconstruction quality while acquiring fewer projections, effectively operating under a dose or time budget. This patient-specific adaptation can reduce radiation exposure and scan duration by focusing acquisition on angles that maximally reduce reconstruction uncertainty or error.

canonical_topics.name: Active Rescanning Strategies for Electron Microscopy
canonical_topics.description: Active rescanning in electron microscopy uses model predictions to determine which pixels or regions to re-acquire at higher fidelity. A pipeline first reconstructs or enhances low-resolution images and estimates both regions of interest and reconstruction errors. A weighted determinantal point process, parameterized by predicted error, then selects a diverse set of high-error pixels to rescan within a fixed acquisition budget. This approach balances informativeness and spatial diversity, concentrating additional imaging resources on areas that most improve overall reconstruction quality.

topics.title: Limitations of Existing AL Evaluations
topics.description: Active learning (AL) for medical image analysis lacks comprehensive and systematic evaluation on realistic medical datasets. Many studies rely on standard benchmark datasets such as CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, or MedMNIST, which do not fully capture the limited data availability and higher complexity of real-world clinical imaging. This mismatch raises concerns about the clinical applicability of reported performance gains.

topics.title: Inconsistent Gains Over Random Sampling
topics.description: Different AL strategies often exhibit inconsistent performance and do not reliably outperform simple random sampling, especially in classification tasks. Studies, including Munjal et al. (2022) and prior discussion in §4.2, report that no single AL method consistently dominates others and that random sampling can be competitive or even superior when the annotation budget is low. This uncertainty makes it difficult to decide which AL method to adopt for a given medical imaging scenario.

topics.title: Active learning for electron microscopy imaging
topics.description: This topic addresses the use of deep active learning in electron microscopy (EM) for brain imaging, including mouse cortex (SNEMI3D) and human cerebrum data. Methods target accelerated acquisition and analysis of EM volumes by prioritizing which regions or samples to acquire at high resolution and to annotate, thus reducing the immense labeling burden typical of EM datasets. The work referenced (Pineda et al. 2020, MICCAI) explores strategies to efficiently reconstruct or segment neural structures from large-scale EM imagery.

topics.title: CT-based reconstruction datasets
topics.description: Several CT reconstruction benchmarks are referenced, covering lung and spine imaging. Lung CT reconstruction is associated with the AAPM dataset, while spine CT reconstruction uses the VerSe dataset. These datasets support evaluation of reconstruction algorithms in different anatomical regions and CT imaging contexts.

topics.title: Accuracy for Multi-Class Classification
topics.description: Accuracy (ACC) is used as the primary evaluation metric for the multi-class classification task on the NCT-CRC-HE-100K dataset. It measures the proportion of correctly classified samples over the total number of samples, providing a straightforward indicator of overall classification performance. This choice is suitable when class distributions are relatively balanced and all classes are equally important.

topics.title: Test-Set Metrics as Final Results
topics.description: Evaluation metrics are ultimately computed on the testing set and reported as the final results. This practice ensures that performance estimates reflect generalization to unseen data and are not biased by training or validation processes. It provides a fair basis for comparing different models or active learning strategies.

topics.title: Random sampling baseline in AL
topics.description: Random sampling is used as the baseline comparison method in the active learning (AL) evaluation. It selects unlabeled samples uniformly at random without using any model-driven informativeness or diversity criteria. This provides a reference to measure the benefit of more sophisticated query strategies.

topics.title: Classic uncertainty-based AL criteria
topics.description: Confidence, Entropy, and Margin are presented as classic uncertainty-based active learning methods. They compute uncertainty scores from prediction probabilities using three different measures: low maximum confidence, high entropy, and small classification margin indicate greater uncertainty. These scores guide the selection of unlabeled samples expected to most improve the model when labeled.

topics.title: Core-Set as a comparison method
topics.description: The Core-Set method by Sener and Savarese (2018) is listed among the comparison methods for evaluating active learning strategies. Although not described in detail in this section, it is treated as an additional baseline/competitor in the experimental setup alongside uncertainty-based and Bayesian methods.

topics.title: k-Center-Greedy for core-set selection
topics.description: k-Center-Greedy is used as the selection algorithm to balance computational cost and active learning performance. At each step, it greedily selects the point that maximizes the minimum distance to already selected points, approximating the k-center objective in embedding space. This yields a diverse and representative labeled set without the cost of exact optimization.

canonical_topics.name: Evaluating Deep Active Learning in Medical Imaging
canonical_topics.description: Deep active learning for medical image analysis is often evaluated on small, generic benchmarks such as CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, or MedMNIST, which fail to capture the data scarcity, label noise, and complexity of real clinical imaging. This limits the clinical relevance of reported performance gains and may overestimate the benefits of sophisticated query strategies. Empirical studies also show that different active learning methods yield highly inconsistent improvements and frequently do not outperform simple random sampling, especially at low annotation budgets. As a result, random sampling must be treated as a strong baseline and carefully compared against, and there is a need for more realistic datasets and standardized evaluation protocols. Addressing these limitations is crucial for determining when and how deep active learning truly adds value in medical imaging workflows.

canonical_topics.name: Uncertainty Sampling and Core-Set Strategies in DAL
canonical_topics.description: Uncertainty-based query strategies, such as maximum confidence, entropy, and margin sampling, select unlabeled examples whose predicted probabilities indicate high model uncertainty, aiming to maximize information gain from each annotation.
