Complementing these, core-set–style methods treat active learning as a geometric coverage problem in feature space, selecting a subset of points that best represents the unlabeled pool. A popular instantiation is k-Center-Greedy, which iteratively chooses the sample that maximizes the minimum distance to already selected points, achieving a diverse and representative labeled set at manageable computational cost. Together, these families of methods form standard baselines and competitors in deep active learning benchmarks. Their comparative performance depends on factors such as feature quality, dataset structure, and annotation budget.

canonical_topics.name: Deep Active Learning for Electron Microscopy Volumes
canonical_topics.description: Deep active learning has been applied to electron microscopy brain imaging to reduce the extreme annotation burden required for accurate 3D reconstruction and segmentation. In this setting, models prioritize which regions or slices of large EM volumes, such as mouse cortex (SNEMI3D) or human cerebrum data, should be acquired at high resolution and labeled. Query strategies can focus on uncertain or structurally informative regions, enabling more efficient reconstruction of neural structures with fewer labeled voxels. This approach accelerates both data acquisition and analysis, making large-scale connectomics studies more feasible. Work such as Pineda et al. (2020, MICCAI) demonstrates how DAL can be integrated into EM pipelines to target the most valuable samples for expert annotation.

topics.title: Uncertainty aggregation in segmentation tasks
topics.description: For segmentation, uncertainty-based methods differ from classification by operating initially at the pixel level. Pixel-wise scores (e.g., probabilities or uncertainty measures per pixel) are first produced, and then aggregated by averaging across pixels to obtain a single uncertainty score per image or sample. This aggregated score is then used for sample selection in active learning.

topics.title: Classification backbone and training setup
topics.description: The classification tasks use ResNet-18 as the backbone network, optimized with stochastic gradient descent with momentum. Training runs for 100 epochs with a batch size of 128, a learning rate of 0.01, momentum of 0.9, and cross-entropy as the loss function. A cosine learning rate decay schedule is applied to achieve smoother convergence during optimization.

topics.title: Dataset-specific augmentations for classification
topics.description: Different data augmentation strategies are applied for two classification datasets to improve generalization. For NCT-CRC-HE-100K, only random horizontal flipping is used, reflecting relatively simple transformations. For ISIC 2020, a richer augmentation pipeline from Zhuang et al. (2018) is followed, including random cropping, flipping, rotation, affine transforms, and color jittering, to model more complex variability in dermoscopic images.

topics.title: U-Net segmentation architecture design
topics.description: Segmentation tasks are handled using a 5-level U-Net architecture, with symmetric encoder and decoder paths. Each level contains two blocks, and each block is composed of a 2D convolution, a dropout layer with probability 0.1, batch normalization, and a leaky ReLU activation. This configuration balances regularization, stable training, and non-linear feature extraction for pixel-wise prediction.

topics.title: Computational environment and software stack
topics.description: Experiments are executed on high-end NVIDIA GPUs (GeForce RTX 3090 and 4090) with CUDA 11.3, indicating requirements for substantial computational resources. The implementation is based on Python 3.8.10 and PyTorch 1.11.0, defining the software environment and deep learning framework used for reproducibility and potential extension.

topics.title: Margin sampling in low-budget regimes
topics.description: This topic describes the behavior of the Margin-based active learning strategy when only a small labeling budget is available. Margin performs well in this regime because it leverages information from wrong predictions between similar classes to select informative samples. This aligns with findings reported in related work (Hu et al. 2023), highlighting the value of uncertainty near decision boundaries for early-stage labeling.

topics.title: Binary skin lesion classification setup
topics.description: The section evaluates deep active learning methods on the ISIC 2020 dataset framed as a binary skin lesion classification task with severe class imbalance. Performance is measured using AUC on a held-out test split, as summarized in Table 7. This setup provides a challenging environment to compare different active learning strategies under realistic clinical class distributions.

topics.title: Equivalence of Confidence and Margin in binaries
topics.description: In the binary classification setting, the Confidence and Margin uncertainty measures become mathematically equivalent, leading the authors to report only Confidence-based results. This reflects that the score ordering induced by these two strategies is identical when only two classes are present. Consequently, Margin is omitted from the comparative analysis.

topics.title: Random vs uncertainty-based query strategies in ASD
topics.description: ASD values are reported for multiple acquisition strategies: Random, Confidence, Entropy, and Margin sampling. Each strategy is associated with mean ± standard deviation ASD values across several budget levels, such as Random (4.71 ± 1.13 down to 2.21 ± 0.73) and Confidence (6.63 ± 2.05 down to 2.22 ± 0.62). These results compare purely random selection with uncertainty-based methods that rely on confidence scores, entropy, or decision margins from the model. The comparison indicates how different query strategies impact boundary accuracy in deep active learning for medical image segmentation.

topics.title: Core-Set Under Low-Budget Early Rounds
topics.description: The Core-Set method performs well on both mean DSC and ASD during early rounds in a lower budget scenario. This suggests that Core-Set is particularly effective when label budgets are small, helping to rapidly improve both overlap and boundary accuracy with limited annotations. Its early-round advantage highlights the role of representative subset selection in data-efficient segmentation.

canonical_topics.name: Pixel-wise uncertainty aggregation in segmentation
canonical_topics.description: In deep active learning for segmentation, uncertainty is first estimated at the pixel or voxel level and then aggregated to obtain a single query score per image. Typical aggregation schemes include averaging or summing pixel-wise uncertainties, or using more sophisticated reductions that emphasize boundaries or highly uncertain regions. The resulting image-level uncertainty score is used to rank unlabeled samples for acquisition. Design choices in aggregation can strongly influence which structures and edge cases are prioritized during annotation. Understanding and calibrating this aggregation step is therefore crucial for effective active learning in dense prediction tasks.

canonical_topics.name: Margin and confidence sampling in classification
canonical_topics.description: Margin-based sampling selects points whose top predicted classes have similar probabilities, thereby targeting examples near the decision boundary. This strategy can be especially effective in low-budget regimes, where early acquisitions around ambiguous boundaries yield rapid performance gains. In binary classification, margin and confidence scores induce the same ranking of unlabeled samples, making the two uncertainty measures mathematically equivalent. As a consequence, reporting only confidence-based results is sufficient in such settings, since margin adds no additional selection behavior. Recognizing these relationships helps simplify experimental design and interpret results across different uncertainty-based query strategies.

canonical_topics.name: Comparing acquisition strategies for medical segmentation
canonical_topics.description: Deep active learning for medical image segmentation often compares random sampling with uncertainty-based and diversity-based query strategies. Uncertainty-driven methods, such as confidence, entropy, and margin sampling, use model outputs to prioritize ambiguous cases and can substantially improve boundary accuracy metrics like ASD relative to random selection. Core-Set approaches, which aim to select a representative and diverse subset of the data, tend to perform particularly well in early rounds under tight labeling budgets, improving both overlap (e.g., DSC) and boundary quality. These comparisons highlight trade-offs between exploration and exploitation, and provide practical guidance for choosing acquisition strategies in data-scarce segmentation scenarios.

topics.title: Sampling Diversity via BADGE and Core-Set
topics.description: Both BADGE and Core-Set are identified as methods that enhance sampling diversity in the active learning process. By diversifying the selected samples, these methods aim to cover different regions of the data space and avoid redundant annotations, which can accelerate model improvement. This diversity-focused selection is presented as a key factor behind their strong early performance in segmentation metrics.

topics.title: Late-Round Superiority of Uncertainty and Random Sampling
topics.description: In later active learning rounds, uncertainty-based methods and even random sampling catch up and improve in both mean DSC and ASD. This suggests that once the model has been sufficiently initialized with diverse, informative samples, simpler selection strategies can still yield strong incremental gains. The observed trend is consistent with earlier findings referenced in the survey, indicating a shift in the relative benefits of complex selection strategies over the course of AL.

topics.title: L2 and cosine distances on embeddings
topics.description: This topic defines how L2 and cosine distances are computed over feature embeddings of images in deep active learning. Each image sample x is mapped to a d-dimensional feature vector z, and the L2 distance is calculated as the Euclidean norm of the difference between two embeddings, while the cosine distance is derived from one minus the cosine similarity between them. These formulas formalize how image similarity is quantified in the feature space for AL methods.

topics.title: Budget-dependent metric performance on datasets
topics.description: This topic summarizes empirical results comparing L2 and cosine distances across multiple medical imaging datasets and labeling budgets. On NCT-CRC-HE-100K, both metrics perform similarly at all budgets, whereas on ISIC 2020 and ACDC, L2 is better in early rounds (low budget) but cosine becomes competitive or superior as more samples are selected (high budget). The findings lead to a recommendation that L2 is generally preferable for low-budget scenarios, while cosine distance may be more advantageous when the annotation budget is high and the model is more mature.

topics.title: Uncertainty as a driver in AL
topics.description: Uncertainty is emphasized as a central signal in active learning, guiding which samples should be queried for annotation. The section suggests that current uncertainty estimates can be improved so that they more directly correspond to where the model is likely to be wrong, instead of merely being numerically high. This reframing positions uncertainty as a tool to expose model weaknesses rather than a generic confidence score.

topics.title: Querying samples with inaccurate predictions
topics.description: The text proposes that active learning performance can be enhanced by preferentially querying samples on which the model currently makes incorrect predictions. This contrasts with querying solely based on high uncertainty and implies a tighter coupling between error detection and query strategy. The idea is that an ideal uncertainty measure should correlate strongly with prediction inaccuracy, making error-prone samples more likely to be selected.

topics.title: Learnable performance estimation for QC
topics.description: This topic describes learnable performance estimation methods for automated quality control (QC) of deep model outputs in medical image analysis. Examples include the Segment Anything Model (SAM) providing IoU estimates per mask, deep generative models predicting Dice scores for cardiac MRI segmentation, and auxiliary networks predicting Dice for brain tissue segmentation. These approaches estimate segmentation quality directly and are proposed as promising tools to support uncertainty-based active learning and mitigate model over-confidence.

topics.title: Probability calibration for uncertainty-based AL
topics.description: This topic covers probability calibration as a means to address over-confidence in deep models used for uncertainty-based active learning. Calibration measures the alignment between predicted probabilities and true outcomes, with over-confident models being poorly calibrated; examples include polyp classifiers where confidence should match actual polyp prevalence. The text discusses that ensembles can be better calibrated than MC Dropout, and Dirichlet-based methods consider all prediction outcomes, but most approaches only propose improved uncertainty metrics and perform post-hoc calibration. Existing calibration methods often require additional labeled datasets, highlighting the open problem of integrating calibration directly into uncertainty-based active learning pipelines.

topics.title: Diffusion models with superior generative quality
topics.description: Diffusion models are highlighted as a newer class of generative models achieving state-of-the-art image quality. They iteratively denoise random noise into coherent images, and recent work (Kazerouni et al., 2023) demonstrates that they can surpass GANs on standard generative benchmarks. This improved fidelity and diversity make them attractive candidates for data generation within active learning frameworks.

topics.title: Text-to-image diffusion for flexible generation
topics.description: Text-to-image diffusion models, exemplified by Stable Diffusion, are described as revolutionizing image generation by conditioning on natural language prompts. Their high-quality, text-guided outputs enable users to specify semantic content and appearance details directly through text. This controllability can support more targeted synthesis of rare or informative cases for active learning in medical imaging contexts.

canonical_topics.name: Evolution of Sampling Strategies Across AL Rounds
canonical_topics.description: Diversity-based methods such as BADGE and Core-Set are highlighted as particularly effective in early active learning rounds because they select heterogeneous samples that cover broad regions of the data space, reducing redundancy and accelerating performance gains. Their strength lies in quickly building a strong initial representation of the problem with limited annotations. As training progresses and the model becomes better initialized, uncertainty-based methods and even random sampling tend to catch up, achieving comparable performance in metrics like Dice and ASD. This late-round convergence suggests that complex, diversity-focused strategies offer the most benefit at low budgets, while simpler strategies can be sufficient once a strong labeled core has been established. Overall, the topic emphasizes the budget- and round-dependent nature of sampling strategy superiority in deep active learning.

canonical_topics.name: Distance Metrics on Deep Embeddings for Sample Selection
canonical_topics.description: In deep active learning, each input image is mapped to a d-dimensional feature embedding on which similarity or diversity is quantified. L2 distance is computed as the Euclidean norm between two embeddings, while cosine distance is derived from one minus their cosine similarity, capturing angular rather than absolute differences. Empirical studies on medical imaging datasets such as NCT-CRC-HE-100K, ISIC 2020, and ACDC show that L2 and cosine can behave differently across labeling budgets, with L2 often performing better in early, low-budget rounds. As more samples are labeled and the representation becomes more stable, cosine distance can become competitive or even superior, especially at higher budgets. These findings motivate using L2 distance for early-stage selection and considering cosine distance once the model is more mature and the annotation budget is larger.

canonical_topics.name: Uncertainty and Error-Aware Querying in Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: Uncertainty is positioned as a central signal in active learning, but its value depends on how well it pinpoints actual model errors rather than merely indicating low confidence. The topic argues that query strategies should ideally focus on samples where the model is wrong, not just where the predicted probability is diffuse or numerically small. This view reframes uncertainty estimation as a tool for exposing model weaknesses and miscalibrated regions of the input space. It further suggests that an ideal uncertainty measure would correlate tightly with prediction inaccuracy, making error-prone samples more likely to be queried. Such error-aware querying could improve label efficiency by directly targeting the model’s blind spots.

canonical_topics.name: Reliability Estimation and Calibration for Uncertainty-Based DAL
canonical_topics.description: Reliable quality and uncertainty estimates are crucial for effective uncertainty-based deep active learning, especially in safety-critical domains like medical imaging. Learnable performance estimation methods, such as auxiliary networks or generative models that predict Dice or IoU for segmentations, can provide sample-wise quality scores to guide querying and quality control. Probability calibration techniques complement these approaches by aligning predicted probabilities with true outcome frequencies, mitigating over-confidence and making uncertainty more trustworthy. The topic compares methods such as ensembles, MC Dropout, and Dirichlet-based approaches, noting that many rely on post-hoc calibration and often require extra labeled data. An open challenge is to integrate calibration and learnable performance estimation natively into active learning loops, so that the querying policy is directly optimized for reliable error prediction under limited annotation budgets.

canonical_topics.name: Diffusion-Based Data Generation for Deep Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: Diffusion models represent a new class of generative models that iteratively denoise random noise to produce high-fidelity images, often surpassing GANs on standard benchmarks. Their strong image quality and sample diversity make them attractive for augmenting datasets and synthesizing informative or rare cases within active learning frameworks. Text-to-image diffusion models, such as Stable Diffusion, extend this capability by conditioning generation on natural language prompts, enabling fine-grained control over semantic content and appearance. This controllability allows practitioners to target specific pathologies or edge cases that are under-represented in the labeled pool, potentially improving model robustness. Integrating diffusion-based synthesis with active learning raises important questions about selection criteria for synthetic samples and how best to combine real and generated data in the querying strategy.

topics.title: ControlNet for structure-conditioned diffusion
topics.description: ControlNet is introduced as an extension that allows diffusion models to follow detailed structural conditions, such as sketches or segmentation masks. By injecting additional control signals, it preserves global semantics from text while aligning local structures to given guidance maps. This mechanism can generate anatomically consistent or label-aligned images that are valuable for annotation-efficient learning and structured data augmentation.

topics.title: Integrating diffusion models into deep AL
topics.description: The section emphasizes that systematically exploring diffusion models within deep active learning remains an open research direction. Potential integrations include using diffusion-based generators to propose informative queries, synthesize hard or underrepresented cases, or model uncertainty in the data space. The authors position this as a promising avenue to surpass current GAN-centric AL strategies, especially in medical image analysis.

topics.title: Foundation models in active learning
topics.description: The section highlights how visual foundation models such as CLIP, SAM, and large language models like GPT-4 are shifting paradigms in medical image analysis and computer vision. These models, rich in prior knowledge, open new opportunities to redesign and improve active learning (AL) pipelines by leveraging their generalizable representations. The focus is on how this new class of models changes the context in which AL is developed and applied.

topics.title: Core methods in deep active learning
topics.description: The survey is described as comprehensively reviewing core methodological approaches in deep active learning. This implies coverage of key query strategies, model architectures, and selection criteria that underpin how deep active learning systems are designed and evaluated. These core methods form the technical foundation upon which more specialized and application-specific techniques are built.

topics.title: Active learning tailored to medical imaging
topics.description: The survey specifically focuses on active learning methods that are customized for medical image analysis tasks. Such tailoring can involve adapting query strategies, model designs, or annotation interfaces to the unique properties of medical images (e.g., 3D volumes, multi-modal data) and clinical labels. The conclusion underscores the importance of domain-specific adaptations rather than generic active learning pipelines.

topics.title: Challenges adapting classical AL to deep learning
topics.description: When transferring traditional active learning methods to deep learning, feature representations become dynamically learned and evolve during training, making pre-computation of pairwise distances or similarities for representativeness-based measures infeasible. Additionally, DNNs tend to be over-confident in their predictions, which can undermine uncertainty estimation for unlabeled samples. Although prior work has comprehensively summarized DAL methods, a lack of cross-dataset, cross-task experimental comparisons makes it difficult to know which DAL algorithms suit which tasks.

topics.title: DeepAL+ benchmarking toolkit for DAL
topics.description: DeepAL+ is a DAL benchmark toolkit that re-implements 19 DAL methods, extending a previous toolkit (DeepAL) that contained 11 highly-cited approaches before 2018. It upgrades prior implementations, adds more recent and highly-cited DAL algorithms, and expands the range of tasks and datasets to include standard image benchmarks (MNIST, CIFAR, SVHN), medical image analysis, and object recognition with spurious correlations. Using DeepAL+, the authors conduct comparative experiments across multiple tasks, analyzing factors such as batch size, number of training epochs per AL iteration, and timing costs. The toolkit is designed to be extensible, enabling easy integration of new tasks, datasets, DAL algorithms, and base models, and is publicly released on GitHub.

topics.title: Gradient-based active learning criteria
topics.description: Gradient-utilizing strategies estimate the impact of labeling a sample by examining gradients of the loss with respect to model parameters. They approximate how much the model would change if a candidate point were labeled and used for training, often via gradient norms or influence scores. This aligns selection with expected parameter updates rather than just prediction scores. Such methods are particularly suited to deep networks where gradients carry rich sensitivity information.

topics.title: Representative diversity-based DAL strategies
topics.description: Representative/diversity-based deep active learning (DAL) aims to select samples that are diverse and representative of the unlabeled pool. The section lists three main mechanisms: clustering, discriminative learning, and point processes. Concrete example methods include K-means-based selection, the Corset approach, Cluster-Margin, DAL, VAAL, WAAL, BADGE (DPPS version), and Active DPP, each operationalizing diversity or representativeness differently.

topics.title: Uncertainty-based deep active learning
topics.description: Uncertainty-based DAL selects unlabeled samples exhibiting high uncertainty, explicitly distinguishing aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Aleatoric uncertainty stems from inherent randomness in data generation processes, while epistemic uncertainty arises from limited model knowledge and can be reduced with more data. The text notes that many such DAL measures are adapted from pool-based active learning techniques developed for classical machine learning tasks, and that these methods form a standard family of querying strategies.

canonical_topics.name: Core Strategies and Challenges in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: Core deep active learning methods are organized around query strategies that directly exploit the properties of deep neural networks. Major families include uncertainty-based selection, representative/diversity-based approaches that cover the data manifold, and gradient- or influence-based criteria that estimate the impact of labeling each candidate sample. Adapting classical active learning ideas to deep settings is non-trivial because feature representations are learned dynamically, making fixed distance or similarity computations unreliable. Deep networks also tend to be over-confident, complicating principled uncertainty estimation for unlabeled data. Furthermore, the lack of standardized, cross-dataset and cross-task benchmarks makes it difficult to assess which deep active learning algorithms are robust and transferable in practice.

canonical_topics.name: DeepAL+ Benchmarking Toolkit for Deep Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: DeepAL+ is a comprehensive benchmarking toolkit that re-implements 19 deep active learning methods, extending an earlier DeepAL framework that covered 11 widely used approaches. It modernizes prior implementations, incorporates more recent and highly cited algorithms, and broadens the scope of tasks and datasets to include standard image benchmarks, medical image analysis, and scenarios with spurious correlations. The toolkit enables controlled comparisons across factors such as query batch size, number of training epochs per iteration, and overall computational cost. Its design emphasizes extensibility, allowing researchers to plug in new datasets, tasks, base models, and acquisition strategies. DeepAL+ is publicly released, supporting reproducible research and facilitating fair empirical evaluation of deep active learning methods.

canonical_topics.name: Deep Active Learning for Medical Image Analysis
canonical_topics.description: Deep active learning in medical imaging tailors query strategies and model designs to the unique characteristics of clinical data and labels. Medical images often appear as 3D volumes or multi-modal scans, and annotations can be highly granular, such as voxel-level segmentations or structured clinical reports. Domain-specific methods adapt acquisition functions, network architectures, and annotation interfaces to cope with these complexities and severe class imbalance. Such customization can substantially reduce labeling effort while maintaining diagnostic performance, compared to directly applying generic deep active learning pipelines. The resulting frameworks better align with clinical workflows and the safety-critical nature of medical decision making.

canonical_topics.name: Foundation Models in Deep Active Learning Pipelines
canonical_topics.description: Large vision and multimodal foundation models such as CLIP, SAM, and large language models like GPT-4 are reshaping how deep active learning pipelines are designed. Their rich, generalizable representations can be exploited to initialize models, construct powerful feature spaces for acquisition functions, or generate pseudo-labels and auxiliary supervision. In medical image analysis and broader computer vision, these priors reduce the burden on task-specific labeled data and may change which samples are truly informative to query. Deep active learning strategies can leverage foundation models through embedding-based diversity measures, uncertainty estimation in foundation feature spaces, or prompt-driven decision rules. This emerging paradigm reframes active learning as a way to specialize broad foundation knowledge to specific downstream tasks with minimal expert annotation.

canonical_topics.name: Diffusion and ControlNet-Based Generative Models for Deep Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: Diffusion models, including structure-conditioned variants like ControlNet, offer new opportunities to integrate powerful generative modeling with deep active learning. By conditioning on detailed structural priors such as sketches, segmentation masks, or anatomical maps, ControlNet can synthesize anatomically consistent or label-aligned images that are valuable for data augmentation and annotation-efficient learning. More broadly, diffusion-based generators can propose informative queries, synthesize hard or underrepresented cases, and help model uncertainty directly in the data space. These capabilities complement or surpass earlier GAN-centric strategies, which have been widely explored in active learning for image analysis. Systematically leveraging diffusion models within deep active learning remains an open research frontier, particularly promising for domains like medical imaging where structure and realism are critical.

topics.title: Predictive entropy over posterior probabilities
topics.description: This topic describes the mathematical formulation of predictive entropy HM[y|x] as −∑_k p_M(y = k | x) log p_M(y = k | x). The entropy is computed over the posterior label probabilities p_M(y | x) given by the classifier M for each class k. It quantifies the uncertainty of the model’s prediction for a given input by measuring how spread out the probability mass is across classes.

topics.title: Least Confidence active learning heuristic
topics.description: Least Confidence (LeastConf) is an uncertainty-based query strategy that selects data points x for which the model M has the lowest posterior probability on its most likely predicted label ŷ. The acquisition function is defined as α_LeastConf(x, M) = − p_M(ŷ | x), so higher acquisition scores correspond to lower model confidence. This method focuses solely on the top predicted class probability as a proxy for uncertainty, without considering the full predictive distribution over labels.

topics.title: Variation Ratios as lack-of-confidence measure
topics.description: Variation Ratios (VarRatio) is presented as a method similar to Least Confidence that also targets the model's lack of confidence in its predictions. Its acquisition function is α_VarRatio(x, M) = 1 − p_M(ŷ | x), which measures how far the top predicted class probability is from full certainty. Like LeastConf, it relies on the most likely label’s posterior probability but expresses uncertainty as a complement (1 minus that probability).

topics.title: Mutual information-based acquisition function
topics.description: The BALD score is defined as the mutual information between the model’s predictions y and the posterior distribution over parameters p(ω|D_l). This is expressed as the difference between the predictive entropy H_M[y|x] and the expected conditional entropy E_{p(ω|D_l)}[H_M[y|x, ω]]. The first term measures overall predictive uncertainty, while the second term averages uncertainty conditioned on specific parameter settings, isolating epistemic uncertainty due to parameter uncertainty. This decomposition is central to how BALD quantifies and selects informative data points.

topics.title: Mean Standard Deviation uncertainty measure
topics.description: Mean Standard Deviation (MeanSTD) is an acquisition function that maximizes the average predictive variance over all k classes for a sample. It computes the variance of class probabilities under a Bayesian posterior over model parameters and averages these variances, prioritizing points with high predictive dispersion across stochastic forward passes. This targets samples where the model’s class probability estimates are most unstable, indicating high epistemic uncertainty.

topics.title: Clustering and CoreSet representative selection
topics.description: Representative/diversity-based strategies such as KMeans and CoreSet aim to select batches that approximate the overall data distribution in a feature space. KMeans iteratively chooses centroids proportional to squared distances from existing centroids, while CoreSet operates in the model’s penultimate layer h(x), repeatedly picking the point farthest from its nearest labeled neighbor. These methods view the selected points as a proxy for the full dataset, emphasizing coverage of the feature space.

topics.title: Cluster-Margin for diverse low-confidence sampling
topics.description: Cluster-Margin combines clustering with margin-based uncertainty to choose diverse, low-confidence samples. It first performs hierarchical agglomerative clustering with average linkage to structure the unlabeled pool, then identifies points within clusters that have the lowest margin scores (least confident predictions). Finally, it filters these to a diverse subset of size b, differing from CoreSet by performing clustering only once as a preprocessing step.

topics.title: Weighted-sum combination and DPP balancing
topics.description: Weighted-sum optimization combines uncertainty and representativeness scores into a single acquisition value via α = α_uncertainty + β α_representative, but introduces a hyperparameter β and mismatched score formats (scalar vs matrix). Exploitation-Exploration is an example that subtracts a similarity term from entropy-based uncertainty to reduce redundancy while promoting diversity. DPPs are highlighted as a natural way to jointly account for per-sample uncertainty and pairwise diversity without extra hyperparameters, though exact sampling incurs O(N³) complexity.

topics.title: Two-stage combined selection strategies
topics.description: Two-stage (or multi-stage) optimization refines candidate sets sequentially using different criteria, often first selecting an informative subset and then enforcing diversity. WAAL first trains a discriminative network on labeled vs unlabeled data and then uses it for batch selection. BADGE computes gradient embeddings in the first stage and clusters them with KMeans++ in the second, whereas DBAL prefilters to the top ρb most uncertain points and then clusters them into b groups, choosing samples near cluster centers.

topics.title: Data-aspect enhancements: pseudo-labeling
topics.description: Data-aspect DAL enhancements use pseudo-labeling to exploit large unlabeled pools without explicit annotation. CEAL assigns pseudo-labels to high-confidence (low-entropy) predictions and includes them in subsequent training iterations, effectively enlarging the labeled set. This approach requires confidence thresholds as hyperparameters; poor tuning can introduce erroneous labels and harm performance.

canonical_topics.name: Uncertainty-Based Acquisition Functions in DAL
canonical_topics.description: Uncertainty-based acquisition functions prioritize unlabeled samples on which a deep model is least certain, making them central to deep active learning. Simple heuristics such as Least Confidence and Variation Ratios use only the highest posterior class probability, either minimizing it or maximizing its complement to estimate lack of confidence. Predictive entropy instead considers the full posterior distribution over labels, measuring how dispersed the probability mass is across classes. Bayesian methods like BALD quantify the mutual information between predictions and model parameters, targeting epistemic uncertainty rather than mere predictive noise. Mean standard deviation and related variance-based scores approximate epistemic uncertainty by aggregating the variability of class probabilities across stochastic forward passes, such as Monte Carlo dropout samples.

canonical_topics.name: Clustering and Core-Set Diversity Sampling
canonical_topics.description: Diversity-based sampling methods in deep active learning aim to select batches that well represent the overall data distribution in a learned feature space. Core-set methods operate in a latent space such as the penultimate layer, iteratively choosing unlabeled points that are farthest from the current labeled set to maximize coverage. Clustering-based approaches, including k-means and hierarchical clustering, group unlabeled points and then select representative elements from each cluster. Techniques like Cluster-Margin combine these ideas by first building a clustering structure over the pool and then picking low-margin (low-confidence) samples within clusters before enforcing additional diversity constraints. This family of methods reduces redundancy in queried labels and often yields more informative batches than purely uncertainty-driven selection.

canonical_topics.name: Hybrid Uncertainty–Diversity Selection Strategies
canonical_topics.description: Hybrid strategies explicitly combine per-sample informativeness with batch-level diversity to form more effective acquisition sets in deep active learning. One approach is scalarization, where uncertainty and representativeness scores are combined via a weighted sum or by subtracting similarity penalties, trading off exploration and exploitation at the cost of extra hyperparameters and score normalization. Determinantal point processes (DPPs) offer a principled probabilistic framework that naturally balances high individual scores with low pairwise similarity, though exact sampling can be computationally expensive. Two-stage methods decouple these objectives, first filtering the pool by an informativeness criterion and then enforcing diversity within the candidate subset. Examples include WAAL’s discriminator-based preselection, BADGE’s gradient-embedding clustering with k-means++, and DBAL’s strategy of clustering only the most uncertain points to obtain a compact, diverse batch.

canonical_topics.name: Pseudo-Labeling Enhancements in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: Pseudo-labeling augments deep active learning by exploiting high-confidence predictions as additional supervision without explicit annotation. Methods such as CEAL identify unlabeled samples whose predictive entropy or similar uncertainty measure falls below a threshold and assign them pseudo-labels for subsequent training rounds. This effectively enlarges the labeled dataset, potentially accelerating convergence and improving generalization when human labeling budgets are limited. However, the approach is sensitive to confidence thresholds and model calibration; overly aggressive pseudo-labeling can introduce systematic errors that degrade performance. Careful scheduling, confidence calibration, and occasional human verification are therefore crucial when integrating pseudo-labels into a deep active learning pipeline.

topics.title: Loss function modification via adversarial objectives
topics.description: Altering the target model’s loss function is proposed as another route to enhancing DAL. WAAL introduces a min–max loss that leverages unlabeled data to better discriminate between labeled and unlabeled samples during training. This adversarial-style objective aims to shape the feature space so that selected unlabeled batches are both diverse and distributionally informative for label acquisition.

topics.title: Ensemble-based uncertainty: MC Dropout and ensembles
topics.description: Ensemble-based techniques counteract the overconfidence of softmax outputs by aggregating predictions from multiple stochastic models. MC Dropout interprets dropout at test time as approximate Bayesian inference, marginalizing over weight uncertainty via Monte Carlo integration to obtain predictive uncertainty; it behaves like an implicit ensemble of subnetworks. Beluch et al. empirically show that explicit ensembles of multiple independently trained classifiers often outperform MC Dropout for estimating uncertainty in DAL.

topics.title: Compared deep active learning strategies
topics.description: The study compares 19 deep active learning methods, spanning random sampling, classic uncertainty-based heuristics (Entropy, Margin, LeastConf and their MC Dropout variants), Bayesian methods like BALD, and other uncertainty measures such as MeanSTD and VarRatio. It also includes pseudo-labeling and hybrid strategies like CEAL(Entropy), diversity-based and core-set-style methods such as KMeans and KCenter, gradient-based BADGE, adversarial query approaches (AdversarialBIM), and more complex frameworks like WAAL, VAAL, and LPL. This broad set enables a comprehensive comparison across different acquisition paradigms and modeling assumptions.

topics.title: GPU-accelerated KMeans for large pools
topics.description: To handle clustering over large unlabeled data pools, the authors replace the standard scikit-learn KMeans implementation, which is too time-consuming, with a GPU-based version implemented using the faiss library. This GPU-accelerated KMeans is used within DeepAL+ to make clustering-based DAL more scalable and better suited to deep learning workloads. It specifically targets the computational bottleneck of clustering in pool-based active learning on large-scale datasets.

topics.title: Common backbone and DAL toolkit
topics.description: All active learning methods share a common backbone model, ResNet18 without pre-training, to ensure a fair comparison across acquisition strategies. The experiments are run within the DeepAL+ toolkit, with consistent classifier settings applied to every DAL method. This controlled setup isolates the effect of the acquisition function from architectural or training differences in the underlying classifier.

topics.title: Experimental protocol and evaluation metrics
topics.description: Each experiment is repeated three times with different random splits of the initial labeled and unlabeled pools (controlled by a fixed seed), and results are averaged to reduce variance. Performance is summarized primarily via the area under the budget curve (AUBC), where the curve relates accuracy to labeling budget, with higher AUBC indicating better overall performance over the entire active learning process. The final accuracy after exhausting the labeling budget (F-acc) is also reported as a terminal performance metric. Additional implementation and dataset details are relegated to an appendix.

topics.title: Task grouping for comparative analysis
topics.description: For analysis, the authors divide the tasks into three groups: standard image classification datasets, medical image analysis datasets, and a group for comparative studies involving MNIST and Waterbird. This grouping structures the interpretation of results by domain characteristics—conventional benchmarks, medical imaging, and tasks with specific comparative or spurious correlation concerns. It underpins how aggregate statistics like AUBC and F-acc are summarized and discussed across different problem types.

topics.title: Uncertainty methods vs. random on benchmarks
topics.description: On standard image classification tasks, typical uncertainty-based strategies such as LeastConf, Margin, and Entropy (including CEAL) outperform random sampling by roughly 1–3% in average AUBC over the active learning process. However, paired t-tests on AUBCs across these methods reveal no single uncertainty-based approach is significantly better than the others, with all p-values above 0.05. This suggests that while uncertainty sampling helps over random, the precise uncertainty heuristic often does not critically affect performance on these benchmarks.

topics.title: Impact of MC Dropout on uncertainty
topics.description: For most standard image classification tasks, MC Dropout versions of uncertainty-based methods show negligible or even counter-intuitive differences compared to their non-dropout counterparts, aligning with earlier observations in the literature. TinyImageNet is an exception, where dropout-based variants outperform original methods by about 1–3% in AUBC. The authors hypothesize that relying on a single backbone’s feature representation yields less accurate uncertainty estimates on this harder dataset, while dropout increases predictive variability and better differentiates uncertainty among unlabeled samples. Thus, MC Dropout appears more beneficial when feature representations are less reliable or the task is more complex.

topics.title: CEAL threshold effects on performance
topics.description: The CEAL(Entropy) method, which augments entropy-based acquisition with pseudo-labeling of confident samples, improves over plain Entropy by about 0.5% on average across eight datasets when using a very small confidence/entropy threshold of 1e-5. While this indicates the approach can be effective, its gains depend sensitively on the choice of threshold. The authors stress that careful tuning of this hyperparameter is necessary to realize performance improvements from CEAL.

canonical_topics.name: Adversarial Loss Design for Deep Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: Adversarially modified loss functions use unlabeled data during training to better separate labeled from unlabeled regions in feature space. Methods such as WAAL introduce a min–max objective where the model is simultaneously encouraged to perform well on labeled data and to distinguish informative unlabeled samples. This adversarial setup aims to shape the representation so that selected batches of unlabeled points are diverse, uncertain, and distributionally representative. By integrating acquisition objectives directly into the training loss, these approaches tighten the coupling between representation learning and query selection in deep active learning.

canonical_topics.name: Ensembles and MC Dropout for DAL Uncertainty
canonical_topics.description: Ensemble-based approaches in deep active learning estimate predictive uncertainty by aggregating outputs from multiple stochastic models. MC Dropout treats dropout at test time as approximate Bayesian inference, drawing multiple subnetworks to marginalize over weight uncertainty. Empirical studies show that explicit ensembles of independently trained networks often yield more reliable uncertainty estimates than MC Dropout on many benchmarks. However, on harder datasets such as TinyImageNet, MC Dropout variants can outperform their deterministic counterparts, likely because increased predictive variability compensates for weaker feature representations. This suggests that the relative benefit of MC Dropout versus explicit ensembles depends on task difficulty and representation quality.

canonical_topics.name: Comparative Evaluation of Deep Active Learning Strategies
canonical_topics.description: Comprehensive DAL studies benchmark a broad spectrum of acquisition strategies, including random sampling, classic uncertainty heuristics (e.g., entropy, margin, least confidence), Bayesian methods like BALD, and alternative uncertainty scores such as MeanSTD and VarRatio. They also cover pseudo-labeling and hybrid approaches like CEAL, diversity-based and core-set-style methods (e.g., KMeans, KCenter), gradient-based selection such as BADGE, adversarial query methods, and more complex frameworks like WAAL, VAAL, and LPL. Across standard image classification benchmarks, uncertainty-based methods typically outperform random sampling by only a few percentage points in AUBC, and no single uncertainty heuristic consistently dominates others statistically. Extensions such as CEAL can provide modest additional gains, but their effectiveness is highly sensitive to hyperparameters like confidence thresholds. These findings highlight that, in many settings, the choice among standard uncertainty heuristics may be less critical than previously assumed, while more structural differences in acquisition paradigms can matter more.

canonical_topics.name: GPU-Accelerated Clustering for Scalable DAL
canonical_topics.description: Clustering-based DAL methods can face severe computational bottlenecks when applied to large unlabeled pools. To address this, GPU-accelerated KMeans implementations, such as those in the Faiss library, are used to replace standard CPU-based clustering routines. Integrated into toolkits like DeepAL+, these GPU methods significantly reduce the runtime of core-set and diversity-based acquisition functions. As a result, clustering-heavy strategies become practical for large-scale deep learning workloads and high-resolution image datasets commonly used in deep active learning research.

canonical_topics.name: Standardized Experimental Protocol for DAL Benchmarks
canonical_topics.description: Fair evaluation of deep active learning methods relies on controlling the underlying model and training setup. Studies often adopt a common backbone, such as an unpretrained ResNet-18, and implement all acquisition functions within a unified toolkit like DeepAL+ to isolate the effect of query strategies. Experiments are typically repeated multiple times with different random splits of labeled and unlabeled pools, using fixed seeds, and results are averaged to reduce variance. Performance is summarized using metrics such as the area under the budget curve (AUBC), which tracks accuracy versus labeling cost, and the final accuracy after exhausting the labeling budget. Datasets are commonly grouped by domain (e.g., standard benchmarks, medical imaging, tasks with spurious correlations) to interpret how DAL methods behave across different problem types.

topics.title: Anomalous behavior on medical image tasks
topics.description: On medical imaging datasets such as Pneumonia-MNIST, some DAL methods perform worse than random sampling; for example, VarRatio underperforms Random by 4.5% in AUBC. The authors also observe that the final accuracy achieved by certain DAL strategies (e.g., KCenter) can exceed the accuracy obtained when training on the full labeled dataset, and that MC Dropout variants often do worse than their non-dropout versions (e.g., Entropy vs. EntropyD). These findings are labeled as abnormal phenomena, suggesting domain shift, data properties, or model–acquisition interactions in medical imaging may fundamentally alter how active learning behaves compared to standard benchmarks.

topics.title: Distribution shift and redundancy in active learning
topics.description: The section attributes some of the observed performance behaviors in DAL experiments to distribution shift between training and test sets and to redundancy in the queried samples during active learning. Distribution shift can cause actively acquired labeled data to be unrepresentative of the test distribution, limiting generalization even when uncertainty criteria are optimized. Redundant acquisitions waste labeling budget on similar or overlapping samples, reducing the efficiency gains expected from active learning. Further technical analysis of these phenomena is deferred to an appendix section.

topics.title: Limitations of representativeness/diversity-based DAL methods
topics.description: Representativeness/diversity-based methods such as KMeans, KCenter, and VAAL are evaluated and found not to show clear performance advantages over uncertainty-based measures. These methods incur substantial computational overhead: KMeans and KCenter repeatedly compute pairwise distance matrices over evolving feature representations, and VAAL requires retraining a variational autoencoder (VAE) each iteration. Large unlabeled pools (e.g., EMNIST) exacerbate memory consumption due to storing full distance matrices, leading to some experiments being infeasible. Thus, their theoretical appeal in diversity and coverage is tempered by practical time and memory costs.

topics.title: Dependence of representativeness-based DAL on feature quality
topics.description: The authors note that representativeness-based active learning strategies perform well in classical machine learning settings but that their success in deep active learning hinges on the quality of learned feature representations. Poor or unstable features can undermine clustering or distance-based selection, leading to weaker gains from methods like KMeans and KCenter. This observation aligns with prior implicit analyses in the literature and is supported by the comparative results in the table. The section also highlights that a GPU-accelerated KMeans implementation is both more time-efficient and slightly better performing than a CPU version, emphasizing the role of scalable feature-space operations.

topics.title: Performance gains and instability of LPL
topics.description: The Loss Prediction Loss (LPL) method shows substantial improvements in final accuracy (F-acc) over full supervised training on several datasets such as SVHN, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and CIFAR10-imb. However, its performance is highly sensitive to hyper-parameters of the LossNet component, particularly the feature size determined by the fully connected layer, and it fails on more complex datasets like EMNIST and TinyImageNet despite extensive tuning. The difficulty is linked to predicting target loss in settings with many categories, but this can be mitigated by using a pre-trained backbone (e.g., pre-trained ResNet18), which provides better feature representations and substantially improves LPL’s effectiveness.

topics.title: WAAL limitations on many-class datasets
topics.description: Weighted Adversarial Active Learning (WAAL) exhibits similar failure patterns to LPL on datasets with many categories, such as EMNIST and TinyImageNet. The method struggles to extract sufficiently diversified features in these high-class-count settings, leading to degraded performance. The comparison on CIFAR100 further supports the explanation that dataset category complexity can hinder WAAL’s ability to construct effective representations.

topics.title: Marginal benefit and high cost of AdvBIM
topics.description: AdvBIM augments DAL training with adversarial samples, computed via an adversarial distance r for each unlabeled sample at every iteration, but does not achieve performance gains comparable to LPL. Because the adversarial examples are crafted using the current backbone model, the additional robustness they provide is limited, resulting in only marginal improvements. The method is extremely time-consuming and computationally prohibitive, to the point that experiments on large datasets like EMNIST and TinyImageNet could not be completed.

topics.title: WAAL robustness to epochs and diversity modeling
topics.description: In the ablation study, WAAL consistently outperforms Entropy and BADGE and is notably less sensitive to the number of training epochs, achieving stable AUBC (around 0.825) even with as few as 5 epochs and showing little change up to 30 epochs. The robustness is attributed to WAAL’s explicit modeling of diversity among samples and its use of unlabeled data to build better representations, which reduces data bias. This property is particularly attractive for DAL, as effective performance can be maintained with fewer training epochs, saving computation time.

topics.title: Group-wise accuracy metrics on Waterbird
topics.description: The Waterbird dataset is partitioned into four groups based on bird type and background: {(waterbird, water), (waterbird, land), (landbird, land), (landbird, water)}. Besides overall accuracy, the study reports mismatch accuracy (for the spurious/background-mismatched groups {(waterbird, land), (landbird, water)}) and worst-group accuracy (the minimum accuracy among all four groups). These metrics quantify performance under distribution shift and group imbalance, revealing robustness and fairness properties of DAL methods.

topics.title: Enhancing techniques in LPL and WAAL
topics.description: LPL and WAAL use additional enhancing mechanisms—loss prediction and leveraging unlabeled-data information—to guide query selection in deep active learning. On Waterbird without pretraining, these techniques can outperform standard uncertainty or clustering-based methods in overall accuracy by extracting more informative signals from the data. However, both methods struggle on the worst group under both pretraining regimes, likely because group imbalance biases loss prediction and unlabeled-data statistics, harming performance on minority or hardest subgroups.

canonical_topics.name: Abnormal DAL Behavior on Medical Imaging Benchmarks
canonical_topics.description: On medical imaging datasets such as Pneumonia-MNIST, several deep active learning (DAL) strategies behave counterintuitively, sometimes performing worse than random sampling in AUBC and final accuracy. Methods like VarRatio can underperform Random by several percentage points, while KCenter can even surpass the accuracy obtained when training on the full labeled dataset. MC Dropout–based variants often lag behind their non-dropout counterparts (e.g., EntropyD vs. Entropy), suggesting that standard uncertainty heuristics do not transfer straightforwardly. These anomalies point to strong interactions between domain shift, dataset properties, and model–acquisition coupling in medical imaging, indicating that DAL benchmarks in this domain may follow qualitatively different dynamics from those in natural image tasks.

canonical_topics.name: Distribution Shift, Redundancy, and Group-Robust DAL
canonical_topics.description: Distribution shift between the actively acquired training set and the test distribution can cause DAL query strategies to optimize uncertainty on a biased subset of the data, limiting gains in generalization. Redundant acquisitions—repeatedly querying highly similar or overlapping samples—further waste labeling budget and reduce the efficiency advantages that active learning is supposed to provide. To analyze robustness under structured shift and spurious correlations, datasets like Waterbird are partitioned into groups (e.g., combinations of bird type and background), and metrics such as mismatch accuracy and worst-group accuracy are reported alongside overall accuracy. These group-wise metrics expose failures that are hidden by aggregate performance, particularly under group imbalance and background–label confounding. Even enhanced DAL methods like LPL and WAAL can improve overall accuracy on such benchmarks while still performing poorly on the worst or minority groups, underscoring the need for group-robust evaluation criteria in DAL research.

canonical_topics.name: Limits of Diversity-Based Deep Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: Representativeness and diversity-based DAL methods such as KMeans, KCenter, and VAAL often fail to show clear performance advantages over simpler uncertainty-based strategies in deep learning settings. Their effectiveness critically depends on the quality and stability of learned feature representations; poor or rapidly shifting features undermine clustering and distance-based selection, leading to weak or inconsistent gains. These methods also impose significant computational and memory burdens, frequently requiring repeated computation of large pairwise distance matrices over evolving feature spaces or retraining auxiliary models like VAEs at each iteration. On large unlabeled pools (e.g., EMNIST), memory limits can make some experiments infeasible, and careful engineering—such as GPU-accelerated KMeans—only partially mitigates these costs. Thus, while conceptually appealing for improving coverage and diversity, these approaches face substantial practical and representational constraints in DAL.

canonical_topics.name: Analysis of LPL, WAAL, and AdvBIM Methods
canonical_topics.description: Loss Prediction Loss (LPL), Weighted Adversarial Active Learning (WAAL), and AdvBIM represent a family of DAL methods that augment standard training with auxiliary losses or adversarial objectives to guide querying. LPL can yield substantial final-accuracy gains over fully supervised training on datasets like SVHN, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and CIFAR10-imb, but it is highly sensitive to LossNet hyperparameters and tends to fail on more complex or many-class datasets such as EMNIST and TinyImageNet unless strong pretrained backbones are used. WAAL exhibits similar difficulties on high-class-count datasets, reflecting challenges in learning sufficiently rich and balanced feature spaces, yet it is relatively robust to the number of training epochs and often outperforms Entropy and BADGE by explicitly modeling diversity and leveraging unlabeled data. AdvBIM augments DAL with adversarially perturbed unlabeled samples, but despite its conceptual appeal, it brings only marginal performance improvements over simpler baselines while incurring extreme computational overhead, making it impractical for large-scale benchmarks. Together, these methods highlight both the promise and fragility of advanced representation-learning and adversarial techniques in DAL, especially under complex data distributions and resource constraints.

topics.title: Enhancement Methods Beyond Acquisition Functions
topics.description: The text discusses the limited gains from solely designing new acquisition functions and highlights alternative enhancement strategies such as learning loss prediction (LPL) and enlarging batch size per acquisition round. It notes that these methods do not generalize well across all tasks and stresses the need for more universal enhancement approaches. Cluster-Margin is cited as a method that scales active learning to very large batch sizes (100K–1M), illustrating both progress and the difficulty of surpassing such scalability.

topics.title: Integrating DAL with Semi- and Self-Supervision
topics.description: There is a research trend toward combining deep active learning (DAL) with semi-supervised and self-supervised learning (S4L) to better exploit unlabeled data. Work by Chan et al. suggests that a significant portion of DAL's benefits can be absorbed by strong S4L techniques, based on extensive empirical comparisons. A key future direction is to design DAL pipelines that more effectively leverage unlabeled data in very low-label regimes.

topics.title: Domain-Specific DAL in Autonomous Driving and Medicine
topics.description: DAL is proposed as a promising tool for data-insufficient, safety-critical domains such as autonomous driving and medical image analysis. In autonomous driving, active learning for nighttime detection of pedestrians and bicycles significantly improved mean average precision compared to manually selected training data. In medical imaging, the prevalence of rare but critical diseases and the high cost of expert annotation make class imbalance and rare-class emphasis central design concerns for DAL strategies. The text underscores that each domain has distinct requirements, motivating task- and domain-specific DAL research.

topics.title: Labeling requirements for deep learning
topics.description: Due to their complex architectures and high capacity, deep learning models require large quantities of labeled samples for effective training. The availability of large-scale annotated datasets has therefore become a key enabler for DL performance. This creates a dependency between DL success and the cost and effort of obtaining high-quality labeled data.

topics.title: Historical evolution of deep learning
topics.description: This topic covers the chronological development of deep learning models from early neural network formulations to modern deep architectures. It mentions the McCulloch-Pitts model, the introduction of backpropagation, the first RNNs, LeNet as an early DNN, Deep Belief Networks, and AlexNet’s breakthrough performance on ImageNet. It highlights how improvements in computing power and architectures led to superior results across visual, language, and speech tasks.

topics.title: Data greed and labeling bottlenecks in DL
topics.description: The text emphasizes that DL’s recent breakthroughs depend heavily on massive labeled datasets, making it highly data-greedy. It explains that while unlabeled data are easy to obtain, manual annotation is costly, especially in expert domains such as COVID-19 lung lesion labeling, medical imaging, speech recognition, remote sensing, robotics, and specialized NLP tasks. This creates a practical bottleneck and motivates methods that maximize performance gains from a small number of labeled samples.

topics.title: Active learning query scenario paradigms
topics.description: The section categorizes AL approaches by application scenario into membership query synthesis, stream-based selective sampling, and pool-based active learning. Membership query synthesis allows the learner to query labels for any point in input space, including synthetically generated samples. Stream-based selective sampling decides online for each incoming sample whether to query its label, whereas pool-based methods evaluate the entire unlabeled pool and select the best samples based on ranking. These paradigms define how and when label queries are made in practice.

topics.title: Convolutional Neural Network as baseline DL
topics.description: The section references a convolutional neural network (CNN) as a common deep learning model used as the baseline architecture when comparing DL, AL, and DeepAL. CNNs serve as the feature extractor and prediction model whose parameters are later adapted within the active learning process.

topics.title: Device resource constraints and AL strategy
topics.description: The text contrasts mobile devices, which require timeliness and have limited storage and computation, with larger devices that have ample resources. It notes that the commonly used pool-based sampling strategy in AL research is more suitable for large, resource-rich devices, implying that alternative strategies may be needed for constrained mobile platforms.

topics.title: Label budget and stopping conditions
topics.description: Both the pool-based AL cycle and the DeepAL workflow are described as iterative processes that terminate when a label budget is exhausted or when predefined stopping conditions are satisfied. This highlights the importance of explicitly modeling annotation cost (budget) and designing stopping strategies to decide when further querying is no longer beneficial.

canonical_topics.name: Beyond Acquisition Functions in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: Focusing solely on designing new acquisition functions often yields limited performance gains in deep active learning. Alternative enhancement strategies include learning loss prediction, adaptive training schemes, and scaling to very large batch sizes per acquisition round. Methods such as Cluster-Margin demonstrate that DAL can be made computationally feasible even with batch sizes in the 100K–1M range. However, many of these techniques do not generalize uniformly across tasks, highlighting the need for more universal improvement strategies. A key research direction is to understand which enhancement components transfer robustly across architectures, datasets, and domains.

canonical_topics.name: Combining Deep Active Learning with Semi- and Self-Supervision
canonical_topics.description: Recent work explores integrating deep active learning with semi-supervised and self-supervised learning to better exploit abundant unlabeled data. Strong self-supervised and semi-supervised techniques can absorb a substantial portion of DAL’s gains, as shown by empirical studies such as those of Chan et al. This raises questions about when explicit querying strategies still provide added value over powerful representation learning alone. Future DAL pipelines must be designed to jointly optimize representation learning, labeling strategies, and consistency regularization in very low-label regimes. Understanding these interactions is crucial for building label-efficient systems that scale to real-world unlabeled corpora.

canonical_topics.name: Deep Active Learning in Safety-Critical Application Domains
canonical_topics.description: Deep active learning is especially promising in safety-critical and data-scarce domains such as autonomous driving and medical imaging. In autonomous driving, DAL has been used to selectively label nighttime pedestrian and bicycle examples, achieving substantial improvements in detection performance over manually curated training sets. In medical image analysis, rare but critical conditions and the high cost of expert annotations make class imbalance and rare-class emphasis central DAL design concerns. These domains require careful consideration of uncertainty, coverage, and risk-sensitive querying, rather than purely accuracy-driven criteria. As a result, domain-specific DAL strategies that respect operational constraints and safety margins are an important research frontier.

canonical_topics.name: Labeling Bottlenecks in Deep Learning and Motivation for DAL
canonical_topics.description: Modern deep learning models are highly data-hungry and typically require massive labeled datasets to achieve strong performance. While raw unlabeled data are plentiful, high-quality annotation is costly, especially in expert domains such as medical imaging, specialized speech recognition, remote sensing, robotics, and domain-specific NLP. This dependency on large annotated corpora creates a practical bottleneck that limits the deployment of deep models in many real-world settings. Deep active learning directly targets this issue by aiming to maximize performance gains from a small number of strategically selected labeled samples. Understanding these labeling bottlenecks provides the motivation and design constraints for DAL algorithms and benchmarks.

canonical_topics.name: Query Paradigms, Budgets, and Stopping in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: Deep active learning inherits several fundamental query paradigms from classical active learning, including membership query synthesis, stream-based selective sampling, and pool-based querying. These paradigms define whether the learner can synthesize new inputs, must decide online for incoming samples, or can rank and select points from a large unlabeled pool. DAL workflows are typically iterative, alternating between model training, scoring unlabeled data, selecting queries, and obtaining new labels. Practical systems must explicitly model annotation budgets and incorporate stopping criteria that determine when additional labeling is no longer cost-effective. Designing DAL strategies that respect these paradigms and constraints is key to building deployable, resource-aware active learning pipelines.

topics.title: Importance of AL query rule design
topics.description: Active learning (AL) begins from unlabeled datasets and relies on carefully designed query rules to select the most informative samples for labeling. These rules aim to minimize labeling cost while maximizing model performance. Consequently, the quality and design of query rules are central to the overall effectiveness of AL methods, and there is extensive research focused on this aspect.

topics.title: Scalability to high-dimensional data
topics.description: Active learning methods face significant challenges when applied to high-dimensional data such as images, text, and video. Many existing approaches were developed and evaluated primarily on low-dimensional problems, limiting their direct applicability to complex, real-world domains. This scalability issue constrains the broader deployment of traditional AL techniques in modern deep learning settings.

topics.title: Feature extraction limitations in AL
topics.description: Traditional active learning typically operates on pre-extracted features and lacks the capability to learn feature representations jointly with querying. In contrast, deep learning models are designed, either manually or automatically, to perform high-performance feature extraction as part of end-to-end training. This gap means that classical AL frameworks often cannot fully exploit the representational power of deep models without additional integration mechanisms.

topics.title: Model uncertainty and overconfident softmax
topics.description: Uncertainty-based query strategies are central in Active Learning, but directly applying them to Deep Learning is problematic because DL models tend to be overconfident. The softmax output (Softmax Response, SR) is an unreliable confidence measure and can perform worse than random sampling when used for sample selection. This highlights a core challenge in using standard DL outputs for AL uncertainty estimation.

topics.title: Batch Query Strategies for Deep AL
topics.description: Empirical work shows that traditional heuristic query strategies designed for one-by-one selection may fail when applied to deep learning in batch settings. Consequently, many researchers develop batch query methods that simultaneously optimize the information content and diversity of selected samples, better matching the training dynamics of deep models.

topics.title: Decomposition of DeepAL research components
topics.description: The DeepAL framework is decomposed into two core parts: active learning (AL) query strategies applied to the unlabeled dataset, and deep learning (DL) model training methods. Additional research axes include methods for improving model generalization and strategies for deciding when to stop querying. This decomposition structures the subsequent survey sections that analyze each component systematically.

topics.title: Pool-based DeepAL optimization formulation
topics.description: In the pool-based setting, DeepAL defines an unlabeled dataset Uₙ with sample space X, label space Y, and joint distribution P(x, y), and a current labeled set Lₘ. Using a deep model f: X → Y, the goal is to design a query strategy Q that selects Lₘ ⊆ Uₙ to minimize the expected loss E(x,y)[ℓ(f(x), y)] while keeping m ≪ n. This formalizes DeepAL as choosing a minimal labeled subset that achieves a desired accuracy, highlighting that the query strategy Q is central to reducing labeling cost.

topics.title: Acquisition function for batch selection
topics.description: Within BMDAL, the acquisition function a_batch(B, f_θ(L)) evaluates a candidate batch B of unlabeled samples given the current labeled training set L (also denoted D_train) and model f_θ. The optimal batch B* is defined as the subset of U that maximizes this acquisition score, formalizing batch selection as an arg max optimization over all possible subsets. This provides a general mathematical template under which specific batch criteria, such as uncertainty or diversity, can be instantiated.

topics.title: Redundancy issue in independent batch selection
topics.description: Constructing batches by independently selecting top-scoring samples can yield sets of highly similar, information-rich points that provide redundant information to the model. Such redundancy wastes labeling resources and does not significantly improve the model’s understanding of the data distribution. This motivates more sophisticated batch acquisition strategies that explicitly account for relationships and diversity among samples, beyond independent uncertainty scores.

topics.title: Exploration-P: balancing uncertainty and redundancy
topics.description: Exploration-P addresses limitations of early BMAL methods that over-rely on similarity and exploitation of boundary samples, leading to batches that poorly represent the feature-space distribution. It uses a deep neural network to learn feature representations, computes sample uncertainty via entropy, and aggregates uncertainty over a selected set S as E(S) = Σ E(xᵢ). Redundancy within S is quantified by R(S), a sum of pairwise similarities Sim(xᵢ, xⱼ) based on learned features and a similarity matrix M. The final objective I(S) = E(S) − α/|S|·R(S) promotes batches with high total uncertainty and low redundancy, explicitly trading off exploration and exploitation.

canonical_topics.name: Core Formulation and Components of Deep AL
canonical_topics.description: Deep active learning is typically formalized in a pool-based setting, where a small labeled set and a large unlabeled pool are drawn from an underlying data distribution. The goal is to design a query strategy that selects a minimal subset of samples for labeling while minimizing the model’s expected loss. This framework naturally decomposes into two main components: the active learning query strategy operating on the unlabeled pool, and the deep learning training procedure that fits a model to the growing labeled set. Additional research axes include improving model generalization and developing principled stopping criteria, but across all of these, the design and quality of the query rules remain central to reducing labeling cost and achieving strong performance.

canonical_topics.name: Uncertainty Estimation Challenges in Deep AL
canonical_topics.description: Uncertainty-based querying is a cornerstone of active learning, but it becomes problematic when applied directly to deep neural networks. Deep models often produce overconfident softmax outputs, making the softmax response an unreliable proxy for predictive uncertainty. When used naively as an acquisition score, such overconfident probabilities can even underperform random sampling. Addressing this issue requires more robust uncertainty estimation methods or calibrated confidence measures tailored to deep active learning.

canonical_topics.name: Scalability and Representation Learning in Deep AL
canonical_topics.description: Classical active learning methods were largely developed for low-dimensional feature spaces and often assume fixed, pre-extracted features. In modern applications with high-dimensional data such as images, text, and video, these methods struggle to scale and cannot fully exploit rich structure in the data. Deep learning, by contrast, learns powerful feature representations end-to-end, suggesting that querying and representation learning should be tightly integrated. Deep active learning therefore focuses on methods that remain computationally feasible in high dimensions while jointly learning features and selecting informative samples.

canonical_topics.name: Batch Acquisition and Diversity in Deep AL
canonical_topics.description: In deep active learning, querying labels one sample at a time is often impractical, and naive extensions of single-point heuristics to batch selection can fail. Simply taking the top-scoring uncertain points tends to produce redundant batches composed of very similar samples, which wastes labeling effort and yields limited performance gains.
