topics.description: One category of semi-supervised methods is unsupervised preprocessing, which applies techniques such as dimensionality reduction, clustering, or feature extraction to the combined labeled and unlabeled dataset before supervised training. This transformation aims to produce a representation where informative samples are easier to identify and model parameters are better estimated when few labels are available. In online active learning, this includes using pre-trained networks to extract salient features from unlabeled instances prior to initiating the sampling routine, thereby guiding more informative query choices.

topics.title: Autoencoders for online active learning
topics.description: An autoencoder is trained on all available unlabeled data to learn a compressed representation that improves downstream online active learning. In this setting, the learned features are then used with linear regression models to enhance prediction and query selection under streaming conditions. This exploits the structure of unlabeled data without requiring additional labels.

topics.title: Wrapper methods with pseudo-labels
topics.description: Wrapper methods rely on one or more supervised learners trained jointly on labeled data and pseudo-labeled unlabeled data. Two core variants are self-training, using a single model that assigns pseudo-labels to confidently predicted examples, and co-training, where multiple models exchange their most confident predictions to generate pseudo-labels for each other. These methods integrate semi-supervised learning into the active learning loop.

topics.title: Pseudo-labels and confirmation bias risk
topics.description: Pseudo-labels help exploit unlabeled data in label-scarce environments but can induce confirmation bias. When models trust their own or peers’ pseudo-labels too strongly, they may reinforce early mistakes, degrading performance. Managing this risk is crucial when incorporating pseudo-labeled data into active learning pipelines.

topics.title: Confirmation bias in active query strategies
topics.description: In a broader active learning context, confirmation bias refers to query strategies that preferentially select examples supporting the current model hypothesis. Such selection neglects challenging or contradictory instances that could drive model improvement, leading to overconfident yet brittle models. Designing acquisition functions that avoid this bias is critical for robust learning.

topics.title: Graph-based regularization and sampling
topics.description: Graph-based methods construct a graph over all data points and train a supervised model with a loss combining standard supervised terms and a regularization that enforces similar predictions for connected nodes. In online active learning, the graph encodes similarity relationships that guide query selection, such as choosing points in low-density regions or far from existing labeled examples. This couples semi-supervised smoothness assumptions with structure-aware active sampling.

topics.title: Industrial quality control as stationary stream
topics.description: Industrial quality control is presented as an example where data streams can be treated as stationary due to controlled operating conditions. Control actions at regular intervals and continuous maintenance of system components stabilize the process, leading to relatively consistent data distributions. Stationary stream classification methods can leverage this stability to monitor product quality and detect anomalies with fewer assumptions about distribution shifts.

topics.title: Human activity recognition from wearable data
topics.description: Human activity recognition using wearable devices is described as another application of stationary data stream classification. Data from sensors on fitness trackers or similar devices generates a continuous stream representing activities like walking, running, or sleeping, assumed to be relatively stable in distribution over time. Models can be updated in real time as new labeled examples arrive, enabling continuous personalization and improvement of activity classification.

canonical_topics.name: Unsupervised Deep Representations for Online Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: Unsupervised and self-supervised deep models, such as autoencoders or pretrained feature extractors, can be trained on large pools of unlabeled or streaming data before or during active learning. These representations compress raw inputs into feature spaces where class structure and informative samples are easier to identify. In online deep active learning, the model incrementally refines these features as new unlabeled instances arrive, while querying labels only for carefully selected points. This improves both prediction quality and the effectiveness of acquisition functions under tight labeling budgets. The approach is especially valuable when labels are scarce but unlabeled data is abundant and continuously arriving.

canonical_topics.name: Pseudo-Labeling and Confirmation Bias in Deep Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: Pseudo-labeling methods, including self-training and co-training, augment a small labeled set by assigning labels to unlabeled examples using confident predictions from deep models. Integrating these techniques into the active learning loop can greatly increase data efficiency, but also introduces confirmation bias, where early model mistakes are reinforced through erroneous pseudo-labels. Similar bias can arise from query strategies that repeatedly select examples aligned with the current hypothesis, neglecting challenging or contradictory instances. Deep active learning systems must therefore manage confidence calibration, re-weight pseudo-labeled data, and design diversity-aware acquisition functions to mitigate confirmation bias. Careful validation and periodic re-evaluation of pseudo-labeled samples are crucial for robust performance.

canonical_topics.name: Graph-Based Regularization and Structure-Aware Sampling
canonical_topics.description: Graph-based semi-supervised methods construct a graph over all labeled and unlabeled instances and enforce smoothness of deep model predictions along the graph structure. A regularization term, often derived from a graph Laplacian, encourages similar predictions for neighboring nodes while allowing sharp changes across low-density regions. In deep active learning, this structure can guide acquisition by prioritizing points near graph-based decision boundaries, in sparse regions, or far from existing labeled nodes. For streaming data, the graph and its embeddings must be updated incrementally, balancing computational cost with representational fidelity. This tight coupling of structural regularization and query selection helps exploit manifold geometry in high-dimensional data.

canonical_topics.name: Online Deep Active Learning for Streaming Text Classification
canonical_topics.description: In streaming NLP tasks such as sentiment analysis or spam detection, text instances arrive continuously and models must adapt in real time. Deep classifiers, for example based on transformers or recurrent networks, can be updated incrementally when selected instances are sent for annotation. Online active learning policies decide on the fly which incoming messages or documents to label, trading off uncertainty, diversity, and annotation cost. The system must handle evolving language patterns and topic drifts while keeping the labeling budget constrained. This setting emphasizes low-latency acquisition functions and efficient incremental training procedures for deep text models.

canonical_topics.name: Sequential Decision-Making in Streaming Deep Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: In domains like video streaming platforms and adaptive clinical trials, data arrive as a sequence of interactions or patients rather than as a fixed pool. Deep active learning must therefore operate in an online, sequential decision-making regime, where each arriving instance is either queried, ignored, or acted upon immediately. The acquisition policy balances information gain against user or patient burden, ethical or regulatory constraints, and strict timing or recruitment requirements. This often leads to formulations that blend deep active learning with contextual bandits or reinforcement learning. Designing such policies requires careful consideration of delayed outcomes, non-stationarity, and the cost of suboptimal decisions during deployment.

topics.title: Real-time intrusion detection under cyberattack drift
topics.description: This topic focuses on real-time intrusion detection systems that monitor computer networks and must detect emerging forms of cyberattacks. Because attack patterns evolve, the underlying data distribution shifts, requiring classification models that adapt over time to maintain detection performance in streaming network data.

topics.title: Random sampling versus specialized strategies
topics.description: This topic contrasts naive random sampling with more advanced online active learning strategies. Random sampling selects instances from the data stream uniformly for annotation, ignoring informativeness. In contrast, specialized strategies target scenarios where labeling resources are limited or costly and where the data distribution may be non-stationary, requiring informed, adaptive selection to maintain model performance over time.

topics.title: General framework and drift adaptation
topics.description: This topic refers to a general framework that captures the main components shared across online active learning algorithms, with configurable options highlighted via callouts. The framework encompasses processes such as instance selection, querying, and model update in a streaming context. It also interfaces with drift detection and adaptation mechanisms that monitor changes in data distribution and trigger model adaptation, as detailed in referenced flowcharts.

topics.title: Mistake-driven perceptron updates with selective labels
topics.description: When a label is queried and the prediction is incorrect, the model is updated via the standard perceptron rule w_t = w_{t−1} + M_t y_t x_t, where M_t is an indicator of a prediction mistake. If the label is not requested, the weight vector remains unchanged, so learning occurs only on queried examples where errors are observed. This couples label querying with mistake-driven updates, reducing annotation cost while maintaining an online learning process.

topics.title: Smoothing-based sampling probability function
topics.description: The section introduces a sampling probability Pt defined as Pt = δ / (δ + |pt|), where δ ≥ 1 is a smoothing parameter. This formulation yields a sampling distribution equivalent to a previously defined one (Eq. 3), but restricts the smoothing parameter to values not smaller than 1. The sampling probability modulates how likely an example is queried based on a score pt, affecting the shape of the sampling distributions illustrated for b-sampling and logistic sampling.

topics.title: Minimax gradient-based conservative selection
topics.description: To mitigate the risks of aggressively focusing on misclassified examples under label noise, Bordes et al. propose a more conservative selection strategy based on a minimax gradient criterion. Instead of directly choosing the most misclassified points, examples are selected for updating wt according to how they influence a worst-case (minimax) gradient objective. This aims to provide more robust updates that are less sensitive to noisy labels and erroneous boundary estimates.

topics.title: Role of model confidence in sampling
topics.description: Beyond label reliability, the section stresses that confidence in the model itself must be considered when sampling is based solely on model predictions. Hao et al. (2018b) argue that margin-based sampling may be suboptimal when the model is not sufficiently confident, implying that query strategies should account for model uncertainty in addition to prediction margins. This connects active sampling quality directly to the model’s calibration and stability over time.

topics.title: Variance-aware soft margin querying strategy
topics.description: The sampling decision uses a variance-adjusted soft margin that combines the absolute margin with a correction term ct depending on the margin variance νt. The correction term ct = −(η/2)(1/(νt + 1/γ)) is designed so that high variance (low confidence) increases the incentive to query labels, while low variance reduces it. A composite quantity ρt = |pt| + ct is computed: if ρt ≤ 0 the label is always queried; if ρt > 0, the label is queried with probability Pt = δ / (δ + ρt), introducing a Bernoulli sampling mechanism that smoothly trades off uncertainty and labeling cost.

topics.title: Cost-sensitive loss for imbalanced data streams
topics.description: To handle class-imbalanced streaming applications, a cost-sensitive variant of the loss function is introduced. This modification assigns different costs to errors from different classes, biasing the learner to pay more attention to minority or more critical classes. The approach is positioned within the broader context of imbalanced data stream analysis.

topics.title: Cold-start with imbalanced multiclass ELMs
topics.description: Qin et al. (2021) highlight the cold-start issue specifically in imbalanced multiclass settings using extreme learning machines (ELMs). In such datasets, some classes have very few instances, severely degrading the model’s predictive ability for those classes, especially early on. They extend an existing active learning framework to multiclass classification and propose a sampling strategy that jointly considers instance uncertainty and diversity, using pairwise diversity measures to avoid redundant queries and to better represent under-represented classes.

canonical_topics.name: Smoothing-Based Probabilistic Sampling in Online AL
canonical_topics.description: This topic covers smoothing-based formulations of sampling probabilities for online active learning in data streams. The sampling probability is modeled as a function of an informativeness score, typically of the form P_t = δ / (δ + s_t), where δ ≥ 1 is a smoothing parameter that regulates how aggressively labels are requested. By constraining δ and choosing appropriate scores (e.g., margins or transformed margins), the same functional form can reproduce different sampling distributions such as b-sampling or logistic sampling. This unified view clarifies how smoothing controls the trade-off between querying highly informative but frequent examples and limiting labeling cost. It is particularly relevant when integrating uncertainty-based sampling into deep or complex models that must operate under strict annotation budgets.

canonical_topics.name: Specialized Active Sampling for Intrusion Detection
canonical_topics.description: This topic focuses on online active learning strategies for real-time intrusion detection under evolving cyberattacks. In streaming network settings, attack patterns induce continual concept drift, making naive random sampling ineffective for maintaining high detection performance. Specialized query strategies selectively request labels for the most informative or suspicious traffic, adapting to non-stationary data distributions while respecting tight annotation budgets. These strategies contrast with uniform random sampling by explicitly modeling informativeness and drift, enabling faster adaptation to emerging attacks. The setting illustrates how domain constraints, such as latency and evolving adversaries, shape the design of active learning policies in practice.

canonical_topics.name: Online Active Learning Frameworks with Drift Adaptation
canonical_topics.description: This topic presents a general framework for online active learning in streaming environments with potential concept drift. The framework decomposes algorithms into key components: instance scoring, querying decisions, and model updates, all operating incrementally as data arrive. It interfaces with drift detection modules that monitor changes in the underlying distribution and trigger adaptation, such as resetting, reweighting, or modifying the active sampling policy. Within this framework, specific mechanisms include mistake-driven perceptron-style updates applied only to queried and misclassified examples, minimax gradient-based selection to be robust under label noise, and variance-aware soft-margin sampling that combines margin magnitude with uncertainty estimates. Together, these elements provide a flexible template for designing and analyzing online (deep) active learning methods under non-stationarity.

canonical_topics.name: Confidence- and Cost-Aware Streaming Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: This topic examines how model confidence and class-dependent costs shape sampling strategies in streaming active learning. Margin-based querying assumes that prediction scores are reliable proxies for uncertainty, which may fail when the underlying model is poorly calibrated or still evolving. To address this, sampling policies explicitly account for model confidence, adjusting query decisions when the learner itself is uncertain or unstable. In parallel, cost-sensitive loss formulations reweight errors for different classes to better handle class imbalance or varying application risks, emphasizing minority or safety-critical classes. Combining confidence awareness with cost sensitivity yields active learners that both respect real-world misclassification costs and avoid over-trusting unreliable model predictions.

canonical_topics.name: Cold-Start Active Learning for Imbalanced Multiclass ELMs
canonical_topics.description: This topic addresses cold-start challenges in imbalanced multiclass classification using extreme learning machines (ELMs) under an active learning regime. When some classes are severely under-represented, early model estimates for those classes are poor, which is especially problematic during initial deployment. The proposed approach extends an existing active learning framework to the multiclass setting and designs a sampling strategy that jointly considers instance uncertainty and diversity. Pairwise diversity measures are used to reduce redundant queries and to better cover rare classes, mitigating the impact of imbalance during the cold-start phase. The ideas generalize to other deep or shallow models facing similar multiclass, imbalanced, and label-scarce streaming scenarios.

topics.title: Differentially private online SVM active learning
topics.description: A differentially private online active learning method based on SVMs randomizes the classical margin-based querying strategy of Tong and Koller. The informativeness of a point x_t is modeled as c(t) = exp(−d(x_t, w_t)), where d(x_t, w_t) = |⟨w_t, x_t⟩| / ||w_t|| is its distance to the current SVM hyperplane. In the non-private setting, labels are queried for points within a margin band around the hyperplane (c(t) > τ, equivalently d(x_t, w_t) ≤ log 1/τ), but to ensure privacy the method replaces this deterministic rule with randomized decisions.

topics.title: Mini-batch strategies for private SGD training
topics.description: For training under differential privacy, the method introduces two mini-batch strategies to mitigate the slow convergence that can result from adding noise in private stochastic gradient descent. By grouping streaming instances into mini-batches before applying noisy updates, the approach aims to balance privacy guarantees with optimization efficiency. This is contextualized with references to prior work on private SGD algorithms.

topics.title: Online active learning with reject option
topics.description: Reject option classifiers allow the learner to abstain from making a prediction when instances are highly ambiguous, mitigating the high cost of misclassification errors, as in medical diagnosis tasks. Shah and Manwani study online active learning for such classifiers, where deciding to reject versus predict is integral to the model’s operation. The framework is tailored to streaming data where each new instance may be predicted, rejected, or queried for a label.

topics.title: Double ramp loss for label querying
topics.description: The reject option classifier uses a non-convex double ramp loss ℓ_dr, where parameter updates occur only in a specific linear region of the loss. The label of the current example xt is queried only if |f_t(xt)| lies within [ρ_t − 1, ρ_t + 1], the interval where the loss is linear and informative for updating. The parameter ρ defines the bandwidth of the rejection region, controlling which instances fall into the 'reject' versus 'predict' zones.

topics.title: Bayesian online active learning framework
topics.description: Fujii and Kashima propose a Bayesian online active learning framework based on policy-adaptive submodularity to handle data streams. It distinguishes between a stream setting, where labeling decisions can be delayed within a time window, and a secretary setting, where decisions must be taken immediately upon arrival. The framework is general enough to cover tasks such as active classification, active clustering, and active feature selection under streaming conditions.

topics.title: Adaptive submodular maximization in streams
topics.description: The Bayesian framework is grounded in adaptive submodular maximization, extending classical submodular maximization characterized by diminishing returns of adding elements to a set. By updating the set function as new observations arrive, the method adapts to the evolving data distribution and current state of knowledge. This adaptivity aims to exploit streaming data more efficiently, improving model performance under limited labeling budgets.

topics.title: Disagreement-based online active learning theory
topics.description: Huang et al. introduce a disagreement-based active learning framework for online settings, formalized over a hypothesis space H with VC dimension d and a Tsybakov noise model. Each classifier h ∈ H maps observations xt to binary labels yt ∈ {0,1}, and pairwise disagreement is quantified by d(h1, h2) = P[h1(x) ≠ h2(x)]. The induced disagreement region, where committee members predict differently, underpins sampling strategies that query labels only on informative, contentious instances.

topics.title: Label complexity and regret objectives
topics.description: Online active learning is formalized as a policy π = ({v_t}, {λ_t}), where v_t encodes whether a label is queried and λ_t is the prediction rule at time t. The performance over a time horizon T is evaluated via label complexity, defined as the expected number of queried labels E[Q(T)], and regret, defined as the expected excess number of classification errors with respect to an optimal hypothesis h*. The algorithm’s goal is to minimize label complexity subject to a constraint on regret, balancing labeling cost and predictive performance.

topics.title: Disagreement-based query region in online learning
topics.description: The learner maintains a version space H_t of candidate hypotheses and defines a region of disagreement D(H_t) as points where at least two hypotheses in H_t predict different labels. Initially, the version space is the full hypothesis class H and the disagreement region is the whole input space X. At each time t, if the current instance x_t falls inside D(H_t), the learner queries its label; otherwise, it predicts with an arbitrary classifier from H_t. This mechanism drives selective querying based on current model uncertainty.

topics.title: Version space pruning via empirical error thresholds
topics.description: After each iteration t, the learner uses the collected labeled set Z_t of size M to estimate the empirical error ε_{Z_t}(h) for all classifiers in H and identify the current best classifier h*_t. The version space is then updated by removing hypotheses whose empirical error exceeds that of h*_t by more than a threshold ε_{Z_t}(h, h*_t). This threshold controls how aggressively the version space is pruned, mediating a trade-off between reducing label complexity (by shrinking the disagreement region) and limiting regret (by avoiding elimination of good classifiers.

canonical_topics.name: Differentially Private Online SVM Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: This topic studies an online margin-based active learning algorithm for SVMs under differential privacy constraints. The informativeness of each incoming instance is modeled as a decreasing function of its distance to the current SVM hyperplane, so that points near the margin are most likely to be queried. In the non-private setting, the algorithm uses a deterministic margin-band rule that queries labels only for points within a fixed distance of the decision boundary. To satisfy differential privacy, this deterministic rule is replaced by a randomized querying strategy whose probability mass is concentrated near the margin but perturbed by carefully calibrated noise. The approach aims to preserve the label efficiency of classic margin-based active learning while providing rigorous privacy guarantees for the labeled data stream.

canonical_topics.name: Online Active Learning with Reject Option
canonical_topics.description: This topic considers online active learning for classifiers equipped with a reject option, allowing the learner to abstain from prediction on highly ambiguous instances. The model uses a non-convex double ramp loss, which has a linear region that is informative for updating parameters and outer regions that correspond to confident predictions or rejections. During streaming operation, the algorithm queries the label of an instance only when the current prediction score falls within the linear band of the double ramp loss. The width and position of this band, controlled by a parameter ρ, determine which examples are rejected, which are predicted, and which are queried for labels. This design explicitly trades off misclassification cost, rejection cost, and labeling cost in sequential decision-making.

canonical_topics.name: Bayesian Streaming Active Learning via Adaptive Submodularity
canonical_topics.description: This topic presents a Bayesian framework for active learning on data streams based on policy-adaptive submodularity. The framework models the expected utility of labeling decisions as an adaptive submodular function, capturing diminishing returns as more labels are acquired. It distinguishes between a stream setting, where decisions can be deferred within a time window, and a secretary setting, where the learner must decide immediately whether to query each arriving instance. By updating the utility function with newly observed labels, the method adapts to the evolving data distribution and information state over time. The approach is general enough to encompass active classification, active clustering, and active feature selection under streaming and budget constraints, while retaining near-optimality guarantees from adaptive submodular maximization.

canonical_topics.name: Disagreement-Based Online Active Learning and Guarantees
canonical_topics.description: This topic develops a disagreement-based framework for online active learning over a hypothesis class with finite VC dimension under Tsybakov noise conditions. The learner maintains a version space of hypotheses consistent with observed labeled data and defines a disagreement region where members of this space predict different labels. Labels are queried only for instances falling inside this region, while outside it the learner predicts using an arbitrary hypothesis from the version space. After each iteration, the version space is pruned by removing hypotheses whose empirical error exceeds that of the current best classifier by more than a data-dependent threshold, thereby shrinking the disagreement region over time. The performance of the resulting policy is analyzed in terms of label complexity and regret, aiming to minimize the expected number of label queries subject to a bound on excess classification errors relative to an optimal hypothesis.

topics.title: Surrogate-loss active learning with pseudo-labels
topics.description: Desalvo et al. (2021) extend disagreement-based online active learning to a framework using surrogate losses and weak labels. At each time step, the learner may either query the true label y_t or assign a pseudo-label ŷ_t, and both true and pseudo-labeled instances form a set S_t that combines Z_t and Ŷ_t. The empirical risk ε_{S_t}(h) is computed over this mixed set, effectively integrating active learning with semi-supervised learning to optimize the sampling and learning strategy.

topics.title: Bayesian active learning for activity recognition
topics.description: For online human activity recognition with sensor data, a semi-supervised active learning strategy leverages a pre-trained conditional restricted Boltzmann machine to extract generic features robust to different sensor layouts. Instance selection follows a Bayesian approach aimed at minimizing uncertainty over model parameters by comparing current model uncertainty (from data up to time t) with the expected risk conditioned on the potential label y_t. The discrepancy between these quantities indicates the impact of acquiring the current label on model uncertainty. A dynamically adaptive threshold is used to decide whether the expected risk justifies querying the label.

topics.title: Decay-weighted expert loss and potential
topics.description: The section discusses how expert advice algorithms maintain a cumulative loss Ri,t−1 for each expert, updated with an exponential decay factor η so that recent mistakes are weighted more heavily than older ones. It explains that the Generalized Forecaster (GF) operates by minimizing, at each time step, the worst-case increase in a potential function over all possible label outcomes. This potential function assigns a value to each expert that reflects the quality of its advice based on its decay-weighted past performance. These mechanisms underpin how expert weights and influence are adapted over time in online prediction.

topics.title: Active multiple kernel learning with random features
topics.description: A related framework applies online active learning to multiple kernel learning (MKL) using random feature approximation. The Active MKL (AMKL) algorithm employs an ensemble of N kernel functions within a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), where each kernel-based function 1fi,t(xt) is optimized independently in a local step. In a subsequent global step, the learner combines these N kernel functions to construct a best-approximation function ft(xt) for prediction on sequentially arriving data. This setup leverages MKL’s ability to capture diverse data characteristics while maintaining online, incremental updates suitable for streaming and active settings.

topics.title: Regret-minimizing kernel ensemble weighting
topics.description: The method constructs a learned kernel-based predictor f̃t(xt) as a weighted combination of N kernel functions fi,t, with weights vi,t chosen to minimize regret over the time horizon T. Weights are computed via exponential weighting of past losses on labeled instances: ωi,t = exp(−ηg ∑_{τ∈A_{t−1}} ℓ(f̂i,τ(xτ), yτ)), where A_{t−1} indexes queried points and ηg is a tunable parameter. Normalizing ωi,t yields vi,t, which balance the contribution of each kernel according to historical performance relative to the best kernel function f*i,t. This framework ties instance labeling decisions to an adaptive ensemble of kernel predictors optimized on previous labeled data.

topics.title: Confidence-based instance selection via kernel agreement
topics.description: Instance selection relies on a confidence condition that measures the similarity of predictions among the weighted kernel ensemble, controlled by a tolerance threshold δ > 0. The criterion max_{1≤j≤N} ∑_{i=1}^N vi,t ℓ(f̃i,t(xt), f̃j,t(xt)) ≤ δ enforces that, for an unlabeled instance, all kernels’ predictions are sufficiently close under the loss ℓ, indicating high agreement. When this condition holds, the system can refrain from querying the label, interpreting high consensus as high confidence. This selection rule is analogous to the condition used in AEWAF by Hao et al. (2018a), adapting expert agreement to a kernel-based ensemble.

topics.title: Distribution shifts in drifting data streams
topics.description: Active learning strategies in this category address online classification in time-varying data streams where the underlying data distribution changes over time. The text distinguishes distribution shifts based on whether they affect the feature distribution p(x) or the conditional distribution p(y|x). A covariate shift is defined as a change that only impacts p(x) while leaving p(y|x) unchanged. This categorization sets the stage for analyzing and designing active learning methods tailored to different types of drift.

topics.title: Limitations of unsupervised drift detection
topics.description: The text explains that purely unsupervised drift detection struggles to capture true concept drifts when the input distribution p(x) remains unchanged but the conditional relationship between x and y changes. In such cases, labels are necessary to recognize that the mapping from features to labels has shifted. This highlights a fundamental limitation of relying only on unlabeled data for detecting concept drift in active learning scenarios. It motivates combining limited supervised signals with unsupervised detectors.

topics.title: Pseudo-label propagation using k-nearest neighbors
topics.description: The section describes augmenting active learning decisions with pseudo-labels inferred from already labeled neighbors. For an unlabeled queried point, its label is estimated through a weighted majority vote among its k-nearest neighbors, propagating known labels through the feature space. Both true labels and these pseudo-labels are then used to assess the utility of incoming data points. This semi-supervised mechanism enriches label information under latency and sparsity, improving utility estimation in streaming active learning.

topics.title: Drift-aware dual-classifier management
topics.description: The algorithm maintains a primary classifier and conditionally spawns a new classifier when the drift detector raises a warning. During a warning phase, the new classifier is trained in the background with labeled examples while the original classifier remains in use. Upon confirmed drift detection, the new classifier replaces the old one, and its training continues, enabling smoother adaptation to concept drift while avoiding abrupt model changes.

canonical_topics.name: Surrogate-Loss Active Learning with Pseudo-Labels
canonical_topics.description: This topic covers online active learning frameworks that allow the learner to either query true labels or assign pseudo-labels while optimizing a surrogate loss. At each time step, instances are added to a mixed set containing both truly labeled and pseudo-labeled examples, and empirical risk is computed over this combined set. This integrates active and semi-supervised learning, enabling the model to leverage weak labels to reduce query rates. Pseudo-labels can be generated by propagating labels from k-nearest neighbors via a weighted majority vote, enriching the training signal when ground-truth labels are sparse or delayed. Such mechanisms aim to preserve model accuracy while tightly controlling labeling cost in streaming settings.

canonical_topics.name: Bayesian Active Learning for Human Activity Recognition
canonical_topics.description: This topic addresses semi-supervised active learning for online human activity recognition from sensor streams. A pre-trained conditional restricted Boltzmann machine is used as a generic feature extractor, providing representations robust to varying sensor layouts. Instance selection follows a Bayesian principle that compares current parameter uncertainty with the expected risk conditioned on each possible label. The discrepancy between these quantities quantifies the value of acquiring the label for the current instance. A dynamically adaptive threshold then decides whether the expected risk reduction justifies querying, balancing recognition performance against labeling cost over time.

canonical_topics.name: Online Active Multiple Kernel Learning with Ensemble Agreement
canonical_topics.description: This topic focuses on active learning with multiple kernel functions in an online setting, often using random feature approximations for efficiency. An ensemble of kernel-based predictors is maintained, each updated locally, and then combined into a single predictor whose kernel weights are learned via exponential weighting to minimize regret over queried, labeled instances. The query strategy is confidence-based, relying on the agreement of the weighted kernel ensemble: when all kernels make similar predictions on an instance, the system treats it as high-confidence and skips querying. A tolerance threshold on this agreement controls the trade-off between label savings and prediction reliability. This framework adapts both instance selection and kernel weights jointly as data arrive in a stream.

canonical_topics.name: Drift-Aware Active Learning and Concept Drift Adaptation
canonical_topics.description: This topic studies active learning in non-stationary data streams where the underlying distribution may drift over time. It distinguishes between covariate shift, which affects only the feature distribution, and true concept drift, which changes the conditional relationship between features and labels. Purely unsupervised drift detection can fail to recognize concept drift when the input distribution is stable, motivating the use of selectively queried labels to validate suspected changes. A drift-aware strategy maintains a primary classifier and spawns a secondary classifier when drift warnings arise, training the new model on queried labeled data during the warning phase. Upon confirmed drift, the new classifier replaces the old one, enabling smoother transitions and focusing label queries on regions most indicative of changing concepts.

topics.title: Simulated labeling via bagging and fuzziness
topics.description: To avoid redundant queries when labels are delayed, the method identifies a region Dn+ = Dn\Wn where queried labels are not yet available. Instead of re-querying similar instances, it simulates incoming labels by using a bagging approach that averages utility estimates over multiple simulated labelings, thus approximating the effect of future supervision. An alternative simulation based on fuzzy labeling is also considered to represent label uncertainty more explicitly.

topics.title: Class-imbalance-aware uncertainty thresholds
topics.description: Instance selection is based on predictive uncertainty measured by the best-versus-second-best margin for multi-class classification. After a passive initialization pool, a per-class threshold θi is computed (Eq. 31) as a function of class-specific sample counts and a constant m controlling threshold size, so that querying behavior can differ across classes. Class imbalance is further addressed through class-specific training weights and dynamic adjustment of these thresholds to bias selection toward minority-class instances.

topics.title: Chunk-based drift detection and selection
topics.description: A data stream S is partitioned into fixed-length chunks whose adjacent distributions are compared to detect concept drift. After a drift is identified, a multi-objective optimization problem is formulated to select query candidates from the current batch that are both relevant and diverse. Relevance is defined as a point’s contribution to the emerging concept, while diversity is quantified via the Pearson correlation coefficient among instances in the same region, encouraging informative yet non-redundant labeling.

topics.title: Meta-learned uncertainty thresholds per window
topics.description: Another approach samples the most uncertain instances from each chunk but uses a meta-learning framework to fine-tune the uncertainty threshold for each window. By adapting this threshold based on meta-level information, the method aims to reduce the number of labels requested while preserving effective adaptation to new concepts. This window-wise tuning balances exploration of changing regions of the feature space with labeling cost constraints.

topics.title: Damped sliding window weight decay
topics.description: Dynamic classifiers are assigned gradually decaying weights based on a damped sliding window mechanism. Each dynamic classifier weight is initialized at 1/D and then updated according to its creation time using the recurrence in Eq. (34). More recent dynamic classifiers receive higher weights to emphasize detection of sudden concept drifts, while older ones have smaller weights and contribute to identifying gradual drifts. This temporal weighting scheme encodes recency into the ensemble’s decision process.

topics.title: Hybrid random–uncertainty instance selection
topics.description: The instance selection strategy combines uncertainty sampling with random sampling to choose which data points in the stream should be labeled. Uncertainty is based on the margin of ensemble predictions, while random sampling ensures coverage of regions far from the current decision boundary. This hybrid design addresses the limitation of pure uncertainty sampling, which may miss concept changes that occur away from the boundary. Similar ideas are reused in chunk-based ensemble active learning, where Zyblewski’s budget labeling strategy selects both random and informative examples measured via a support function threshold (interpreted as distance to the decision boundary in binary problems).

topics.title: Clustering-based active learning with stable classifiers
topics.description: Halder et al. (2023) extend a framework with stable and dynamic classifiers by inserting a clustering step on each data block. The goal is to train a new stable classifier on instances that are simultaneously informative and representative, selected from clusters formed in each incoming block. This integrates cluster structure into the design of online active learning for time-varying data streams.

topics.title: Density-peak clustering for representative sample selection
topics.description: Zhang et al. (2023) employ density-peak clustering to identify the most representative data points in each batch of a data stream. They detect incomplete clusters in the dynamic feature space via the 'altitude' of data points and then query labels from those regions in subsequent iterations. This targets areas that are underrepresented or poorly formed in the current clustering structure.

topics.title: Bi-criteria GGMM-based active learning with drift handling
topics.description: Mohamad et al. (2018) introduce a bi-criteria active learning algorithm that combines input-space density and label uncertainty. Density is modeled with a growing Gaussian mixture model (GGMM) that forms clusters and estimates data density, creating a new cluster when a point’s Mahalanobis distance to its nearest cluster exceeds a closeness threshold. Label uncertainty and concept drift are handled via a Bayesian logistic regression model whose parameters evolve over time, linking evolving class boundaries with the streaming data’s cluster structure.

topics.title: Discrepancy-based incremental model updating
topics.description: The model is updated incrementally using a discrepancy measure defined as the difference between the model’s uncertainty on an instance xt before and after its true label yt is added to the training set. The query strategy uses a b-sampling approach to preferentially select instances that are expected to contribute most to the current error. This couples an uncertainty-change metric with error-focused sampling for online active learning in data streams.

canonical_topics.name: Simulation-Based Label Forecasting for Delayed Feedback
canonical_topics.description: This topic addresses active learning in streaming scenarios where queried labels are delayed. Instead of repeatedly querying similar instances from a region where labels are still pending, it simulates incoming labels using a bagging strategy that averages utility estimates over multiple hypothetical labelings. An alternative fuzzy-labeling scheme explicitly encodes label uncertainty by assigning soft labels rather than hard class decisions. These simulation mechanisms approximate the effect of future supervision, allowing the learner to avoid redundant queries and maintain progress while waiting for ground-truth labels.

canonical_topics.name: Adaptive Uncertainty Criteria Under Imbalance and Drift
canonical_topics.description: This topic focuses on advanced uncertainty-based querying strategies that adapt to class imbalance and temporal variation. A margin-based uncertainty measure (best-versus-second-best prediction) is controlled by per-class thresholds that depend on class-specific sample counts and a tunable parameter, so rare classes are more aggressively queried. The thresholds are further adjusted over time, for example via meta-learning on each data window, to balance label budget against responsiveness to evolving concepts. In addition, a discrepancy measure compares model uncertainty on an instance before and after its label is incorporated, and b-sampling prioritizes points expected to yield the largest uncertainty (and error) reduction. Together, these mechanisms create a family of active learning policies that tailor uncertainty criteria to class frequencies, temporal windows, and expected impact on model performance.

canonical_topics.name: Concept-Drift-Aware Stream Active Learning with Hybrid Sampling
canonical_topics.description: This topic covers stream-based active learning methods that explicitly detect and track concept drift while selecting informative labels. Incoming data are processed in fixed-length chunks whose adjacent distributions are compared to identify drifts, after which a multi-objective optimization selects instances that are both highly relevant to the emerging concept and mutually diverse, with diversity quantified via measures such as Pearson correlation. Instance selection often combines margin-based uncertainty sampling with random sampling so that the learner captures both changes near the current decision boundary and shifts occurring in previously unexplored regions. Density is modeled with a growing Gaussian mixture model that forms and splits clusters based on Mahalanobis distance, while a Bayesian logistic regressor with time-varying parameters tracks evolving class boundaries. An ensemble of dynamic classifiers is maintained with damped sliding-window weights, emphasizing recent models for abrupt drifts while retaining older ones to better handle gradual changes.

canonical_topics.name: Clustering and Density-Peak Selection in Streaming Active Learning
canonical_topics.description: This topic uses clustering structure to guide representative and informative querying in data streams. Each incoming data block is clustered, and points are chosen that are simultaneously informative for the current decision boundary and representative of their clusters, providing training data for more stable base classifiers. Density-peak clustering identifies high-density exemplars and uses an altitude-like measure to detect incomplete or weakly formed clusters in the evolving feature space. Labels are then requested from these underrepresented regions in subsequent iterations, improving coverage of emerging or poorly modeled areas. By targeting both cluster exemplars and incomplete clusters, the method balances representativeness and exploration in non-stationary streaming environments.

topics.title: Cognitive dual density-uncertainty query strategy
topics.description: Liu et al. (2021) propose an online active learning strategy that combines local density and classifier uncertainty to select informative and representative instances under concept drift and noise. Local density is defined as the number of times an observation is the nearest neighbor of other instances, computed within a sliding 'cognition window' over the stream. Inspired by Ebbinghaus’s law of human memory, the method uses a memory-strength-based policy to decide when the cognition window is refreshed, addressing both gradual and abrupt drifts. Labeling decisions are controlled by two thresholds, one on local density and one on classifier uncertainty.

topics.title: Time-decay Bayesian probit framework for streams
topics.description: Chu et al. (2011) propose an online framework based on a Bayesian probit model with time-decay to handle evolving data streams. Online Bayesian learning maintains a posterior distribution over the linear classifier’s weight vector wt, while time-decay strategies downweight older examples to cope with concept drift and emphasize recent data. An online approximation technique supports weighted examples, following Minka (2001), and various sampling strategies are explored using entropy-based, function-value-based, and random selection criteria. This integrates probabilistic modeling, temporal weighting, and multiple query heuristics for streaming active learning.

topics.title: Conflict and ignorance for stream active learning
topics.description: In single-pass active learning for evolving classification models, query decisions are based on conflict and ignorance. Conflict captures when an incoming instance lies near the decision boundary between classes, indicating label ambiguity, while ignorance measures the distance of the instance from the labeled training data in feature space, indicating unexplored regions. These two criteria guide which streaming instances should be labeled to most effectively improve the classifier.

topics.title: Uncertainty-driven active learning for evolving regression
topics.description: For evolving regression models, online active learning combines ignorance in the input space with uncertainty in model outputs and parameters. Predictive uncertainty is quantified using confidence intervals via locally adaptive error bars, and overlapping fuzzy rules are merged with a dedicated approach to refine the rule base. Parameter uncertainty is assessed using the A-optimality criterion, an alphabetic optimality measure that aims to minimize the average variance of parameter estimates.

topics.title: Variable uncertainty thresholds and low-support rules
topics.description: An alternative active learning strategy for recurrent fuzzy classifiers uses a dynamic threshold based on the variable uncertainty strategy. Instead of directly exploiting output uncertainty, the method adaptively adjusts the threshold that determines when to query labels, focusing updates on rules with low support formed from few observations. This emphasizes improving underrepresented regions of the rule base and addresses the what-to-learn question in recurrent fuzzy model training.

topics.title: D-optimality for fuzzy model parameter selection
topics.description: A recent online active learning strategy for fuzzy models introduces criteria based on D-optimality in the consequent space. D-optimality is used to reduce parameter uncertainty by selecting instances that maximize the determinant of the information matrix, thereby improving the precision of parameter estimates in the consequents of fuzzy rules. This embeds classical optimal experimental design principles into active learning for evolving fuzzy systems.

topics.title: Spherical potential-based novelty thresholds
topics.description: Subramanian et al. propose a meta-cognitive component that evaluates the novelty of incoming data points using a knowledge measure called spherical potential, a concept studied in kernel-based methods. This spherical potential is used to set a threshold deciding whether a new fuzzy rule should be added to capture the knowledge in the current sample. The work contrasts this label-efficient novelty criterion with a prediction-error-based threshold relying on hinge loss, which is less suitable under label scarcity.

topics.title: Certainty-based querying in visual inspection streams
topics.description: For visual inspection quality control, images are evaluated in a single pass and those selected for querying are stored in a buffer to be labeled later by an oracle. The buffer size defines a trade-off between promptly updating the classifier and limiting frequent human interventions. An active learning strategy is used that queries samples when model certainty, computed differently for a random forest (best-versus-second-best margin) and an evolving fuzzy classifier (conflict and ignorance measures), falls below a threshold.

topics.title: Hotelling T² and SPE for AL sampling
topics.description: Cernuda et al. employ a latent-structure-based query strategy using Hotelling T² and squared prediction error (SPE) statistics, classical tools from multivariate statistical process control and anomaly detection. These statistics measure the distance between the current labeled training set and a new unlabeled data point; high values indicate that the observation violates the current model and is thus informative to query. Implementations combine these criteria with principal component regression or partial least squares, and newly labeled samples trigger retraining of a Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy model using a sliding window over the data stream.

topics.title: Optimal experimental design and active learning
topics.description: Optimal experimental design is presented as a closely related field to active learning, focusing on designing experiments that enable efficient parameter estimation or improved prediction while minimizing the number of labeled runs N. It develops optimality criteria that balance resource efficiency with model performance. The traditional framework considered here is based on linear regression models, connecting classical design of experiments with active learning objectives.

canonical_topics.name: Density and Novelty-Based Streaming Query Strategies
canonical_topics.description: This topic covers online active learning strategies that combine local density, classifier uncertainty, and novelty measures to select informative instances in data streams with concept drift and noise. One approach defines a local density score based on how often an observation appears as the nearest neighbor within a sliding cognition window, which is refreshed according to a memory-strength policy inspired by Ebbinghaus’s forgetting curve to handle gradual and abrupt drifts. Another approach uses a spherical potential measure, derived from kernel-based methods, to quantify the novelty of incoming samples and decide when to create new fuzzy rules. Labeling and structure-adaptation decisions are governed by thresholds on density, uncertainty, and spherical potential, aiming to remain label-efficient while maintaining a representative and adaptive model.

canonical_topics.name: Conflict and Ignorance Criteria in Stream Learning
canonical_topics.description: This topic focuses on conflict and ignorance as complementary criteria for single-pass active learning in evolving classifiers, including applications to visual inspection. Conflict quantifies how close an instance lies to the current decision boundary, indicating label ambiguity and motivating queries for boundary refinement. Ignorance measures the distance of a new sample from the labeled training set in feature space, highlighting unexplored regions where the model is poorly supported. In a visual quality-control setting, instances are processed once, and samples whose certainty (computed via conflict–ignorance for fuzzy models or best-versus-second-best margins for random forests) falls below a threshold are stored in a buffer for later labeling. The buffer size and certainty threshold jointly control the trade-off between rapid model updates and the frequency of human annotation.

canonical_topics.name: Active Learning for Evolving Regression in Data Streams
canonical_topics.description: This topic addresses active learning for regression models that evolve over streaming data. A Bayesian probit framework with time-decay maintains an online posterior over classifier or regressor weights while downweighting older observations, enabling adaptation to concept drift and supporting query strategies such as entropy-based, function-value-based, and random sampling. For fuzzy and rule-based regressors, predictive uncertainty is quantified through locally adaptive error bars, and parameter uncertainty is assessed using alphabetic optimality criteria such as A-optimality, guiding which samples most reduce expected parameter variance. Latent-structure-based statistics like Hotelling T² and squared prediction error (SPE) further measure how strongly a new point violates the current latent subspace, indicating informative outliers for labeling. These ideas are implemented with models such as principal component regression, partial least squares, and Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy systems within sliding-window or single-pass streaming settings.

canonical_topics.name: Adaptive Uncertainty Thresholds and Optimal Design in AL
canonical_topics.description: This topic links adaptive query control in active learning with principles from optimal experimental design. In recurrent fuzzy classifiers, a variable uncertainty strategy adjusts the querying threshold over time, focusing labeling effort on rules with low support that are formed from few observations, thereby improving underrepresented regions of the input space. From an optimal design perspective, active learning is framed as choosing experiments or samples that maximize information gain for parameter estimation or prediction quality while minimizing the number of labeled runs. Classical optimality criteria from linear regression design provide a theoretical basis for these strategies, formalizing trade-offs between resource efficiency and model performance. Together, dynamic thresholds and design-based criteria address the what-to-learn question in a principled and data-efficient way.

canonical_topics.name: D-Optimality Criteria for Fuzzy Model Queries
canonical_topics.description: This topic introduces D-optimality-based query strategies for evolving fuzzy models. The core idea is to reduce parameter uncertainty in the consequents of fuzzy rules by selecting samples that maximize the determinant of the information matrix, a classical D-optimal design criterion. Such samples are expected to yield the greatest reduction in the volume of the confidence ellipsoid for the parameters, improving estimation precision. Embedding D-optimality into online active learning allows fuzzy systems to grow and update using the most informative observations, rather than relying solely on heuristic uncertainty or error-based measures. This bridges optimal experimental design theory with practical stream-based active learning for fuzzy and rule-based models.

topics.title: Linear regression and OLS estimation
topics.description: The section defines a linear regression model y = Xβ + ε with N observations and d input variables, where ε is Gaussian noise with covariance σ²I. It explains that if XᵀX is full rank, the ordinary least squares (OLS) estimator for the regression coefficients β is given by (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy. This sets the foundation for later discussion of design properties and parameter uncertainty.

topics.title: Moment matrix and design geometry
topics.description: The moment matrix M = XᵀX / N is introduced as a key object in design optimality criteria, encapsulating information about the design geometry. Since XᵀX governs the estimation of β, its structure (eigenvalues, determinant) reflects how informative the design is for parameter estimation. Optimal design methods exploit these properties to evaluate and compare experimental designs.

topics.title: Confidence ellipsoid for regression parameters
topics.description: Assuming Gaussian noise, the estimator β̂ has a Normal distribution with covariance σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹, which induces a confidence ellipsoid for the true parameter vector β. The ellipsoid is defined via quadratic forms in (b − β̂) involving XᵀX, and its volume is inversely proportional to √det(XᵀX), while the axis lengths scale with 1/λᵢ, the eigenvalues of XᵀX. This geometric interpretation underlies how optimality criteria assess designs via ellipsoid size and shape.

topics.title: From offline to streaming optimal design
topics.description: Traditional optimal design methods are used in offline experimental settings, where all design points can be pre-determined before data collection. In streaming scenarios, data points arrive sequentially and the design must be adapted online, requiring modifications of classical optimality-based approaches. This motivates strategies that incrementally select which incoming observations to label to approximate an optimal design.

topics.title: Online A-optimal design under heteroskedasticity
topics.description: Fontaine et al. extend online optimal design to settings with heteroskedastic noise, where the variance of the response depends on the covariates. Their objective is to optimally allocate a fixed labeling budget across covariates so that the variances of the estimated regression coefficients are balanced, in line with A-optimality principles. This results in adaptive selection policies that consider both design geometry and non-constant error variance.

topics.title: Conditional D-optimality for streaming selection
topics.description: Cacciarelli et al. propose a Conditional D-optimality (CDO) algorithm that extends norm-thresholding ideas to D-optimal design in streaming settings. The design is made marginally D-optimal given an initial labeled set, and incoming observations are selected by applying a D-optimality-based thresholding rule to augment this set. The method exploits the link between D-optimality and prediction variance, yielding a sequential selection strategy that improves the determinant of the information matrix as new data arrive.

topics.title: Warm-up set and KDE threshold estimation
topics.description: Before starting active querying, the learner passively collects a warm-up set of j unlabeled observations from the stream to estimate the covariance structure of the data. Using eigendecomposition and whitening of both the initial design X and warm-up set W, the algorithm computes representations Z and V in a normalized space. Kernel density estimation (KDE) over V is then used to select a threshold τ such that the norm-thresholding rule achieves the desired sampling rate α. This procedure initializes τ and is periodically updated as the labeled design grows.

topics.title: Outlier-robust double-threshold sampling region
topics.description: To mitigate the tendency of design-optimality sampling to focus on outliers, the authors describe bounding the selection region with two thresholds τ1 and τ2. Only points whose leverage x_t^T (X^T X)^{-1} x_t falls between these bounds are eligible for labeling, defining an annular region in the transformed feature space. The upper threshold τ2 controls a trade-off between avoiding high-leverage outliers and still exploring uncertain regions of the input space. This modification aims to preserve predictive performance in the presence of outliers.

topics.title: MAB as sequential experimental design
topics.description: Multi-armed bandit (MAB) problems are framed as a special case of sequential experimental design, where each arm pull is an experiment chosen to maximize an outcome over time. The learner must identify the arm with the highest expected reward among several arms with different reward distributions. This setting parallels active learning, as both involve sequential decisions (arm pulls or label queries) with feedback guiding future choices to optimize reward or model accuracy.

topics.title: Regret minimization in bandits
topics.description: Regret minimization in MAB focuses on maximizing cumulative reward across many trials, equivalently minimizing the loss relative to always playing the best arm. Algorithms must carefully balance exploration of lesser-known arms to improve reward estimates with exploitation of the currently best-estimated arm. This paradigm is suited to applications such as treatment design, online advertising, and recommender systems, where ongoing rewards are critical.

canonical_topics.name: Linear Regression Geometry for Optimal Design
canonical_topics.description: A linear regression model y = Xβ + ε with Gaussian noise provides a convenient foundation for design-based active learning. The ordinary least squares (OLS) estimator β̂ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy depends on the information matrix XᵀX, or equivalently the moment matrix M = XᵀX / N. The eigenvalues and determinant of this matrix encode how informative the design is for estimating β, linking directly to classical A- and D-optimality criteria. Under Gaussian assumptions, β̂ is Normal with covariance σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹, inducing a confidence ellipsoid whose volume and axis lengths are governed by the spectrum of XᵀX. This geometric view connects parameter uncertainty to design quality and underlies many optimal-design-inspired active learning strategies.

canonical_topics.name: Streaming Optimal Design for Sequential Labeling
canonical_topics.description: Optimal experimental design can be adapted from offline batch settings to streaming scenarios where candidate points arrive sequentially. In this setting, the learner must decide online which observations to label in order to approximate A- or D-optimal designs under a fixed labeling budget. Extensions to heteroskedastic regression allocate labels to balance coefficient variances when noise depends on the covariates, generalizing A-optimality to non-constant error variance. Conditional D-optimality methods further refine selection by making the design marginally D-optimal relative to an existing labeled set and updating decisions as new points arrive. Together, these approaches provide principled sequential selection rules that align active querying with classical design optimality in dynamic data streams.

canonical_topics.name: Norm-Thresholding and Robust Streaming Sampling
canonical_topics.description: Norm-thresholding methods use the geometry of a whitened feature space to decide which streaming points to label. A passive warm-up phase collects an initial unlabeled set to estimate the data covariance, whiten both the design and warm-up features, and tune a norm threshold via kernel density estimation to achieve a target sampling rate. During active querying, points whose leverage or whitened norm lies within a prescribed range are selected, effectively targeting regions that are informative for reducing prediction variance. Introducing a double-threshold scheme bounds the sampling region, discarding very low-leverage points as uninformative and very high-leverage points as potential outliers. This annular selection region improves robustness, preventing optimal-design-inspired samplers from over-focusing on extreme observations while maintaining strong predictive performance.

topics.title: Pure exploration bandit strategies
topics.description: Pure exploration methods aim to identify the best arm with high confidence or under a fixed budget of arm pulls, rather than maximizing cumulative reward. The main objective is to learn an accurate model of the reward structure while minimizing the number of measurements or labels, often motivated by safety or cost constraints on interventions. This setting is relevant to domains such as drug discovery and soft sensor development, where safe and efficient experimentation is crucial.

topics.title: G-optimality and XY-allocation for bandits
topics.description: In the offline pure exploration setting for linear bandits, Soare et al. analyze the problem using the G-optimality criterion from experimental design, which seeks to minimize the maximum prediction variance over a design space. They introduce the XY-allocation algorithm, a specific strategy for allocating pulls across arms to achieve near G-optimal experimental designs. This connects classical optimal design theory with sample-efficient bandit exploration.

topics.title: LSTM-based policy for label vs. predict
topics.description: Woodward and Finn (2017) propose a reinforcement learning approach in which, at each time step, the learner must choose between predicting a label for xt or paying to query its true label yt. The policy π*(st) is optimized over states st to balance the cost of label requests versus the cost of incorrect predictions, with rewards assigned for requesting a label (Rreq), making a correct prediction (Rcorr), or an incorrect prediction (Rinc), where Rcorr and Rinc are modeled as negative due to associated costs. The action-value function is approximated using an LSTM neural network with a linear output layer, enabling the policy to exploit temporal dependencies in the sequence of decisions.

topics.title: Learning-curve evaluation of active learning
topics.description: Active learning strategies are evaluated by comparing them to passive random sampling through learning curves that track model performance versus the number of labeled examples. Metrics such as accuracy, F1 score, or root mean square error on a holdout test set are plotted. The curve’s asymptote and slope capture overall performance and sample efficiency, with steeper slopes indicating faster performance gains per labeled example.

topics.title: Non-parametric tests for strategy comparison
topics.description: To rigorously compare multiple active learning sampling strategies, non-parametric statistical tests are recommended. For pairwise comparisons, the sign test and the Wilcoxon signed-ranks test are proposed, while for more than two strategies, Friedman tests (including aligned-ranks and Iman–Davenport correction) and the Quade test are suggested. These tests assess whether observed performance differences between active and passive strategies are statistically significant across tasks or datasets.

topics.title: MOA framework for stream evaluation
topics.description: MOA (Massive Online Analysis) is an open-source software suite for data stream mining that implements both holdout and prequential evaluation strategies. It provides infrastructure to run and compare online learning and active learning algorithms on streaming data. Many studies in the survey use MOA as their experimental platform for evaluating online active learning strategies. Its inclusion of multiple evaluation protocols makes it a de facto standard tool in this research area.

topics.title: Train-on-queried, test-on-full-dataset protocol
topics.description: Some works adopt a non-standard protocol where models are trained only on queried (labeled) data but evaluated on the entire dataset, including instances seen during training. This differs from strict prequential test-then-train, where each instance is tested before becoming part of the training set. Such a protocol can lead to partial overlap between training and test data, which may bias performance estimates. It reflects a batch-style evaluation layered on top of an active querying process.

topics.title: Window-based batch evaluation in streams
topics.description: Window-based evaluation assesses prediction accuracy over all observations within the current batch or window of a data stream. Models are evaluated on each window as a unit, reflecting performance over recent data rather than on a per-instance basis. This approach can smooth short-term fluctuations and is useful when data naturally arrive in batches. It diverges from strictly online, instance-level prequential evaluation while still respecting temporal structure.

topics.title: Network protocol identification with AL
topics.description: Online active learning is used for network protocol identification, where traffic data streams must be classified into protocol types under changing conditions. Zhang et al. (2020a) propose a method to select the most representative instances on the fly, focusing labeling effort where it most benefits the model. This approach enables continual adaptation of the protocol classifier to dynamic data distributions.

topics.title: Limits of deep AL in stream settings
topics.description: Many effective deep active learning strategies for computer vision rely on clustering or computing pairwise similarities between image embeddings to select diverse or informative samples. Such operations typically require multiple passes over the dataset or substantial storage, making them ill-suited to single-pass, stream-based scenarios. Consequently, these deep AL methods are not easily adaptable to online learning from data streams.

canonical_topics.name: Deep Active Learning for Streaming Decisions
canonical_topics.description: Deep active learning in streaming settings studies how deep models decide when to query labels while processing data sequentially. One approach formulates the label-versus-predict choice as a reinforcement learning problem, where an LSTM-based policy observes the current state of the learner and chooses between requesting a label or issuing a prediction, trading off annotation cost against prediction errors. At the same time, many successful deep active learning methods for images rely on clustering or computing pairwise similarities in deep embedding space, which typically assumes multiple passes over a static dataset and substantial storage. These operations are often infeasible in single-pass, memory-constrained data streams, limiting the direct applicability of pool-based deep active learning methods. Research in this area seeks new architectures, objectives, and selection mechanisms that both exploit deep representations and respect strict streaming constraints.

topics.title: Uncertainty-based AL for 3D objects
topics.description: For stream-based classification of 3D objects, online active learning can rely on traditional models combined with uncertainty sampling. Narr et al. (2016) employ a Mondrian forest classifier, an efficient online alternative to random forests, and query labels for images with high classification uncertainty. This design balances computational efficiency with focused labeling of the most ambiguous 3D object instances.

topics.title: Vision-based process monitoring with AL
topics.description: Online active learning is applied to vision-based process monitoring to reduce the effort required for manual image labeling while tracking industrial or operational processes. Rožanec et al. (2022) first extract visual features using a pre-trained ResNet-18 model, then employ online active learning to decide which images should be annotated. This combination leverages deep feature representations with selective labeling to make process monitoring more scalable.

topics.title: Feature-filtered streaming active learning
topics.description: A mutual-information-based feature selection step retains only √n of the original features to train an online classifier, where n is the number of observations in the training set. This reduced feature set is then used with a simple uncertainty-based active learning strategy. The approach is combined with several streaming classification algorithms, including Hoeffding trees, Hoeffding adaptive trees, stochastic gradient trees, streaming logistic regression, and streaming k-nearest neighbors.

topics.title: Gradient-based diversity sampling for DNNs
topics.description: For deep streaming active learning, each incoming example is represented by the gradient of the cross-entropy loss with respect to the last-layer parameters, using the model’s argmax prediction as a pseudo-label. The selection probability of a point is made proportional to the determinant of the updated covariance matrix of gradient representations, favoring examples that contribute novel information. This determinant-based criterion encourages diversity and coverage in the gradient space of the selected batch.

topics.title: Slice-aware budgeting in streaming object detection
topics.description: In autonomous driving scenarios, streaming camera data includes heterogeneous and imbalanced conditions such as clear, foggy, and rainy weather. A streamline approach is proposed to actively allocate labeling budget across these slices, prioritizing those where the model underperforms rather than sampling proportionally to their frequency. This counters the tendency of passive sampling to under-represent rare but critical conditions in the training data.

topics.title: Diversity-based online AL for vehicle faults
topics.description: For autonomous cars, a diversity-based online active learning strategy is used to improve fault detection. The method focuses on selecting diverse informative examples to reduce the false alarm rate while enabling the system to learn about previously unseen faults. This tailors active sampling to safety-critical anomaly and fault detection in automotive systems.

topics.title: Active learning in compressor optimization loops
topics.description: An industrial framework is introduced that couples a thermodynamics-based simulator of a centrifugal compressor with a Gaussian Process surrogate model and an online active learning module. The goal is to minimize the power absorbed during the boil-off process by adaptively selecting new experimental operating points. Simulator, surrogate, and optimizer interact in real time, with active learning guiding which experiments to run to efficiently explore and optimize compressor behavior.

topics.title: SBAD framework single-pass sampling
topics.description: The SBAD framework (Manjah et al., 2023) structures online active learning for data streams into sampling, fine-tuning, and evaluation phases. Sampling is performed in a single pass over the stream using a thresholding mechanism to decide which instances to query. This design aims to respect streaming constraints while still selecting informative examples.

topics.title: Scalability of online active learning
topics.description: Online active learning algorithms must remain computationally efficient and scalable to cope with large datasets and high-velocity data streams. The time to make sampling decisions must be lower than the process feed rate; otherwise, buffers are required, which undermines the benefits of true online operation. As data volume and speed increase, computational demands can become prohibitive, limiting real-world deployment.

topics.title: Model interpretability in active querying
topics.description: Beyond selecting the most informative instances, it can be important to explain why particular samples are queried, especially in high-stakes domains. Providing interpretable rationales for query choices helps practitioners in areas like healthcare and manufacturing better understand both the model behavior and the underlying problem. This links active learning with explainability and user trust requirements.

canonical_topics.name: Deep Feature Online Active Learning for Process Monitoring
canonical_topics.description: Vision-based process monitoring can leverage deep feature extractors together with online active learning to reduce labeling costs on industrial image streams.
